1st-metacarpal-bone.name: 1st Metacarpal (Thumb)
1st-metacarpal-bone.summary: The metacarpal of the thumb. It is shorter and thicker than the others and is not tied to the second metacarpal, so the thumb moves freely.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the thumb (metacarpophalangeal joint)
landmarks: Two grooves on the palmar head for sesamoid bones
attachments: Abductor pollicis longus on the lateral side of the base
Opponens pollicis along the lateral shaft
First dorsal interosseous (part) on the shaft
Joint capsule and collateral ligaments of the metacarpophalangeal joint
1st-metacarpal-bone.ossification: Primary center in the shaft, plus a growth plate at the base (it behaves like a phalanx). It fuses by about age 16 to 18.
1st-metacarpal-bone.clinical: A break through the base that enters the joint (Bennett fracture) is unstable. Abductor pollicis longus pulls the shaft toward the wrist.

2nd-metacarpal-bone.name: 2nd Metacarpal (Index)
2nd-metacarpal-bone.summary: The metacarpal of the index finger. It is the longest metacarpal and forms the fixed, stable center of the hand.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the index finger (metacarpophalangeal joint)
attachments: Extensor carpi radialis longus on the back of the base
Flexor carpi radialis on the palmar base
Oblique head of adductor pollicis at the base
First and second dorsal interossei on the sides of the shaft
First palmar interosseous on the palmar shaft
2nd-metacarpal-bone.ossification: Primary center in the shaft; growth plate at the head. It fuses by about age 16 to 18.
2nd-metacarpal-bone.clinical: Together with the third metacarpal it forms a rigid central pillar. Shaft fractures here are less common than at the 5th metacarpal.

3rd-metacarpal-bone.name: 3rd Metacarpal (Middle)
3rd-metacarpal-bone.summary: The metacarpal of the middle finger. It sits in the center of the hand and has a small styloid process on its base.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger (metacarpophalangeal joint)
attachments: Extensor carpi radialis brevis on the styloid process of the base
Oblique head of adductor pollicis at the base
Transverse head of adductor pollicis along the palmar shaft
Second and third dorsal interossei on the sides of the shaft
3rd-metacarpal-bone.ossification: Primary center in the shaft; growth plate at the head. It fuses by about age 16 to 18.
3rd-metacarpal-bone.clinical: Its styloid process can form a bony bump on the back of the wrist (carpal boss). The bump is often mistaken for a ganglion cyst.

4th-metacarpal-bone.name: 4th Metacarpal (Ring)
4th-metacarpal-bone.summary: The metacarpal of the ring finger. Its base is more mobile than those of the 2nd and 3rd metacarpals.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger (metacarpophalangeal joint)
attachments: Third and fourth dorsal interossei on the sides of the shaft
Second palmar interosseous on the palmar shaft
No long forearm tendon inserts on this bone
4th-metacarpal-bone.ossification: Primary center in the shaft; growth plate at the head. It fuses by about age 16 to 18.
4th-metacarpal-bone.clinical: The neck of this bone can break after a punch, as can the 5th metacarpal. Rotation of the finger after a fracture must be checked.

5th-metacarpal-bone.name: 5th Metacarpal (Little)
5th-metacarpal-bone.summary: The metacarpal of the little finger. Its base is the most mobile, which lets the hand cup around an object.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the little finger (metacarpophalangeal joint)
attachments: Extensor carpi ulnaris on the tubercle of the base
Opponens digiti minimi along the ulnar shaft
Fourth dorsal interosseous and third palmar interosseous
Pisometacarpal ligament on the base
5th-metacarpal-bone.ossification: Primary center in the shaft; growth plate at the head. It fuses by about age 16 to 18.
5th-metacarpal-bone.clinical: A break through the neck, often after a punch, is called a boxer's fracture. The knuckle sinks and the finger can rotate.

capitate-bone.name: Capitate
capitate-bone.summary: The largest carpal bone, in the center of the wrist. Its rounded head fits into the cup formed by the scaphoid and lunate.
attachments: Oblique head of adductor pollicis (origin)
Palmar and dorsal intercarpal ligaments
Carpometacarpal ligaments
capitate-bone.ossification: First carpal to ossify, at about 1 to 3 months of age.
capitate-bone.clinical: Its head has a poor blood supply, like the scaphoid. It is the first carpal to ossify.

clavicle.name: Clavicle (Collarbone)
clavicle.summary: The S-shaped collarbone. It links the arm to the trunk and keeps the shoulder held out to the side.
articulations: Manubrium of sternum and first costal cartilage (sternoclavicular joint)
attachments: Sternocleidomastoid (clavicular head) on the upper medial third
Pectoralis major (clavicular head) on the front of the medial half
Deltoid on the front of the lateral third
Trapezius on the back of the lateral third
Subclavius in the groove on the underside
Coracoclavicular ligaments (conoid and trapezoid) on the underside of the lateral end
Costoclavicular ligament on the costal tuberosity
clavicle.ossification: First bone in the body to begin ossifying (about week 5 of fetal life). The medial end fuses last, near age 25.
clavicle.clinical: Fractures are common, usually at the junction of the middle and lateral thirds. The medial piece is often pulled upward by the sternocleidomastoid.

distal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.name: Thumb - Distal Phalanx
distal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.summary: The last bone of the thumb. It supports the thumb pad and nail, and it has no middle phalanx before it.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the thumb (interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Flexor pollicis longus on the palmar base
Extensor pollicis longus on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the interphalangeal joint
distal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
distal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.clinical: Crush injuries can fracture the tuft. Cutting the flexor pollicis longus tendon prevents bending of the thumb tip.

distal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.name: Index Finger - Distal Phalanx
distal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.summary: The last bone of the index finger. It supports the fingertip pad and the nail.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the index finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Flexor digitorum profundus on the palmar base
Terminal tendon of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the distal interphalangeal joint
distal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
distal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.clinical: Tearing the extensor tendon from its base causes mallet finger, and the tip cannot be straightened. Crush injuries can fracture the tuft.

distal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.name: Middle Finger - Distal Phalanx
distal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.summary: The last bone of the middle finger. It supports the fingertip pad and the nail.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the middle finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Flexor digitorum profundus on the palmar base
Terminal tendon of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the distal interphalangeal joint
distal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
distal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.clinical: Tearing the extensor tendon from its base causes mallet finger, and the tip cannot be straightened. Crush injuries can fracture the tuft.

distal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.name: Ring Finger - Distal Phalanx
distal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.summary: The last bone of the ring finger. It supports the fingertip pad and the nail.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the ring finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Flexor digitorum profundus on the palmar base
Terminal tendon of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the distal interphalangeal joint
distal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
distal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.clinical: A forceful pull can tear flexor digitorum profundus from the base (jersey finger), and the tip cannot bend. The ring finger is most often involved.

distal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.name: Little Finger - Distal Phalanx
distal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.summary: The last bone of the little finger. It supports the fingertip pad and the nail.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the little finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Flexor digitorum profundus on the palmar base
Terminal tendon of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the distal interphalangeal joint
distal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
distal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.clinical: Tearing the extensor tendon from its base causes mallet finger, and the tip cannot be straightened. Crush injuries can fracture the tuft.

hamate-bone.name: Hamate
hamate-bone.summary: A wedge-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the distal row. It has a hook on its palmar surface.
attachments: Flexor retinaculum on the hook
Flexor digiti minimi brevis on the hook
Opponens digiti minimi on the hook
Pisohamate ligament
Pisometacarpal ligament
hamate-bone.ossification: Begins ossifying at about 2 to 4 months of age.
hamate-bone.clinical: The hook can fracture in golf, baseball and racquet sports. The ulnar nerve and flexor tendons next to it can be damaged.

humerus.name: Humerus
humerus.summary: The long bone of the arm. It forms the shoulder joint above and the elbow joint below.
articulations: Scapula (glenohumeral joint, head into glenoid cavity)
Ulna (humeroulnar joint, trochlea into trochlear notch)
Radius (humeroradial joint, capitulum onto radial head)
attachments: Rotator cuff tendons on the tubercles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor on greater; subscapularis on lesser)
Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major along the intertubercular sulcus
Deltoid on the deltoid tuberosity
Coracobrachialis on the medial mid-shaft
Brachialis on the lower front of the shaft
Triceps (lateral and medial heads) on the back of the shaft
Common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle
Common extensor origin on the lateral epicondyle
Brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus on the lateral supracondylar ridge
humerus.ossification: Shaft ossifies before birth. Epiphyses appear in childhood, and the ends fuse to the shaft by about age 20.
humerus.clinical: A fracture of the surgical neck can injure the axillary nerve. A midshaft fracture can injure the radial nerve in the radial groove.

lunate-bone.name: Lunate
lunate-bone.summary: The crescent-shaped carpal bone in the middle of the proximal row. It sits in the lunate fossa of the radius at the wrist joint.
attachments: Scapholunate interosseous ligament
Lunotriquetral interosseous ligament
Palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments
No muscles attach
lunate-bone.ossification: Begins ossifying at about age 2 to 4 years.
lunate-bone.clinical: It is the carpal bone most often dislocated, usually toward the palm. It can press on the median nerve and cause carpal tunnel symptoms.

middle-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.name: Index Finger - Middle Phalanx
middle-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.summary: The middle bone of the index finger. It lies between the proximal and distal phalanges.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the index finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
Distal phalanx of the index finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
landmarks: Ridges for the flexor digitorum superficialis
attachments: Flexor digitorum superficialis by two slips on the sides of the palmar shaft
Central slip of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the interphalangeal joints
middle-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
middle-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.clinical: Tearing the central slip at its base causes a boutonniere deformity. The proximal joint bends and the distal joint extends.

middle-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.name: Middle Finger - Middle Phalanx
middle-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.summary: The middle bone of the middle finger. It lies between the proximal and distal phalanges.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the middle finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
Distal phalanx of the middle finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
landmarks: Ridges for the flexor digitorum superficialis
attachments: Flexor digitorum superficialis by two slips on the sides of the palmar shaft
Central slip of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the interphalangeal joints
middle-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
middle-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.clinical: This bone and the one beside it are often hurt in ball sports. A torn central slip at the base gives a boutonniere deformity.

middle-phalanx-of-4th-finger.name: Ring Finger - Middle Phalanx
middle-phalanx-of-4th-finger.summary: The middle bone of the ring finger. It lies between the proximal and distal phalanges.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the ring finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
Distal phalanx of the ring finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
landmarks: Ridges for the flexor digitorum superficialis
attachments: Flexor digitorum superficialis by two slips on the sides of the palmar shaft
Central slip of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the interphalangeal joints
middle-phalanx-of-4th-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
middle-phalanx-of-4th-finger.clinical: Dislocation of the proximal interphalangeal joint is common in sport. Early movement helps prevent stiffness.

middle-phalanx-of-5th-finger.name: Little Finger - Middle Phalanx
middle-phalanx-of-5th-finger.summary: The middle bone of the little finger. It lies between the proximal and distal phalanges.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the little finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
Distal phalanx of the little finger (distal interphalangeal joint)
landmarks: Ridges for the flexor digitorum superficialis
attachments: Flexor digitorum superficialis by two slips on the sides of the palmar shaft
Central slip of the extensor expansion on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the interphalangeal joints
middle-phalanx-of-5th-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
middle-phalanx-of-5th-finger.clinical: It is the shortest middle phalanx. The proximal interphalangeal joint is easily injured in sport.

pisiform-bone.name: Pisiform
pisiform-bone.summary: A small pea-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the palm. It is a sesamoid bone inside the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.
landmarks: Single facet on the dorsal surface (for triquetrum)
Palmar prominence (palpable at the base of the hypothenar eminence)
attachments: Flexor carpi ulnaris tendon (insertion)
Abductor digiti minimi (origin)
Flexor retinaculum
Pisohamate ligament
Pisometacarpal ligament (to the base of the 5th metacarpal)
pisiform-bone.ossification: Last carpal to ossify, at about age 9 to 12 years.
pisiform-bone.clinical: The ulnar nerve and artery pass beside it through the ulnar tunnel (Guyon's canal). It can be fractured by a direct blow or fall.

proximal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.name: Thumb - Proximal Phalanx
proximal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.summary: The first bone of the thumb beyond the metacarpal. The thumb has only two phalanges, a proximal and a distal.
articulations: Distal phalanx of the thumb (interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Abductor pollicis brevis on the lateral base
Flexor pollicis brevis on the lateral base
Adductor pollicis on the medial base (through a sesamoid bone)
Extensor pollicis brevis on the dorsal base
Collateral ligaments of the metacarpophalangeal joint
proximal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-1st-finger.clinical: Tearing the ulnar collateral ligament at its base (gamekeeper's or skier's thumb) makes pinching weak and painful.

proximal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.name: Index Finger - Proximal Phalanx
proximal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.summary: The first bone of the index finger beyond the metacarpal. It is the longest of the three phalanges of the finger.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the index finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: First dorsal interosseous on the radial side of the base
First palmar interosseous into the extensor expansion
Fibrous flexor sheath on the palmar shaft
Extensor expansion over the back
proximal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-2nd-finger.clinical: The proximal interphalangeal joint is often dislocated or sprained in ball sports. Trigger finger occurs when the tendon catches at the A1 pulley at the metacarpal head.

proximal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.name: Middle Finger - Proximal Phalanx
proximal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.summary: The first bone of the middle finger beyond the metacarpal. It is the longest of the three phalanges of the finger.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the middle finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Second and third dorsal interossei on the radial and ulnar sides of the base
Fibrous flexor sheath on the palmar shaft
Extensor expansion over the back
proximal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-3rd-finger.clinical: Fractures of the proximal phalanx can heal with a rotated finger, which makes the fingers overlap when the fist is closed.

proximal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.name: Ring Finger - Proximal Phalanx
proximal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.summary: The first bone of the ring finger beyond the metacarpal. It is the longest of the three phalanges of the finger.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the ring finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Fourth dorsal interosseous on the ulnar side of the base
Second palmar interosseous into the extensor expansion
Fibrous flexor sheath on the palmar shaft
Extensor expansion over the back
proximal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-4th-finger.clinical: Shaft fractures often angle with the point toward the palm, because the interossei flex the upper fragment.

proximal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.name: Little Finger - Proximal Phalanx
proximal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.summary: The first bone of the little finger beyond the metacarpal. It is the longest of the three phalanges of the finger.
articulations: Middle phalanx of the little finger (proximal interphalangeal joint)
attachments: Abductor digiti minimi on the ulnar side of the base
Flexor digiti minimi brevis on the base
Third palmar interosseous into the extensor expansion
Fibrous flexor sheath on the palmar shaft
Extensor expansion over the back
proximal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.ossification: Primary center in the shaft before birth. The growth plate at the base fuses by about age 16 to 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-5th-finger.clinical: Fractures are common in sport. After a break, check that the finger is not rotated, which makes it cross its neighbor.

radius.name: Radius
radius.summary: The lateral forearm bone, on the thumb side. It is small at the elbow and wide at the wrist, and it rotates around the ulna.
articulations: Ulna (proximal radioulnar joint, head in radial notch)
Ulna (distal radioulnar joint, ulnar notch around ulnar head)
Scaphoid and lunate (radiocarpal joint, the wrist joint)
attachments: Biceps brachii on the radial tuberosity
Supinator on the upper lateral shaft
Pronator teres on the pronator tuberosity (mid-lateral shaft)
Flexor digitorum superficialis on the anterior oblique line
Flexor pollicis longus on the front of the shaft
Pronator quadratus on the lower front of the shaft
Brachioradialis on the lower lateral end near the styloid process
Interosseous membrane on the interosseous border
Annular ligament around the head (attaches to the ulna)
radius.ossification: Shaft ossifies before birth. The distal end appears at about age 1 and fuses by about age 20.
radius.clinical: A fall on the outstretched hand can break the distal radius (Colles fracture), tilting the hand backward like a dinner fork. A child can pull the radial head out of the annular ligament (nursemaid's elbow).

scaphoid-bone.name: Scaphoid
scaphoid-bone.summary: The boat-shaped carpal bone on the thumb side of the proximal row. It bridges the two rows of carpal bones.
attachments: Radial collateral ligament of the wrist
Flexor retinaculum on the tubercle
Scapholunate interosseous ligament
scaphoid-bone.ossification: Begins ossifying at about age 4 to 6 years.
scaphoid-bone.clinical: It is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, with pain in the anatomical snuffbox. Waist fractures can cut off the blood supply and cause bone death.

scapula.name: Scapula (Shoulder Blade)
scapula.summary: A flat, triangular bone on the back of the rib cage. It forms the socket of the shoulder joint and anchors many shoulder muscles.
articulations: Humerus (glenohumeral joint, at the glenoid cavity)
attachments: Rotator cuff: supraspinatus (supraspinous fossa), infraspinatus (infraspinous fossa), subscapularis (subscapular fossa), teres minor (lateral border)
Long head of biceps on the supraglenoid tubercle
Long head of triceps on the infraglenoid tubercle
Short head of biceps, coracobrachialis and pectoralis minor on the coracoid process
Trapezius and deltoid on the spine and acromion
Levator scapulae, rhomboid minor and rhomboid major on the medial border
Serratus anterior on the front of the medial border
Teres major on the back of the inferior angle
scapula.ossification: Body begins ossifying about week 8 of fetal life. Other centers (coracoid, acromion, glenoid) appear after birth and fuse by about age 20 to 25.
scapula.clinical: Injury to the long thoracic nerve paralyzes serratus anterior. The medial border then lifts off the rib cage (winged scapula).

trapezium-bone.name: Trapezium
trapezium-bone.summary: The four-sided carpal bone on the thumb side of the distal row. It forms the saddle joint at the base of the thumb.
landmarks: Groove for flexor carpi radialis tendon
attachments: Flexor retinaculum on the tubercle
Abductor pollicis brevis
Opponens pollicis
Flexor pollicis brevis
Radial collateral ligament of the wrist
trapezium-bone.ossification: Begins ossifying at about age 4 to 6 years.
trapezium-bone.clinical: Osteoarthritis of the thumb carpometacarpal joint is very common. It causes pain at the base of the thumb when pinching or gripping.

trapezoid-bone.name: Trapezoid
trapezoid-bone.summary: The smallest carpal bone of the distal row. It is wedge-shaped and sits in front of the base of the index metacarpal.
attachments: Carpal and carpometacarpal ligaments only
No muscles attach
trapezoid-bone.ossification: Begins ossifying at about age 4 to 6 years.
trapezoid-bone.clinical: It is rarely injured because it is wedged tightly between its neighbors. When it dislocates, it usually moves toward the back of the hand.

triquetrum-bone.name: Triquetrum
triquetrum-bone.summary: The pyramid-shaped carpal bone on the little-finger side of the proximal row. It carries the pisiform on its palmar surface.
articulations: Articular disc of the wrist (ulnocarpal side)
attachments: Ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist
Lunotriquetral interosseous ligament
Pisotriquetral ligaments
Palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments
triquetrum-bone.ossification: Begins ossifying at about age 2 to 3 years.
triquetrum-bone.clinical: A small chip fracture on the back of the bone is the second most common carpal fracture. It follows a fall on the outstretched hand.

ulna.name: Ulna
ulna.summary: The medial forearm bone, on the little-finger side. It is large at the elbow and forms the hinge with the humerus.
articulations: Humerus (humeroulnar joint, trochlear notch around trochlea)
Radius (distal radioulnar joint, ulnar head in ulnar notch)
Articular disc of the wrist (the ulna does not touch the carpal bones directly)
attachments: Triceps brachii on the olecranon
Brachialis on the ulnar tuberosity
Anconeus on the lateral olecranon and upper posterior shaft
Supinator on the supinator crest
Flexor digitorum profundus on the front and medial shaft
Pronator quadratus on the lower front of the shaft
Flexor carpi ulnaris on the olecranon and posterior border
Abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis on the back of the shaft
Ulnar collateral ligament of the elbow on the coronoid process and olecranon
Annular ligament on the edges of the radial notch
ulna.ossification: Shaft ossifies before birth. The olecranon fuses at about age 16, and the distal end by about age 20.
ulna.clinical: An olecranon fracture is common after a fall on the elbow. The triceps can pull the broken piece upward. A broken ulnar shaft with a dislocated radial head is a Monteggia fracture.

abdominal-part-of-pectoralis-major-muscl.name: Pectoralis Major — Abdominal Part
abdominal-part-of-pectoralis-major-muscl.summary: The lowest slip of the pectoralis major. It pulls the raised arm down and forward.
abdominal-part-of-pectoralis-major-muscl.origin: Aponeurosis of the external oblique muscle (anterior layer of the rectus sheath)
abdominal-part-of-pectoralis-major-muscl.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus. The lowest fibers fold under the others to reach it.
action: Depresses the raised arm against resistance
blood: Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
Perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery
abdominal-part-of-pectoralis-major-muscl.clinical: The twisted tendon can rupture during bench pressing. Poland syndrome is a birth defect in which the sternocostal and abdominal parts are absent.

abductor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.name: Abductor Digiti Minimi (Hand)
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.summary: The outermost muscle of the little finger side of the palm. It spreads the little finger away from the ring finger.
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.clinical: Wasting flattens the little finger side of the palm in ulnar nerve palsy. Wartenberg sign is an abducted little finger that cannot be adducted.
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.origin: Pisiform bone and the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger, and the extensor expansion
action: Weakly flexes the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint

abductor-pollicis-brevis.name: Abductor Pollicis Brevis
abductor-pollicis-brevis.summary: A thenar muscle on the outer edge of the palm. It moves the thumb straight forward, away from the palm.
abductor-pollicis-brevis.clinical: Weakness and thenar wasting occur in severe carpal tunnel syndrome. Test by lifting the thumb straight up from a flat palm.
abductor-pollicis-brevis.origin: Flexor retinaculum, and the tubercles of the scaphoid and trapezium
abductor-pollicis-brevis.insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
action: Helps with opposition of the thumb
blood: Superficial palmar branch of radial artery

abductor-pollicis-longus.name: Abductor Pollicis Longus
abductor-pollicis-longus.summary: A deep muscle on the back of the forearm. Its tendon runs to the base of the thumb and pulls the thumb away from the hand.
abductor-pollicis-longus.clinical: Its tendon and the extensor pollicis brevis tendon are involved in de Quervain tenosynovitis. This causes pain at the radial side of the wrist.
abductor-pollicis-longus.origin: Posterior surfaces of the ulna and radius, and the interosseous membrane
abductor-pollicis-longus.insertion: Lateral side of the base of the first metacarpal
action: Abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint
Extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint
abductor-pollicis-longus.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

acromial-part-of-deltoid-muscle.name: Deltoid — Middle (Acromial) Part
acromial-part-of-deltoid-muscle.summary: The middle part of the deltoid. It is the main muscle that lifts the arm out to the side.
action: Abducts the arm at the shoulder (about 15°–90°)
blood: Deltoid branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
acromial-part-of-deltoid-muscle.clinical: The axillary nerve can be injured in a surgical neck fracture or shoulder dislocation. The shoulder then looks flat and the skin over it is numb.

anconeus-muscle.name: Anconeus
anconeus-muscle.summary: A small triangular muscle behind the elbow. It helps the triceps straighten the elbow and steadies the joint.
anconeus-muscle.clinical: Pain over the lateral elbow can arise here, so it is part of the differential for tennis elbow. It also tenses the elbow joint capsule.
anconeus-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the lateral epicondyle of the humerus
anconeus-muscle.insertion: Lateral surface of the olecranon and the upper posterior surface of the ulna
action: Assists triceps brachii in extending the elbow
Abducts the ulna during forearm pronation
anconeus-muscle.nerve: Radial nerve (branch from the nerve to the medial head of triceps)

ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.name: Trapezius — Lower (Ascending) Part
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.summary: The lower fibers of the trapezius. They pull the shoulder blade down and help turn it upward.
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of vertebrae T4–T12 (some texts: T3–T12)
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.insertion: Tubercle at the medial end of the spine of the scapula, through a small aponeurosis
action: Rotates the scapula upward (with the upper part and serratus anterior)
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3–C4 proprioceptive fibers
blood: Dorsal scapular artery (deep branch of the transverse cervical artery)
ascending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.clinical: Weak lower trapezius is common with poor shoulder posture. Damage to CN XI weakens the whole muscle and causes a drooping shoulder.

brachialis-muscle.name: Brachialis
brachialis-muscle.summary: A thick muscle under the biceps. It is the main muscle that bends the elbow.
brachialis-muscle.origin: Distal half of the anterior surface of the humerus, and the intermuscular septa
brachialis-muscle.insertion: Tuberosity of the ulna and the coronoid process of the ulna
action: Flexes the forearm at the elbow in all positions (forearm pronated, supinated or neutral)
brachialis-muscle.nerve: Musculocutaneous nerve (small lateral part: radial nerve)
blood: Muscular branches of the brachial artery
brachialis-muscle.clinical: Called the workhorse of elbow flexion. Bone may form in it after elbow injury (myositis ossificans), which limits movement.

brachioradialis-muscle.name: Brachioradialis
brachioradialis-muscle.summary: The muscle that forms the rounded outer bulge of the upper forearm. It flexes the elbow, most strongly when the thumb points up.
brachioradialis-muscle.clinical: It is supplied by the radial nerve but flexes the elbow. The brachioradialis reflex tests C5 and C6.
brachioradialis-muscle.origin: Proximal two thirds of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus
brachioradialis-muscle.insertion: Lateral surface of the distal radius, just above the styloid process
action: Flexes the forearm at the elbow
Most effective with the forearm in mid-pronation
Returns the forearm toward mid-position from pronation or supination

clavicular-head-of-pectoralis-major-musc.name: Pectoralis Major — Clavicular Head
clavicular-head-of-pectoralis-major-musc.summary: The upper part of the pectoralis major. It lifts the arm forward and turns it inward.
clavicular-head-of-pectoralis-major-musc.origin: Anterior surface of the medial half of the clavicle
clavicular-head-of-pectoralis-major-musc.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
action: Flexes the arm at the shoulder
blood: Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
clavicular-head-of-pectoralis-major-musc.clinical: This head works most in an incline press. It can still work when other parts of the muscle are absent or torn.

clavicular-part-of-deltoid-muscle.name: Deltoid — Front (Clavicular) Part
clavicular-part-of-deltoid-muscle.summary: The front part of the deltoid. It lifts the arm forward and turns it inward.
clavicular-part-of-deltoid-muscle.origin: Lateral third of the anterior border of the clavicle
action: Flexes the arm at the shoulder
blood: Deltoid branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
clavicular-part-of-deltoid-muscle.clinical: The front deltoid is often strained in overhead lifting. Axillary nerve injury weakens the whole deltoid.

coracobrachialis-muscle.name: Coracobrachialis
coracobrachialis-muscle.summary: A small muscle on the upper inner arm. It flexes and adducts the arm. The musculocutaneous nerve passes through it.
coracobrachialis-muscle.origin: Tip of the coracoid process of the scapula (with the short head of biceps)
coracobrachialis-muscle.insertion: Middle third of the medial surface of the humerus
action: Flexes the arm at the shoulder
blood: Muscular branches of the brachial artery
coracobrachialis-muscle.clinical: The musculocutaneous nerve pierces this muscle. The muscle also serves as a guide to the axillary artery.

deep-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brevis.name: Flexor Pollicis Brevis — Deep Head
deep-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brevis.latin: Caput profundum musculi flexoris pollicis brevis
deep-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brevis.summary: The deeper part of flexor pollicis brevis. It joins the superficial head to bend the thumb at its base joint.
deep-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brevis.clinical: The deep head is usually ulnar-supplied, so flexor pollicis brevis can survive a median nerve injury. Some people vary from this pattern.
deep-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brevis.origin: Trapezoid and capitate bones, and the palmar carpal ligaments
deep-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brevis.insertion: Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, with the superficial head
action: Flexes the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint
blood: Superficial palmar branch of radial artery

deep-head-of-pronator-teres.name: Pronator Teres — Deep (Ulnar) Head
deep-head-of-pronator-teres.summary: The small deep head of pronator teres. It joins the superficial head to turn the palm downward.
deep-head-of-pronator-teres.clinical: The median nerve passes between the two heads. Entrapment here causes pronator teres syndrome, with forearm pain and hand numbness.
deep-head-of-pronator-teres.origin: Medial side of the coronoid process of the ulna
deep-head-of-pronator-teres.insertion: Pronator tuberosity on the middle of the lateral surface of the radius, with the superficial head

descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.name: Trapezius — Upper (Descending) Part
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.summary: The upper fibers of the trapezius. They lift the shoulder, as in a shrug, and move the neck.
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.origin: Medial third of the superior nuchal line, external occipital protuberance, nuchal ligament, and spinous process of C7
action: Extends and laterally flexes the neck; turns the face to the opposite side
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3–C4 proprioceptive fibers
blood: Superficial branch of the transverse cervical artery
descending-part-of-trapezius-muscle.clinical: Often tight and sore from desk work and stress. A weak shrug and a drooping shoulder suggest CN XI injury, for example after neck surgery.

dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-hand.name: Dorsal Interossei of the Hand
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-hand.summary: Four small muscles between the metacarpals, each with two heads. They spread the fingers apart from the middle finger.
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-hand.clinical: Ulnar nerve palsy causes weakness of finger spreading and hollowing between the metacarpals. Test by spreading the fingers against resistance.
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-hand.origin: Adjacent sides of two neighboring metacarpals, with two heads each
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-hand.insertion: Extensor expansions and bases of the proximal phalanges of digits 2 to 4
action: Abduct digits 2 to 4 away from the middle finger (DAB)
Extend the interphalangeal joints with the lumbricals
blood: Palmar metacarpal arteries (from deep palmar arch)

extensor-carpi-radialis-brevis.name: Extensor Carpi Radialis Brevis
extensor-carpi-radialis-brevis.summary: A wrist extensor on the back of the forearm. It extends the wrist and tilts the hand toward the thumb side.
extensor-carpi-radialis-brevis.clinical: Its origin is the usual site of lateral epicondylitis, or tennis elbow. It often causes pain on the outer elbow when gripping.
extensor-carpi-radialis-brevis.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
extensor-carpi-radialis-brevis.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the third metacarpal
action: Fixes the wrist during finger flexion
extensor-carpi-radialis-brevis.nerve: Radial nerve (deep branch or posterior interosseous nerve)

extensor-carpi-radialis-longus.name: Extensor Carpi Radialis Longus
extensor-carpi-radialis-longus.summary: A wrist extensor that lies beside brachioradialis. It extends the wrist and tilts the hand toward the thumb side.
extensor-carpi-radialis-longus.clinical: It is spared in posterior interosseous nerve palsy. The wrist then extends weakly and deviates toward the thumb side.
extensor-carpi-radialis-longus.origin: Distal third of the lateral supracondylar ridge of the humerus
extensor-carpi-radialis-longus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the second metacarpal

extensor-digiti-minimi.name: Extensor Digiti Minimi
extensor-digiti-minimi.summary: A slender muscle that extends the little finger. It lets the little finger straighten independently.
extensor-digiti-minimi.clinical: It lets a person extend the little finger on its own, as when pointing the index and little finger. Its tendon passes in the fifth dorsal compartment.
extensor-digiti-minimi.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
extensor-digiti-minimi.insertion: Extensor expansion of the little finger
action: Extends the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal and interphalangeal joints
extensor-digiti-minimi.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

extensor-digitorum.name: Extensor Digitorum
extensor-digitorum.summary: The main muscle that straightens the four fingers. Its four tendons spread out over the back of the fingers.
extensor-digitorum.clinical: Posterior interosseous nerve palsy causes finger drop, with the metacarpophalangeal joints unable to extend. Wrist extension is still possible.
extensor-digitorum.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
extensor-digitorum.insertion: Extensor expansions of digits 2 to 5, reaching the middle and distal phalanges
action: Extends digits 2 to 5 at the metacarpophalangeal joints
Extends the interphalangeal joints with the interossei and lumbricals
extensor-digitorum.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

extensor-indicis.name: Extensor Indicis
extensor-indicis.summary: A small deep muscle that extends the index finger. It allows the index finger to point on its own.
extensor-indicis.clinical: Surgeons often transfer this tendon to replace a ruptured extensor pollicis longus tendon. It is a convenient donor because extensor digitorum also extends the index finger.
extensor-indicis.origin: Posterior surface of the ulna and the interosseous membrane, below the extensor pollicis longus
extensor-indicis.insertion: Extensor expansion of the index finger, joining the tendon of extensor digitorum
extensor-indicis.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

extensor-pollicis-brevis.name: Extensor Pollicis Brevis
extensor-pollicis-brevis.summary: A deep muscle whose tendon runs along the thumb. It straightens the first thumb joint and pulls the thumb outward.
extensor-pollicis-brevis.clinical: Its tendon is involved in de Quervain tenosynovitis. A positive Finkelstein test causes sharp pain at the radial wrist.
extensor-pollicis-brevis.origin: Posterior surface of the radius and the interosseous membrane, below abductor pollicis longus
extensor-pollicis-brevis.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb
action: Extends the proximal phalanx of the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint
Extends and abducts the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint
extensor-pollicis-brevis.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

extensor-pollicis-longus.name: Extensor Pollicis Longus
extensor-pollicis-longus.summary: A deep muscle that straightens the thumb tip. Its tendon turns around Lister tubercle on the radius.
extensor-pollicis-longus.clinical: The tendon can rupture after a distal radius fracture or in rheumatoid arthritis. It forms the ulnar border of the anatomical snuffbox.
extensor-pollicis-longus.origin: Lateral part of the middle third of the posterior ulna and the interosseous membrane
extensor-pollicis-longus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
action: Extends the distal phalanx of the thumb
Extends the proximal phalanx and the carpometacarpal joint
extensor-pollicis-longus.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

flexor-carpi-radialis.name: Flexor Carpi Radialis
flexor-carpi-radialis.summary: A superficial forearm muscle. Its tendon is easily felt at the front of the wrist, beside the radial artery pulse.
flexor-carpi-radialis.clinical: The radial artery pulse is felt just lateral to its tendon. The tendon is also a landmark for wrist surgery approaches.
flexor-carpi-radialis.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
flexor-carpi-radialis.insertion: Palmar surfaces of the bases of the second and third metacarpals

flexor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.name: Flexor Digiti Minimi Brevis (Hand)
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.latin: Musculus flexor digiti minimi brevis manus
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.summary: A small muscle on the little finger side of the palm. It bends the little finger at its base.
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.clinical: It weakens with ulnar nerve injury at the wrist or elbow. Its origin is near the hook of the hamate, which is a fracture site.
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.origin: Hook of the hamate and the flexor retinaculum
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-hand.insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the little finger
action: Flexes the little finger at the metacarpophalangeal joint

flexor-digitorum-profundus.name: Flexor Digitorum Profundus
flexor-digitorum-profundus.summary: The deep finger flexor. It is the only muscle that bends the fingertip joints of digits 2 to 5.
flexor-digitorum-profundus.clinical: Jersey finger is a rupture of its tendon from the distal phalanx, usually the ring finger. The fingertip cannot flex.
flexor-digitorum-profundus.origin: Proximal three quarters of the medial and anterior surfaces of the ulna, and the interosseous membrane
flexor-digitorum-profundus.insertion: Palmar surfaces of the bases of the distal phalanges of digits 2 to 5
action: Flexes the distal interphalangeal joints of digits 2 to 5
Assists flexion of the proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints
flexor-digitorum-profundus.nerve: Dual supply: median nerve (anterior interosseous branch) to digits 2 and 3; ulnar nerve to digits 4 and 5

flexor-digitorum-superficialis.name: Flexor Digitorum Superficialis
flexor-digitorum-superficialis.summary: A superficial finger flexor. It bends the middle joints of the four fingers, and its tendons split to let deep tendons pass.
flexor-digitorum-superficialis.clinical: Each tendon splits into two slips so the flexor digitorum profundus tendon can pass through. Test it by holding the other fingers straight.
flexor-digitorum-superficialis.origin: Humeroulnar head: medial epicondyle, ulnar collateral ligament and coronoid process. Radial head: anterior oblique line of the radius
flexor-digitorum-superficialis.insertion: Sides of the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2 to 5
action: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 2 to 5

flexor-pollicis-longus.name: Flexor Pollicis Longus
flexor-pollicis-longus.summary: A deep forearm muscle for the thumb. It is the only muscle that bends the tip of the thumb.
flexor-pollicis-longus.clinical: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy prevents making an OK sign. The thumb and index fingertips cannot pinch together.
flexor-pollicis-longus.origin: Anterior surface of the radius and the adjacent interosseous membrane
flexor-pollicis-longus.insertion: Palmar surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the thumb
action: Flexes the interphalangeal joint of the thumb
Flexes the metacarpophalangeal joint of the thumb

humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.name: Extensor Carpi Ulnaris — Humeral Head
humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.latin: Caput humerale musculi extensoris carpi ulnaris
humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.summary: The upper head of extensor carpi ulnaris. It extends the wrist and tilts the hand toward the little finger side.
humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.clinical: Tendon problems cause pain on the ulnar side of the wrist. It is often affected in racket sports and golf.
humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus (common extensor tendon)
humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.insertion: Medial side of the base of the fifth metacarpal, shared with the ulnar head
humeral-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

humeral-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.name: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris — Humeral Head
humeral-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.latin: Caput humerale musculi flexoris carpi ulnaris
humeral-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.summary: The humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris. It flexes the wrist and tilts the hand toward the little finger side.
humeral-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.clinical: The ulnar nerve passes between the humeral and ulnar heads. Compression here is part of cubital tunnel syndrome.
humeral-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
humeral-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.insertion: Pisiform, hook of the hamate and the base of the fifth metacarpal (via the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments)

infraspinatus-muscle.name: Infraspinatus
infraspinatus-muscle.summary: A rotator cuff muscle on the back of the scapula. It turns the arm outward and holds the humeral head in its socket.
infraspinatus-muscle.insertion: Middle facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
action: Stabilizes the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity
infraspinatus-muscle.clinical: Tears are common in older adults. The suprascapular nerve can be trapped at the spinoglenoid notch, which wastes this muscle only.

lateral-head-of-triceps-brachii.name: Triceps Brachii — Lateral Head
lateral-head-of-triceps-brachii.summary: The outer head of the triceps. It extends the elbow and covers the radial nerve in its groove.
lateral-head-of-triceps-brachii.origin: Posterior surface of the humerus above the radial groove, and the lateral intermuscular septum
lateral-head-of-triceps-brachii.insertion: Proximal end of the olecranon of the ulna, through the common triceps tendon
action: Extends the forearm at the elbow
lateral-head-of-triceps-brachii.clinical: A fracture of the humeral shaft at the radial groove can injure the radial nerve and cause wrist drop.

latissimus-dorsi-muscle.name: Latissimus Dorsi
latissimus-dorsi-muscle.group: Back muscles acting on the arm
latissimus-dorsi-muscle.summary: A broad muscle of the back. It pulls the raised arm down and back, as in climbing or rowing.
latissimus-dorsi-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of T7–T12, thoracolumbar fascia, posterior iliac crest, lower three or four ribs, and inferior angle of the scapula
latissimus-dorsi-muscle.insertion: Floor of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
blood: Posterior intercostal and lumbar arteries (lower part)
latissimus-dorsi-muscle.clinical: Surgeons use it as a muscle flap for breast reconstruction. Damage to the thoracodorsal nerve weakens climbing and pulling.

levator-scapulae.name: Levator Scapulae
levator-scapulae.summary: A strap muscle at the side of the neck. It lifts the shoulder blade.
levator-scapulae.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1–C4
levator-scapulae.insertion: Superior angle and upper medial border of the scapula, down to the root of the spine
action: Bends the neck to the same side (when the scapula is fixed)
levator-scapulae.nerve: Dorsal scapular nerve and cervical spinal nerves C3–C4
levator-scapulae.roots: C3, C4 (and C5 via the dorsal scapular nerve)
levator-scapulae.clinical: A tight levator scapulae often causes a stiff neck and pain at the top corner of the shoulder blade.

long-head-of-biceps-brachii.name: Biceps Brachii — Long Head
long-head-of-biceps-brachii.summary: The outer head of the biceps. Its tendon runs through the shoulder joint and bends the elbow.
long-head-of-biceps-brachii.origin: Supraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and the glenoid labrum
long-head-of-biceps-brachii.insertion: Radial tuberosity, and the bicipital aponeurosis (shared with the short head)
action: Flexes the forearm at the elbow
Weakly flexes the arm at the shoulder
Helps hold the humeral head in the glenoid cavity
blood: Muscular branches of the brachial artery
long-head-of-biceps-brachii.clinical: Tendon rupture causes a bulging "Popeye" muscle. Tendinitis in the intertubercular groove causes shoulder pain.

long-head-of-triceps-brachii.name: Triceps Brachii — Long Head
long-head-of-triceps-brachii.summary: The longest head of the triceps. It crosses both the shoulder and the elbow, so it extends both.
long-head-of-triceps-brachii.insertion: Proximal end of the olecranon of the ulna, through the common triceps tendon
action: Extends the forearm at the elbow
Extends the arm at the shoulder
Helps stop the humeral head from sliding downward
long-head-of-triceps-brachii.clinical: It forms a border of the quadrangular and triangular spaces. The triceps reflex mainly tests C7.

lumbrical-muscles-of-hand.name: Lumbricals of the Hand
lumbrical-muscles-of-hand.summary: Four worm-like muscles that arise from the deep flexor tendons. They bend the finger bases and straighten the finger tips.
lumbrical-muscles-of-hand.clinical: Ulnar nerve injury paralyzes the third and fourth lumbricals. The ring and little fingers form a claw with hyperextended metacarpophalangeal joints.
lumbrical-muscles-of-hand.origin: Tendons of flexor digitorum profundus: first and second from the lateral sides of tendons 2 and 3; third and fourth from adjacent sides of tendons 3 to 5
lumbrical-muscles-of-hand.insertion: Lateral side of the extensor expansions of digits 2 to 5
lumbrical-muscles-of-hand.nerve: First and second: median nerve. Third and fourth: ulnar nerve (deep branch)

medial-head-of-triceps-brachii.name: Triceps Brachii — Medial Head
medial-head-of-triceps-brachii.summary: The deep head of the triceps. It works in all elbow extension and is the main workhorse of the muscle.
medial-head-of-triceps-brachii.origin: Posterior surface of the humerus below the radial groove, and both intermuscular septa
medial-head-of-triceps-brachii.insertion: Proximal end of the olecranon of the ulna, through the common triceps tendon
action: Extends the forearm at the elbow
medial-head-of-triceps-brachii.clinical: The radial nerve passes between the lateral and medial heads in the radial groove. Humeral shaft fractures here can cause wrist drop.

oblique-head-of-adductor-pollicis.name: Adductor Pollicis — Oblique Head
oblique-head-of-adductor-pollicis.summary: The oblique head of the thumb adductor. It lies deep in the palm and pulls the thumb toward the palm.
oblique-head-of-adductor-pollicis.clinical: Weakness causes Froment sign. The patient substitutes flexor pollicis longus and bends the thumb tip when gripping paper.
oblique-head-of-adductor-pollicis.origin: Bases of the second and third metacarpals, the capitate and adjacent carpal bones
oblique-head-of-adductor-pollicis.insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, through a sesamoid bone, with the transverse head

opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-hand.name: Opponens Digiti Minimi
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-hand.summary: A small hypothenar muscle. It draws the fifth metacarpal forward to cup the palm and bring the little finger toward the thumb.
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-hand.clinical: It weakens with ulnar nerve injury, flattening the hand. The ability to cup the palm for carrying water is reduced.
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-hand.origin: Hook of the hamate and the flexor retinaculum
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-hand.insertion: Medial border and adjacent palmar surface of the fifth metacarpal
action: Draws the fifth metacarpal forward and rotates it (opposition of the little finger)
Deepens the hollow of the palm

opponens-pollicis-muscle.name: Opponens Pollicis
opponens-pollicis-muscle.summary: A deep thenar muscle. It rotates the thumb across the palm so the thumb pad meets the fingertips.
opponens-pollicis-muscle.clinical: Loss of opposition is a key sign of a median nerve injury at the wrist. The thumb stays flat beside the index finger (ape hand).
opponens-pollicis-muscle.origin: Flexor retinaculum and the tubercle of the trapezium
opponens-pollicis-muscle.insertion: Lateral border and adjacent palmar surface of the first metacarpal
action: Opposes the thumb by drawing the first metacarpal across the palm and rotating it
blood: Superficial palmar branch of radial artery

palmar-interossei-muscles.name: Palmar Interossei
palmar-interossei-muscles.summary: Three small muscles on the palm side between the metacarpals. They pull the index, ring and little fingers toward the middle finger.
palmar-interossei-muscles.clinical: Weakness lets the fingers drift apart when held together. Test by gripping a piece of paper between extended fingers.
palmar-interossei-muscles.origin: Palmar surfaces of the second, fourth and fifth metacarpals (second on its ulnar side; fourth and fifth on their radial sides)
palmar-interossei-muscles.insertion: Extensor expansions and bases of the proximal phalanges of digits 2, 4 and 5
action: Adduct digits 2, 4 and 5 toward the middle finger (PAD)
Extend the interphalangeal joints with the lumbricals
blood: Palmar metacarpal arteries (from deep palmar arch)

palmaris-longus-muscle.name: Palmaris Longus
palmaris-longus-muscle.summary: A slender superficial forearm muscle with a long tendon. It tightens the palm and weakly flexes the wrist.
palmaris-longus-muscle.clinical: It is absent in about 15% of people on at least one side. Surgeons often use its tendon as a graft.
palmaris-longus-muscle.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon)
palmaris-longus-muscle.insertion: Distal half of the flexor retinaculum and the palmar aponeurosis

pectoralis-minor-muscle.name: Pectoralis Minor
pectoralis-minor-muscle.summary: A thin triangular muscle under the pectoralis major. It pulls the shoulder blade forward and down.
pectoralis-minor-muscle.origin: Outer surfaces of ribs 3–5, near the costal cartilages
pectoralis-minor-muscle.insertion: Medial border and upper surface of the coracoid process of the scapula
action: Depresses the scapula (draws it forward and down)
Elevates ribs 3–5 in forced breathing, when the scapula is fixed
blood: Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
pectoralis-minor-muscle.clinical: Its tendon crosses the axillary artery and brachial plexus. A tight muscle can compress them (pectoralis minor syndrome).

pronator-quadratus.name: Pronator Quadratus
pronator-quadratus.summary: A flat, square muscle just above the wrist on the front of the forearm. It turns the palm downward and binds the radius to the ulna.
pronator-quadratus.clinical: It is the prime mover of pronation, with pronator teres helping against resistance. Anterior interosseous nerve palsy weakens pronation with the elbow flexed.
pronator-quadratus.origin: Distal quarter of the anterior surface of the ulna
pronator-quadratus.insertion: Distal quarter of the anterior surface of the radius
action: Holds the distal radius and ulna together

radial-head-of-flexor-digitorum-superfic.name: Flexor Digitorum Superficialis — Radial Head
radial-head-of-flexor-digitorum-superfic.latin: Caput radiale musculi flexoris digitorum superficialis
radial-head-of-flexor-digitorum-superfic.summary: The radial head of flexor digitorum superficialis. It lies on the radius and joins the humeroulnar head to bend the finger middle joints.
radial-head-of-flexor-digitorum-superfic.clinical: The fibrous arch joining the heads of this muscle can compress the median nerve. Test the whole muscle by flexing one finger with the others held straight.
radial-head-of-flexor-digitorum-superfic.origin: Anterior oblique line of the radius
radial-head-of-flexor-digitorum-superfic.insertion: Sides of the shafts of the middle phalanges of digits 2 to 5, shared with the humeroulnar head
action: Flexes the proximal interphalangeal joints of digits 2 to 5

rhomboid-major-muscle.name: Rhomboid Major
rhomboid-major-muscle.summary: A flat muscle between the spine and the shoulder blade. It pulls the scapula toward the spine.
rhomboid-major-muscle.insertion: Medial border of the scapula, from the root of the spine to the inferior angle
action: Holds the scapula against the chest wall
rhomboid-major-muscle.clinical: Weakness lets the medial border of the scapula lift away from the chest, so the scapula looks winged.

rhomboid-minor-muscle.name: Rhomboid Minor
rhomboid-minor-muscle.summary: A small flat muscle above the rhomboid major. It pulls the shoulder blade toward the spine.
rhomboid-minor-muscle.origin: Lower part of the nuchal ligament and spinous processes of C7–T1
rhomboid-minor-muscle.insertion: Medial border of the scapula at the root of the spine
action: Holds the scapula against the chest wall
rhomboid-minor-muscle.clinical: Strain can cause pain between the shoulder blades. The dorsal scapular nerve can be injured during neck surgery.

scapular-spinal-part-of-deltoid-muscle.name: Deltoid — Back (Spinal) Part
scapular-spinal-part-of-deltoid-muscle.summary: The back part of the deltoid. It pulls the arm backward and turns it outward.
scapular-spinal-part-of-deltoid-muscle.origin: Lower lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula
action: Extends the arm at the shoulder
blood: Deltoid branch of the profunda brachii artery
scapular-spinal-part-of-deltoid-muscle.clinical: Axillary nerve injury weakens this part along with the rest of the deltoid. The posterior deltoid is often tested in extension.

serratus-anterior-muscle.name: Serratus Anterior
serratus-anterior-muscle.summary: A broad muscle on the side of the chest. It pulls the shoulder blade forward and holds it against the ribs.
serratus-anterior-muscle.origin: External surfaces of the lateral parts of ribs 1–8 (some texts: 1–9)
serratus-anterior-muscle.insertion: Costal surface of the medial border of the scapula
action: Holds the scapula against the thoracic wall
serratus-anterior-muscle.clinical: Long thoracic nerve injury, for example in breast surgery, causes winged scapula and difficulty raising the arm above the head.

short-head-of-biceps-brachii.name: Biceps Brachii — Short Head
short-head-of-biceps-brachii.summary: The inner head of the biceps. It bends and turns the forearm.
short-head-of-biceps-brachii.origin: Tip of the coracoid process of the scapula (with the coracobrachialis)
short-head-of-biceps-brachii.insertion: Radial tuberosity, and the bicipital aponeurosis (shared with the long head)
action: Flexes the forearm at the elbow
Weakly flexes the arm at the shoulder
blood: Muscular branches of the brachial artery
short-head-of-biceps-brachii.clinical: The biceps reflex tests C5–C6. The common tendon can rupture at the radial tuberosity, which weakens supination.

sternocostal-head-of-pectoralis-major-mu.name: Pectoralis Major — Sternocostal Head
sternocostal-head-of-pectoralis-major-mu.summary: The large middle part of the pectoralis major. It pulls the arm across the chest and turns it inward.
sternocostal-head-of-pectoralis-major-mu.origin: Anterior surface of the sternum and the upper six costal cartilages
sternocostal-head-of-pectoralis-major-mu.insertion: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
action: Extends the flexed arm to the side of the trunk
blood: Pectoral branch of the thoraco-acromial artery
Perforating branches of the internal thoracic artery
sternocostal-head-of-pectoralis-major-mu.clinical: This head is missing in Poland syndrome. A tear at the humeral insertion is a known weightlifting injury.

subscapularis-muscle.name: Subscapularis
subscapularis-muscle.summary: A rotator cuff muscle on the front of the scapula. It turns the arm inward and supports the front of the shoulder.
action: Stabilizes the humeral head, especially at the front
subscapularis-muscle.clinical: The lift-off test and belly-press test check it. It may tear in anterior shoulder dislocation.

superficial-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brev.name: Flexor Pollicis Brevis — Superficial Head
superficial-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brev.latin: Caput superficiale musculi flexoris pollicis brevis
superficial-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brev.summary: The larger, outer head of flexor pollicis brevis. It bends the thumb at its base joint.
superficial-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brev.clinical: A recurrent branch injury from a palm laceration paralyzes the thenar muscles. The thumb then cannot oppose.
superficial-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brev.origin: Distal border of the flexor retinaculum and the tubercle of the trapezium
superficial-head-of-flexor-pollicis-brev.insertion: Radial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, through a sesamoid bone
action: Flexes the thumb at the metacarpophalangeal joint
blood: Superficial palmar branch of radial artery

superficial-head-of-pronator-teres.name: Pronator Teres — Superficial (Humeral) Head
superficial-head-of-pronator-teres.summary: The main head of pronator teres. It forms the medial edge of the cubital fossa and turns the palm downward.
superficial-head-of-pronator-teres.clinical: The median nerve usually passes between the two heads. This is a site of pronator teres syndrome.
superficial-head-of-pronator-teres.origin: Medial epicondyle of the humerus (common flexor tendon) and the antebrachial fascia
superficial-head-of-pronator-teres.insertion: Pronator tuberosity on the middle of the lateral surface of the radius

supinator.name: Supinator
supinator.summary: A deep muscle that wraps around the upper radius. It turns the palm upward.
supinator.clinical: The posterior interosseous nerve passes through it at the arcade of Frohse. Compression here causes finger drop with sparing of wrist extension.
supinator.origin: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus, radial collateral and annular ligaments, and the supinator fossa and crest of the ulna
supinator.insertion: Lateral, posterior and anterior surfaces of the proximal third of the radius
supinator.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

supraspinatus-muscle.name: Supraspinatus
supraspinatus-muscle.summary: A rotator cuff muscle above the scapular spine. It starts arm abduction and holds the humeral head in place.
supraspinatus-muscle.insertion: Superior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
action: Stabilizes the head of the humerus in the glenoid cavity
supraspinatus-muscle.clinical: It is the rotator cuff muscle most often torn. It can be pinched under the acromion (impingement). The empty can test checks it.

teres-major-muscle.name: Teres Major
teres-major-muscle.summary: A thick muscle on the lower back of the scapula. It pulls the arm down and turns it inward.
teres-major-muscle.origin: Dorsal surface of the inferior angle of the scapula
teres-major-muscle.insertion: Medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus of the humerus
teres-major-muscle.clinical: Often called the little helper of the latissimus dorsi. It forms the lower border of the quadrangular and triangular spaces.

teres-minor-muscle.name: Teres Minor
teres-minor-muscle.summary: A small rotator cuff muscle on the back of the scapula. It turns the arm outward.
teres-minor-muscle.origin: Upper two-thirds of the dorsal surface of the lateral border of the scapula
teres-minor-muscle.insertion: Inferior facet of the greater tubercle of the humerus
teres-minor-muscle.clinical: The axillary nerve passes through the quadrangular space beside it. Injury to the nerve weakens this muscle and the deltoid.

transverse-head-of-adductor-pollicis.name: Adductor Pollicis — Transverse Head
transverse-head-of-adductor-pollicis.summary: The transverse head of the thumb adductor. It is a fan-shaped sheet deep in the palm that pulls the thumb toward the index finger.
transverse-head-of-adductor-pollicis.clinical: Weakness causes Froment sign. The patient cannot hold paper between the thumb and index finger with a straight thumb.
transverse-head-of-adductor-pollicis.origin: Palmar surface of the shaft of the third metacarpal
transverse-head-of-adductor-pollicis.insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the thumb, through a sesamoid bone, with the oblique head

transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.name: Trapezius — Middle (Transverse) Part
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.summary: The middle fibers of the trapezius. They pull the shoulder blades together.
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of C7–T3 (some texts: C7–T4)
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.insertion: Medial margin of the acromion and the upper lip of the crest of the spine of the scapula
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.nerve: Spinal accessory nerve (CN XI), with C3–C4 proprioceptive fibers
blood: Superficial branch of the transverse cervical artery
transverse-part-of-trapezius-muscle.clinical: Weakness reduces scapular retraction and can contribute to rounded shoulders. CN XI injury weakens the whole trapezius.

ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.name: Extensor Carpi Ulnaris — Ulnar Head
ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.latin: Caput ulnare musculi extensoris carpi ulnaris
ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.summary: The smaller ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris. It joins the humeral head to extend the wrist toward the little finger side.
ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.clinical: Tendon inflammation or instability causes pain on the ulnar side of the wrist. It can snap over the ulnar groove with rotation.
ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.origin: Posterior border of the ulna, through an aponeurosis
ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.insertion: Medial side of the base of the fifth metacarpal, shared with the humeral head
ulnar-head-of-extensor-carpi-ulnaris.nerve: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial nerve)

ulnar-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.name: Flexor Carpi Ulnaris — Ulnar Head
ulnar-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.latin: Caput ulnare musculi flexoris carpi ulnaris
ulnar-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.summary: The ulnar head of flexor carpi ulnaris. It arises from the elbow and ulna and joins the humeral head to bend the wrist.
ulnar-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.clinical: The ulnar nerve runs under the aponeurosis joining the two heads. This is the cubital tunnel, a site of nerve compression.
ulnar-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.origin: Medial margin of the olecranon and the posterior border of the ulna, through an aponeurosis
ulnar-head-of-flexor-carpi-ulnaris.insertion: Pisiform, hook of the hamate and the base of the fifth metacarpal (via the pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments)

anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.name: Medial Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve — Anterior Branch
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.latin: Ramus anterior nervi cutanei antebrachii medialis
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.summary: The larger of the two terminal branches of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve. It carries sensation from the front and inner side of the forearm.
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.from: Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (medial cord of the brachial plexus)
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.course: It arises in the arm and passes in front of, or beside, the median cubital vein. It then runs down the anteromedial forearm toward the wrist.
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.sensory: Skin of the anteromedial (front and inner) forearm, down toward the wrist.
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.injury: Numbness or tingling of the inner front forearm. There is no muscle weakness.
anterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-c.clinical: Branches of this nerve lie close to the median cubital and basilic veins. They can be injured during blood draws or vein surgery, causing a patch of numb skin.

anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.name: Inferior Trunk — Anterior Division
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.latin: Divisio anterior trunci inferioris plexus brachialis
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.parent: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.summary: The front half of the inferior trunk. It carries fibers for the flexor (front) muscles of the arm, forearm and hand.
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.from: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.course: It forms behind the clavicle as the inferior trunk splits. It continues as the medial cord, which then gives off the ulnar nerve and other medial branches.
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.sensory: None (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.injury: Lower plexus injury (Klumpke palsy) causes weak finger flexion and small hand muscles, often with a claw hand.
anterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-b.clinical: Pressure from a cervical rib or a lung apex tumor can injure the inferior trunk and cause weakness of the small hand muscles.

anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.name: Middle Trunk — Anterior Division
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.latin: Divisio anterior trunci medii plexus brachialis
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.parent: Middle trunk of the brachial plexus
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.summary: The front half of the middle trunk. It carries C7 fibers for the flexor (front) side of the limb.
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.from: Middle trunk of the brachial plexus
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.course: It forms behind the clavicle. It joins the anterior division of the superior trunk to form the lateral cord.
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.sensory: None (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.injury: Isolated damage is rare. Its C7 fibers pass to the lateral cord and mainly the lateral root of the median nerve, so loss can weaken pronator teres and flexor carpi radialis.
anterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-bra.clinical: Together with the superior trunk, it forms the lateral cord. That cord gives the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.

anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.name: Superior Trunk — Anterior Division
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.latin: Divisio anterior trunci superioris plexus brachialis
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.parent: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.summary: The front half of the superior trunk. It carries C5 and C6 fibers for the flexor (front) side of the limb.
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.from: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.course: It forms behind the clavicle. It joins the anterior division of the middle trunk to form the lateral cord.
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.sensory: None (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.injury: Upper plexus injury (Erb palsy) causes weak elbow flexion and an arm held at the side, turned inward.
anterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-b.clinical: Injury to the upper trunk (Erb palsy) weakens the biceps, brachialis and deltoid. The arm hangs by the side in the waiter-tip position.

anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.name: Anterior Interosseous Nerve
anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.summary: A deep motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm. It supplies the deep flexors of the thumb, index finger and middle finger, and the pronator quadratus.
anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.from: Median nerve, in the upper forearm just below the elbow
anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.course: It runs down the front of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous artery, between flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus. It ends deep to pronator quadratus.
motor: Flexor digitorum profundus (lateral half: index and middle fingers)
anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.sensory: No skin supply. It sends fibers to the wrist joint for deep pain sense.
anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.injury: Loss of flexion at the thumb tip and index fingertip. The patient cannot form an OK sign.
anterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.clinical: Anterior interosseous syndrome causes a weak pinch. The patient cannot make an OK sign because the thumb and index tips do not flex.

axillary-nerve.name: Axillary Nerve
axillary-nerve.group: Terminal branches of the brachial plexus
axillary-nerve.summary: A terminal branch of the posterior cord. It supplies the deltoid and teres minor and the skin over the lower deltoid.
axillary-nerve.from: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
axillary-nerve.course: It leaves the axilla through the quadrangular space with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. It wraps around the surgical neck of the humerus under the deltoid.
axillary-nerve.sensory: Skin over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area), via the superior lateral brachial cutaneous nerve. Also the shoulder joint capsule.
axillary-nerve.injury: Weak arm abduction beyond the first 15°, a flattened shoulder, and numbness over the lower deltoid.
axillary-nerve.clinical: It is injured by surgical neck fractures, anterior shoulder dislocation, or poorly fitted crutches. The deltoid wastes and the round shoulder contour is lost.

common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.name: Median Nerve — Common Palmar Digital Branches
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.latin: Nervi digitales palmares communes nervi mediani
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.summary: The branches of the median nerve in the palm. Each divides near a finger web into proper palmar digital nerves.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.from: Median nerve, after it leaves the carpal tunnel
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.course: Three branches run toward the thumb web, the second web and the third web. Each splits into proper palmar digital nerves for adjacent digits.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.sensory: Palmar skin of the thumb, index finger, middle finger and the lateral half of the ring finger, with their nail beds.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.injury: Numbness of the lateral three and a half fingers, and weak index and middle finger lumbricals.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses the median nerve before these branches arise. It causes numbness and tingling in the lateral three and a half fingers.

common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.name: Ulnar Nerve — Common Palmar Digital Branches
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.latin: Nervi digitales palmares communes nervi ulnaris
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.summary: A palm branch of the superficial ulnar nerve. It runs to the fourth finger web and splits into proper digital nerves.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.from: Superficial branch of the ulnar nerve
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.course: It runs toward the web between the ring and little fingers. There it divides into proper palmar digital nerves.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.sensory: Palmar skin of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.injury: Numbness of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.
common-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.clinical: A lesion of the ulnar nerve at the wrist or elbow numbs the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.

communicating-branch-of-median-nerve-wit.name: Median Nerve — Communicating Branch to Ulnar Nerve
communicating-branch-of-median-nerve-wit.summary: A small connecting branch between the median nerve and the ulnar nerve. Most often it lies in the palm and links their digital branches.
communicating-branch-of-median-nerve-wit.from: Median nerve (third common palmar digital nerve)
communicating-branch-of-median-nerve-wit.course: In the palm it crosses to join the ulnar common palmar digital nerve to the fourth web. A forearm version (Martin–Gruber) also occurs in some people.
communicating-branch-of-median-nerve-wit.sensory: Mixed sensory fibers that overlap the ring finger skin supplied by both nerves.
communicating-branch-of-median-nerve-wit.clinical: This link explains why some people have unusual sensation or muscle weakness patterns after median or ulnar nerve injury.

deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.name: Radial Nerve — Deep Branch
deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.summary: The motor branch of the radial nerve in the forearm. It supplies the supinator and then continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.from: Radial nerve, in front of the lateral epicondyle
deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.course: It winds around the radius through the supinator muscle. After the muscle it continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
motor: Then continues as the posterior interosseous nerve to the finger and thumb extensors
deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.sensory: No skin supply. Small branches go to the wrist joint.
deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.injury: Finger drop with the wrist still able to extend weakly toward the thumb side.
deep-branch-of-radial-nerve.clinical: The nerve passes through a tendinous arch of the supinator (arcade of Frohse). Compression there can cause weak finger extension.

deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve — Deep Branch
deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.summary: The motor branch of the ulnar nerve in the hand. It supplies most of the small intrinsic muscles of the hand.
deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.from: Ulnar nerve, near the pisiform bone
deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.course: It passes between the hypothenar muscles and curves around the hook of the hamate. It then crosses the palm with the deep palmar arch.
