deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.sensory: None (motor only), apart from small branches to wrist joints.
deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.injury: Clawing of the ring and little fingers, weak finger spreading, and weak pinch (Froment sign).
deep-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.clinical: Compression in Guyon canal, for example from handlebars (cyclist palsy), weakens the hand muscles but leaves skin sensation normal.

dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve — Dorsal Branch
dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.summary: A sensory branch of the ulnar nerve. It supplies the back of the medial hand and the back of the little finger and half of the ring finger.
dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.from: Ulnar nerve, about 5 cm above the wrist
dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.course: It passes deep to flexor carpi ulnaris and winds to the back of the wrist. It then divides into dorsal digital nerves.
dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial dorsum of the hand and the dorsal little finger and medial half of the ring finger.
dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.injury: Numbness of the back of the medial hand and the little finger.
dorsal-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.clinical: Numbness on the back of the medial hand suggests a lesion proximal to the wrist. A lesion in Guyon canal spares this area.

dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.name: Radial Nerve — Dorsal Digital Branches
dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.summary: The terminal sensory twigs of the superficial radial nerve. They supply the skin on the back of the thumb and lateral fingers.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.from: Superficial branch of the radial nerve
dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.course: They arise on the back of the hand. They run along the sides of the thumb, index finger, middle finger and radial half of the ring finger.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.sensory: Skin on the back of the thumb and the proximal parts of the index finger, middle finger and lateral ring finger.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.injury: Numbness on the back of the thumb and index finger web, without muscle weakness.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-radial-nerve.clinical: The skin of the first dorsal web space is the radial nerve autonomous zone. It is the usual place to test radial sensation.

dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve — Dorsal Digital Branches
dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.summary: The terminal twigs of the dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve. They supply skin on the back of the little finger and half of the ring finger.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.from: Dorsal branch of the ulnar nerve
dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.course: They run along the back of the medial hand toward the little finger and ring finger. They supply the skin as far as the proximal finger joints.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.sensory: Skin on the back of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger, proximal to the nail beds.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.injury: Numbness on the back of the little finger and ring finger.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.clinical: The nail bed area is supplied by palmar digital nerves instead, so the fingertip may keep feeling when the dorsal branch is cut.

dorsal-scapular-nerve.name: Dorsal Scapular Nerve
dorsal-scapular-nerve.group: Branches from the roots of the brachial plexus
dorsal-scapular-nerve.summary: A small nerve from the C5 root. It supplies the rhomboid muscles that pull the scapula toward the spine.
dorsal-scapular-nerve.from: Root C5 of the brachial plexus
dorsal-scapular-nerve.course: It pierces the middle scalene muscle and runs deep to levator scapulae. It then runs along the medial border of the scapula under the rhomboids.
dorsal-scapular-nerve.injury: Weak scapular retraction and slight winging of the scapula.
dorsal-scapular-nerve.clinical: Entrapment as it crosses the middle scalene can cause deep, dull pain along the medial border of the scapula.

inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.name: Inferior Lateral Brachial Cutaneous Nerve
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.group: Cutaneous branches of the radial nerve
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.summary: A sensory branch of the radial nerve. It supplies skin on the lower outer part of the arm.
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.from: Radial nerve, in or near the spiral groove
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.course: It pierces the lateral head of triceps and the deep fascia. It then runs down the lateral arm to the elbow.
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.sensory: Skin of the lower lateral arm, down to the elbow.
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.injury: Numb patch over the lower outer arm.
inferior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.clinical: It can be damaged along with the radial nerve in a humeral shaft fracture, causing a numb patch on the outer arm.

inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.name: Inferior Trunk of the Brachial Plexus
inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.summary: The lowest trunk of the brachial plexus. It is formed by the C8 and T1 ventral rami.
inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.from: Union of the ventral rami of C8 and T1
inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.course: It arches over the first rib behind the subclavian artery. Behind the clavicle it divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.sensory: None directly (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.injury: Klumpke palsy: weak hand muscles with a claw hand and numbness on the inner arm and forearm.
inferior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.clinical: Pressure from a cervical rib or a lung apex tumor (Pancoast tumor) can injure it. T1 involvement may also cause Horner syndrome.

lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.name: Lateral Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.summary: The continuation of the musculocutaneous nerve below the elbow. It is a skin nerve for the outer forearm.
lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.from: Musculocutaneous nerve (lateral cord of the brachial plexus)
lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.course: It emerges lateral to the biceps tendon and pierces the deep fascia. It then runs with the cephalic vein down the lateral forearm to the wrist.
lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the lateral (thumb side) forearm, reaching the base of the thenar eminence.
lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.injury: Numbness over the lateral forearm. There is no weakness.
lateral-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.clinical: It can be injured during biceps tendon repair or radial artery puncture, causing numbness on the thumb side of the forearm.

lateral-pectoral-nerve.name: Lateral Pectoral Nerve
lateral-pectoral-nerve.summary: A branch of the lateral cord. It mainly supplies the pectoralis major muscle on the chest.
lateral-pectoral-nerve.from: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
lateral-pectoral-nerve.course: It crosses in front of the axillary artery and pierces the clavipectoral fascia. It supplies pectoralis major and joins a loop with the medial pectoral nerve.
motor: Pectoralis minor (through the loop with the medial pectoral nerve)
lateral-pectoral-nerve.injury: Weak arm adduction and inward rotation.
lateral-pectoral-nerve.clinical: It can be injured during breast or axillary surgery. Weakness of the pectoral muscles is then noticed when pushing or adducting the arm.

long-thoracic-nerve.name: Long Thoracic Nerve
long-thoracic-nerve.group: Branches from the roots of the brachial plexus
long-thoracic-nerve.summary: A motor nerve to the serratus anterior muscle. It arises from the roots of the plexus and runs down the side of the chest.
long-thoracic-nerve.from: Roots C5, C6 and C7 of the brachial plexus
long-thoracic-nerve.course: It pierces the middle scalene and passes behind the plexus. It then descends on the outer surface of serratus anterior along the midaxillary line.
long-thoracic-nerve.injury: Winged scapula, and difficulty raising the arm above horizontal.
long-thoracic-nerve.clinical: It lies on the side of the chest wall and is easily hurt in breast surgery or axillary node dissection. Injury causes a winged scapula.

medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.name: Medial Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.summary: A skin nerve from the medial cord. It supplies the inner side of the forearm.
medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.from: Medial cord of the brachial plexus
medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.course: It runs down the arm medial to the brachial artery. It pierces the deep fascia with the basilic vein and splits into anterior and posterior branches.
medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial (little finger side) forearm.
medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.injury: Numbness of the medial forearm. There is no weakness.
medial-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.clinical: It lies close to the basilic vein and can be injured during vein surgery. The result is numbness on the inner forearm.

medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.name: Medial Brachial Cutaneous Nerve
medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.summary: A small sensory branch of the medial cord. It supplies skin on the inner side of the arm.
medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.from: Medial cord of the brachial plexus
medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.course: It runs down the medial arm and joins the intercostobrachial nerve (T2) in the axilla. It pierces the deep fascia in the lower arm.
medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial arm, reaching as far as the medial epicondyle.
medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.injury: Numb patch on the inner arm.
medial-brachial-cutaneous-nerve.clinical: Numbness here after axillary surgery usually involves the neighboring intercostobrachial nerve as well.

median-nerve.name: Median Nerve
median-nerve.group: Terminal branches of the brachial plexus
median-nerve.summary: A main nerve of the front of the forearm and hand. It flexes the wrist and fingers, pronates the forearm, and moves the thumb.
median-nerve.from: Lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus (two roots that join around the axillary artery)
median-nerve.course: It runs down the arm beside the brachial artery and passes through the cubital fossa. It then runs between flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus and through the carpal tunnel.
motor: Forearm: pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis
Anterior interosseous branch: flexor pollicis longus, lateral half of flexor digitorum profundus, pronator quadratus
Hand: abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head), first and second lumbricals
median-nerve.sensory: Palmar skin of the lateral three and a half digits and the lateral palm. Also the fingertip skin on the back of the index, middle and ring fingers.
median-nerve.injury: At the wrist: ape hand and weak thumb opposition. High lesion: hand of benediction when making a fist.
median-nerve.clinical: Carpal tunnel syndrome compresses it at the wrist. It causes night-time tingling and weak thumb opposition.

middle-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.name: Middle Trunk of the Brachial Plexus
middle-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.summary: The middle trunk of the brachial plexus. It is the continuation of the C7 ventral ramus.
middle-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.course: It passes laterally across the posterior triangle of the neck. Behind the clavicle it divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
middle-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.sensory: None directly (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
middle-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.injury: Weak elbow, wrist and finger extension, and possible numbness of the middle finger.
middle-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.clinical: Isolated injury is rare. Damage to C7 weakens extension of the elbow, wrist and fingers.

muscular-branches-of-axillary-nerve.name: Axillary Nerve — Muscular Branches
muscular-branches-of-axillary-nerve.summary: The motor branches of the axillary nerve. They supply the deltoid and the teres minor.
muscular-branches-of-axillary-nerve.from: Axillary nerve (posterior cord of the brachial plexus)
muscular-branches-of-axillary-nerve.course: An anterior branch winds around the surgical neck to the deltoid. A posterior branch supplies teres minor and the back of the deltoid.
muscular-branches-of-axillary-nerve.injury: Weak abduction of the arm beyond the first 15° and weak outward rotation.
muscular-branches-of-axillary-nerve.clinical: These branches are at risk in surgical neck fractures and anterior dislocations. The deltoid then wastes and the shoulder looks flattened.

muscular-branches-of-median-nerve.name: Median Nerve — Muscular Branches
muscular-branches-of-median-nerve.summary: The motor branches of the median nerve to the front of the forearm. A recurrent branch in the hand supplies the thenar muscles.
muscular-branches-of-median-nerve.course: Branches leave near the elbow to the pronator and superficial flexors. The recurrent branch loops back at the lower edge of the flexor retinaculum to the thenar muscles.
motor: Thenar muscles: abductor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis, flexor pollicis brevis (superficial head)
muscular-branches-of-median-nerve.injury: Weak pronation and wrist flexion. Wasting of the thenar muscles and loss of thumb opposition.
muscular-branches-of-median-nerve.clinical: The recurrent thenar branch lies just under the skin of the palm. A shallow cut there can paralyze the thumb muscles.

muscular-branches-of-radial-nerve.name: Radial Nerve — Muscular Branches
muscular-branches-of-radial-nerve.summary: The motor branches of the radial nerve above the elbow. They supply the triceps, anconeus, brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus.
muscular-branches-of-radial-nerve.course: The triceps branches leave in the axilla and spiral groove. Branches to brachioradialis and extensor carpi radialis longus arise near the elbow.
muscular-branches-of-radial-nerve.injury: Wrist drop. High lesions in the axilla also weaken elbow extension.
muscular-branches-of-radial-nerve.clinical: A midshaft humeral fracture damages the nerve below the triceps branches. Triceps works, but the wrist and fingers cannot extend.

muscular-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve — Muscular Branches
muscular-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.summary: The motor branches of the ulnar nerve in the forearm. They supply flexor carpi ulnaris and half of flexor digitorum profundus.
muscular-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.from: Ulnar nerve, just below the elbow
muscular-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.course: They arise after the nerve passes between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris. They enter flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of flexor digitorum profundus.
motor: Flexor digitorum profundus (medial half: ring and little fingers)
muscular-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.injury: Weak wrist flexion with ulnar deviation, and weak ring and little finger tip flexion.
muscular-branches-of-ulnar-nerve.clinical: Compression at the cubital tunnel at the elbow can weaken grip and wrist flexion on the inner side.

musculocutaneous-nerve.name: Musculocutaneous Nerve
musculocutaneous-nerve.group: Terminal branches of the brachial plexus
musculocutaneous-nerve.summary: The nerve of the front compartment of the arm. It flexes the elbow and supplies the skin of the outer forearm.
musculocutaneous-nerve.from: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus
musculocutaneous-nerve.course: It pierces coracobrachialis and runs between biceps brachii and brachialis. It then continues as the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.
musculocutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the lateral forearm, through the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve.
musculocutaneous-nerve.injury: Weak elbow flexion and supination, loss of the biceps reflex, and numbness of the lateral forearm.
musculocutaneous-nerve.clinical: The biceps tendon reflex tests C5–C6 through this nerve. Isolated injury is uncommon and may follow shoulder dislocation.

palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.name: Median Nerve — Palmar Cutaneous Branch
palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.summary: A small skin branch of the median nerve. It supplies the base of the thumb and the center of the palm.
palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.from: Median nerve, in the lower forearm, about 5 cm above the wrist
palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.course: It passes over the flexor retinaculum rather than under it. It supplies the skin of the thenar eminence and the central palm.
palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.sensory: Skin over the thenar eminence and the central palm.
palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.injury: Numbness over the thenar eminence is not seen in carpal tunnel syndrome. It occurs with a lesion above the wrist.
palmar-branch-of-median-nerve.clinical: Because it passes over the carpal tunnel, thenar skin sensation is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

palmar-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve — Palmar Cutaneous Branch
palmar-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.summary: A small skin branch of the ulnar nerve. It supplies the skin of the medial palm.
palmar-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.course: It runs down in front of the ulnar artery and pierces the deep fascia near the wrist. It supplies the skin over the hypothenar eminence.
palmar-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial palm over the hypothenar eminence.
palmar-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.injury: Numbness of the medial palm when the ulnar nerve is cut above mid-forearm.
palmar-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.clinical: It passes over Guyon canal, so palm skin sensation can remain even when the ulnar nerve is compressed at the canal.

posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.name: Posterior Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.group: Cutaneous branches of the radial nerve
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.summary: A skin branch of the radial nerve. It supplies the back of the forearm.
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.from: Radial nerve, in the spiral groove of the humerus
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.course: It pierces the lateral head of triceps and runs down the back of the arm. It continues down the middle of the posterior forearm to the wrist.
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the posterior forearm, from the elbow to the wrist.
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.injury: Numbness on the back of the forearm.
posterior-antebrachial-cutaneous-nerve.clinical: It is often spared in forearm-level radial nerve injuries because it branches off higher up the arm.

posterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-.name: Medial Antebrachial Cutaneous Nerve — Posterior Branch
posterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-.latin: Ramus posterior nervi cutanei antebrachii medialis
posterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-.summary: The smaller terminal branch of the medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve. It supplies the back and inner side of the forearm.
posterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-.from: Medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve (medial cord of the brachial plexus)
posterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-.course: It passes in front of the medial epicondyle and runs down the medial and back side of the forearm to the wrist.
posterior-branch-of-medial-antebrachial-.clinical: It passes near the medial epicondyle and can be hurt in elbow surgery, giving numbness of the inner forearm.

posterior-cord-of-brachial-plexus.name: Posterior Cord of the Brachial Plexus
posterior-cord-of-brachial-plexus.summary: The cord behind the axillary artery. It is formed by all three posterior divisions and supplies the extensor side of the upper limb.
posterior-cord-of-brachial-plexus.from: Union of the posterior divisions of the superior, middle and inferior trunks
posterior-cord-of-brachial-plexus.course: It lies behind the second part of the axillary artery. It gives the upper and lower subscapular nerves, thoracodorsal nerve, axillary nerve and radial nerve.
posterior-cord-of-brachial-plexus.injury: Wrist drop, weak elbow extension and shoulder weakness, with numbness over the back of the arm and hand.
posterior-cord-of-brachial-plexus.clinical: A crutch pressed into the axilla can injure it. This weakens shoulder abduction, and the elbow, wrist and finger extensors.

posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.name: Inferior Trunk — Posterior Division
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.latin: Divisio posterior trunci inferioris plexus brachialis
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.parent: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.summary: The back half of the inferior trunk. It carries C8 and T1 fibers for the extensor (back) side of the limb.
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.from: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.course: It forms behind the clavicle. It joins the other two posterior divisions to form the posterior cord.
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.sensory: None (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.injury: Part of lower plexus injury, with weakness of the lowest radial nerve muscles.
posterior-division-of-inferior-trunk-of-.clinical: Lower trunk injury can affect these fibers. This can weaken finger and thumb extensors supplied by the radial nerve.

posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.name: Middle Trunk — Posterior Division
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.latin: Divisio posterior trunci medii plexus brachialis
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.parent: Middle trunk of the brachial plexus
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.summary: The back half of the middle trunk. It carries C7 fibers for the extensor (back) side of the limb.
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.from: Middle trunk of the brachial plexus
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.course: It forms behind the clavicle. It joins the other two posterior divisions to form the posterior cord.
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.sensory: None (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.injury: Part of a C7 injury, with weak elbow and wrist extension.
posterior-division-of-middle-trunk-of-br.clinical: C7 contributes much of the power to the triceps and wrist extensors through the radial nerve.

posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.name: Superior Trunk — Posterior Division
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.latin: Divisio posterior trunci superioris plexus brachialis
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.parent: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.summary: The back half of the superior trunk. It carries C5 and C6 fibers for the extensor (back) side of the limb.
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.from: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.course: It forms behind the clavicle. It joins the other two posterior divisions to form the posterior cord.
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.sensory: None (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.injury: Part of Erb palsy, with a weak deltoid and teres minor.
posterior-division-of-superior-trunk-of-.clinical: These fibers supply the deltoid, teres minor and brachioradialis through the axillary and radial nerves. Upper plexus injury weakens them.

posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.name: Posterior Interosseous Nerve
posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.summary: The continuation of the deep radial nerve after the supinator. It supplies most of the extensor muscles on the back of the forearm.
posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.from: Deep branch of the radial nerve
posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.course: It emerges from the supinator and runs between the superficial and deep extensors. It lies on the interosseous membrane and ends at the wrist joint.
posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.sensory: No skin supply. It carries deep pain and position sense from the wrist joint.
posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.injury: Finger drop and weak thumb extension. Wrist extension remains but deviates toward the thumb side.
posterior-interosseous-nerve-of-forearm.clinical: Compression at the arcade of Frohse or a Monteggia fracture can injure it. The result is finger drop with no wrist drop.

proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.name: Median Nerve — Proper Palmar Digital Branches
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.latin: Nervi digitales palmares proprii nervi mediani
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.summary: The final sensory nerves of the median nerve to the digits. Each digit has one on each side.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.from: Common palmar digital branches of the median nerve
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.course: They run along the sides of the thumb, index finger, middle finger and lateral ring finger. They also send twigs to the back of the fingertips.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.sensory: Palmar skin of the thumb, index finger, middle finger and lateral half of the ring finger. Also the nail bed and fingertip skin on the dorsum.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.injury: Fingertip numbness from cuts at the sides of the lateral three and a half fingers.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-median.clinical: A digital nerve block at the base of the finger numbs the finger by anesthetizing these nerves on both sides.

proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.name: Ulnar Nerve — Proper Palmar Digital Branches
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.latin: Nervi digitales palmares proprii nervi ulnaris
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.summary: The final sensory nerves of the ulnar nerve to the little finger and half of the ring finger.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.from: Superficial branch of the ulnar nerve (via the common palmar digital branch)
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.course: They run along the sides of the little finger and the medial side of the ring finger. They also send twigs to the back of the fingertips.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.sensory: Palmar skin of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger, with the fingertip skin on the dorsum.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.injury: Numbness of the palmar little finger and medial half of the ring finger.
proper-palmar-digital-branches-of-ulnar-.clinical: Ulnar nerve damage at the wrist or elbow causes numbness of the little finger. This is the best skin test for the ulnar nerve.

radial-nerve.name: Radial Nerve
radial-nerve.group: Terminal branches of the brachial plexus
radial-nerve.summary: The largest branch of the brachial plexus. It supplies the extensor muscles of the arm, forearm and hand.
radial-nerve.from: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus
radial-nerve.course: It runs behind the humerus in the spiral groove with the deep brachial artery. In front of the lateral epicondyle it divides into superficial and deep branches.
motor: Supinator and the forearm extensors, via the deep branch
radial-nerve.sensory: Skin of the back of the arm and forearm. Also the lateral back of the hand and thumb, via the superficial branch.
radial-nerve.injury: Wrist drop, loss of finger extension, and numbness over the first dorsal web space.
radial-nerve.clinical: A midshaft humeral fracture or a long period of arm pressure (Saturday night palsy) damages it. It causes wrist drop.

roots-of-brachial-plexus.name: Roots of the Brachial Plexus
roots-of-brachial-plexus.summary: The five nerve roots that start the brachial plexus. They are the ventral rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1.
roots-of-brachial-plexus.from: Ventral rami of spinal nerves C5 to T1
roots-of-brachial-plexus.course: They leave the spine between the anterior and middle scalene muscles. They then pass above the first rib toward the armpit.
roots-of-brachial-plexus.sensory: None directly (carried by branches such as the dorsal scapular nerve)
roots-of-brachial-plexus.injury: C5–C6 injury causes Erb palsy. C8–T1 injury causes Klumpke palsy.
roots-of-brachial-plexus.clinical: Roots can be torn from the spinal cord in motorcycle crashes or birth traction. This is called a root avulsion.

subclavian-nerve.name: Nerve to Subclavius
subclavian-nerve.group: Branches from the trunks of the brachial plexus
subclavian-nerve.summary: A small motor nerve to the subclavius muscle under the clavicle.
subclavian-nerve.from: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
subclavian-nerve.course: It descends in front of the plexus and subclavian artery to reach subclavius. Sometimes it sends a branch to the phrenic nerve.
subclavian-nerve.clinical: Its accessory phrenic branch is present in some people and is of minor clinical importance.

superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.name: Radial Nerve — Superficial Branch
superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.summary: The sensory branch of the radial nerve. It supplies the skin of the thumb side of the back of the hand.
superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.from: Radial nerve, in front of the lateral epicondyle
superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.course: It runs under brachioradialis beside the radial artery. In the lower forearm it moves to the back of the wrist and divides into dorsal digital nerves.
superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.sensory: Skin of the lateral back of the hand and the proximal dorsum of the thumb and lateral two and a half fingers.
superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.injury: Numbness over the thumb side of the back of the hand without any muscle weakness.
superficial-branch-of-radial-nerve.clinical: A tight watch band or handcuffs can compress it (Wartenberg syndrome). It causes tingling at the base of the thumb.

superficial-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve — Superficial Branch
superficial-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.summary: The sensory branch of the ulnar nerve in the hand. It supplies the palmar skin of the little finger and half of the ring finger.
superficial-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.course: It leaves the nerve beside the pisiform and runs into the hypothenar palm. It gives a twig to palmaris brevis and then divides into digital nerves.
superficial-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.sensory: Palmar skin of the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.
superficial-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.injury: Numbness of the palmar little finger and medial half of the ring finger.
superficial-branch-of-ulnar-nerve.clinical: Compression in Guyon canal can numb the little finger and the medial half of the ring finger.

superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.name: Superior Lateral Brachial Cutaneous Nerve
superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.summary: A skin branch of the axillary nerve. It supplies the skin over the lower deltoid.
superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.from: Axillary nerve (posterior cord of the brachial plexus)
superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.course: It winds around the posterior border of the deltoid and pierces the deep fascia. It runs to the skin over the lateral arm.
superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.sensory: Skin over the lower deltoid and the upper lateral arm (the regimental badge area).
superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.injury: Numbness over the lower deltoid (regimental badge area).
superior-lateral-brachial-cutaneous-nerv.clinical: A patch of numb skin here is a quick test of the axillary nerve after shoulder injury.

superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.name: Superior Trunk of the Brachial Plexus
superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.summary: The highest trunk of the brachial plexus. It is formed by the C5 and C6 ventral rami.
superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.from: Union of the ventral rami of C5 and C6
superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.course: It forms at Erb point in the lower neck. It gives the suprascapular nerve and the nerve to subclavius, then divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.sensory: None directly (a conduit for fibers to later branches)
superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.injury: Erb palsy: the arm hangs at the side, turned inward, with the forearm pronated (waiter-tip position).
superior-trunk-of-brachial-plexus.clinical: Hard traction on the neck and shoulder, for example in a fall or during a difficult birth, can injure it.

suprascapular-nerve.name: Suprascapular Nerve
suprascapular-nerve.group: Branches from the trunks of the brachial plexus
suprascapular-nerve.summary: A nerve from the superior trunk. It supplies the supraspinatus and infraspinatus muscles of the rotator cuff.
suprascapular-nerve.from: Superior trunk of the brachial plexus
suprascapular-nerve.course: It passes through the suprascapular notch under the superior transverse scapular ligament. It then curves around the spine of the scapula to infraspinatus.
suprascapular-nerve.sensory: No skin supply. It supplies the shoulder joint and the acromioclavicular joint.
suprascapular-nerve.injury: Weak start of arm abduction and weak outward rotation, with wasting above and below the scapular spine.
suprascapular-nerve.clinical: Entrapment at the suprascapular notch is common in overhead athletes. It causes deep shoulder pain and weak abduction and external rotation.

ulnar-nerve.name: Ulnar Nerve
ulnar-nerve.group: Terminal branches of the brachial plexus
ulnar-nerve.summary: The nerve of the inner forearm and hand. It supplies most of the small muscles of the hand and the skin of the little finger side.
ulnar-nerve.from: Medial cord of the brachial plexus
ulnar-nerve.course: It runs down the medial arm and behind the medial epicondyle. It passes between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris, then through Guyon canal at the wrist.
motor: Forearm: flexor carpi ulnaris, flexor digitorum profundus (medial half)
Hand: hypothenar muscles, third and fourth lumbricals, interossei, adductor pollicis, palmaris brevis, flexor pollicis brevis (deep head)
ulnar-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial one and a half digits, both palmar and dorsal, and the medial palm and back of the hand.
ulnar-nerve.injury: Ulnar claw of the ring and little fingers, weak finger spreading, Froment sign, and numbness of the little finger.
ulnar-nerve.clinical: Pressure behind the medial epicondyle (the funny bone) gives tingling in the little finger. Cubital tunnel syndrome is a common compression.

anterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.name: Anterior circumflex humeral artery
anterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.summary: A small branch of the axillary artery that wraps around the front of the surgical neck of the humerus.
anterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.course: It runs laterally under coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps, then around the surgical neck. It meets the posterior circumflex artery.
branches: Ascending branch along the bicipital groove
anterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.clinical: A fracture of the surgical neck can injure it. Both circumflex arteries help supply the humeral head.

anterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.name: Anterior circumflex humeral vein
anterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.summary: A small vein that accompanies the anterior circumflex humeral artery.
drains: Front of the upper arm and shoulder joint
anterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.course: It wraps around the front of the surgical neck of the humerus and empties into the axillary vein.
anterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.clinical: It lies close to the humeral neck, so it can be torn in surgical neck fractures.

axillary-artery.name: Axillary artery
axillary-artery.summary: The continuation of the subclavian artery through the armpit. Pectoralis minor divides it into three parts.
axillary-artery.from: Subclavian artery (at the lateral border of the first rib)
axillary-artery.course: It runs from the first rib to the lower border of teres major, where it becomes the brachial artery. Part 1 is above, part 2 behind, and part 3 below pectoralis minor.
branches: Part 2: thoraco-acromial artery and lateral thoracic artery
Part 3: subscapular, anterior circumflex humeral, and posterior circumflex humeral arteries
axillary-artery.clinical: Rich anastomoses around the scapula keep the arm alive if the artery is blocked or tied between the subscapular and thoraco-acromial branches.

axillary-vein.name: Axillary vein
axillary-vein.summary: The main vein of the armpit. It lies next to the axillary artery.
drains: Arm (through the brachial and basilic veins)
axillary-vein.into: Subclavian vein (at the lateral border of the first rib)
axillary-vein.course: It begins where the basilic vein joins the brachial veins, at the lower border of teres major. It ends at the lateral border of the first rib.
axillary-vein.clinical: A clot here, often after hard repeated arm effort, causes a swollen painful arm (effort thrombosis or Paget-Schroetter syndrome).

basilic-vein.name: Basilic vein
basilic-vein.group: Superficial veins of the upper limb
basilic-vein.summary: The main superficial vein on the little-finger side of the arm.
drains: Medial side of the dorsal venous network
basilic-vein.into: Axillary vein (by joining the brachial veins)
basilic-vein.course: It runs up the medial forearm, passes in front of the medial epicondyle, and pierces the deep fascia in the mid-arm. It joins the brachial veins to form the axillary vein.
basilic-vein.clinical: It is often used for PICC lines. The median cubital vein usually joins it at the elbow.

brachial-artery.name: Brachial artery
brachial-artery.summary: The main artery of the arm. It is the continuation of the axillary artery.
brachial-artery.from: Axillary artery (at the lower border of teres major)
brachial-artery.course: It runs down the medial arm on brachialis. The median nerve crosses it from lateral to medial. In the cubital fossa it divides into the radial and ulnar arteries.
brachial-artery.clinical: Its pulse and blood pressure are taken in the cubital fossa, just medial to the biceps tendon. Supracondylar fractures can damage it.

brachial-veins.name: Brachial veins
brachial-veins.summary: A pair of deep veins that run on either side of the brachial artery.
brachial-veins.into: Axillary vein (after joining the basilic vein)
brachial-veins.course: They begin in the cubital fossa where the radial and ulnar veins unite. They ascend with the brachial artery and join the basilic vein to form the axillary vein.
brachial-veins.clinical: These deep veins are a site of deep vein thrombosis in the arm. Catheters placed in the arm often pass through them.

cephalic-vein.name: Cephalic vein
cephalic-vein.group: Superficial veins of the upper limb
cephalic-vein.summary: The main superficial vein on the thumb side of the arm.
drains: Lateral side of the dorsal venous network
cephalic-vein.course: It starts on the thumb side of the hand and ascends along the lateral forearm and the lateral edge of biceps. It runs in the deltopectoral groove and pierces the clavipectoral fascia to enter the axillary vein.
cephalic-vein.clinical: It is a common IV site, and surgeons find it in the deltopectoral groove. It is also used for dialysis fistulas.

circumflex-scapular-artery.name: Circumflex scapular artery
circumflex-scapular-artery.summary: A branch of the subscapular artery that winds around the lateral border of the scapula.
circumflex-scapular-artery.course: It passes backward through the triangular space, between subscapularis, teres minor, and teres major. Then it enters the infraspinous fossa.
circumflex-scapular-artery.clinical: It joins the suprascapular artery in the scapular anastomosis, a key collateral route around the shoulder.

circumflex-scapular-vein.name: Circumflex scapular vein
circumflex-scapular-vein.summary: A vein that accompanies the circumflex scapular artery around the border of the scapula.
drains: Muscles on the back of the scapula
circumflex-scapular-vein.course: It follows the artery through the triangular space and joins the subscapular vein, which drains into the axillary vein.
circumflex-scapular-vein.clinical: It travels in the triangular space with its artery. It matters mainly in surgery around the scapula.

common-interosseous-artery.name: Common interosseous artery
common-interosseous-artery.summary: A short branch of the ulnar artery that divides into the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries.
common-interosseous-artery.course: It is only about 1 cm long. It ends near the upper border of the interosseous membrane by splitting into two branches.
supplies: Deep flexor and extensor muscles of the forearm
common-interosseous-artery.clinical: It is the source of blood to the deep forearm. Damage in the proximal forearm can contribute to compartment syndrome.

common-palmar-digital-arteries.name: Common palmar digital arteries
common-palmar-digital-arteries.summary: Three arteries that leave the superficial palmar arch. They run toward the webs between the fingers.
common-palmar-digital-arteries.from: Superficial palmar arch (with contributions from the palmar metacarpal arteries)
common-palmar-digital-arteries.course: They run distally over the lumbricals toward the webs of the second to fourth spaces. Each splits into two proper palmar digital arteries.
supplies: Adjacent sides of the index, middle, ring, and little fingers
common-palmar-digital-arteries.clinical: They lie close to the common digital nerves. A deep palm cut can injure both.

deep-brachial-artery.name: Deep brachial artery
deep-brachial-artery.summary: The largest branch of the brachial artery. It supplies the back of the arm.
deep-brachial-artery.from: Brachial artery (near the lower border of teres major)
deep-brachial-artery.course: It passes behind the humerus in the radial groove with the radial nerve, between the heads of triceps. It ends as the middle and radial collateral arteries.
deep-brachial-artery.clinical: A mid-shaft humerus fracture in the radial groove can injure this artery and the radial nerve together.

deep-palmar-arch.name: Deep palmar arch
deep-palmar-arch.summary: An arterial arch deep in the palm. The radial artery forms most of it.
deep-palmar-arch.from: Radial artery (completed by the deep palmar branch of the ulnar artery)
deep-palmar-arch.course: It crosses the palm at the bases of the metacarpals, deep to the long flexor tendons. It lies about 1 cm closer to the wrist than the superficial arch.
deep-palmar-arch.clinical: It lies deeper than the superficial arch. Its main source is the radial artery, so radial injuries can reduce its flow.

deep-venous-palmar-arch.name: Deep venous palmar arch
deep-venous-palmar-arch.summary: A pair of veins that accompany the deep palmar arterial arch.
deep-venous-palmar-arch.into: Radial and ulnar veins (deep veins that run with the arteries)
deep-venous-palmar-arch.course: It lies deep in the palm at the bases of the metacarpals, beside the deep palmar arterial arch.
deep-venous-palmar-arch.clinical: It is a deep vein, so it cannot be seen through the skin.

dorsal-carpal-anastomosis.name: Dorsal carpal arch (anastomosis)
dorsal-carpal-anastomosis.summary: A network of arteries on the back of the wrist. It is formed by the radial and ulnar dorsal carpal branches.
dorsal-carpal-anastomosis.from: Dorsal carpal branches of the radial and ulnar arteries (with the anterior and posterior interosseous arteries)
dorsal-carpal-anastomosis.course: It lies on the back of the carpus under the extensor tendons. It gives off the second to fourth dorsal metacarpal arteries.
supplies: Back of the hand (through its branches)
dorsal-carpal-anastomosis.clinical: It provides collateral flow around the wrist and feeds the arteries of the back of the hand.

dorsal-carpal-branch-of-ulnar-artery.name: Dorsal carpal branch of the ulnar artery
dorsal-carpal-branch-of-ulnar-artery.summary: A branch of the ulnar artery that winds to the back of the wrist.
dorsal-carpal-branch-of-ulnar-artery.course: It passes deep to the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, around the ulnar side of the wrist, and joins the dorsal carpal network.
dorsal-carpal-branch-of-ulnar-artery.clinical: It helps form the dorsal carpal network. This is a collateral route if the radial or ulnar artery is injured.

dorsal-digital-arteries-of-hand.name: Dorsal digital arteries of the hand
dorsal-digital-arteries-of-hand.summary: Small arteries on the backs of the fingers. They arise from the dorsal metacarpal arteries.
dorsal-digital-arteries-of-hand.from: Dorsal metacarpal arteries (also directly from the radial artery for the thumb)
dorsal-digital-arteries-of-hand.course: Each pair runs along the sides of a finger on its back. They usually reach only the proximal and middle segments.
supplies: Skin of the back of the fingers (proximal parts)
Extensor tendons and joints of the fingers
dorsal-digital-arteries-of-hand.clinical: The fingertips are mainly supplied from the palmar side, so loss of the dorsal arteries rarely harms the fingertip.

dorsal-digital-veins-of-hand.name: Dorsal digital veins of the hand
dorsal-digital-veins-of-hand.summary: Small veins on the backs of the fingers. They collect blood from the fingers.
dorsal-digital-veins-of-hand.into: Dorsal venous network of the hand (through the dorsal metacarpal veins)
dorsal-digital-veins-of-hand.course: They run along the sides of the fingers and join near the webs to form dorsal metacarpal veins. These empty into the dorsal venous network.
dorsal-digital-veins-of-hand.clinical: They join the network used for hand IV access. Swelling of the hand shows first on the back, where these veins lie.

dorsal-metacarpal-arteries.name: Dorsal metacarpal arteries
dorsal-metacarpal-arteries.summary: Three or four small arteries on the back of the hand. They run over the dorsal interossei.
dorsal-metacarpal-arteries.from: Dorsal carpal arch (the first comes from the radial artery)
dorsal-metacarpal-arteries.course: They run distally on the dorsal interossei. Each divides into two dorsal digital arteries near the finger webs. Perforating branches join the deep palmar arch.
branches: Perforating branches to the deep palmar arch
dorsal-metacarpal-arteries.clinical: Perforating branches link the back and palm of the hand, so injury to one side may be partly offset by the other.

dorsal-venous-network-of-hand.name: Dorsal venous network of the hand
dorsal-venous-network-of-hand.summary: A web of veins under the skin on the back of the hand. It gives rise to the cephalic and basilic veins.
dorsal-venous-network-of-hand.into: Cephalic vein (lateral side) and basilic vein (medial side)
dorsal-venous-network-of-hand.course: It lies on the back of the hand. Its lateral part continues up the arm as the cephalic vein and its medial part as the basilic vein.
dorsal-venous-network-of-hand.clinical: The veins are easy to see here, so the back of the hand is a common site for IV cannulation.

inferior-ulnar-collateral-artery.name: Inferior ulnar collateral artery
inferior-ulnar-collateral-artery.summary: A branch of the brachial artery just above the elbow. It passes in front of the medial epicondyle.
inferior-ulnar-collateral-artery.from: Brachial artery (about 5 cm above the elbow)
inferior-ulnar-collateral-artery.course: It runs medially in front of the medial epicondyle and meets the anterior ulnar recurrent artery. It also joins the superior ulnar collateral artery.
inferior-ulnar-collateral-artery.clinical: It is a link in the elbow anastomosis. This network helps the forearm if the brachial artery is blocked below the collaterals.

lateral-thoracic-artery.name: Lateral thoracic artery
lateral-thoracic-artery.summary: A branch of the axillary artery that runs down the side of the chest wall.
lateral-thoracic-artery.from: Axillary artery (second part); sometimes the subscapular artery
lateral-thoracic-artery.course: It follows the lateral border of pectoralis minor down to the side of the chest, in company with the long thoracic nerve.
lateral-thoracic-artery.clinical: It supplies the outer breast. Surgeons see it during axillary node dissection, and it must be protected near the long thoracic nerve.

lateral-thoracic-vein.name: Lateral thoracic vein
lateral-thoracic-vein.summary: A vein that drains the side of the chest wall and the outer breast.
lateral-thoracic-vein.course: It follows the lateral thoracic artery along the lateral border of pectoralis minor.
lateral-thoracic-vein.clinical: It links with the superficial thoraco-epigastric vein. This gives a route between the upper and lower body if a main vein is blocked.

median-antebrachial-vein.name: Median antebrachial vein
median-antebrachial-vein.group: Superficial veins of the upper limb
median-antebrachial-vein.summary: A small superficial vein that runs up the middle of the front of the forearm.
drains: Palmar venous plexus of the hand
median-antebrachial-vein.into: Median cubital vein, basilic vein, or cephalic vein (this varies)
median-antebrachial-vein.course: It starts from the palmar venous plexus and ascends the front of the forearm between the cephalic and basilic veins. Its end varies from person to person.
median-antebrachial-vein.clinical: It is sometimes used for IV access when other veins are not available. Its pattern varies a lot.

median-cubital-vein.name: Median cubital vein
median-cubital-vein.group: Superficial veins of the upper limb
median-cubital-vein.summary: A short superficial vein that links the cephalic and basilic veins across the front of the elbow.
median-cubital-vein.course: It runs obliquely from the cephalic vein up and medially over the cubital fossa. It lies on top of the bicipital aponeurosis.
median-cubital-vein.clinical: It is the most common site for blood draws and IV access. The bicipital aponeurosis protects the brachial artery below it.

middle-collateral-artery.name: Middle collateral artery
middle-collateral-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the deep brachial artery. It runs down the back of the arm toward the elbow.
middle-collateral-artery.course: It descends in the medial head of triceps behind the elbow and meets the recurrent interosseous artery.
middle-collateral-artery.clinical: It joins the arterial network around the elbow. This network keeps the forearm supplied if the brachial artery is blocked.

palmar-carpal-branch-of-radial-artery.name: Palmar carpal branch of the radial artery
palmar-carpal-branch-of-radial-artery.summary: A small branch of the radial artery that crosses the front of the wrist.
palmar-carpal-branch-of-radial-artery.from: Radial artery (near the lower border of pronator quadratus)
palmar-carpal-branch-of-radial-artery.course: It runs medially across the front of the carpus, deep to the flexor tendons. It joins the palmar carpal branch of the ulnar artery.
palmar-carpal-branch-of-radial-artery.clinical: Together with the ulnar branch it forms the palmar carpal arch, a collateral network at the wrist.

palmar-digital-veins.name: Palmar digital veins
palmar-digital-veins.summary: Small veins on the palm side of the fingers. They accompany the proper palmar digital arteries.
palmar-digital-veins.into: Superficial venous palmar arch (through the common palmar digital veins)
palmar-digital-veins.course: They run along the fingers and join near the finger webs to form common palmar digital veins. Many also drain to the back of the hand.
palmar-digital-veins.clinical: Much finger blood drains to the back of the hand, so a tight band at the finger base can cause swelling.

palmar-metacarpal-arteries.name: Palmar metacarpal arteries
palmar-metacarpal-arteries.summary: Three small arteries that leave the deep palmar arch. They run toward the fingers on the palmar interossei.
palmar-metacarpal-arteries.course: They pass distally along the second to fourth metacarpal spaces. Near the finger webs they join the common palmar digital arteries.
palmar-metacarpal-arteries.clinical: They link the deep and superficial arches, which helps the hand keep its blood flow.

pectoral-branches-of-thoraco-acromial-ar.name: Pectoral branches of the thoraco-acromial artery
pectoral-branches-of-thoraco-acromial-ar.summary: These branches of the thoraco-acromial artery supply the pectoral muscles. They also help feed the breast.
pectoral-branches-of-thoraco-acromial-ar.course: They run down between pectoralis major and pectoralis minor and enter the deep surface of both muscles.
pectoral-branches-of-thoraco-acromial-ar.clinical: They are cut or cauterized in surgery on the pectoral muscles. They are also part of the blood supply that surgeons use for pectoral flaps.

posterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.name: Posterior circumflex humeral artery
posterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.summary: A branch of the axillary artery that passes through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve.
posterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.course: It leaves the axilla through the quadrangular space and winds around the surgical neck of the humerus under deltoid.
posterior-circumflex-humeral-artery.clinical: A surgical neck fracture or shoulder dislocation can injure it together with the axillary nerve.

posterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.name: Posterior circumflex humeral vein
posterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.summary: A small vein that accompanies the posterior circumflex humeral artery.
posterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.course: It passes through the quadrangular space with the axillary nerve and artery, then joins the axillary vein.
posterior-circumflex-humeral-vein.clinical: It can be damaged with the axillary nerve in a shoulder dislocation or surgical neck fracture.

posterior-interosseus-artery.name: Posterior interosseous artery
posterior-interosseus-artery.summary: The artery of the extensor compartment of the forearm. It passes through the gap above the interosseous membrane.
posterior-interosseus-artery.course: It passes backward above the interosseous membrane and runs between the superficial and deep extensor muscles. It gives off the recurrent interosseous artery.
supplies: Dorsal wrist (through the dorsal carpal network)
posterior-interosseus-artery.clinical: It travels with the deep branch of the radial nerve, so injuries to the proximal forearm can affect both.

proper-palmar-digital-arteries.name: Proper palmar digital arteries
proper-palmar-digital-arteries.summary: The arteries that run along the sides of each finger on the palm side. They give the fingers most of their blood.
proper-palmar-digital-arteries.from: Common palmar digital arteries (for the thumb and index finger, branches of the radial artery)
proper-palmar-digital-arteries.course: A pair runs along each finger beside the flexor sheath, just behind the proper palmar digital nerves. They join over the fingertip.
proper-palmar-digital-arteries.clinical: Digital nerve blocks are given at the base of the finger, close to these vessels. Deep finger cuts can sever both artery and nerve.

radial-artery.name: Radial artery
radial-artery.summary: The smaller terminal branch of the brachial artery. It runs along the thumb side of the forearm.
radial-artery.course: It descends under brachioradialis, then lies beside the flexor carpi radialis tendon at the wrist. It crosses the anatomical snuffbox and enters the palm to form the deep palmar arch.
branches: Princeps pollicis and radialis indicis arteries
radial-artery.clinical: The radial pulse is felt lateral to the flexor carpi radialis tendon. The Allen test checks flow through the radial and ulnar arteries.

radial-collateral-artery.name: Radial collateral artery
radial-collateral-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the deep brachial artery. It follows the radial nerve to the front of the lateral epicondyle.
radial-collateral-artery.course: It accompanies the radial nerve through the lateral intermuscular septum. It then runs in front of the lateral epicondyle and meets the radial recurrent artery.
radial-collateral-artery.clinical: It is part of the elbow anastomosis that provides collateral flow around the joint.

radial-veins.name: Radial veins
radial-veins.summary: A pair of deep veins that accompany the radial artery.
drains: Deep structures of the lateral forearm
radial-veins.into: Brachial veins (after joining the ulnar veins)
radial-veins.course: They start from the deep venous palmar arch and run up the lateral forearm beside the radial artery. They unite with the ulnar veins near the elbow.
radial-veins.clinical: Because they are small and deep, they are rarely used for needle access. They matter when a radial artery line is placed.

recurrent-interosseus-artery.name: Recurrent interosseous artery
recurrent-interosseus-artery.summary: A branch of the posterior interosseous artery that runs back up to the back of the elbow.
recurrent-interosseus-artery.course: It ascends behind the elbow, deep to anconeus, and meets the middle collateral artery.
recurrent-interosseus-artery.clinical: It joins the middle collateral artery in the elbow anastomosis, giving the forearm a backup blood supply.

subscapular-artery.name: Subscapular artery
subscapular-artery.summary: The largest branch of the axillary artery. It runs along the lower edge of the subscapularis muscle.
subscapular-artery.course: It descends along the lateral border of subscapularis. About 2 to 3 cm from its origin it gives off the circumflex scapular artery and continues as the thoracodorsal artery.
subscapular-artery.clinical: It links the axillary artery to the scapular anastomosis. This route can carry blood around a blockage higher in the axillary artery.

subscapular-vein.name: Subscapular vein
subscapular-vein.summary: A vein that collects blood from the back of the shoulder blade region. It follows the subscapular artery.
subscapular-vein.course: It runs with the subscapular artery along the lateral border of subscapularis and empties into the axillary vein.
subscapular-vein.clinical: It is a deep tributary that surgeons may meet during axillary lymph node surgery.

superficial-palmar-arch.name: Superficial palmar arch
superficial-palmar-arch.summary: An arterial arch in the palm. The ulnar artery forms most of it.
superficial-palmar-arch.from: Ulnar artery (completed by the superficial palmar branch of the radial artery or another branch)
superficial-palmar-arch.course: It crosses the palm under the palmar aponeurosis and over the long flexor tendons. It lies roughly level with the distal border of the fully extended thumb.
branches: Proper palmar digital artery to the little finger
superficial-palmar-arch.clinical: It can be cut by deep palm lacerations and heavy bleeding may follow. The Allen test checks whether the arches are complete.

superficial-venous-palmar-arch.name: Superficial venous palmar arch
superficial-venous-palmar-arch.summary: A pair of veins that accompany the superficial palmar arterial arch.
superficial-venous-palmar-arch.course: It lies in the palm beside the superficial palmar arterial arch and drains mostly toward the ulnar side of the forearm.
superficial-venous-palmar-arch.clinical: It lies below the palmar aponeurosis, so it is at risk in deep cuts of the palm.

superior-ulnar-collateral-artery.name: Superior ulnar collateral artery
superior-ulnar-collateral-artery.summary: A branch of the brachial artery that runs with the ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle.
superior-ulnar-collateral-artery.from: Brachial artery (near the middle of the arm)
superior-ulnar-collateral-artery.course: It pierces the medial intermuscular septum with the ulnar nerve. It passes behind the medial epicondyle and meets the posterior ulnar recurrent artery.
superior-ulnar-collateral-artery.clinical: It lies next to the ulnar nerve. Surgeons protect it during ulnar nerve transposition at the elbow.

suprascapular-artery.name: Suprascapular artery
suprascapular-artery.summary: A branch of the thyrocervical trunk that supplies the muscles on the back of the scapula.
suprascapular-artery.from: Thyrocervical trunk (first part of the subclavian artery)
suprascapular-artery.course: It runs across the root of the neck and passes over the superior transverse scapular ligament. The suprascapular nerve passes under it.
suprascapular-artery.clinical: Memory aid: the artery goes over the ligament and the nerve goes under. It meets the circumflex scapular artery.

suprascapular-vein.name: Suprascapular vein
suprascapular-vein.summary: A vein that follows the suprascapular artery and drains the back of the scapula.
suprascapular-vein.into: External jugular vein (sometimes the subclavian vein)
suprascapular-vein.course: It accompanies the suprascapular artery across the top of the scapula and drains into the external jugular vein in the neck.
suprascapular-vein.clinical: It lies in the lower neck behind the clavicle, so it can be injured in clavicle fractures or neck surgery.

thoraco-acromial-artery.name: Thoraco-acromial artery
thoraco-acromial-artery.summary: A short, wide branch of the axillary artery. It pierces the clavipectoral fascia and splits into four branches.
thoraco-acromial-artery.from: Axillary artery (second part, behind pectoralis minor)
thoraco-acromial-artery.course: It emerges at the upper border of pectoralis minor, pierces the clavipectoral membrane, and divides at once into its branches.
thoraco-acromial-artery.clinical: It is a landmark vessel in the deltopectoral approach. It can bleed when surgeons release the clavipectoral fascia.

thoracodorsal-artery.name: Thoracodorsal artery
thoracodorsal-artery.summary: The continuation of the subscapular artery. It travels with the thoracodorsal nerve to latissimus dorsi.
thoracodorsal-artery.course: It runs down the posterior axillary wall with the thoracodorsal nerve and enters the deep surface of latissimus dorsi.
thoracodorsal-artery.clinical: Surgeons use it as the pedicle of the latissimus dorsi flap for breast reconstruction.

thoracodorsal-vein.name: Thoracodorsal vein
thoracodorsal-vein.summary: A vein that drains latissimus dorsi. It runs with the thoracodorsal artery and nerve.
thoracodorsal-vein.into: Subscapular vein (or directly into the axillary vein)
thoracodorsal-vein.course: It runs up the posterior axillary wall beside the thoracodorsal artery and nerve.
thoracodorsal-vein.clinical: Surgeons use it with its artery as the vascular pedicle of a latissimus dorsi flap.

ulnar-artery.name: Ulnar artery
ulnar-artery.summary: The larger terminal branch of the brachial artery. It runs along the little finger side of the forearm.
ulnar-artery.course: It passes deep to pronator teres and runs between flexor carpi ulnaris and flexor digitorum superficialis. At the wrist it lies beside the ulnar nerve and continues as the superficial palmar arch.
branches: Anterior and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries
supplies: Deep forearm muscles (via the interosseous arteries)
Palm and little finger side of the hand
ulnar-artery.clinical: A fracture of the hook of the hamate or a cut at the wrist can injure it with the ulnar nerve. The Allen test uses it.

ulnar-recurrent-artery.name: Ulnar recurrent arteries
ulnar-recurrent-artery.summary: Small branches of the ulnar artery that turn back up toward the elbow. They have anterior and posterior parts.
ulnar-recurrent-artery.course: The anterior branch runs up in front of the medial epicondyle. The posterior branch runs up behind it, near the ulnar nerve.
ulnar-recurrent-artery.clinical: They join the collateral arteries to form the elbow anastomosis, which supplies the joint and protects blood flow.

ulnar-veins.name: Ulnar veins
ulnar-veins.summary: A pair of deep veins that accompany the ulnar artery.
drains: Deep structures of the medial forearm
ulnar-veins.into: Brachial veins (after joining the radial veins)
ulnar-veins.course: They start from the superficial venous palmar arch, run up the medial forearm beside the ulnar artery, and unite with the radial veins.
ulnar-veins.clinical: They run with the ulnar artery, so a deep forearm wound on the medial side can injure the artery and its veins together.

sacrum.name: Sacrum
sacrum.summary: The sacrum is a triangular bone made of five fused sacral vertebrae. It forms the back of the pelvis and links the spine to the hip bones.
sacrum.clinical: The sacral hiatus, a gap at the lower end of the canal, is the entry point for caudal epidural anesthesia.
articulations: Ilium on each side (sacroiliac joint, auricular surface)
landmarks: Four pairs of anterior and posterior sacral foramina
Median, intermediate, and lateral sacral crests
attachments: Piriformis (anterior surface)
Gluteus maximus (posterior surface and lateral border)
Erector spinae and multifidus (posterior surface)
Sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments (lateral border)
Sacroiliac ligaments
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
sacrum.ossification: Each sacral vertebra ossifies from several centers. Fusion begins after puberty and is usually complete by about age 30.

coccyx.name: Coccyx
coccyx.summary: The coccyx, or tailbone, is a small triangular bone made of three to five fused rudimentary vertebrae (usually four). It lies below the sacrum.
coccyx.clinical: A fall onto the buttocks can bruise or fracture the coccyx and cause lasting pain when sitting (coccydynia).
articulations: Sacrum above (sacrococcygeal joint, usually a fibrocartilage joint)
landmarks: Rudimentary transverse processes of the first coccygeal vertebra
attachments: Coccygeus and levator ani (via the anococcygeal body)
Gluteus maximus (lowest fibers)
External anal sphincter (tip)
Sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments
Anococcygeal ligament
coccyx.ossification: Each segment ossifies from one center after birth. The segments fuse with age, and the coccyx may fuse to the sacrum in older adults.

vertebra-c6.name: Vertebra C6
vertebra-c6.summary: C6 is a typical cervical vertebra with a large anterior tubercle on its transverse process. The vertebral artery usually enters the column through its transverse foramen.
vertebra-c6.clinical: The large anterior tubercle (carotid tubercle) allows the common carotid artery to be compressed against it. The cricoid cartilage lies at this level.
articulations: C5 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
C7 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Small wide body with uncinate processes
attachments: Anterior scalene (anterior tubercle)
Middle and posterior scalene (posterior tubercle)
Longus colli and longus capitis (anterior tubercle)
Nuchal ligament and semispinalis cervicis (spinous process)
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-c6.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-c7.name: Vertebra C7
vertebra-c7.summary: C7 is a transitional vertebra with a long spinous process that is not bifid. This process forms the prominent bump at the base of the neck.
vertebra-c7.clinical: A cervical rib, present in about 1 percent of people, can arise from C7. It may compress the lower brachial plexus or the subclavian artery.
articulations: C6 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T1 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Small transverse foramen (transmits accessory veins, not the vertebral artery)
attachments: Nuchal ligament (spinous process)
Trapezius and rhomboid minor (spinous process)
Serratus posterior superior (spinous process)
Middle scalene (transverse process)
Semispinalis and multifidus
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-c7.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t1.name: Vertebra T1
vertebra-t1.summary: T1 is the first thoracic vertebra. It has a complete facet for rib 1 and a long, almost horizontal spinous process.
vertebra-t1.clinical: Damage to the T1 root can weaken the small hand muscles and, with the sympathetic fibers, cause Horner syndrome.
articulations: Head of rib 1 (complete superior costal facet)
C7 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T2 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Body with a complete superior costal facet and an inferior demifacet
attachments: Rhomboid minor, trapezius, and serratus posterior superior (spinous process)
Longus colli (body)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t1.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t2.name: Vertebra T2
vertebra-t2.summary: T2 is a typical upper thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 2 and 3. It supports the upper back of the thorax.
vertebra-t2.clinical: The superior angle of the scapula lies at about the T2 level when the arm is at the side.
articulations: T1 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T3 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius and rhomboid major (spinous process)
Serratus posterior superior (spinous process)
Longus colli (body)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t2.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t3.name: Vertebra T3
vertebra-t3.summary: T3 is a typical thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 3 and 4. Its spinous process begins to slope downward.
vertebra-t3.clinical: The root of the spine of the scapula lies at about the T3 level, a surface landmark for counting levels.
articulations: T2 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T4 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius and rhomboid major (spinous process)
Serratus posterior superior (spinous process)
Longus colli (body)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t3.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t4.name: Vertebra T4
vertebra-t4.summary: T4 is a typical thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 4 and 5. Its spinous process slopes downward.
vertebra-t4.clinical: The sternal angle lies at the level of the T4-T5 disc, which also marks the tracheal bifurcation and the aortic arch.
articulations: T3 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T5 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius and rhomboid major (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t4.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t5.name: Vertebra T5
vertebra-t5.summary: T5 is a typical mid-thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 5 and 6. Its long spinous process slopes steeply downward.
vertebra-t5.clinical: The tip of a mid-thoracic spinous process lies level with the body of the vertebra below, which can mislead level counting by touch.
articulations: T4 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T6 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius and rhomboid major (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t5.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t6.name: Vertebra T6
vertebra-t6.summary: T6 is a typical mid-thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 6 and 7. Its spinous process is long and slopes steeply downward.
vertebra-t6.clinical: Rib attachments make the mid-thoracic spine stiff, so disc herniation is less common here than in the neck or lower back.
articulations: T5 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T7 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t6.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t7.name: Vertebra T7
vertebra-t7.summary: T7 is a typical mid-thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 7 and 8. Its spinous process is long and slopes downward.
vertebra-t7.clinical: The inferior angle of the scapula lies at about the T7 level when the arm is at the side.
articulations: T6 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T8 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius (spinous process)
Latissimus dorsi (spinous process, via thoracolumbar fascia)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t7.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t8.name: Vertebra T8
vertebra-t8.summary: T8 is a typical lower mid-thoracic vertebra with demifacets for ribs 8 and 9. Its spinous process slopes downward.
vertebra-t8.clinical: The opening for the inferior vena cava in the diaphragm lies at about the T8 level.
articulations: T7 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T9 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius and latissimus dorsi (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t8.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t9.name: Vertebra T9
vertebra-t9.summary: T9 is a lower thoracic vertebra. It usually has only a superior demifacet for rib 9, and its inferior demifacet is often absent.
vertebra-t9.clinical: The xiphisternal joint lies at about the T9 level, a surface landmark on the front of the trunk.
articulations: T8 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T10 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
attachments: Trapezius and latissimus dorsi (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t9.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t10.name: Vertebra T10
vertebra-t10.summary: T10 has a single complete costal facet on the body for rib 10. It also has a transverse costal facet.
vertebra-t10.clinical: The T10 dermatome includes the umbilicus, and the esophageal hiatus of the diaphragm lies at about this level.
articulations: Head of rib 10 (single complete facet at the body-pedicle junction)
T9 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T11 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Body with a single complete costal facet
attachments: Trapezius and latissimus dorsi (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t10.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t11.name: Vertebra T11
vertebra-t11.summary: T11 has a single complete costal facet for rib 11 and no facet on its transverse process. Its body is larger than the vertebrae above.
vertebra-t11.clinical: The thoracolumbar junction (T11 to L2) is a common site for spinal compression and burst fractures.
articulations: Head of rib 11 (single complete facet at the body-pedicle junction)
T10 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
T12 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Large body with a single complete costal facet
attachments: Latissimus dorsi (spinous process)
Serratus posterior inferior (spinous process)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t11.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-t12.name: Vertebra T12
vertebra-t12.summary: T12 is a transitional vertebra. It has a single costal facet for rib 12 and lumbar-type features, such as inferior facets that face sideways.
vertebra-t12.clinical: T12 lies at the thoracolumbar junction, a common site of compression fractures. The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at about this level.
articulations: Head of rib 12 (single complete facet at the body-pedicle junction)
T11 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
L1 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Large body with a single costal facet
Superior facets face backward, inferior facets face sideways
attachments: Latissimus dorsi and serratus posterior inferior (spinous process)
Diaphragm (median arcuate ligament and crura, at the body)
Psoas major (body)
Erector spinae and transversospinalis muscles
Levator costarum (transverse process)
Costotransverse and radiate ligaments
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
vertebra-t12.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-l1.name: Vertebra L1
vertebra-l1.summary: L1 is the first lumbar vertebra, with a massive kidney-shaped body and no costal facets. The transpyloric plane passes through this level.
vertebra-l1.clinical: L1 lies at the thoracolumbar junction, where burst and compression fractures are common. The spinal cord usually ends at L1 to L2.
articulations: T12 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
L2 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Superior facets face medially, inferior facets face laterally
attachments: Crura of the diaphragm (anterior body)
Medial and lateral arcuate ligaments (transverse process)
Psoas major (transverse process and body)
Quadratus lumborum (transverse process tip)
Erector spinae and multifidus
Thoracolumbar fascia
Supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, ligamenta flava
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
