vertebra-l1.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-l2.name: Vertebra L2
vertebra-l2.summary: L2 is a lumbar vertebra with a large kidney-shaped body. The spinal cord usually ends at its upper border or at the L1-L2 level.
vertebra-l2.clinical: The conus medullaris usually ends at the L1-L2 level, so lumbar punctures are done below L2 to avoid the cord.
articulations: L1 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
L3 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Superior facets face medially, inferior facets face laterally

Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-l2.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-l3.name: Vertebra L3
vertebra-l3.summary: L3 is a central lumbar vertebra. The subcostal plane, at the lowest edge of the rib cage, passes through this level.
vertebra-l3.clinical: Lumbar punctures are usually done between L3 and L4 or L4 and L5, below the end of the spinal cord.
articulations: L2 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
L4 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Superior facets face medially, inferior facets face laterally
attachments: Right crus of the diaphragm (anterior body)
Psoas major (transverse process and body)

Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-l3.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-l4.name: Vertebra L4
vertebra-l4.summary: L4 is a lumbar vertebra with a large body and a short spinous process. The aorta divides into the common iliac arteries at about this level.
vertebra-l4.clinical: A line joining the highest points of the iliac crests crosses the L4 spinous process, a guide for lumbar puncture. Disc herniation at L4-L5 often compresses the L5 root.
articulations: L3 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
L5 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)

vertebra-l4.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-l5.name: Vertebra L5
vertebra-l5.summary: L5 is the largest and lowest lumbar vertebra. Its wedge-shaped body and large transverse processes join the spine to the sacrum.
vertebra-l5.clinical: L5 is the usual site of spondylolysis and spondylolisthesis, where the vertebra slips forward on the sacrum. The inferior vena cava forms at this level.
articulations: L4 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)

vertebra-l5.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

arytenoid-cartilage.name: Arytenoid Cartilage
arytenoid-cartilage.summary: The arytenoid cartilages are two small pyramid-shaped cartilages on the back of the larynx. They pivot and slide to open, close, and tension the vocal folds.
arytenoid-cartilage.clinical: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves the arytenoid cartilage unable to move, which causes a hoarse voice. Intubation can dislocate it.
arytenoid-cartilage.bone_type: Hyaline cartilage (apex and vocal process are elastic cartilage)
articulations: Upper border of the cricoid lamina (cricoarytenoid joint)
landmarks: Anterior surface for the vestibular ligament
attachments: Vocal ligament and vocalis (vocal process)
Thyroarytenoid (anterolateral surface)
Posterior and lateral cricoarytenoid (muscular process)
Transverse and oblique arytenoids (posterior surface)
Aryepiglottic fold (apex)
arytenoid-cartilage.ossification: The hyaline parts may calcify and ossify from early adulthood.

corniculate-cartilage.name: Corniculate Cartilage
corniculate-cartilage.summary: The corniculate cartilages are two tiny nodules of elastic cartilage that sit on the apex of each arytenoid cartilage. They lie within the aryepiglottic folds.
corniculate-cartilage.clinical: The corniculate tubercles form small bumps at the back of the laryngeal inlet and serve as landmarks during laryngoscopy.
landmarks: Raises the corniculate tubercle in the mucosa
attachments: Aryepiglottic fold
Mucous membrane at the back of the laryngeal inlet

thyroid-cartilage.name: Thyroid Cartilage
thyroid-cartilage.summary: The thyroid cartilage is the largest laryngeal cartilage. Its two laminae meet in front to form the laryngeal prominence and shield the vocal folds.
thyroid-cartilage.clinical: The laryngeal prominence is larger and sharper in males. The cricothyroid membrane just below it is the site for emergency airway access.
articulations: Cricoid cartilage below (cricothyroid joint, at the inferior horn)
attachments: Thyrohyoid membrane (upper border)
Sternothyroid, thyrohyoid, and inferior pharyngeal constrictor (oblique line)
Cricothyroid (lower border)
Vocal and vestibular ligaments (inner surface at the angle)
Thyroarytenoid and thyroepiglottic muscles (inner surface)
thyroid-cartilage.ossification: It ossifies progressively from early adulthood, often earlier in males.

atlas-c1.name: Atlas (C1)
atlas-c1.summary: The atlas is the first cervical vertebra. It is a ring with no body and no spinous process, and it carries the skull.
atlas-c1.clinical: A burst fracture of the ring (Jefferson fracture) follows axial loading, such as diving into shallow water. Rupture of the transverse ligament causes atlantoaxial instability.
articulations: Axis (C2) below (atlantoaxial joints; dens at the median joint, turning)
landmarks: Lateral masses with superior and inferior articular facets
Facet for the dens (on the back of the anterior arch)
attachments: Transverse ligament of the atlas (lateral masses)
Anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes
Rectus capitis anterior and lateralis
Rectus capitis posterior minor (posterior tubercle)
Obliquus capitis superior and inferior (transverse process)
Levator scapulae and splenius cervicis (transverse process)
atlas-c1.ossification: It ossifies from three centers: one in each lateral mass before birth and one in the anterior arch in the first year. The ring fuses by about age 7.

ethmoid-bone.name: Ethmoid Bone
ethmoid-bone.summary: The ethmoid is a light, air-filled bone between the orbits. It forms part of the anterior cranial floor, the nasal septum, and the walls of the nasal cavity and orbit.
ethmoid-bone.clinical: Fracture of the cribriform plate can cause loss of smell and cerebrospinal fluid leak from the nose. The thin medial orbital wall lets ethmoid infection spread to the orbit.
landmarks: Ethmoidal labyrinth with ethmoid air cells
attachments: Falx cerebri (crista galli)
Olfactory bulb rests on the cribriform plate
Nasal septal cartilage (perpendicular plate)
ethmoid-bone.ossification: It ossifies from three centers: one in each labyrinth before birth and one midline center in the first year after birth.

frontal-bone.name: Frontal Bone
frontal-bone.summary: The frontal bone forms the forehead, the roof of the orbits, and part of the anterior cranial floor. It contains the frontal sinuses.
frontal-bone.clinical: A blow to the forehead can fracture the frontal sinus wall. The supraorbital nerve passes through the supraorbital notch at the brow.
attachments: Falx cerebri (frontal crest)
Corrugator supercilii (medial brow)
Orbicularis oculi (orbital margin)
Temporal fascia (temporal line)
Trochlea for superior oblique (trochlear fovea)
frontal-bone.ossification: It forms from two halves that fuse at the metopic suture in early childhood. The suture persists in a minority of adults.

hyoid-bone.name: Hyoid Bone
hyoid-bone.summary: The hyoid is a U-shaped bone in the front of the neck at the level of C3. It does not touch any other bone and anchors the tongue and larynx.
hyoid-bone.clinical: A fractured hyoid in an adult raises suspicion of strangulation. The hyoid rises and falls during swallowing.
articulations: No bony articulation (suspended by the stylohyoid ligaments and muscles)
attachments: Suprahyoid muscles: mylohyoid, geniohyoid, digastric (by a sling), and stylohyoid
Infrahyoid muscles: sternohyoid, omohyoid, and thyrohyoid
Hyoglossus and middle pharyngeal constrictor
Stylohyoid ligament (lesser horn)
Thyrohyoid membrane
hyoid-bone.ossification: It ossifies from several centers around birth. The greater horns fuse to the body in middle age.

inferior-nasal-concha-bone.name: Inferior Nasal Concha
inferior-nasal-concha-bone.summary: The inferior nasal concha is a thin, curled bone on the lateral wall of the nasal cavity. It is a separate bone, not part of the ethmoid.
inferior-nasal-concha-bone.clinical: The nasolacrimal duct opens beneath it, into the inferior meatus. Swelling of the concha is a common cause of nasal blockage.
attachments: Nasal mucous membrane covers its surface

lacrimal-bone.name: Lacrimal Bone
lacrimal-bone.summary: The lacrimal bone is a small, fragile bone in the front of the medial orbital wall. It helps form the fossa for the lacrimal sac.
lacrimal-bone.clinical: Blocked tear drainage can be treated by making a new passage through this thin bone into the nose (dacryocystorhinostomy).
landmarks: Fossa for the lacrimal sac (with the maxilla)
attachments: Lacrimal part of orbicularis oculi (posterior lacrimal crest)
Lacrimal fascia and lacrimal sac

lateral-process-of-nasal-septal-cartilag.name: Lateral Process of Nasal Septal Cartilage
lateral-process-of-nasal-septal-cartilag.summary: This is the wing-like extension of the septal cartilage that forms the upper side wall of the nose, also called the upper lateral cartilage. It lies below the nasal bone.
lateral-process-of-nasal-septal-cartilag.clinical: The gap between this cartilage and the septum is the internal nasal valve. Collapse of the valve blocks nasal breathing.
articulations: Nasal bone and maxilla (frontal process, by fibrous tissue)
Nasal septal cartilage (continuous at the midline)
Major alar cartilage (overlaps its lower edge)
landmarks: Upper edge under the nasal bone
attachments: Procerus and nasalis (overlying muscle attachments)
Fibrous tissue to the maxilla and nasal bone

major-alar-cartilage.name: Major Alar Cartilage
major-alar-cartilage.summary: The major alar cartilage is a U-shaped cartilage that shapes the nostril and the tip of the nose. Its medial crus lies in the columella.
major-alar-cartilage.clinical: Its shape controls the nasal tip and the external nasal valve. Weakness or surgery can cause nostril collapse on breathing in.
articulations: Nasal septal cartilage (medial crus, by fibrous tissue)
Lateral process of the septal cartilage (overlap)
Frontal process of the maxilla (lateral crus, by fibrous tissue)
attachments: Nasalis (alar part)
Depressor septi nasi (medial crus)
Fibrofatty tissue of the nostril wing

malleus.name: Malleus
malleus.summary: The malleus is the largest and outermost of the three middle ear ossicles. Its handle is attached to the eardrum.
malleus.clinical: The handle and umbo of the malleus can be seen through the eardrum during otoscopy. The chorda tympani nerve crosses the malleus neck.
attachments: Tympanic membrane (handle and lateral process)
Tensor tympani tendon (handle)
Anterior, superior, and lateral ligaments of the malleus
malleus.ossification: It ossifies before birth and is nearly adult size at birth.

incus.name: Incus
incus.summary: The incus is the middle bone of the three middle ear ossicles. It links the malleus to the stapes and has a body and two crura.
incus.clinical: Its long limb has a poor blood supply. It can die after trauma or chronic ear infection, which breaks the chain and causes hearing loss.
attachments: Posterior ligament of the incus (short crus)
Superior ligament of the incus (body)
incus.ossification: It ossifies before birth and is adult size at birth.

stapes.name: Stapes
stapes.summary: The stapes is the smallest bone in the body. Its footplate sits in the oval window and passes vibrations to the fluid of the inner ear.
stapes.clinical: Otosclerosis fixes the footplate in the oval window and causes conductive hearing loss. It is treated by stapedotomy or stapedectomy.
articulations: Oval window of the vestibule (at the base, held by the annular ligament)
attachments: Stapedius tendon (neck)
Annular ligament (footplate rim)
stapes.ossification: It ossifies before birth and is adult size at birth.

mandible.name: Mandible
mandible.summary: The mandible is the lower jaw, the largest and strongest facial bone. It holds the lower teeth and is the only movable skull bone.
mandible.clinical: Fractures often occur at two sites because the jaw forms a ring, for example at the angle and at the opposite condylar neck or body.
articulations: Temporal bone (temporomandibular joint, via an articular disc)
Lower teeth (in alveolar sockets, a gomphosis)
attachments: Masseter (lateral ramus and angle)
Temporalis (coronoid process)
Medial pterygoid (medial angle)
Lateral pterygoid (neck of the condyle)
Mylohyoid, geniohyoid, genioglossus, and anterior digastric (inner and lower body)
Buccinator and platysma
Sphenomandibular ligament (lingula)
Stylomandibular ligament (angle)
mandible.ossification: It ossifies in membrane from one center per half before birth. The halves fuse at the symphysis in the first year of life.

maxilla.name: Maxilla
maxilla.summary: The maxilla is the upper jaw bone. It forms most of the hard palate, the floor of the orbit, and the side of the nose, and it contains the maxillary sinus.
maxilla.clinical: Le Fort fractures separate the maxilla from the rest of the skull. The roots of upper molars lie close to the maxillary sinus floor.
articulations: Frontal, nasal, lacrimal, ethmoid, and zygomatic bones
attachments: Masseter (zygomatic process)
Buccinator (alveolar process)
Orbicularis oculi and levator labii superioris alaeque nasi (frontal process)
Levator labii superioris and levator anguli oris
Nasalis and depressor septi nasi
Medial pterygoid (tuberosity)
Inferior oblique (orbital floor)
maxilla.ossification: It ossifies in membrane before birth. The maxillary sinus is tiny at birth and reaches full size after the permanent teeth erupt.

nasal-bone.name: Nasal Bone
nasal-bone.summary: The nasal bones are two small rectangular bones that form the bridge of the nose. They meet in the midline.
nasal-bone.clinical: They are the most commonly fractured facial bones because they project from the face.
attachments: Procerus (upper surface)
Nasal septal and lateral cartilages (lower edge)

nasal-septal-cartilage.name: Nasal Septal Cartilage
nasal-septal-cartilage.summary: The septal cartilage is a flat, roughly quadrangular plate that forms the front part of the nasal septum. It supports the nasal dorsum.
nasal-septal-cartilage.clinical: A deviated septum can block one side of the nose. A septal hematoma can destroy the cartilage and collapse the nasal bridge.
articulations: Perpendicular plate of the ethmoid (above and behind)
Maxilla (nasal crest and anterior nasal spine, below)
Major alar cartilages (medial crura, in front)
attachments: Perichondrium and nasal mucosa
Fibrous attachments to the surrounding bones

occipital-bone.name: Occipital Bone
occipital-bone.summary: The occipital bone forms the back and base of the skull. It surrounds the foramen magnum, where the brainstem becomes the spinal cord.
occipital-bone.clinical: Raised pressure can push the cerebellar tonsils through the foramen magnum and compress the medulla (tonsillar herniation).
attachments: Trapezius and sternocleidomastoid (nuchal lines)
Semispinalis capitis and splenius capitis
Rectus capitis posterior major and minor, obliquus capitis superior
Occipital belly of occipitofrontalis
Rectus capitis anterior and lateralis, longus capitis
Superior pharyngeal constrictor (pharyngeal tubercle)
Nuchal ligament, falx cerebri, tentorium cerebelli, tectorial membrane
occipital-bone.ossification: It forms from four parts around the foramen magnum that fuse in childhood. The basilar part fuses with the sphenoid in early adulthood.

palatine-bone.name: Palatine Bone
palatine-bone.summary: The palatine bone is an L-shaped bone behind the maxilla. It forms the back of the hard palate, part of the nasal wall, and part of the orbital floor.
palatine-bone.clinical: The greater palatine nerve emerges at the greater palatine foramen, which is the site for a palatal nerve block.
attachments: Palatine aponeurosis (posterior border of the horizontal plate)
Musculus uvulae (posterior nasal spine)
Palatopharyngeus
Medial pterygoid (pyramidal process, superficial head)

parietal-bone.name: Parietal Bone
parietal-bone.summary: The parietal bones are two curved, four-sided plates that form most of the roof and upper sides of the skull.
parietal-bone.clinical: A blow to the pterion, where the parietal, frontal, sphenoid, and temporal bones meet, can tear the middle meningeal artery and cause an epidural hematoma.
landmarks: Grooves for the middle meningeal vessels
attachments: Temporalis (inferior temporal line)
Temporal fascia (superior temporal line)
Epicranial aponeurosis
parietal-bone.ossification: It ossifies in membrane from one center at the parietal eminence. Unossified gaps (fontanelles) close within the first two years.

sinus-of-frontal-bone.name: Frontal Sinus
sinus-of-frontal-bone.summary: The frontal sinuses are air-filled cavities in the frontal bone above the eyebrows. They are usually paired and drain into the nose through the frontonasal duct.
sinus-of-frontal-bone.clinical: Frontal sinusitis causes pain and tenderness above the eyebrow. Infection can spread to the orbit or the anterior cranial fossa.
sinus-of-frontal-bone.bone_type: Air-filled cavity within the frontal bone
articulations: Nasal cavity (through the frontonasal duct to the middle meatus)
landmarks: Septum between right and left sinuses
attachments: Lined by respiratory mucosa
sinus-of-frontal-bone.ossification: It is absent at birth, appears in early childhood, and grows until after puberty.

sinus-of-sphenoid-bone.name: Sphenoid Sinus
sinus-of-sphenoid-bone.summary: The sphenoid sinuses are air-filled cavities in the body of the sphenoid bone. They open into the sphenoethmoidal recess of the nasal cavity.
sinus-of-sphenoid-bone.clinical: The pituitary gland lies just above this sinus, so surgeons remove pituitary tumors through the nose and sphenoid sinus.
sinus-of-sphenoid-bone.bone_type: Air-filled cavity within the sphenoid bone
landmarks: Septum between right and left sinuses
Relations: sella turcica, cavernous sinus, optic canal
attachments: Lined by respiratory mucosa
sinus-of-sphenoid-bone.ossification: It is small at birth and enlarges through childhood and adolescence.

sphenoid-bone.name: Sphenoid Bone
sphenoid-bone.summary: The sphenoid is a bat-shaped bone in the middle of the skull base. It links the cranial and facial bones and holds the pituitary gland.
sphenoid-bone.clinical: A pituitary tumor in the sella turcica can compress the optic chiasm and cause loss of the outer visual fields (bitemporal hemianopia).
landmarks: Body with sella turcica and sphenoid sinuses
Lesser wings and anterior clinoid processes
Pterygoid processes (medial and lateral plates, hamulus)
attachments: Lateral and medial pterygoid (pterygoid plates, greater wing)
Temporalis (infratemporal surface of the greater wing)
Tensor veli palatini (scaphoid fossa and spine)
Superior pharyngeal constrictor (medial plate and hamulus)
Extraocular muscles (common tendinous ring and wings)
Tentorium cerebelli and diaphragma sellae
Sphenomandibular ligament (spine)
sphenoid-bone.ossification: It forms from several centers that fuse before and shortly after birth. The basilar part of the occipital bone fuses to the body in early adulthood.

temporal-bone.name: Temporal Bone
temporal-bone.summary: The temporal bone forms part of the side and base of the skull. It houses the middle and inner ear, the facial canal, and the carotid canal.
temporal-bone.clinical: Fractures of the petrous part can injure the facial nerve or the inner ear. Middle ear infection can spread into the mastoid air cells (mastoiditis).
landmarks: Mastoid process and mastoid air cells
attachments: Sternocleidomastoid, splenius capitis, and longissimus capitis (mastoid process)
Posterior digastric (mastoid notch)
Stylohyoid, styloglossus, and stylopharyngeus (styloid process)
Temporalis (temporal fossa)
Masseter (zygomatic arch)
Levator veli palatini (petrous apex)
Tentorium cerebelli (petrous ridge)
Stylohyoid and stylomandibular ligaments
temporal-bone.ossification: It forms from squamous, petromastoid, and tympanic parts that fuse around birth. The mastoid process develops in the second year.

vomer.name: Vomer
vomer.summary: The vomer is a thin, flat midline bone that forms the lower and back part of the bony nasal septum. It separates the two choanae.
vomer.clinical: A deviated septum often involves the vomer and the septal cartilage. The nasopalatine nerve runs in a groove on its surface.
landmarks: Groove for the nasopalatine nerve and vessels
Anterior border groove for the septal cartilage
attachments: Nasal septal cartilage (anterior border)
Nasal mucous membrane covers both sides

zygomatic-bone.name: Zygomatic Bone
zygomatic-bone.summary: The zygomatic bone forms the prominence of the cheek and part of the lateral wall and floor of the orbit. It joins the zygomatic arch.
zygomatic-bone.clinical: Tripod (zygomaticomaxillary complex) fractures flatten the cheek and can cause numbness below the eye (infraorbital nerve), double vision, or trouble opening the mouth.
articulations: Temporal bone (temporal process, forming the zygomatic arch)
attachments: Masseter (lower border and arch)
Zygomaticus major and minor
Temporal fascia (upper border)
Lateral palpebral ligament (orbital tubercle)
Lateral check ligament of the lateral rectus

upper-medial-incisor.name: Upper Central Incisor
upper-medial-incisor.summary: The upper central incisor is the widest front tooth. It has a chisel-shaped crown for cutting and one long root. The anterior superior alveolar nerve supplies it.
upper-medial-incisor.clinical: It is the front tooth most often broken by a blow to the mouth. A knocked-out tooth may be replanted if kept moist.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
Opposes the lower incisors in biting
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-medial-incisor.ossification: Erupts at about 7 to 8 years. Eruption times vary between people.

upper-lateral-incisor.name: Upper Lateral Incisor
upper-lateral-incisor.summary: The upper lateral incisor is smaller than the central incisor and lies beside it. It has one root and is supplied by the anterior superior alveolar nerve.
upper-lateral-incisor.clinical: Its crown is often small and peg-shaped, and the tooth is sometimes missing from birth.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-lateral-incisor.ossification: Erupts at about 8 to 9 years. Eruption times vary between people.

upper-canine.name: Upper Canine
upper-canine.summary: The upper canine has a single pointed cusp and the longest root of any tooth. It tears food and guides the jaw during sideways movement.
upper-canine.clinical: The upper canine is the most commonly impacted tooth after the third molar. Its long root makes extraction difficult.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-canine.ossification: Erupts at about 11 to 12 years. Eruption times vary between people.

upper-first-premolar.name: Upper First Premolar
upper-first-premolar.summary: The upper first premolar has a buccal and a palatal cusp for crushing food. It usually has two roots and is supplied by the middle superior alveolar nerve.
upper-first-premolar.clinical: Its two thin roots can fracture during extraction. Premolars are often removed to relieve crowding in orthodontic treatment.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-first-premolar.ossification: Erupts at about 10 to 11 years. Eruption times vary between people.

upper-second-premolar.name: Upper Second Premolar
upper-second-premolar.summary: The upper second premolar has a buccal and a palatal cusp, similar to the first premolar. It usually has a single root.
upper-second-premolar.clinical: The root tip can lie close to the floor of the maxillary sinus. Extraction or infection there may involve the sinus.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-second-premolar.ossification: Erupts at about 10 to 12 years. Eruption times vary between people.

upper-first-molar-tooth.name: Upper First Molar
upper-first-molar-tooth.summary: The upper first molar is the largest upper tooth. It has four main cusps and usually three roots. The posterior superior alveolar nerve mainly supplies it.
upper-first-molar-tooth.clinical: Its roots lie very close to the maxillary sinus floor, so extraction can open a connection between the mouth and the sinus.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
landmarks: Four main cusps (mesiobuccal, distobuccal, mesiopalatal, distopalatal)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-first-molar-tooth.ossification: Erupts at about 6 to 7 years, before any baby tooth is lost. Eruption times vary between people.

upper-second-molar-tooth.name: Upper Second Molar
upper-second-molar-tooth.summary: The upper second molar resembles the first but is slightly smaller. It usually has four cusps and three roots, which may be fused.
upper-second-molar-tooth.clinical: The parotid duct opens into the mouth on the cheek lining opposite this tooth.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the maxilla (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
landmarks: Four cusps (the distopalatal cusp is often small)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
upper-second-molar-tooth.ossification: Erupts at about 12 to 13 years. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-medial-incisor.name: Lower Central Incisor
lower-medial-incisor.summary: The lower central incisor is the smallest tooth. It has a narrow chisel-shaped crown and one flattened root. The inferior alveolar nerve supplies it.
lower-medial-incisor.clinical: Plaque and tartar often build up on its tongue side, near the openings of the salivary ducts.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
landmarks: Narrow crown with an incisal edge
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-medial-incisor.ossification: Erupts at about 6 to 7 years. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-lateral-incisor.name: Lower Lateral Incisor
lower-lateral-incisor.summary: The lower lateral incisor is slightly larger than the lower central incisor. It has one flattened root and a chisel-shaped crown.
lower-lateral-incisor.clinical: Crowding of the lower front teeth often involves this tooth, which may be tilted or rotated.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-lateral-incisor.ossification: Erupts at about 7 to 8 years. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-canine.name: Lower Canine
lower-canine.summary: The lower canine has a single pointed cusp and one long root. It is narrower than the upper canine.
lower-canine.clinical: Along with the upper canine, it guides the jaw during sideways movement. Its root sometimes has a fork at the tip.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-canine.ossification: Erupts at about 9 to 10 years. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-first-premolar.name: Lower First Premolar
lower-first-premolar.summary: The lower first premolar has a large buccal cusp and a small lingual cusp. It has one root and is supplied by the inferior alveolar nerve.
lower-first-premolar.clinical: The mental foramen lies near its root. First premolars are often extracted to relieve crowding in orthodontic treatment.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-first-premolar.ossification: Erupts at about 10 to 12 years. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-second-premolar.name: Lower Second Premolar
lower-second-premolar.summary: The lower second premolar has a buccal cusp and one or two lingual cusps. It has one root.
lower-second-premolar.clinical: It is the most common permanent tooth to be missing from birth, apart from the third molars. The mental foramen lies close to its root.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-second-premolar.ossification: Erupts at about 11 to 12 years. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-first-molar-tooth.name: Lower First Molar
lower-first-molar-tooth.summary: The lower first molar is the largest lower tooth. It usually has five cusps and two roots, one in front and one behind.
lower-first-molar-tooth.clinical: It is the first permanent tooth to appear, around age 6, and is among the teeth most often affected by decay.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
landmarks: Five cusps (mesiobuccal, distobuccal, distal, mesiolingual, distolingual)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-first-molar-tooth.ossification: Erupts at about 6 to 7 years, behind the last baby tooth. Eruption times vary between people.

lower-second-molar-tooth.name: Lower Second Molar
lower-second-molar-tooth.summary: The lower second molar is slightly smaller than the first. It usually has four cusps and two roots.
lower-second-molar-tooth.clinical: Its roots lie close to the inferior alveolar canal, so extraction or implant work here can injure the inferior alveolar nerve.
articulations: Alveolar socket of the mandible (a gomphosis, held by the periodontal ligament)
landmarks: Two roots (mesial and distal, sometimes fused)
attachments: Periodontal ligament to the alveolar bone
Gingiva around the neck
lower-second-molar-tooth.ossification: Erupts at about 11 to 13 years. Eruption times vary between people.

vertebra-c3.name: Vertebra C3
vertebra-c3.summary: C3 is a typical cervical vertebra. It lies at about the level of the hyoid bone.
vertebra-c3.clinical: A spinal cord injury at or above C3 usually stops breathing, because the phrenic nerve arises from C3 to C5.
articulations: C2 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
C4 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Small, wide body with uncinate processes
Superior facets face upward and backward
attachments: Levator scapulae and splenius cervicis (transverse process)
Anterior and middle scalene
Longus capitis and longus colli
Semispinalis cervicis and nuchal ligament (spinous process)
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-c3.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-c4.name: Vertebra C4
vertebra-c4.summary: C4 is a typical cervical vertebra. It lies at about the level of the upper border of the thyroid cartilage.
vertebra-c4.clinical: The common carotid artery divides near this level. Plaque at the bifurcation is a common cause of stroke.
articulations: C3 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
C5 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Small, wide body with uncinate processes
Superior facets face upward and backward
attachments: Levator scapulae (transverse process)
Anterior and middle scalene
Longus capitis and longus colli
Semispinalis cervicis and nuchal ligament (spinous process)
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-c4.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

vertebra-c5.name: Vertebra C5
vertebra-c5.summary: C5 is a typical cervical vertebra with a short, usually bifid spinous process. The C5 nerve root passes just above it.
vertebra-c5.clinical: C5 root injury weakens shoulder abduction and elbow flexion (deltoid and biceps). Disc disease at C4-C5 can compress it.
articulations: C4 above (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
C6 below (intervertebral disc and paired zygapophysial (facet) joints)
landmarks: Small, wide body with uncinate processes
Superior facets face upward and backward
attachments: Anterior, middle, and posterior scalene
Longus capitis and longus colli
Semispinalis cervicis and nuchal ligament (spinous process)
Anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments
vertebra-c5.ossification: Three primary centers (body and two halves of the arch) form before birth. Five secondary centers appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.

femur.name: Femur
femur.summary: The femur is the thigh bone. It is the longest, heaviest, and strongest bone in the body.
femur.clinical: Femoral neck fractures can cut off blood supply to the head and cause avascular necrosis.
attachments: Gluteus medius and minimus: greater trochanter
Iliopsoas: lesser trochanter
Gluteus maximus: gluteal tuberosity
Adductor muscles: linea aspera and adductor tubercle
Vastus muscles: shaft
Collateral ligaments: epicondyles
Cruciate ligaments: intercondylar fossa walls
femur.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 7. The distal epiphysis appears near birth and the head within the first year. Growth plates close by about age 18 to 20.

patella.name: Patella
patella.summary: The patella is the kneecap. It is the largest sesamoid bone and sits within the quadriceps tendon.
patella.clinical: Patellar dislocation usually occurs laterally, and patellofemoral pain is a common cause of anterior knee pain.
articulations: Patellar surface of the femur (patellofemoral joint)
attachments: Quadriceps tendon: base and anterior surface
Patellar ligament: apex
Medial and lateral patellar retinacula: sides
patella.ossification: Ossifies from one or more centers between about ages 3 and 6. A bipartite patella is a common variant.

tibia.name: Tibia
tibia.summary: The tibia is the shinbone. It lies medially in the leg and carries almost all the body weight transmitted through the leg.
tibia.clinical: Its anterior border lies just under the skin, so tibial fractures are often open. Compartment syndrome can follow injury.
attachments: Patellar ligament: tibial tuberosity
Sartorius, gracilis, semitendinosus (pes anserinus): proximal medial surface
Iliotibial tract: Gerdy tubercle
Cruciate ligaments: intercondylar area
Soleus: soleal line
Deltoid ligament: medial malleolus
Interosseous membrane: interosseous border
tibia.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 7. The proximal epiphysis appears near birth and the distal epiphysis in the first year. Fusion occurs by about age 16 to 20.

fibula.name: Fibula
fibula.summary: The fibula is the slender lateral bone of the leg. It carries little weight but anchors muscles and forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise.
fibula.clinical: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck, so injury there can cause foot drop. Ankle fractures often involve the lateral malleolus.
attachments: Biceps femoris tendon and fibular collateral ligament: head
Fibularis longus and brevis: lateral shaft
Extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus: anterior shaft
Soleus, tibialis posterior, flexor hallucis longus: posterior shaft
Lateral ankle ligaments: lateral malleolus
Interosseous membrane: interosseous border
fibula.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 8. The distal epiphysis appears about age 2 and the proximal about age 4. Fusion occurs by about age 15 to 20.

calcaneus.name: Calcaneus
calcaneus.summary: The calcaneus is the heel bone. It is the largest tarsal bone and bears the first load of body weight at heel strike.
calcaneus.clinical: It is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone, usually after a fall from a height. Plantar fasciitis causes heel pain at its underside.
landmarks: Medial and lateral processes of the tuberosity
attachments: Calcaneal (Achilles) tendon: posterior surface
Plantar aponeurosis, flexor digitorum brevis, abductor hallucis: medial process
Abductor digiti minimi: lateral process
Spring ligament: sustentaculum tali
Long and short plantar ligaments: plantar surface
Extensor digitorum brevis: dorsolateral surface
Interosseous talocalcaneal ligament: sinus tarsi
calcaneus.ossification: Primary center appears in fetal month 3 to 4. A secondary center at the tuberosity appears about age 6 to 10 and fuses by about 15.

talus.name: Talus
talus.summary: The talus links the leg to the foot. It sits between the tibia and fibula above and the calcaneus and navicular below. No muscles attach to it.
talus.clinical: Its blood supply enters mainly through the neck and runs backward, so talar neck fractures risk avascular necrosis of the body.
landmarks: Posterior process with groove for flexor hallucis longus
attachments: No muscle attachments
Deltoid ligament: medial side
Anterior and posterior talofibular ligaments: lateral side
Interosseous talocalcaneal ligament: inferior surface
Joint capsules
talus.ossification: Primary center appears in fetal month 6 to 7. A separate os trigonum behind the posterior process is a common variant.

navicular-bone.name: Navicular Bone
navicular-bone.summary: The navicular is a boat-shaped tarsal bone on the medial side of the foot. It lies between the talar head and the three cuneiforms.
navicular-bone.clinical: An accessory navicular can cause medial foot pain. Navicular stress fractures occur in athletes because the central bone has a limited blood supply.
landmarks: Three distal facets for the cuneiforms
attachments: Tibialis posterior tendon: tuberosity
Spring ligament: plantar surface
Deltoid ligament (tibionavicular part): medial side
navicular-bone.ossification: Begins to ossify at about age 3 (range 1 to 5), later than other tarsal bones.

cuboid-bone.name: Cuboid Bone
cuboid-bone.summary: The cuboid is a tarsal bone on the lateral side of the foot. It supports the lateral longitudinal arch.
cuboid-bone.clinical: Cuboid syndrome, a mild subluxation, causes lateral foot pain. A nutcracker fracture can occur when the cuboid is crushed between adjacent bones.
attachments: Fibularis longus tendon: runs in the plantar groove
Long and short plantar ligaments: plantar surface
Tibialis posterior tendon slip
Flexor hallucis brevis: part of origin
cuboid-bone.ossification: Usually begins to ossify around the time of birth.

medial-cuneiform-bone.name: Medial Cuneiform Bone
medial-cuneiform-bone.summary: The medial cuneiform is the largest of the three cuneiforms. It lies on the medial side of the midfoot, in front of the navicular.
medial-cuneiform-bone.clinical: The Lisfranc ligament runs from this bone to the base of the second metatarsal. Midfoot injuries often tear it.
landmarks: Wedge shape with the base directed downward
Facets for the first metatarsal and navicular
attachments: Tibialis anterior: medial and plantar surface
Fibularis longus: plantar surface
Tibialis posterior tendon slip
Lisfranc ligament: to second metatarsal base
medial-cuneiform-bone.ossification: Begins to ossify at about age 2.

intermediate-cuneiform-bone.name: Intermediate Cuneiform Bone
intermediate-cuneiform-bone.summary: The intermediate cuneiform is the smallest cuneiform. It sits between the other two and forms the keystone of the transverse arch.
intermediate-cuneiform-bone.clinical: Its recessed position helps lock the second metatarsal base in place. Midfoot injuries often involve this region.
landmarks: Wedge shape with the base directed upward
attachments: Tibialis posterior tendon slip
Interosseous cuneometatarsal and intercuneiform ligaments
Dorsal and plantar ligaments
intermediate-cuneiform-bone.ossification: Begins to ossify at about age 3.

lateral-cuneiform-bone.name: Lateral Cuneiform Bone
lateral-cuneiform-bone.summary: The lateral cuneiform is the middle-sized cuneiform. It lies between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, in front of the navicular.
lateral-cuneiform-bone.clinical: It forms part of the Lisfranc joint line. Midfoot fractures and dislocations often involve it.
landmarks: Wedge shape with the base directed upward
attachments: Tibialis posterior tendon slip
Flexor hallucis brevis: part of origin
Intercuneiform and cuneocuboid ligaments
lateral-cuneiform-bone.ossification: Begins to ossify at about age 1.

first-metatarsal-bone.name: First Metatarsal Bone
first-metatarsal-bone.summary: The first metatarsal is the shortest and thickest metatarsal. It supports the great toe and bears much of the weight in push-off.
first-metatarsal-bone.clinical: Hallux valgus (bunion) involves the first metatarsal drifting medially. Gout often affects the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the great toe
Two sesamoid bones (plantar surface of head)
attachments: Tibialis anterior: medial base
Fibularis longus: lateral base
First dorsal interosseous: origin
first-metatarsal-bone.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 9. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.

second-metatarsal-bone.name: Second Metatarsal Bone
second-metatarsal-bone.summary: The second metatarsal is the longest metatarsal. Its base is wedged into a recess between the cuneiforms.
second-metatarsal-bone.clinical: It is the longest metatarsal and a common site of stress (march) fractures. Its locked base makes it central to Lisfranc injuries.
articulations: All three cuneiforms (base is recessed between the medial and lateral cuneiforms)
Proximal phalanx of the second toe
attachments: Tibialis posterior tendon slip: base
Lisfranc ligament: base, from medial cuneiform
First and second dorsal interossei: origin
Adductor hallucis (oblique head): origin
second-metatarsal-bone.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 9. A secondary center at the head appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.

third-metatarsal-bone.name: Third Metatarsal Bone
third-metatarsal-bone.summary: The third metatarsal articulates with the lateral cuneiform. It is a central weight-bearing ray of the forefoot.
third-metatarsal-bone.clinical: Morton neuroma usually forms in the space between the third and fourth metatarsal heads. Stress fractures can also occur.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the third toe
attachments: Tibialis posterior tendon slip: base
Adductor hallucis (oblique head): origin
Dorsal and plantar interossei: origin
third-metatarsal-bone.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 9. A secondary center at the head appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.

fourth-metatarsal-bone.name: Fourth Metatarsal Bone
fourth-metatarsal-bone.summary: The fourth metatarsal articulates mainly with the cuboid. It lies between the third and fifth metatarsals.
fourth-metatarsal-bone.clinical: Its head lies beside the third interspace, where Morton neuroma commonly develops. Stress fractures are less common than in the second.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the fourth toe
attachments: Tibialis posterior tendon slip: base
Adductor hallucis (oblique head): origin
Dorsal and plantar interossei: origin
fourth-metatarsal-bone.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 9. A secondary center at the head appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.

fifth-metatarsal-bone.name: Fifth Metatarsal Bone
fifth-metatarsal-bone.summary: The fifth metatarsal forms the lateral border of the foot. Its base has a prominent tuberosity that can be felt under the skin.
fifth-metatarsal-bone.clinical: Avulsion fractures of the tuberosity are common after ankle inversion. A Jones fracture lies slightly farther along the proximal shaft and heals poorly.
articulations: Proximal phalanx of the fifth toe
landmarks: Tuberosity of the fifth metatarsal (lateral base)
attachments: Fibularis brevis: tuberosity
Fibularis tertius: dorsal base and shaft
Plantar aponeurosis lateral band: tuberosity
Abductor digiti minimi: origin
Plantar interosseous and flexor digiti minimi brevis: origin
fifth-metatarsal-bone.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal week 9. A secondary center at the head appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.

proximal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.name: Proximal Phalanx of Great Toe
proximal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal months 3 to 4. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.summary: The proximal phalanx of the great toe is short and broad. It forms the first metatarsophalangeal joint with the first metatarsal.
proximal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.clinical: The first metatarsophalangeal joint is often affected by gout, hallux rigidus, and bunion deformity.
articulations: First metatarsal head and sesamoids (metatarsophalangeal joint)
attachments: Abductor hallucis and medial head of flexor hallucis brevis: medial base
Adductor hallucis and lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis: lateral base
Extensor hallucis brevis: dorsal base

distal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.name: Distal Phalanx of Great Toe
distal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal weeks 8 to 10, earlier than the other phalanges. A secondary center at the base fuses by about age 18.
distal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.summary: The distal phalanx of the great toe is broad and strong. It supports the nail and the pad of the toe.
distal-phalanx-of-first-finger-of-foot.clinical: Ingrown toenails most often affect the great toe. Subungual hematoma follows crushing injuries.
attachments: Flexor hallucis longus: plantar base
Extensor hallucis longus: dorsal base

proximal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foo.name: Proximal Phalanx of Second Toe
proximal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foo.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal months 3 to 4. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foo.summary: The proximal phalanx of the second toe is the longest bone of that toe. It joins the metatarsal head and the middle phalanx.
proximal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foo.clinical: The second toe is the most common site of hammer toe deformity.
articulations: Head of the second metatarsal (metatarsophalangeal joint)
attachments: First dorsal interosseous: medial base
Second dorsal interosseous: lateral base
Lumbrical and extensor expansion

distal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.name: Distal Phalanx of Second Toe
distal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal weeks 8 to 10, earlier than the other phalanges. A secondary center at the base fuses by about age 18.
distal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.summary: The distal phalanx of the second toe is the small end bone of the toe. It supports the nail and the toe pad.
distal-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.clinical: Mallet toe bends the distal interphalangeal joint. Stubbing injuries can fracture this bone or cause subungual hematoma.
attachments: Flexor digitorum longus: plantar base
Extensor expansion (extensor digitorum longus and brevis): dorsal base

middle-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.name: Middle Phalanx of Second Toe
middle-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in the late fetal period. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
middle-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.summary: The middle phalanx of the second toe is a short bone between the proximal and distal phalanges. The great toe has no middle phalanx.
middle-phalanx-of-second-finger-of-foot.clinical: Hammer toe bends the proximal interphalangeal joint of this toe.
attachments: Flexor digitorum brevis: sides of the shaft
Extensor expansion (central slip): dorsal base

proximal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.name: Proximal Phalanx of Third Toe
proximal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal months 3 to 4. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.summary: The proximal phalanx of the third toe is the longest bone of that toe. It joins the metatarsal head and the middle phalanx.
proximal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.clinical: Toe deformities such as claw toe can involve this phalanx.
articulations: Head of the third metatarsal (metatarsophalangeal joint)
attachments: Third dorsal interosseous: lateral base
First plantar interosseous: medial base
Lumbrical and extensor expansion

distal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.name: Distal Phalanx of Third Toe
distal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal weeks 8 to 10, earlier than the other phalanges. A secondary center at the base fuses by about age 18.
distal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.summary: The distal phalanx of the third toe is the small end bone of the toe. It supports the nail and the toe pad.
distal-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.clinical: Mallet toe bends the distal interphalangeal joint. Stubbing injuries can fracture this bone or cause subungual hematoma.
attachments: Flexor digitorum longus: plantar base
Extensor expansion (extensor digitorum longus and brevis): dorsal base

middle-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.name: Middle Phalanx of Third Toe
middle-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in the late fetal period. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
middle-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.summary: The middle phalanx of the third toe is a short bone between the proximal and distal phalanges. The great toe has no middle phalanx.
middle-phalanx-of-third-finger-of-foot.clinical: Hammer or claw toe deformities can affect this joint.
attachments: Flexor digitorum brevis: sides of the shaft
Extensor expansion (central slip): dorsal base

proximal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foo.name: Proximal Phalanx of Fourth Toe
proximal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foo.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal months 3 to 4. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foo.summary: The proximal phalanx of the fourth toe is the longest bone of that toe. It joins the metatarsal head and the middle phalanx.
proximal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foo.clinical: This phalanx can be injured when the toe is stubbed.
articulations: Head of the fourth metatarsal (metatarsophalangeal joint)
attachments: Fourth dorsal interosseous: lateral base
Second plantar interosseous: medial base
Lumbrical and extensor expansion

distal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.name: Distal Phalanx of Fourth Toe
distal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal weeks 8 to 10, earlier than the other phalanges. A secondary center at the base fuses by about age 18.
distal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.summary: The distal phalanx of the fourth toe is the small end bone of the toe. It supports the nail and the toe pad.
distal-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.clinical: Mallet toe bends the distal interphalangeal joint. Stubbing injuries can fracture this bone or cause subungual hematoma.
attachments: Flexor digitorum longus: plantar base
Extensor expansion (extensor digitorum longus and brevis): dorsal base

middle-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.name: Middle Phalanx of Fourth Toe
middle-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in the late fetal period. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
middle-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.summary: The middle phalanx of the fourth toe is a short bone between the proximal and distal phalanges. The great toe has no middle phalanx.
middle-phalanx-of-fourth-finger-of-foot.clinical: Hammer or claw toe deformities can affect this joint.
attachments: Flexor digitorum brevis: sides of the shaft
Extensor expansion (central slip): dorsal base

proximal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.name: Proximal Phalanx of Little Toe
proximal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal months 3 to 4. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
proximal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.summary: The proximal phalanx of the little toe is the longest bone of that toe. It joins the metatarsal head and the middle phalanx.
proximal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.clinical: The fifth toe is the most often broken toe, usually by stubbing.
articulations: Head of the fifth metatarsal (metatarsophalangeal joint)
attachments: Third plantar interosseous: medial base
Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi brevis: lateral base
Lumbrical and extensor expansion

distal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.name: Distal Phalanx of Little Toe
distal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in fetal weeks 8 to 10, earlier than the other phalanges. A secondary center at the base fuses by about age 18.
distal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.summary: The distal phalanx of the little toe is the small end bone of the toe. It supports the nail and the toe pad.
distal-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.clinical: Mallet toe bends the distal interphalangeal joint. Stubbing injuries can fracture this bone or cause subungual hematoma.
attachments: Flexor digitorum longus: plantar base
Extensor expansion (extensor digitorum longus and brevis): dorsal base

middle-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.name: Middle Phalanx of Little Toe
middle-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.ossification: Shaft begins in the late fetal period. A secondary center at the base appears in early childhood and fuses by about age 18.
middle-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.summary: The middle phalanx of the little toe is a short bone between the proximal and distal phalanges. The great toe has no middle phalanx.
middle-phalanx-of-fifth-finger-of-foot.clinical: This phalanx is often very small and may fuse with the distal phalanx.
attachments: Flexor digitorum brevis: sides of the shaft
Extensor expansion (central slip): dorsal base

sesamoid-bones-of-foot.name: Sesamoid Bones of the Foot
sesamoid-bones-of-foot.summary: Two small sesamoid bones lie in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons under the head of the first metatarsal. Other sesamoids may occur in the foot.
sesamoid-bones-of-foot.clinical: Sesamoiditis and fractures cause pain under the ball of the foot. The medial sesamoid is injured more often and is often bipartite.
articulations: Plantar grooves on the first metatarsal head (medial and lateral)
landmarks: Groove between them for flexor hallucis longus
attachments: Flexor hallucis brevis tendons
Abductor hallucis: medial sesamoid
Adductor hallucis: lateral sesamoid
Plantar plate and intersesamoid ligament
sesamoid-bones-of-foot.ossification: Ossify from one or more centers between about ages 7 and 11, earlier in girls.

tenth-rib.name: Tenth Rib
tenth-rib.summary: The tenth rib is a false rib. Its cartilage joins the cartilage above, and its head has a single facet for the tenth thoracic vertebra.
tenth-rib.clinical: Slipping rib syndrome can involve the lower false ribs, where loose cartilage attachments cause sharp lower chest pain.
attachments: External oblique: outer surface
Internal oblique: lower border
Transversus abdominis: costal cartilage
Diaphragm: inner surface
Serratus posterior inferior and latissimus dorsi: outer surface
Iliocostalis and intercostal muscles
tenth-rib.ossification: Primary center in the shaft at about fetal week 8 to 10. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear around puberty and fuse by about age 25.

eleventh-rib.name: Eleventh Rib
eleventh-rib.summary: The eleventh rib is a short floating rib. It has no neck or tubercle and does not reach the sternum or the costal margin.
eleventh-rib.clinical: Because it lies behind the lower pleura and kidney region, flank injuries can involve the pleura and kidney.
attachments: External and internal oblique: outer surface and lower border
Serratus posterior inferior and latissimus dorsi: outer surface
Diaphragm: inner surface
Intercostal muscles
Iliocostalis lumborum
eleventh-rib.ossification: Primary center in the shaft at about fetal week 8 to 10. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear around puberty and fuse by about age 25.

twelfth-rib.name: Twelfth Rib
twelfth-rib.summary: The twelfth rib is the shortest and lowest floating rib. It has no neck, tubercle, or costal groove, and its end is free in the flank.
twelfth-rib.clinical: The pleura reaches below it posteriorly, so flank incisions near this rib risk pneumothorax. The subcostal nerve runs beneath it.
attachments: Quadratus lumborum: lower medial border
Diaphragm: inner surface and lateral arcuate ligament
Latissimus dorsi, external oblique, serratus posterior inferior
Lumbocostal ligament and iliocostalis lumborum
twelfth-rib.ossification: Primary center in the shaft at about fetal week 8 to 10. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear around puberty and fuse by about age 25.

costal-cartilage-of-8th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of the 8th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-8th-rib.summary: The eighth costal cartilage is a false rib cartilage. It does not reach the sternum but joins the cartilage above.
costal-cartilage-of-8th-rib.clinical: Slipping rib syndrome involves hypermobile false rib cartilages such as this one, causing pain and clicking.
articulations: Ninth costal cartilage (interchondral joint or fibrous band)
attachments: External and internal oblique: costal margin
Transversus abdominis and diaphragm: inner surface
Rectus abdominis sheath and fascia near the margin

costal-cartilage-of-9th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of the 9th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-9th-rib.summary: The ninth costal cartilage is a false rib cartilage. It joins the eighth cartilage and forms part of the costal margin.
costal-cartilage-of-9th-rib.clinical: Slipping rib syndrome can involve this cartilage, and the costal margin is a landmark for subcostal incisions.
attachments: External and internal oblique: costal margin
Transversus abdominis and diaphragm: inner surface

costal-cartilage-of-10th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of the 10th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-10th-rib.summary: The tenth costal cartilage is the last cartilage to join the costal margin. It attaches to the ninth cartilage above.
costal-cartilage-of-10th-rib.clinical: Its attachment is loose in some people, which contributes to slipping rib syndrome. Cartilage calcifies with age.
attachments: External and internal oblique: costal margin
Transversus abdominis and diaphragm: inner surface

hip-bone.name: Hip Bone
hip-bone.summary: The hip bone is formed by the ilium, ischium, and pubis. It joins the sacrum behind and the other hip bone in front.
hip-bone.clinical: Pelvic fractures can cause major bleeding. Avulsion fractures of the apophyses are common in adolescent athletes.
landmarks: Anterior and posterior superior iliac spines
Anterior and posterior inferior iliac spines
attachments: Abdominal wall muscles: iliac crest
Sartorius: anterior superior iliac spine
Rectus femoris: anterior inferior iliac spine
Gluteal muscles: outer ilium
Hamstrings: ischial tuberosity
Iliacus: iliac fossa
Inguinal ligament: anterior superior iliac spine to pubic tubercle
hip-bone.ossification: Three primary centers (ilium, ischium, pubis) meet at the Y-shaped triradiate cartilage in the acetabulum. They fuse by about age 15 to 17.

manubrium-of-sternum.name: Manubrium of Sternum
manubrium-of-sternum.summary: The broad, upper part of the sternum. It joins the clavicles, the first ribs, and the body of the sternum.
articulations: 2nd costal cartilage (upper half of its notch)
Body of sternum at the manubriosternal joint
landmarks: Jugular (suprasternal) notch, at about the T2-T3 level
Costal notch for the 1st costal cartilage
Sternal angle where it meets the body, at about the T4-T5 disc level
attachments: Sternocleidomastoid (sternal head)
Sternohyoid
Sternothyroid
Pectoralis major (upper fibres)
Interclavicular ligament (at the jugular notch)
manubrium-of-sternum.ossification: Ossifies from one or two centers in the fetus. It usually stays separate from the body until late adult life.
manubrium-of-sternum.clinical: The sternal angle marks the 2nd rib, the tracheal bifurcation, and the start and end of the aortic arch.

body-of-sternum.name: Body of Sternum
body-of-sternum.summary: The long, flat middle part of the sternum. The 2nd to 7th costal cartilages attach along its edges.
articulations: Xiphoid process at the xiphisternal joint
2nd to 7th costal cartilages at the costal notches
landmarks: Costal notches along both lateral borders
Transverse ridges marking the fused sternebrae
Sternal angle at its upper end
Lies at about the T5-T9 vertebral levels
attachments: Pectoralis major (sternocostal head)
Transversus thoracis (inner surface)
Sternopericardial ligaments
Aponeurosis of the external oblique and rectus sheath (lower part)
body-of-sternum.ossification: Forms from four sternebrae with centers appearing from the fifth fetal month to the first year. They fuse from puberty to about age 25.
body-of-sternum.clinical: Surgeons split the body in a median sternotomy for heart surgery. CPR compressions are given over its lower half.

xiphoid-process.name: Xiphoid Process
xiphoid-process.summary: The small, pointed lower end of the sternum. It is cartilage in youth and slowly ossifies in adults.
articulations: Body of sternum at the xiphisternal joint, at about the T9 level
landmarks: Tip felt in the epigastrium at the infrasternal angle
Shape varies and may be bifid or perforated
attachments: Rectus abdominis
Linea alba
Diaphragm (sternal part)
Transversus thoracis (lowest fibres)
xiphoid-process.ossification: Stays cartilage in youth. It usually ossifies after about age 40 and may fuse with the body.
xiphoid-process.clinical: Pressing on the tip during CPR can injure the liver. A prominent xiphoid is often mistaken for an abdominal mass.

cricoid-cartilage.name: Cricoid Cartilage
cricoid-cartilage.summary: A signet-ring-shaped cartilage at the base of the larynx. It is the only complete ring of cartilage around the airway.
articulations: Inferior horns of the thyroid cartilage at the cricothyroid joints
Arytenoid cartilages at the cricoarytenoid joints
First tracheal ring through the cricotracheal ligament
landmarks: Facets for the thyroid inferior horn and the arytenoid cartilage
Lies at about the C6 vertebral level
attachments: Cricothyroid ligament (upper border of the arch)
Cricothyroid muscle (outer arch)
Posterior cricoarytenoid (back of lamina)
Lateral cricoarytenoid (upper arch)
Inferior pharyngeal constrictor
Cricotracheal ligament
cricoid-cartilage.ossification: Hyaline cartilage that may ossify gradually in adult life.
cricoid-cartilage.clinical: An emergency cricothyrotomy is cut through the cricothyroid ligament just above the arch. Narrowing below the vocal folds can occur after long intubation.

costal-cartilage-of-1st-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 1st Rib
costal-cartilage-of-1st-rib.summary: The shortest costal cartilage. It joins the first rib directly to the manubrium with almost no movement.
landmarks: Lies just below the medial end of the clavicle
attachments: Subclavius (from the rib-cartilage junction)
Costoclavicular ligament
First intercostal muscles
costal-cartilage-of-1st-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-1st-rib.clinical: It often calcifies early in adult life and can look like a lesion on chest imaging.

costal-cartilage-of-2nd-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 2nd Rib
costal-cartilage-of-2nd-rib.summary: Connects the second rib to the sternum at the sternal angle. This joint is the usual starting point for counting ribs.
articulations: Manubrium and body of sternum at the sternal angle (synovial joint)
landmarks: Meets the sternum at the sternal angle
Lies at the level of the T4-T5 disc
attachments: Intercostal muscles
Pectoralis major (sternocostal head)
Transversus thoracis
costal-cartilage-of-2nd-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-2nd-rib.clinical: Tietze syndrome causes painful swelling here, most often at the 2nd or 3rd cartilage.

costal-cartilage-of-3rd-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 3rd Rib
costal-cartilage-of-3rd-rib.summary: Joins the third rib to the body of the sternum. It is longer than the first two cartilages.
articulations: Body of sternum at the 3rd costal notch (synovial joint)
landmarks: Slopes slightly upward toward the sternum
May join neighboring cartilages in some people
attachments: Intercostal muscles
Pectoralis major (sternocostal head)
Transversus thoracis
costal-cartilage-of-3rd-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-3rd-rib.clinical: Costochondritis causes chest wall pain and tenderness here. It can mimic cardiac pain.

costal-cartilage-of-4th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 4th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-4th-rib.summary: Joins the fourth rib to the body of the sternum. It lies in front of the upper heart.
articulations: Body of sternum at the 4th costal notch (synovial joint)
landmarks: Runs nearly horizontally to the sternum
Lies in front of the heart and mediastinum
attachments: Intercostal muscles
Pectoralis major (sternocostal head)
Transversus thoracis
Pectoralis minor (near the rib junction)
costal-cartilage-of-4th-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-4th-rib.clinical: Injury to the anterior chest wall cartilages can cause pain that mimics cardiac disease.

costal-cartilage-of-5th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 5th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-5th-rib.summary: Joins the fifth rib to the body of the sternum. The rectus abdominis begins on its outer surface.
articulations: Body of sternum at the 5th costal notch (synovial joint)
May form a small joint with the 6th cartilage
landmarks: Rectus abdominis attaches to its outer surface
attachments: Intercostal muscles
Rectus abdominis
Pectoralis major (sternocostal head)
Transversus thoracis
costal-cartilage-of-5th-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-5th-rib.clinical: The cardiac apex beat is usually felt in the left 5th intercostal space near here.

costal-cartilage-of-6th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 6th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-6th-rib.summary: Joins the sixth rib to the lower part of the sternal body. It often touches the 7th cartilage.
articulations: Body of sternum at the 6th costal notch (synovial joint)
Small interchondral joint with the 7th cartilage
landmarks: Rectus abdominis attaches to its outer surface
attachments: Intercostal muscles
Rectus abdominis
Pectoralis major (sternocostal head)
Transversus thoracis
costal-cartilage-of-6th-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-6th-rib.clinical: Costochondral injury here is painful with deep breathing or twisting, and it can resemble pleurisy.

costal-cartilage-of-7th-rib.name: Costal Cartilage of 7th Rib
costal-cartilage-of-7th-rib.summary: The lowest costal cartilage that reaches the sternum. It begins the costal margin together with the 8th to 10th cartilages.
articulations: Lower body of sternum near the xiphisternal joint (synovial joint)
8th costal cartilage joins its lower edge
landmarks: Longest costal cartilage to reach the sternum
attachments: Rectus abdominis
External oblique
Transversus abdominis (inner surface)
Diaphragm (inner surface)
Transversus thoracis
costal-cartilage-of-7th-rib.ossification: Calcifies gradually with age, which makes the chest wall stiffer.
costal-cartilage-of-7th-rib.clinical: Clinicians palpate the liver and spleen edges just below the costal margin.

first-rib.name: First Rib
first-rib.summary: The shortest, broadest, and most curved rib. It is flat from top to bottom and sits just under the clavicle.
articulations: Head with a single facet articulates with the T1 vertebral body
Tubercle articulates with the T1 transverse process
landmarks: Groove for the subclavian vein (in front of the tubercle)
Groove for the subclavian artery and lower trunk of the brachial plexus (behind the tubercle)
attachments: Scalenus anterior
Scalenus medius
Serratus anterior (first digitation)
Subclavius
Costoclavicular ligament
Suprapleural membrane
first-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
first-rib.clinical: Thoracic outlet syndrome can arise when the first rib or a cervical rib compresses the subclavian vessels or the lower trunk of the plexus.

second-rib.name: Second Rib
second-rib.summary: Thinner and longer than the first rib. Its costal cartilage joins the sternum at the sternal angle.
articulations: Head with two facets articulates with the T1 and T2 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T2 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the sternum at the sternal angle
landmarks: Rough tuberosity for serratus anterior on the outer surface
attachments: Scalenus posterior
Serratus anterior
Serratus posterior superior
Intercostal muscles
second-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
second-rib.clinical: Because the first rib is hidden under the clavicle, clinicians start counting ribs from the second rib at the sternal angle.

third-rib.name: Third Rib
third-rib.summary: A typical true rib. It runs from the T2-T3 vertebrae around the chest to the sternal body through its costal cartilage.
articulations: Head articulates with the T2 and T3 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T3 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the body of the sternum
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: Pectoralis minor
Serratus anterior
Serratus posterior superior
Intercostal muscles
third-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
third-rib.clinical: The intercostal vein, artery, and nerve run in the costal groove, so needles pass just above the rib below the space.

fourth-rib.name: Fourth Rib
fourth-rib.summary: A typical true rib. It articulates with the T3 and T4 vertebrae and reaches the sternal body through its cartilage.
articulations: Head articulates with the T3 and T4 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T4 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the body of the sternum
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: Pectoralis minor
Serratus anterior
Serratus posterior superior
Intercostal muscles
fourth-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
fourth-rib.clinical: The nipple usually overlies the 4th intercostal space in men. The 4th to 5th space is a common site for a chest drain.

fifth-rib.name: Fifth Rib
fifth-rib.summary: A typical true rib. It articulates with the T4 and T5 vertebrae and reaches the sternal body through its cartilage.
articulations: Head articulates with the T4 and T5 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T5 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the body of the sternum
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: Pectoralis minor
Serratus anterior
Serratus posterior superior
External oblique
Intercostal muscles
fifth-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
fifth-rib.clinical: The safe triangle for chest drain insertion lies at the 5th intercostal space in the midaxillary line.

sixth-rib.name: Sixth Rib
sixth-rib.summary: A typical true rib. It articulates with the T5 and T6 vertebrae and reaches the lower sternal body through its cartilage.
articulations: Head articulates with the T5 and T6 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T6 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the body of the sternum
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: Serratus anterior
External oblique
Intercostal muscles
sixth-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
sixth-rib.clinical: In the midclavicular line the lower border of the lung crosses the 6th rib. The pleura extends lower, to the 8th rib.

seventh-rib.name: Seventh Rib
seventh-rib.summary: The lowest true rib. Its costal cartilage reaches the sternum near the xiphisternal joint.
articulations: Head articulates with the T6 and T7 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T7 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the lower body of the sternum
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: Serratus anterior
External oblique
Iliocostalis thoracis (angle)
Intercostal muscles
seventh-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
seventh-rib.clinical: Multiple adjacent rib fractures can produce a flail chest, in which a chest wall segment moves paradoxically with breathing.

heighth-rib.name: Eighth Rib
heighth-rib.summary: The first false rib. Its costal cartilage joins the 7th cartilage instead of the sternum.
articulations: Head articulates with the T7 and T8 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T8 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the 7th costal cartilage
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: Serratus anterior
External oblique
Iliocostalis thoracis (angle)
Intercostal muscles
heighth-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
heighth-rib.clinical: Slipping rib syndrome can cause pain when the loosely attached cartilages of the 8th to 10th ribs move too much.

ninth-rib.name: Ninth Rib
ninth-rib.summary: A false rib. Its costal cartilage joins the 8th cartilage instead of the sternum.
articulations: Head articulates with the T8 and T9 vertebral bodies
Tubercle articulates with the T9 transverse process
Costal cartilage joins the 8th costal cartilage
landmarks: Costal groove on the lower inner border
attachments: External oblique
Latissimus dorsi (variable)
Serratus posterior inferior
Iliocostalis thoracis (angle)
Intercostal muscles
ninth-rib.ossification: A primary center near the angle appears in the fetus. Secondary centers for the head and tubercle appear at puberty and fuse by about age 25.
ninth-rib.clinical: The tip of the 9th costal cartilage marks the transpyloric plane (L1) and often the gallbladder fundus.

posterior-transverse-collateral-sulcus.name: Posterior Transverse Collateral Sulcus
posterior-transverse-collateral-sulcus.summary: A short sulcus on the underside of the occipital lobe near the back end of the collateral sulcus. It is a surface landmark only.
posterior-transverse-collateral-sulcus.location: Inferior surface of the occipital lobe, near the occipitotemporal junction
function: Surface fold that increases cortical area
Landmark for locating adjacent visual association cortex
blood: Posterior cerebral artery (inferior temporal and occipital branches)
posterior-transverse-collateral-sulcus.clinical: Sulcal patterns like this are used as landmarks on MRI parcellation. They have no direct clinical syndrome.

temporal-pole.name: Temporal Pole
temporal-pole.summary: The rounded front tip of the temporal lobe. It sits in the middle cranial fossa behind the greater wing of the sphenoid.
temporal-pole.location: Anterior end of the temporal lobe, in front of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle
function: Semantic memory and word meaning
Social and emotional processing
Links the limbic system with sensory association cortex
blood: Middle cerebral artery (temporopolar and anterior temporal branches)
temporal-pole.clinical: It is often removed in anterior temporal lobectomy for drug-resistant epilepsy. Herpes simplex encephalitis commonly damages it.
temporal-pole.connections: Joined to the amygdala and orbitofrontal cortex by the uncinate fasciculus.

accessory-nucleus-of-oculomotor-nucleus.name: Accessory Nucleus of Oculomotor Nerve (Edinger-Westphal Nucleus)
accessory-nucleus-of-oculomotor-nucleus.summary: A small parasympathetic nucleus of the midbrain. It sends fibres with the oculomotor nerve to constrict the pupil and focus the lens.
accessory-nucleus-of-oculomotor-nucleus.location: Midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, close to the oculomotor nucleus
function: Parasympathetic supply to the sphincter pupillae
Parasympathetic supply to the ciliary muscle for accommodation
blood: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip and posterior cerebral arteries
accessory-nucleus-of-oculomotor-nucleus.clinical: Damage to its fibres in CN III causes a dilated pupil that does not react to light. Aneurysms of the posterior communicating artery can compress them.
parts: Preganglionic fibres run with CN III to the ciliary ganglion
accessory-nucleus-of-oculomotor-nucleus.connections: Receives input from the pretectal nuclei for the pupillary light reflex.

amygdaloid-body.name: Amygdala
amygdaloid-body.summary: An almond-shaped group of nuclei in the front of the temporal lobe. It links emotion with memory and body responses.
amygdaloid-body.location: Medial temporal lobe, in front of the hippocampus and the temporal horn, near the tail of the caudate nucleus
function: Processes fear and other emotions
Attaches emotional meaning to memories
Drives autonomic and hormonal responses through the hypothalamus
blood: Branches of the middle cerebral artery
amygdaloid-body.clinical: Bilateral temporal lobe damage can cause Kluver-Bucy syndrome, with placidity and hypersexuality. Amygdala overactivity is linked to anxiety and PTSD.
amygdaloid-body.connections: Sends fibres to the hypothalamus through the stria terminalis and the ventral amygdalofugal pathway.

angular-gyrus.name: Angular Gyrus
