angular-gyrus.summary: A gyrus in the lower back part of the parietal lobe. It arches over the end of the superior temporal sulcus (Brodmann area 39).
angular-gyrus.location: Posterior inferior parietal lobule, at the junction of parietal, temporal, and occipital lobes
function: Reading and understanding written words
Calculation and number processing
Spatial attention and integration of sensory information
blood: Angular artery (middle cerebral artery, inferior division)
angular-gyrus.clinical: Damage on the dominant side can cause Gerstmann syndrome, with finger agnosia, left-right confusion, agraphia, and acalculia.

anterior-cochlear-nucleus.name: Anterior (Ventral) Cochlear Nucleus
anterior-cochlear-nucleus.summary: A brainstem nucleus that receives the first auditory input from the cochlear nerve. It lies on the surface of the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
anterior-cochlear-nucleus.location: Pontomedullary junction, lateral to the inferior cerebellar peduncle
function: First relay for hearing from the cochlear nerve (CN VIII)
Sends sound signals to both superior olivary complexes
anterior-cochlear-nucleus.clinical: Because the pathway crosses and splits, deafness in one ear usually means a lesion of the ear, the nerve, or the cochlear nuclei.
anterior-cochlear-nucleus.connections: Fibres cross in the trapezoid body and ascend in the lateral lemniscus.

anterior-commissure.name: Anterior Commissure
anterior-commissure.summary: A small, rounded bundle of white matter that crosses the midline just in front of the columns of the fornix. It joins the two temporal lobes.
anterior-commissure.location: Midline, in the lamina terminalis, in front of the fornix columns and below the rostrum of the corpus callosum
function: Connects the anterior temporal lobes and the amygdalae
Carries some olfactory fibres between the two sides
blood: Branches of the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries
anterior-commissure.clinical: Together with the posterior commissure, it defines the AC-PC line used for stereotactic brain mapping.
anterior-commissure.connections: Anterior part joins the olfactory regions. Posterior part joins the temporal lobes.

anterior-occipital-sulcus.name: Anterior Occipital Sulcus
anterior-occipital-sulcus.summary: A shallow sulcus on the lateral surface near the front of the occipital lobe. It is a landmark near the occipitotemporal boundary.
anterior-occipital-sulcus.location: Lateral surface, near the junction of the occipital and temporal lobes, close to the preoccipital notch
function: Surface fold that increases cortical area
Landmark for the boundary between occipital and temporal lobes
blood: Branches of the middle cerebral and posterior cerebral arteries
anterior-occipital-sulcus.clinical: It has no direct clinical syndrome. Sulcal landmarks help surgeons and radiologists describe lesion locations.

aqueduct-of-midbrain-cerebral-aqueduct.name: Cerebral Aqueduct
aqueduct-of-midbrain-cerebral-aqueduct.summary: A narrow channel about 1.5 cm long that carries cerebrospinal fluid through the midbrain. It joins the third and fourth ventricles.
aqueduct-of-midbrain-cerebral-aqueduct.location: Midline of the midbrain, between the tectum behind and the tegmentum in front
function: Conducts cerebrospinal fluid from the third ventricle to the fourth ventricle
Surrounded by periaqueductal grey matter
blood: Paramedian branches of the basilar and posterior cerebral arteries supply the surrounding grey matter
aqueduct-of-midbrain-cerebral-aqueduct.clinical: Aqueductal stenosis blocks CSF flow and causes obstructive hydrocephalus. The lateral and third ventricles enlarge, but the fourth does not.

calcarine-sulcus.name: Calcarine Sulcus
calcarine-sulcus.summary: A deep sulcus on the medial surface of the occipital lobe. The primary visual cortex (area V1) lies along its banks.
calcarine-sulcus.location: Medial occipital lobe, running forward from the occipital pole to meet the parieto-occipital sulcus
function: Houses the primary visual cortex
Separates the cuneus above from the lingual gyrus below
blood: Calcarine branch of the posterior cerebral artery
calcarine-sulcus.clinical: A posterior cerebral artery stroke here causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.
calcarine-sulcus.connections: Receives the optic radiation from the lateral geniculate body. The upper bank receives the lower visual field.

caudate-nucleus.name: Caudate Nucleus
caudate-nucleus.summary: A C-shaped nucleus that arches along the wall of the lateral ventricle. It is a main input station of the basal ganglia.
caudate-nucleus.location: Along the floor of the frontal horn and the lateral wall of the lateral ventricle, medial to the internal capsule
function: Planning and control of movement
Learning habits and reward-based behavior
Cognitive and executive functions
blood: Medial and lateral striate arteries (head and body)
caudate-nucleus.clinical: In Huntington disease the caudate shrinks, which enlarges the frontal horns and causes chorea and cognitive decline.
caudate-nucleus.connections: Receives cortical, thalamic, and dopaminergic nigral input. Projects to the globus pallidus and substantia nigra.

central-canal.name: Central Canal
central-canal.summary: A tiny, fluid-filled channel running through the center of the spinal cord. It is lined with ependymal cells.
central-canal.location: Center of the grey commissure of the spinal cord, continuous above with the fourth ventricle
function: Carries a small amount of cerebrospinal fluid
Remnant of the neural tube lumen
blood: Sulcal branches of the anterior spinal artery supply the surrounding grey matter
central-canal.clinical: Syringomyelia is a fluid cavity near the canal. It causes a cape-like loss of pain and temperature in the arms with touch preserved.
central-canal.connections: Opens above into the fourth ventricle and ends below in the terminal ventricle of the conus medullaris.

central-sulcus.name: Central Sulcus
central-sulcus.summary: A long groove on the lateral brain surface that separates the frontal lobe from the parietal lobe. It lies between the precentral and postcentral gyri.
central-sulcus.location: Runs obliquely downward and forward from near the midline of the top of the hemisphere toward the lateral sulcus
function: Divides the primary motor cortex from the primary somatosensory cortex
Key landmark for mapping brain function
blood: Rolandic (central sulcus) branches of the middle cerebral artery
central-sulcus.clinical: Surgeons and radiologists first find the central sulcus to locate motor cortex before surgery.

cerebellum.name: Cerebellum
cerebellum.summary: The large structure behind the brainstem that coordinates movement, balance, and posture. It acts on the same side of the body.
cerebellum.location: Posterior cranial fossa, below the tentorium cerebelli and behind the pons and medulla
function: Coordinates smooth, accurate movement
Maintains balance and posture
Supports motor learning and muscle tone
cerebellum.clinical: Cerebellar damage causes same-side ataxia, intention tremor, and nystagmus. A raised pressure can push the tonsils through the foramen magnum.
cerebellum.connections: Joined to the brainstem by the superior, middle, and inferior cerebellar peduncles.

cingulate-gyrus-posteroventral-part.name: Cingulate Gyrus, Posteroventral Part
cingulate-gyrus-posteroventral-part.summary: The lower back part of the cingulate gyrus, curving around the back end of the corpus callosum toward the parahippocampal gyrus.
cingulate-gyrus-posteroventral-part.location: Medial surface, below and behind the splenium of the corpus callosum (the isthmus region)
function: Part of the limbic system
Supports memory and links to the hippocampal region
blood: Pericallosal branches of the anterior cerebral artery
Splenial branches of the posterior cerebral artery
cingulate-gyrus-posteroventral-part.clinical: Early Alzheimer disease reduces activity in the nearby posterior cingulate and retrosplenial regions.

cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-anteri.name: Cingulate Gyrus and Sulcus, Middle Anterior Part
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-anteri.latin: Gyrus et sulcus cinguli, pars media anterior
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-anteri.summary: The front middle section of the cingulate gyrus and its sulcus. It lies above the front half of the body of the corpus callosum.
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-anteri.location: Medial frontal lobe surface, above the anterior body of the corpus callosum
function: Pain processing and emotional response
Error and conflict monitoring
Autonomic and motivational control
blood: Pericallosal and callosomarginal branches of the anterior cerebral artery
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-anteri.clinical: Cingulotomy in this region has been used for severe, treatment-resistant pain or obsessive-compulsive disorder. Bilateral damage can cause akinetic mutism.

cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-poster.name: Cingulate Gyrus and Sulcus, Middle Posterior Part
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-poster.latin: Gyrus et sulcus cinguli, pars media posterior
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-poster.summary: The back middle section of the cingulate gyrus and its sulcus. It lies above the posterior body of the corpus callosum.
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-poster.location: Medial surface, above the posterior body of the corpus callosum, behind the middle anterior part
function: Motor planning and movement-related processing
Pain and attention
Links limbic and motor areas
blood: Pericallosal and callosomarginal branches of the anterior cerebral artery
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-middle-poster.clinical: It is supplied by the anterior cerebral artery, so a stroke in that territory may disturb motivation and movement.

cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-posterior-dor.name: Cingulate Gyrus and Sulcus, Posterior Dorsal Part
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-posterior-dor.latin: Gyrus et sulcus cinguli, pars posterior dorsalis
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-posterior-dor.summary: The upper back part of the cingulate gyrus and its sulcus. It is the posterior cingulate cortex, above the splenium.
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-posterior-dor.location: Medial surface, above the splenium of the corpus callosum and in front of the precuneus
function: Key hub of the default mode network
Memory retrieval and self-related thought
Attention and awareness
blood: Pericallosal branches of the anterior cerebral artery
Branches of the posterior cerebral artery
cingulate-gyrus-and-sulcus-posterior-dor.clinical: Reduced metabolism in the posterior cingulate is an early finding on PET scans in Alzheimer disease.

cingulate-sulcus-marginal-part.name: Cingulate Sulcus, Marginal Part
cingulate-sulcus-marginal-part.summary: The back end of the cingulate sulcus. It turns upward to reach the top edge of the hemisphere behind the paracentral lobule.
cingulate-sulcus-marginal-part.location: Medial surface, between the paracentral lobule in front and the precuneus behind
function: Separates the paracentral lobule from the precuneus
Landmark for finding the central sulcus on MRI
blood: Branches of the anterior cerebral artery (paracentral and precuneal)
cingulate-sulcus-marginal-part.clinical: On axial MRI, the marginal ramus is the sulcus just behind the central sulcus and helps identify it.

circular-sulcus-of-insula.name: Circular Sulcus of Insula
circular-sulcus-of-insula.summary: A groove that surrounds the insula like a ring. It separates the insula from the overlying frontal, parietal, and temporal opercula.
circular-sulcus-of-insula.location: Deep within the lateral sulcus, around the margin of the insula
function: Marks the boundary of the insular cortex
Landmark for surgical approaches to the insula
blood: Insular branches of the middle cerebral artery
circular-sulcus-of-insula.clinical: Surgeons follow it when operating on insular tumours through the lateral sulcus.

collateral-sulcus.name: Collateral Sulcus
collateral-sulcus.summary: A long groove on the underside of the temporal and occipital lobes. It lies between the parahippocampal and fusiform gyri.
collateral-sulcus.location: Inferior surface of the hemisphere, from the occipital pole forward toward the temporal pole
function: Separates the lingual and parahippocampal gyri from the lateral occipitotemporal gyrus
Raises the collateral eminence in the temporal horn
blood: Branches of the posterior cerebral artery
collateral-sulcus.clinical: Its depth and shape are used as landmarks in MRI studies of the medial temporal lobe, including in epilepsy and dementia.

corpus-callosum.name: Corpus Callosum
corpus-callosum.summary: The largest white matter bundle in the brain. It connects the two cerebral hemispheres across the midline.
corpus-callosum.location: Deep in the longitudinal fissure, forming the roof of the lateral ventricles and the floor of the fissure
function: Transfers information between the two hemispheres
Coordinates sensory, motor, and cognitive activity
blood: Pericallosal and callosomarginal arteries (anterior cerebral artery)
Splenial branches of the posterior cerebral artery
corpus-callosum.clinical: Callosotomy can limit severe seizures. A glioma that spreads across the genu has a butterfly shape on MRI.

cuneus.name: Cuneus
cuneus.summary: A wedge-shaped area on the medial surface of the occipital lobe. It lies above the calcarine sulcus.
cuneus.location: Medial occipital lobe, between the parieto-occipital sulcus and the calcarine sulcus
function: Primary and early visual processing
Receives input from the lower visual field of the opposite side
blood: Parieto-occipital and calcarine branches of the posterior cerebral artery
cuneus.clinical: A lesion causes a contralateral inferior quadrantanopia, sometimes called pie on the floor.

fornix.name: Fornix
fornix.summary: A C-shaped bundle of white matter that carries output from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies and septal area.
fornix.location: Arches from the temporal lobe under the corpus callosum, above the thalamus, and down in front of the interventricular foramen
function: Main output pathway of the hippocampus
Supports memory formation
blood: Branches of the anterior cerebral and anterior communicating arteries
Posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
fornix.clinical: Damage causes memory loss. A colloid cyst of the third ventricle can compress the columns of the fornix.
fornix.connections: Runs from the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies, then onward through the mammillothalamic tract.

fourth-ventricle.name: Fourth Ventricle
fourth-ventricle.summary: A diamond-shaped, fluid-filled cavity between the brainstem and the cerebellum. It connects with the aqueduct above and the central canal below.
fourth-ventricle.location: Posterior cranial fossa, behind the pons and upper medulla and in front of the cerebellum
function: Carries cerebrospinal fluid toward the subarachnoid space
Contains choroid plexus that makes CSF
blood: Posterior inferior cerebellar artery supplies the choroid plexus
fourth-ventricle.clinical: Blockage by a tumour, such as a medulloblastoma, causes obstructive hydrocephalus.
fourth-ventricle.connections: Drains through the median aperture and two lateral apertures into the subarachnoid space.

globus-pallidus.name: Globus Pallidus
globus-pallidus.summary: A pale nucleus in the basal ganglia. It is the main output station to the thalamus and helps regulate movement.
globus-pallidus.location: Medial part of the lentiform nucleus, between the putamen and the internal capsule
function: Main output of the basal ganglia
Inhibits the thalamus to help scale and select movements
blood: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
globus-pallidus.clinical: The internal segment is a deep brain stimulation target in Parkinson disease and dystonia. Carbon monoxide poisoning often damages it.
globus-pallidus.connections: Receives striatal and subthalamic input. Projects to the ventral anterior and ventral lateral thalamus.

habenula.name: Habenula
habenula.summary: A small nucleus at the back of the thalamus, next to the pineal gland. It links the forebrain with the midbrain.
habenula.location: Epithalamus, in the habenular trigone at the back of the third ventricle roof beside the pineal gland
function: Processes reward and aversion
Links limbic forebrain areas to midbrain monoamine nuclei
blood: Medial posterior choroidal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
habenula.clinical: Calcification of the habenular commissure is a common, normal finding on CT scans of adults.
habenula.connections: Receives the stria medullaris thalami. Projects through the fasciculus retroflexus to the interpeduncular nucleus.

hippocampal-commissure.name: Hippocampal Commissure
hippocampal-commissure.summary: A thin sheet of fibres that crosses the midline between the two crura of the fornix. It lies below the splenium.
hippocampal-commissure.location: Midline, beneath the splenium of the corpus callosum, between the posterior parts of the fornix
function: Connects the hippocampal formations of the two sides
blood: Splenial branches of the posterior cerebral artery
hippocampal-commissure.clinical: It is small in humans and rarely a focus of disease. It may be involved with splenial or fornix injuries.

hippocampus.name: Hippocampus
hippocampus.summary: A curved fold of cortex in the medial temporal lobe. It is essential for forming new memories and for spatial navigation.
hippocampus.location: Floor of the temporal horn of the lateral ventricle, in the medial temporal lobe
function: Forms new long-term declarative memories
Supports spatial navigation
blood: Hippocampal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
hippocampus.clinical: Bilateral damage causes severe anterograde amnesia. It is damaged early in Alzheimer disease and in temporal lobe epilepsy.
hippocampus.connections: Receives input from the entorhinal cortex. Sends output through the fornix to the mammillary bodies.

hypothalamus.name: Hypothalamus
hypothalamus.summary: A small region at the base of the brain that controls body balance. It regulates temperature, hunger, thirst, sleep, and hormones.
hypothalamus.location: Below the thalamus, forming the floor and lower walls of the third ventricle, above the pituitary gland
function: Regulates body temperature, hunger, and thirst
Controls the autonomic nervous system
Controls the pituitary gland and releases ADH and oxytocin
Sets circadian rhythms
blood: Small branches of the anterior cerebral, anterior communicating, posterior communicating, and posterior cerebral arteries
hypothalamus.clinical: Damage can cause diabetes insipidus, abnormal temperature control, or severe changes in appetite and sleep.
hypothalamus.connections: Linked to the pituitary through the infundibulum and to the limbic system through the fornix.

inferior-colliculus.name: Inferior Colliculus
inferior-colliculus.summary: One of two lower bumps on the back of the midbrain. It is a key relay for hearing.
inferior-colliculus.location: Dorsal midbrain tectum, below the superior colliculus
function: Relay and integration of auditory signals
Sound localization
Auditory reflexes such as the startle response
blood: Quadrigeminal branches of the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries
inferior-colliculus.clinical: Damage on both sides can impair hearing centrally. A pineal tumour compressing the tectum mainly affects upward gaze.
inferior-colliculus.connections: Receives the lateral lemniscus. Projects through the brachium of the inferior colliculus to the medial geniculate body.

inferior-frontal-sulcus.name: Inferior Frontal Sulcus
inferior-frontal-sulcus.summary: A groove on the side of the frontal lobe. It separates the middle frontal gyrus above from the inferior frontal gyrus below.
inferior-frontal-sulcus.location: Lateral frontal lobe, running forward from the precentral sulcus
function: Separates the middle and inferior frontal gyri
Landmark for the inferior frontal gyrus
blood: Prefrontal and opercular branches of the middle cerebral artery
inferior-frontal-sulcus.clinical: It marks the upper edge of the inferior frontal gyrus, which contains Broca area on the dominant side.

inferior-occipital-gyrus-and-sulcus.name: Inferior Occipital Gyrus and Sulcus
inferior-occipital-gyrus-and-sulcus.summary: The lower lateral part of the occipital lobe. It takes part in visual association processing.
inferior-occipital-gyrus-and-sulcus.location: Inferolateral occipital lobe, below the lateral occipital gyrus
function: Visual association processing
Early recognition of objects and faces
blood: Posterior temporal and occipital branches of the middle cerebral artery
inferior-occipital-gyrus-and-sulcus.clinical: Damage here, especially on both sides, can impair visual recognition of objects or faces.

inferior-salivatory-nucleus.name: Inferior Salivatory Nucleus
inferior-salivatory-nucleus.summary: A small parasympathetic nucleus in the lower brainstem. It sends fibres in the glossopharyngeal nerve to the parotid gland.
inferior-salivatory-nucleus.location: Rostral medulla, close to the nucleus ambiguus (exact location varies by source)
function: Parasympathetic supply of the parotid gland through CN IX
Stimulates watery saliva
blood: Branches of the vertebral and posterior inferior cerebellar arteries
inferior-salivatory-nucleus.clinical: Frey syndrome is sweating and flushing when eating, after parotid surgery damages the nearby parasympathetic fibres.
inferior-salivatory-nucleus.connections: Fibres run in CN IX, the lesser petrosal nerve, and the otic ganglion.

inferior-temporal-gyrus.name: Inferior Temporal Gyrus
inferior-temporal-gyrus.summary: The lowest long gyrus on the side of the temporal lobe. It continues onto the underside of the brain.
inferior-temporal-gyrus.location: Lateral and inferior temporal lobe, below the inferior temporal sulcus
function: Object and face recognition
Visual memory and meaning
blood: Anterior and posterior temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery
Inferior temporal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
inferior-temporal-gyrus.clinical: Bilateral damage to this ventral visual pathway can cause visual agnosia or prosopagnosia.
inferior-temporal-gyrus.connections: Part of the ventral visual stream.

inferior-temporal-sulcus.name: Inferior Temporal Sulcus
inferior-temporal-sulcus.summary: A groove on the side of the temporal lobe. It separates the middle temporal gyrus from the inferior temporal gyrus.
inferior-temporal-sulcus.location: Lateral temporal lobe, running front to back below the middle temporal gyrus
function: Separates the middle and inferior temporal gyri
Surface fold that increases cortical area
blood: Temporal branches of the middle cerebral artery
inferior-temporal-sulcus.clinical: It has no direct clinical syndrome. It serves as a landmark in imaging and surgery.

insula-subcentral-gyrus-and-ant-and-post.name: Insula
insula-subcentral-gyrus-and-ant-and-post.summary: A buried lobe of cortex deep inside the lateral sulcus. The frontal, parietal, and temporal opercula cover it.
insula-subcentral-gyrus-and-ant-and-post.location: Floor of the lateral sulcus, deep to the opercula, lateral to the lentiform nucleus
function: Taste (primary gustatory cortex)
Awareness of internal body states
Pain, emotion, and autonomic control
Speech articulation (dominant side)
blood: Insular branches of the middle cerebral artery
insula-subcentral-gyrus-and-ant-and-post.clinical: Insular stroke can disturb taste and autonomic control, and it can cause cardiac rhythm changes.

interpeduncular-fossa.name: Interpeduncular Fossa
interpeduncular-fossa.summary: A depression on the underside of the midbrain between the two cerebral peduncles. It lies in the interpeduncular cistern.
interpeduncular-fossa.location: Ventral midbrain, between the cerebral peduncles, behind the mammillary bodies and in front of the pons
function: Gateway for small perforating arteries
Exit area of the oculomotor nerve
blood: Posterior perforating branches of the basilar and posterior communicating arteries
interpeduncular-fossa.clinical: Basilar tip aneurysms in this cistern can compress the oculomotor nerve and cause a dilated pupil with a down-and-out eye.

intraparietal-sulcus.name: Intraparietal Sulcus
intraparietal-sulcus.summary: A long groove on the parietal lobe. It separates the superior parietal lobule from the inferior parietal lobule.
intraparietal-sulcus.location: Lateral parietal lobe, running backward from the postcentral sulcus
function: Separates the superior and inferior parietal lobules
Nearby cortex helps with spatial attention, eye movements, and reaching
blood: Posterior parietal and angular branches of the middle cerebral artery
intraparietal-sulcus.clinical: Damage to nearby parietal cortex can cause contralateral neglect, more often on the non-dominant side.

lat-fis-ant-horizont.name: Lateral Sulcus, Anterior Horizontal Ramus
lat-fis-ant-horizont.summary: A short branch of the lateral sulcus that runs forward into the inferior frontal gyrus. It separates the pars orbitalis from the pars triangularis.
lat-fis-ant-horizont.location: Inferior frontal gyrus, running forward from the front end of the lateral sulcus
function: Divides parts of the inferior frontal gyrus
Landmark for Broca area
blood: Prefrontal and orbitofrontal branches of the middle cerebral artery
lat-fis-ant-horizont.clinical: Along with the ascending ramus, it outlines the pars triangularis, part of Broca area on the dominant side.

lat-fis-ant-vertical.name: Lateral Sulcus, Anterior Ascending Ramus
lat-fis-ant-vertical.summary: A short branch of the lateral sulcus that runs upward into the inferior frontal gyrus. It separates the pars triangularis from the pars opercularis.
lat-fis-ant-vertical.location: Inferior frontal gyrus, rising upward from the front end of the lateral sulcus
function: Divides parts of the inferior frontal gyrus
Landmark for Broca area
blood: Prefrontal and precentral branches of the middle cerebral artery
lat-fis-ant-vertical.clinical: Along with the horizontal ramus, it outlines the pars triangularis, part of Broca area on the dominant side.

lat-fis-post.name: Lateral Sulcus, Posterior Ramus
lat-fis-post.summary: The long, main part of the lateral sulcus. It runs backward and slightly upward, separating the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes.
lat-fis-post.location: Lateral surface of the hemisphere, from the anterior rami backward into the parietal lobe
function: Separates the temporal lobe from the frontal and parietal lobes
Overlies the insula and the auditory cortex
blood: Branches of the middle cerebral artery run within it
lat-fis-post.clinical: The middle cerebral artery branches run in this sulcus. Language areas lie along its borders on the dominant side.

lateral-geniculate-body.name: Lateral Geniculate Body
lateral-geniculate-body.summary: A small part of the thalamus that relays visual signals from the optic tract to the visual cortex.
lateral-geniculate-body.location: Posterolateral thalamus, under the pulvinar, at the end of the optic tract
function: Relay nucleus for the visual pathway
Sorts signals from each eye into six layers
blood: Lateral posterior choroidal artery (posterior cerebral artery)
lateral-geniculate-body.clinical: Damage causes a contralateral homonymous visual field defect.
lateral-geniculate-body.connections: Receives the optic tract. Projects through the optic radiation to the primary visual cortex.

lateral-occipital-gyrus-middle-occipital.name: Lateral Occipital Gyrus
lateral-occipital-gyrus-middle-occipital.summary: The main gyrus on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe. It takes part in visual association and object recognition.
lateral-occipital-gyrus-middle-occipital.location: Lateral occipital lobe, between the superior and inferior occipital sulci
function: Visual association processing
Recognition of object shape
blood: Posterior temporal and parieto-occipital branches of the middle cerebral artery
lateral-occipital-gyrus-middle-occipital.clinical: It lies near the border between the middle and posterior cerebral artery territories. Border-zone infarcts here can impair visual perception.

lateral-occipitotemporal-gyrus.name: Lateral Occipitotemporal Gyrus (Fusiform Gyrus)
lateral-occipitotemporal-gyrus.summary: A long gyrus on the underside of the temporal and occipital lobes. It is commonly called the fusiform gyrus.
lateral-occipitotemporal-gyrus.location: Inferior surface, between the collateral sulcus and the occipitotemporal sulcus
function: Face recognition
Word form recognition (left side)
Object and color processing
blood: Inferior temporal and posterior temporal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
lateral-occipitotemporal-gyrus.clinical: Damage on both sides can cause prosopagnosia, which is the inability to recognize faces.

lateral-ventricle.name: Lateral Ventricle
lateral-ventricle.summary: A C-shaped, fluid-filled cavity inside each cerebral hemisphere. It contains choroid plexus that produces cerebrospinal fluid.
lateral-ventricle.location: Deep within the cerebral hemisphere, curving around the thalamus from the frontal lobe back to the temporal lobe
function: Makes and holds cerebrospinal fluid
Passes CSF to the third ventricle
lateral-ventricle.clinical: Enlarged ventricles show hydrocephalus or brain atrophy. Hemorrhage into the ventricles is often serious.
lateral-ventricle.connections: Drains through the interventricular foramen (of Monro) into the third ventricle.

lentiform-nucleus.name: Lentiform Nucleus
lentiform-nucleus.summary: A lens-shaped mass of grey matter made of the putamen and the globus pallidus. It lies lateral to the internal capsule.
lentiform-nucleus.location: Deep in the hemisphere, lateral to the internal capsule and medial to the external capsule and insula
function: Motor control and movement selection
Part of the basal ganglia loops
blood: Lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
lentiform-nucleus.clinical: The putamen is the most common site of hypertensive brain hemorrhage. Wilson disease damages the lentiform nuclei.

lingual-gyrus.name: Lingual Gyrus
lingual-gyrus.summary: A gyrus on the underside of the medial occipital lobe. It lies below the calcarine sulcus and takes part in visual processing.
lingual-gyrus.location: Medial occipital and temporal lobe, between the calcarine sulcus and the collateral sulcus
function: Early visual processing of the upper visual field
Visual memory and word recognition
blood: Calcarine and posterior temporal branches of the posterior cerebral artery
lingual-gyrus.clinical: A lesion causes a contralateral superior quadrantanopia, sometimes called pie in the sky.

lunate-sulcus.name: Lunate Sulcus
lunate-sulcus.summary: A small, variable curved sulcus on the lateral surface of the occipital lobe, near the occipital pole.
lunate-sulcus.clinical: Prominent in apes, where it marks the front edge of primary visual cortex. In humans it is often small or absent.
lunate-sulcus.location: Lateral surface of the occipital lobe, a short distance in front of the occipital pole.
function: Surface landmark of the occipital lobe
Marks the approximate edge of visual cortex in apes

mamillary-body.name: Mamillary Body
mamillary-body.summary: A small rounded bump on the underside of the brain, behind the tuber cinereum. There are two, one on each side of the midline.
mamillary-body.clinical: Damage from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency is a hallmark of Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, causing severe memory loss.
mamillary-body.location: Posterior hypothalamus, on the floor of the brain between the cerebral peduncles and the tuber cinereum.
function: Relay in the limbic memory circuit (Papez circuit)
Helps form new episodic memories
blood: Posterior cerebral artery (premamillary and thalamoperforating branches)
mamillary-body.connections: Receives the fornix from the hippocampus. Projects through the mamillothalamic tract to the anterior nucleus of the thalamus.

medial-geniculate-body.name: Medial Geniculate Body
medial-geniculate-body.summary: The thalamic relay nucleus for hearing. It is a small oval swelling on the back-underside of the thalamus.
medial-geniculate-body.clinical: Lesions near it rarely cause deafness alone, because the auditory pathway is bilateral. Bilateral damage can cause cortical deafness.
medial-geniculate-body.location: Posterolateral underside of the thalamus, beside the pulvinar and lateral to the superior colliculus.
function: Relays auditory information to the cortex
Helps analyze sound pitch, timing, and location
blood: Thalamogeniculate branches of the posterior cerebral artery
medial-geniculate-body.connections: Receives from the inferior colliculus through the brachium of the inferior colliculus. Projects through the acoustic radiation to the transverse temporal gyrus.

medial-occipitotemporal-gyrus-parahippoc.name: Parahippocampal Gyrus (Medial Occipitotemporal Gyrus)
medial-occipitotemporal-gyrus-parahippoc.summary: A gyrus on the medial underside of the temporal lobe, between the hippocampal and collateral sulci. Its front end curves into the hook-like uncus.
medial-occipitotemporal-gyrus-parahippoc.clinical: Early Alzheimer disease affects the entorhinal cortex here. In uncal herniation, the uncus presses on the oculomotor nerve and midbrain.
medial-occipitotemporal-gyrus-parahippoc.location: Medial temporal lobe, below the hippocampus and bordered laterally by the collateral sulcus.
function: Memory encoding and retrieval
Spatial and scene processing
Pathway between the cortex and the hippocampus

medulla-oblongata.name: Medulla Oblongata
medulla-oblongata.summary: The lowest part of the brainstem. It continues from the spinal cord at the foramen magnum and ends at the pons.
medulla-oblongata.clinical: Lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome follows a stroke here. It causes vertigo, dysphagia, hoarseness, and crossed loss of pain and temperature.
medulla-oblongata.location: Lowest brainstem segment, in the posterior cranial fossa, between the spinal cord and the pons.
function: Controls breathing, heart rate, and blood pressure
Contains nuclei of cranial nerves IX to XII
Carries motor and sensory tracts between brain and cord
parts: Cranial nerve nuclei IX to XII
medulla-oblongata.connections: Corticospinal fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation. Dorsal column fibers synapse in the gracile and cuneate nuclei.

midbrain.name: Midbrain
midbrain.summary: The shortest brainstem segment, between the pons and the diencephalon. It has a tectum, tegmentum, and cerebral peduncles.
midbrain.clinical: Compression of the oculomotor nerve at the midbrain, as in uncal herniation, causes a dilated pupil and a down-and-out eye.
midbrain.location: Upper brainstem, passing through the tentorial notch, with the cerebral aqueduct running through it.
function: Visual and auditory reflexes (colliculi)
Eye movement control (cranial nerves III and IV)
Motor relay and dopamine production (substantia nigra)

middle-frontal-gyrus.name: Middle Frontal Gyrus
middle-frontal-gyrus.summary: The broad gyrus between the superior and inferior frontal sulci. It forms much of the lateral prefrontal cortex.
middle-frontal-gyrus.clinical: Damage to its dorsolateral part can impair planning and working memory. Its posterior part contains the frontal eye field.
middle-frontal-gyrus.location: Lateral surface of the frontal lobe, between the superior frontal sulcus and the inferior frontal sulcus.
function: Working memory and planning (dorsolateral prefrontal cortex)
Voluntary eye movements (frontal eye field, posterior part)
blood: Middle cerebral artery (superior division, prefrontal branches)

middle-temporal-gyrus.name: Middle Temporal Gyrus
middle-temporal-gyrus.summary: The gyrus between the superior and inferior temporal sulci on the lateral temporal lobe.
middle-temporal-gyrus.clinical: Damage in the dominant hemisphere can impair word meaning. Its posterior end helps process visual motion.
middle-temporal-gyrus.location: Lateral surface of the temporal lobe, between the superior temporal sulcus and the inferior temporal sulcus.
function: Understanding word meaning (language-dominant side)
Visual motion processing (posterior part)
Recognition of faces and objects

motor-nucleus-of-facial-nerve.name: Motor Nucleus of Facial Nerve
motor-nucleus-of-facial-nerve.summary: A column of motor neurons in the lower pons that sends axons to the muscles of facial expression.
motor-nucleus-of-facial-nerve.clinical: Upper motor neuron lesions spare the forehead because it has bilateral input. Lower motor neuron lesions, as in Bell palsy, paralyze the whole side.
motor-nucleus-of-facial-nerve.location: Ventrolateral pontine tegmentum, in the caudal pons. Its axons loop around the abducens nucleus before exiting.
function: Supplies muscles of facial expression
Supplies stapedius, stylohyoid, and posterior belly of digastric
blood: Pontine branches of the basilar artery
motor-nucleus-of-facial-nerve.connections: Receives corticobulbar fibers. The forehead part gets input from both hemispheres, the lower face mainly from the opposite hemisphere.

nucleus-ambiguus.name: Nucleus Ambiguus
nucleus-ambiguus.summary: A column of motor neurons deep in the medulla. Its axons travel in the glossopharyngeal and vagus nerves.
nucleus-ambiguus.clinical: Damage in lateral medullary syndrome causes hoarseness, difficulty swallowing, and a drooping soft palate on the same side.
nucleus-ambiguus.location: Deep lateral medulla, in the reticular formation, between the inferior olive and the spinal trigeminal nucleus.
function: Moves pharyngeal, palatal, and laryngeal muscles (swallowing, speech)
Gives parasympathetic fibers that slow the heart
nucleus-ambiguus.connections: Receives bilateral corticobulbar input. Axons leave via cranial nerves IX and X. The soft palate muscle tensor veli palatini is excluded.

nucleus-of-abducens-nerve.name: Nucleus of Abducens Nerve
nucleus-of-abducens-nerve.summary: A motor nucleus in the lower pons, beneath the floor of the fourth ventricle. It controls sideways eye movement.
nucleus-of-abducens-nerve.clinical: A lesion here causes loss of gaze to the same side, not just a lateral rectus palsy, because interneurons are also damaged.
nucleus-of-abducens-nerve.location: Caudal pontine tegmentum, at the facial colliculus in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
function: Moves the eye outward through the lateral rectus
Drives horizontal gaze via interneurons to the opposite oculomotor nucleus
blood: Pontine branches of the basilar artery
nucleus-of-abducens-nerve.connections: Interneurons cross and ascend in the medial longitudinal fasciculus to the opposite medial rectus subnucleus. The facial nerve loops around this nucleus.

nucleus-of-accessory-nerve.name: Nucleus of Accessory Nerve
nucleus-of-accessory-nerve.summary: A column of motor neurons in the anterior horn of the upper cervical spinal cord. It supplies two large neck and shoulder muscles.
nucleus-of-accessory-nerve.clinical: Injury to the nerve, often in the posterior neck triangle, causes a drooping shoulder and weak shoulder shrugging.
nucleus-of-accessory-nerve.location: Lateral part of the anterior horn of the spinal cord, from about C1 to C5 (sometimes C6).
function: Supplies the sternocleidomastoid muscle
Supplies the trapezius muscle
nucleus-of-accessory-nerve.connections: Rootlets emerge laterally, ascend through the foramen magnum, and leave the skull through the jugular foramen.

nucleus-of-hypoglossal-nerve.name: Nucleus of Hypoglossal Nerve
nucleus-of-hypoglossal-nerve.summary: A long motor column near the midline of the medulla. It controls the muscles of the tongue.
nucleus-of-hypoglossal-nerve.clinical: A lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the side of the damage when protruded. Medial medullary stroke is one cause.
nucleus-of-hypoglossal-nerve.location: Dorsomedial medulla, beneath the hypoglossal trigone in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
function: Moves the tongue (all intrinsic muscles and most extrinsic muscles)
Supports speech, chewing, and swallowing
nucleus-of-hypoglossal-nerve.connections: Axons pass ventrally between the pyramid and the olive. The palatoglossus muscle is not supplied by this nucleus.

nucleus-of-oculomotor-nerve.name: Nucleus of Oculomotor Nerve
nucleus-of-oculomotor-nerve.summary: A group of motor neurons in the midbrain at the level of the superior colliculus. It supplies most eye muscles and the eyelid lifter.
nucleus-of-oculomotor-nerve.clinical: Damage causes ptosis, a dilated pupil, and an eye turned down and out. Aneurysms of the posterior communicating artery can compress the nerve.
nucleus-of-oculomotor-nerve.location: Midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, ventral to the cerebral aqueduct.
function: Moves the eye through the superior, medial, and inferior rectus and inferior oblique
Lifts the eyelid (levator palpebrae superioris)
Gives pupil constriction and lens focusing via the Edinger-Westphal part
blood: Perforating branches of the basilar tip
nucleus-of-oculomotor-nerve.connections: The superior rectus is supplied from the opposite nucleus. The levator subnucleus is a single midline group.

nucleus-of-solitary-tract.name: Nucleus of Solitary Tract
nucleus-of-solitary-tract.group: Cranial nerve nuclei (CN VII, IX, X)
nucleus-of-solitary-tract.summary: The main sensory nucleus for taste and visceral input. It wraps around the solitary tract in the medulla.
nucleus-of-solitary-tract.clinical: It drives reflexes such as the baroreflex, gag, and cough. Damage may disturb blood pressure control and taste.
nucleus-of-solitary-tract.location: Dorsolateral medulla, beside the solitary tract, lateral to the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus.
function: Receives taste from cranial nerves VII, IX, and X
Receives visceral input from the heart, lungs, and gut
Relays baroreceptor and chemoreceptor signals
nucleus-of-solitary-tract.connections: Projects to the reticular formation, hypothalamus, ventral posteromedial thalamus (taste), and vagal motor nuclei.

nucleus-of-trochlear-nerve.name: Nucleus of Trochlear Nerve
nucleus-of-trochlear-nerve.summary: A small motor nucleus in the midbrain at the level of the inferior colliculus. It supplies the superior oblique muscle of the opposite eye.
nucleus-of-trochlear-nerve.clinical: Damage causes vertical double vision and a head tilt away from the affected eye. The fourth nerve is the longest intracranial nerve.
nucleus-of-trochlear-nerve.location: Caudal midbrain tegmentum at the inferior colliculus level, just below the oculomotor nucleus.
function: Moves the eye down and in via the superior oblique muscle of the opposite side
blood: Perforating branches of the basilar tip
nucleus-of-trochlear-nerve.connections: Axons curve dorsally, cross in the superior medullary velum, and exit behind the brainstem. It is the only cranial nerve to exit dorsally.

occipital-pole.name: Occipital Pole
occipital-pole.summary: The rounded posterior tip of each cerebral hemisphere, formed by the occipital lobe.
occipital-pole.clinical: Damage here causes a central blind spot. Macular sparing in posterior cerebral artery stroke occurs because the pole also gets middle cerebral flow.
occipital-pole.location: Most posterior tip of the occipital lobe, behind the lunate and transverse occipital sulci.
function: Processes central (macular) vision
Part of primary and secondary visual cortex

occipitotemporal-sulcus-lateral-part.name: Occipitotemporal Sulcus (Lateral Part)
occipitotemporal-sulcus-lateral-part.summary: A long sulcus on the underside of the temporal lobe. It separates the fusiform gyrus from the inferior temporal gyrus.
occipitotemporal-sulcus-lateral-part.clinical: Its landmark role helps surgeons and imaging readers locate the fusiform gyrus, which handles face recognition.
occipitotemporal-sulcus-lateral-part.location: Inferior surface of the temporal and occipital lobes, lateral to the fusiform gyrus.
function: Surface landmark between fusiform and inferior temporal gyri
Adds cortical surface area through folding

olfactory-sulcus.name: Olfactory Sulcus
olfactory-sulcus.summary: A straight groove on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe. It holds the olfactory bulb and tract.
olfactory-sulcus.clinical: A tumor here, such as an olfactory groove meningioma, can cause loss of smell. Head trauma may tear the olfactory fibers.
olfactory-sulcus.location: Orbital (underside) surface of the frontal lobe, lateral to the gyrus rectus.
function: Houses the olfactory bulb and tract
Separates the gyrus rectus from the orbital gyri

olive.name: Olive
olive.summary: An oval bulge on the side of the upper medulla, lateral to the pyramid. It overlies the inferior olivary nucleus.
olive.clinical: Damage to the olivary-red nucleus-cerebellar loop can cause palatal tremor and later olivary enlargement.
olive.location: Anterolateral medulla, between the pyramid and the rootlets of the glossopharyngeal, vagus, and accessory nerves.
function: Houses the inferior olivary nucleus
Sends climbing fibers to the cerebellum for motor learning
olive.connections: Olivary axons cross and enter the opposite cerebellum through the inferior cerebellar peduncle.

opercular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.name: Opercular Part of Inferior Frontal Gyrus
opercular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.summary: The posterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, in front of the precentral gyrus. It forms part of Broca area (Brodmann area 44).
opercular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.clinical: Damage in the dominant hemisphere can cause Broca aphasia, with halting, effortful speech but fairly good comprehension.
opercular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.location: Lateral frontal lobe, above the lateral sulcus, behind the triangular part and in front of the inferior precentral sulcus.
function: Speech production and motor planning for speech
Syntax and language processing
blood: Middle cerebral artery (superior division, precentral branch)

optic-chiasm.name: Optic Chiasm
optic-chiasm.summary: An X-shaped crossing of the two optic nerves, where fibers from the inner (nasal) half of each retina cross.
optic-chiasm.clinical: Pituitary tumors press on it from below and cause bitemporal hemianopia, loss of the outer half of both visual fields.
optic-chiasm.location: Above the pituitary gland, in front of the infundibulum, at the floor of the third ventricle.
function: Sends information from each visual field to the opposite hemisphere
Allows combined input from both eyes
optic-chiasm.connections: Receives the optic nerves and continues as the optic tracts. Nasal retinal fibers cross, temporal retinal fibers stay on the same side.

optic-tract.name: Optic Tract
optic-tract.summary: A band of fibers that carries visual information from the optic chiasm around the cerebral peduncle to the lateral geniculate body.
optic-tract.clinical: A lesion causes loss of the opposite half of the visual field in both eyes (contralateral homonymous hemianopia).
optic-tract.location: From the posterior chiasm, around the side of the hypothalamus and cerebral peduncle, to the thalamus.
function: Carries opposite visual field information from both eyes
Sends fibers to the superior colliculus and pretectum for reflexes
optic-tract.connections: Most fibers end in the lateral geniculate body. Others reach the pretectal area and the superior colliculus.

orbital-gyri-frontomarginal-gyrus-and-su.name: Orbital Gyri (Frontomarginal Gyrus and Sulcus)
orbital-gyri-frontomarginal-gyrus-and-su.summary: A small gyrus and sulcus near the frontal pole at the edge of the orbital surface. It is a minor, variable cortical feature.
orbital-gyri-frontomarginal-gyrus-and-su.clinical: No specific clinical syndrome. Damage to nearby orbitofrontal cortex can cause disinhibition and poor judgment.
orbital-gyri-frontomarginal-gyrus-and-su.location: Front edge of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe, near the frontal pole.
function: Surface landmark of the anterior orbitofrontal region
Part of orbitofrontal cortex
blood: Anterior cerebral artery (frontopolar and orbitofrontal branches)

orbital-gyri.name: Orbital Gyri
orbital-gyri.summary: The group of gyri on the underside of the frontal lobe, resting on the orbital roof. They are the medial, anterior, lateral, and posterior orbital gyri.
orbital-gyri.clinical: Injury, often from head trauma, can cause disinhibition, poor judgment, and loss of smell.
orbital-gyri.location: Orbital (inferior) surface of the frontal lobe, above the orbital roof, lateral to the olfactory sulcus.
function: Reward, emotion, and decision-making (orbitofrontal cortex)
Taste and smell integration

orbital-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.name: Orbital Part of Inferior Frontal Gyrus
orbital-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.summary: The lowest and most anterior part of the inferior frontal gyrus, below the triangular part (Brodmann area 47).
orbital-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.clinical: Involved in language meaning. Damage in the dominant hemisphere can affect word retrieval and meaning.
orbital-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyrus.location: Lateral and orbital frontal lobe, below the anterior horizontal ramus of the lateral sulcus.
function: Semantic processing of language
Selecting among competing word meanings
blood: Middle cerebral artery (inferior division, orbitofrontal branches)

orbital-sulci-h-shaped-orbital-sulci.name: Orbital Sulci (H-Shaped Orbital Sulci)
orbital-sulci-h-shaped-orbital-sulci.summary: A set of grooves on the orbital surface of the frontal lobe that form an H shape. They divide the orbital gyri.
orbital-sulci-h-shaped-orbital-sulci.clinical: Their pattern varies between people, which is a point of attention in surgery or imaging of the orbitofrontal area.
orbital-sulci-h-shaped-orbital-sulci.location: Orbital surface of the frontal lobe, lateral to the olfactory sulcus.
function: Separate medial, anterior, lateral, and posterior orbital gyri
Landmarks of the orbitofrontal cortex

orbital-sulci-lateral-orbital-sulcus.name: Orbital Sulci (Lateral Orbital Sulcus)
orbital-sulci-lateral-orbital-sulcus.summary: The outer limb of the H-shaped orbital sulci. It separates the lateral orbital gyrus from the more medial gyri.
orbital-sulci-lateral-orbital-sulcus.clinical: No specific clinical syndrome. It serves as a landmark for orbitofrontal cortex.
orbital-sulci-lateral-orbital-sulcus.location: Lateral part of the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
function: Surface landmark of the orbital gyri
Adds cortical surface area through folding

paracentral-gyrus-and-sulcus.name: Paracentral Gyrus and Sulcus
paracentral-gyrus-and-sulcus.summary: The part of the paracentral lobule and its adjoining groove on the medial surface of the hemisphere, around the end of the central sulcus.
paracentral-gyrus-and-sulcus.clinical: Anterior cerebral artery stroke here causes weakness and sensory loss in the opposite leg and foot, with possible bladder control problems.
paracentral-gyrus-and-sulcus.location: Medial surface of the hemisphere, above the cingulate sulcus, where the central sulcus reaches the top edge.
function: Motor control of the opposite leg and foot
Sensation from the opposite leg and foot
Bladder and bowel control
blood: Anterior cerebral artery (paracentral branch of the callosomarginal artery)

paracentral-sulcus.name: Paracentral Sulcus
paracentral-sulcus.summary: A groove on the medial surface of the frontal lobe. It lies in front of the paracentral lobule and branches off the cingulate sulcus.
paracentral-sulcus.clinical: No specific syndrome. It is a landmark for finding the medial motor and sensory leg area.
paracentral-sulcus.location: Medial surface of the hemisphere, rising from the cingulate sulcus in front of the paracentral lobule.
function: Separates the paracentral lobule from the superior frontal gyrus
Surface landmark on the medial hemisphere

parieto-occipital-sulcus.name: Parieto-occipital Sulcus
parieto-occipital-sulcus.summary: A deep groove on the medial surface of the hemisphere. It separates the parietal precuneus from the occipital cuneus.
parieto-occipital-sulcus.clinical: It is a key landmark on brain scans for the boundary between parietal and occipital lobes.
parieto-occipital-sulcus.location: Medial surface of the hemisphere, joining the calcarine sulcus at a Y-shaped junction.
function: Boundary between parietal and occipital lobes
Separates the precuneus from the cuneus
parieto-occipital-sulcus.connections: Meets the calcarine sulcus to form a Y. The cuneus lies between the two.

pons.name: Pons
pons.summary: The middle part of the brainstem, between the midbrain and medulla. Its bulging front surface carries fibers to the cerebellum.
pons.clinical: A basilar artery stroke can cause locked-in syndrome, with paralysis of all limbs but preserved eye movements and awareness.
pons.location: Brainstem, in front of the cerebellum and fourth ventricle, in the posterior cranial fossa.
function: Relays cortical information to the cerebellum
Contains nuclei of cranial nerves V to VIII
Helps regulate breathing
pons.connections: Pontine nuclei send crossing fibers into the opposite cerebellum through the middle cerebellar peduncle.

postcentral-gyrus.name: Postcentral Gyrus
postcentral-gyrus.summary: The gyrus just behind the central sulcus. It is the primary somatosensory cortex (Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2).
postcentral-gyrus.clinical: Damage causes loss of touch, position sense, and discrimination on the opposite side of the body.
postcentral-gyrus.location: Anterior parietal lobe, between the central sulcus and the postcentral sulcus.
function: Receives touch, pressure, and position sense
Arranged as a sensory map of the body (homunculus)
blood: Middle cerebral artery (lateral surface, face and arm)
postcentral-gyrus.connections: Receives input from the ventral posterior nuclei of the thalamus.

postcentral-sulcus.name: Postcentral Sulcus
postcentral-sulcus.summary: The groove that forms the back edge of the postcentral gyrus. It often joins the intraparietal sulcus.
postcentral-sulcus.clinical: A landmark for locating the primary sensory cortex on scans and during surgery.
postcentral-sulcus.location: Lateral surface of the parietal lobe, behind the postcentral gyrus.
function: Separates the postcentral gyrus from the superior and inferior parietal lobules
Surface landmark
blood: Middle cerebral artery (postcentral and anterior parietal branches)

posterior-cochlear-nucleus.name: Posterior Cochlear Nucleus
posterior-cochlear-nucleus.summary: The auditory nucleus on the back surface of the inferior cerebellar peduncle. Cochlear nerve fibers synapse here first.
posterior-cochlear-nucleus.clinical: Damage to the cochlear nerve or nuclei causes hearing loss on the same side. Central lesions rarely cause one-sided deafness.
posterior-cochlear-nucleus.location: Pontomedullary junction, on the dorsolateral surface of the inferior cerebellar peduncle.
function: First relay for high-frequency hearing signals
Helps analyze sound quality and pitch
posterior-cochlear-nucleus.connections: Projects across the midline through the dorsal acoustic stria to the lateral lemniscus and inferior colliculus.

posterior-commissure.name: Posterior Commissure
posterior-commissure.summary: A small bundle of crossing fibers at the junction of the third ventricle and the cerebral aqueduct, just below the pineal gland.
posterior-commissure.clinical: Pineal tumors can compress it and cause Parinaud syndrome, with loss of upward gaze and abnormal pupil responses.
posterior-commissure.location: Posterior wall of the third ventricle, above the opening of the cerebral aqueduct and below the pineal recess.
function: Carries crossing fibers for the consensual pupillary light reflex
Connects centers for vertical eye movements
posterior-commissure.connections: Links the pretectal nuclei of both sides, and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal and nuclei involved in vertical gaze.

posterior-nucleus-of-vagus-nerve.name: Posterior Nucleus of Vagus Nerve
posterior-nucleus-of-vagus-nerve.summary: The parasympathetic motor nucleus of the vagus nerve, in the floor of the fourth ventricle in the medulla.
posterior-nucleus-of-vagus-nerve.clinical: Vagal injury can alter heart rate and gut movement. Vagotomy was once used to reduce stomach acid.
posterior-nucleus-of-vagus-nerve.location: Dorsal medulla, beneath the vagal trigone in the floor of the fourth ventricle.
function: Sends parasympathetic fibers to the thoracic and abdominal organs
Controls gut motility and glandular secretion
Slows the heart together with the nucleus ambiguus
posterior-nucleus-of-vagus-nerve.connections: Receives input from the nucleus of the solitary tract and hypothalamus. Its fibers reach organs up to the left colic flexure.

precentral-gyrus.name: Precentral Gyrus
precentral-gyrus.summary: The gyrus just in front of the central sulcus. It is the primary motor cortex (Brodmann area 4).
precentral-gyrus.clinical: A stroke or lesion causes weakness or paralysis of the opposite side. Irritation can cause focal motor seizures that spread along the body map.
precentral-gyrus.location: Posterior frontal lobe, between the precentral sulcus and the central sulcus.
function: Controls voluntary movement of the opposite side
Arranged as a motor map of the body (homunculus)
blood: Middle cerebral artery (lateral surface, face and arm)
precentral-gyrus.connections: Upper motor neurons here form the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts.

precentral-sulcus-inferior-part.name: Precentral Sulcus (Inferior Part)
precentral-sulcus-inferior-part.summary: The lower part of the groove in front of the precentral gyrus. It lies next to the pars opercularis of Broca area.
precentral-sulcus-inferior-part.clinical: A landmark when mapping motor and speech areas during brain surgery.
precentral-sulcus-inferior-part.location: Lateral surface of the frontal lobe, in front of the lower precentral gyrus.
function: Separates the lower precentral gyrus from the inferior frontal gyrus
Surface landmark
blood: Middle cerebral artery (precentral and prerolandic branches)

precentral-sulcus-superior-part.name: Precentral Sulcus (Superior Part)
precentral-sulcus-superior-part.summary: The upper part of the groove in front of the precentral gyrus. It meets the superior frontal sulcus, near the frontal eye field.
precentral-sulcus-superior-part.clinical: A landmark for the frontal eye field, which controls voluntary eye movements toward the opposite side.
precentral-sulcus-superior-part.location: Lateral surface of the frontal lobe, in front of the upper precentral gyrus.
function: Separates the upper precentral gyrus from the middle frontal gyrus
Surface landmark

precuneus.name: Precuneus
precuneus.summary: The square-shaped part of the medial parietal lobe, between the paracentral lobule and the parieto-occipital sulcus.
precuneus.clinical: Reduced activity here is an early sign on imaging in Alzheimer disease.
precuneus.location: Medial surface of the parietal lobe, above the subparietal sulcus and in front of the parieto-occipital sulcus.
function: Visuospatial imagery and self-related thinking
Episodic memory retrieval
Part of the default mode network

putamen.name: Putamen
putamen.summary: The larger, outer part of the lentiform nucleus. Together with the caudate nucleus it forms the dorsal striatum.
putamen.clinical: A common site of hypertensive brain hemorrhage. Degeneration is involved in Parkinson and Huntington disease.
putamen.location: Deep in the cerebral hemisphere, lateral to the internal capsule and medial to the external capsule.
function: Planning and smooth control of movement
Part of the motor loop with the cortex and thalamus
blood: Lateral lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery
putamen.connections: Receives cortical and nigral input. Projects to the globus pallidus.

pyramid-of-medulla-oblongata.name: Pyramid of Medulla Oblongata
pyramid-of-medulla-oblongata.summary: A paired ridge on the front of the medulla formed by the corticospinal tracts.
pyramid-of-medulla-oblongata.clinical: A stroke in the medial medulla causes opposite-side weakness of the arm and leg, with weakness of the tongue on the same side.
pyramid-of-medulla-oblongata.location: Anteromedial medulla, on either side of the anterior median fissure.
function: Carries corticospinal fibers to the spinal cord
Site of the pyramidal decussation at its lower end
pyramid-of-medulla-oblongata.connections: About 75 to 90 percent of fibers cross in the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract.

red-nucleus.name: Red Nucleus
red-nucleus.summary: A rounded nucleus in the midbrain tegmentum. It looks pink in fresh tissue because of its rich blood supply and iron content.
red-nucleus.clinical: Damage can cause an opposite-side tremor, as in Benedikt syndrome, along with an oculomotor palsy on the same side.
red-nucleus.location: Midbrain tegmentum at the level of the superior colliculus, near the substantia nigra.
function: Relay for cerebellar output to motor pathways
Gives rise to the rubrospinal tract
blood: Paramedian branches of the basilar tip
red-nucleus.connections: Receives from the opposite dentate nucleus via the superior cerebellar peduncle. The rubrospinal tract crosses and influences flexor tone in the arm.

septal-nuclei.name: Septal Nuclei
septal-nuclei.summary: A group of nuclei at the base of the septum pellucidum, in front of the anterior commissure. They are part of the limbic system.
septal-nuclei.clinical: Linked to reward and emotion. Damage in animals causes rage, and in humans it may alter mood or reward response.
septal-nuclei.location: Medial basal forebrain, below the rostrum of the corpus callosum and in front of the anterior commissure.
function: Reward and pleasure circuits
Regulate emotion and autonomic responses
Link the hippocampus with the hypothalamus
blood: Anterior cerebral artery (medial striate and anterior communicating branches)
septal-nuclei.connections: Connects with the hippocampus via the fornix and with the habenula via the stria medullaris.

septum-pellucidum.name: Septum Pellucidum
septum-pellucidum.summary: A thin, double-layered membrane between the two lateral ventricles. It stretches from the corpus callosum down to the fornix.
septum-pellucidum.clinical: A fluid-filled gap between its layers (cavum septum pellucidum) is common in infants. Absence may suggest midline malformations.
septum-pellucidum.location: Midline, between the frontal horns and bodies of the lateral ventricles, below the corpus callosum.
function: Separates the two lateral ventricles
Forms the medial wall of the frontal horns
septum-pellucidum.connections: Contains the septal nuclei at its base and attaches to the fornix below.

straight-gyrus-gyrus-rectus.name: Straight Gyrus (Gyrus Rectus)
straight-gyrus-gyrus-rectus.summary: A narrow gyrus on the inferior surface of the frontal lobe, along the longitudinal fissure, medial to the olfactory sulcus.
straight-gyrus-gyrus-rectus.clinical: Often involved in olfactory groove tumors and frontal trauma, which can cause smell loss and personality change.
straight-gyrus-gyrus-rectus.location: Orbital (inferior) surface of the frontal lobe, next to the longitudinal fissure.
function: Part of orbitofrontal cortex
Takes part in emotion and decision-making
blood: Anterior cerebral artery (orbitofrontal and frontopolar branches)

stria-medullaris-thalami.name: Stria Medullaris Thalami
stria-medullaris-thalami.summary: A white matter band along the upper medial edge of the thalamus. It carries fibers to the habenula.
stria-medullaris-thalami.clinical: It links the limbic system with the habenula, which is of interest in mood disorders.
stria-medullaris-thalami.location: Along the junction of the medial and dorsal surfaces of the thalamus, beside the third ventricle.
function: Carries input from the septal nuclei and hypothalamus to the habenula
Part of a limbic pathway to the brainstem
stria-medullaris-thalami.connections: Ends in the habenular nuclei. Fibers cross to the opposite side through the habenular commissure.

stria-terminalis.name: Stria Terminalis
stria-terminalis.summary: A C-shaped fiber bundle that runs from the amygdala along the groove between the caudate nucleus and thalamus.
stria-terminalis.clinical: It carries emotional and stress signals from the amygdala. It is a key pathway in fear and anxiety circuits.
stria-terminalis.location: Floor of the lateral ventricle, in the groove between the thalamus and caudate nucleus, beside the thalamostriate vein.
function: Carries amygdala output to the hypothalamus and septal area
Links to the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis
stria-terminalis.connections: Runs from the amygdala, arches over the thalamus, and ends in the hypothalamus, septal nuclei, and bed nucleus.

subparietal-sulcus.name: Subparietal Sulcus
subparietal-sulcus.summary: A groove on the medial surface of the parietal lobe. It separates the precuneus from the cingulate gyrus below it.
subparietal-sulcus.clinical: A landmark for locating the precuneus and posterior cingulate region on brain scans.
subparietal-sulcus.location: Medial surface of the hemisphere, above the posterior cingulate gyrus and below the precuneus.
function: Boundary between the precuneus and the cingulate gyrus
Surface landmark

sulcus-interm-prim-jensen.name: Sulcus Intermedius Primus (Jensen)
sulcus-interm-prim-jensen.summary: A short groove that branches from the intraparietal sulcus into the inferior parietal lobule. It marks the border between the supramarginal and angular gyri.
sulcus-interm-prim-jensen.clinical: A landmark for locating the angular gyrus, whose damage in the dominant hemisphere can cause reading and writing problems.
sulcus-interm-prim-jensen.location: Lateral surface of the parietal lobe, in the inferior parietal lobule, rising from the intraparietal sulcus.
function: Separates the supramarginal gyrus from the angular gyrus
Surface landmark
blood: Middle cerebral artery (posterior parietal and angular branches)

superior-cerebellar-peduncle.name: Superior Cerebellar Peduncle
superior-cerebellar-peduncle.summary: A thick fiber bundle connecting the cerebellum to the midbrain. It is the main output pathway of the cerebellum.
superior-cerebellar-peduncle.clinical: Damage causes limb tremor and poor coordination on the same side as the lesion (ataxia).
superior-cerebellar-peduncle.location: Between the cerebellum and the upper pons and midbrain, forming the upper lateral wall of the fourth ventricle.
function: Carries cerebellar output to the red nucleus and thalamus
Carries some input from the spinal cord (ventral spinocerebellar tract)
superior-cerebellar-peduncle.connections: Fibers from the dentate nucleus cross in the midbrain (decussation) and go to the opposite red nucleus and thalamus.

superior-colliculus.name: Superior Colliculus
superior-colliculus.summary: One of two paired bumps on the upper tectum of the midbrain. It directs quick eye and head movements toward visual targets.
superior-colliculus.clinical: Pressure from pineal tumors on this area can cause Parinaud syndrome, with loss of upward gaze.
superior-colliculus.location: Dorsal midbrain, above the inferior colliculus and below the pineal gland.
function: Controls rapid eye movements (saccades)
Directs the head and eyes toward visual stimuli
Receives retinal and visual cortex input
superior-colliculus.connections: Projects to the spinal cord through the tectospinal tract and to brainstem gaze centers. Receives input from the optic tract through the brachium.

superior-frontal-gyrus.name: Superior Frontal Gyrus
superior-frontal-gyrus.summary: The uppermost frontal gyrus, running along the top edge of the hemisphere above the superior frontal sulcus. It extends onto the medial surface.
superior-frontal-gyrus.clinical: Damage to the supplementary motor area on its medial part can cause temporary loss of speech and weakness on the opposite side.
superior-frontal-gyrus.location: Upper lateral and medial frontal lobe, above the superior frontal sulcus.
function: Planning and starting movement (supplementary motor area, posterior part)
Executive functions and self-awareness

superior-frontal-sulcus.name: Superior Frontal Sulcus
superior-frontal-sulcus.summary: A groove running forward from the precentral sulcus. It separates the superior frontal gyrus from the middle frontal gyrus.
superior-frontal-sulcus.clinical: A landmark used on scans and in surgery to find the frontal eye field and prefrontal areas.
superior-frontal-sulcus.location: Lateral surface of the frontal lobe, running front to back above the middle frontal gyrus.
function: Separates the superior and middle frontal gyri
Surface landmark
blood: Middle cerebral artery (prefrontal and precentral branches)

superior-occipital-gyri.name: Superior Occipital Gyri
superior-occipital-gyri.summary: The gyri on the upper lateral surface of the occipital lobe. They form part of the visual association cortex.
superior-occipital-gyri.clinical: Damage can impair visual processing, such as motion or spatial awareness, without total blindness.
superior-occipital-gyri.location: Upper lateral occipital lobe, above the lateral occipital sulcus and behind the transverse occipital sulcus.
function: Visual association processing
Spatial vision and the dorsal visual stream

superior-parietal-lobule.name: Superior Parietal Lobule
superior-parietal-lobule.summary: The part of the parietal lobe above the intraparietal sulcus and behind the postcentral gyrus (Brodmann areas 5 and 7).
superior-parietal-lobule.clinical: Damage can cause trouble recognizing objects by touch (astereognosis) and difficulty reaching for things (optic ataxia).
superior-parietal-lobule.location: Posterior superior parietal lobe, above the intraparietal sulcus.
function: Integrates touch and position sense
Guides reaching and hand movements
Spatial attention

superior-salivatory-nucleus.name: Superior Salivatory Nucleus
superior-salivatory-nucleus.summary: A parasympathetic nucleus in the pons. It controls tear and salivary gland secretion via the facial nerve.
superior-salivatory-nucleus.clinical: Facial nerve damage near the geniculate ganglion can reduce tearing and salivation on the same side.
superior-salivatory-nucleus.location: Pontine tegmentum, near the facial motor nucleus and the nucleus of the solitary tract.
function: Drives the lacrimal gland (tears)
Drives the submandibular and sublingual glands (saliva)
Drives nasal and palatine glands
blood: Pontine branches of the basilar artery
superior-salivatory-nucleus.connections: Fibers travel in the nervus intermedius. Some go via the greater petrosal nerve, others via the chorda tympani.

superior-temporal-gyrus-lateral-part.name: Superior Temporal Gyrus (Lateral Part)
superior-temporal-gyrus-lateral-part.summary: The uppermost gyrus on the lateral surface of the temporal lobe, below the lateral sulcus. Its rear part contains Wernicke area.
superior-temporal-gyrus-lateral-part.clinical: Damage to the posterior part in the dominant hemisphere causes Wernicke aphasia, with fluent but meaningless speech and poor comprehension.
superior-temporal-gyrus-lateral-part.location: Lateral surface of the temporal lobe, between the lateral sulcus and the superior temporal sulcus.
function: Auditory association and speech comprehension (Wernicke area, posterior part)
Processing of complex sounds
blood: Middle cerebral artery (inferior division, temporal branches)

superior-temporal-sulcus.name: Superior Temporal Sulcus
superior-temporal-sulcus.summary: A long groove on the lateral temporal lobe that separates the superior and middle temporal gyri.
superior-temporal-sulcus.clinical: Its cortex helps read faces, voices, and body movement. Differences here are studied in autism research.
superior-temporal-sulcus.location: Lateral surface of the temporal lobe, running parallel to the lateral sulcus.
function: Separates the superior and middle temporal gyri
Cortex within it processes social and biological motion cues

supramarginal-gyrus.name: Supramarginal Gyrus
supramarginal-gyrus.summary: A gyrus of the inferior parietal lobule that arches over the end of the lateral sulcus (Brodmann area 40).
supramarginal-gyrus.clinical: Damage in the dominant hemisphere can cause conduction aphasia and apraxia. Right-sided damage can contribute to neglect.
supramarginal-gyrus.location: Inferior parietal lobule, curving around the posterior end of the lateral sulcus.
function: Language processing (phonology) on the dominant side
Touch and body awareness
Skilled movement planning
blood: Middle cerebral artery (inferior division, posterior parietal branches)

temporal-plane.name: Temporal Plane
temporal-plane.latin: Facies superior gyri temporalis superioris (planum temporale)
temporal-plane.summary: The flat upper surface of the temporal lobe, buried inside the lateral sulcus. It holds the transverse temporal gyri and the planum temporale.
temporal-plane.clinical: The planum temporale is usually larger on the left, linked to language. It is not seen without opening the lateral sulcus.
temporal-plane.location: Superior surface of the temporal lobe, hidden within the lateral sulcus.
function: Primary and secondary auditory processing
Language-related sound analysis
blood: Middle cerebral artery (inferior division, temporal branches)

thalamus.name: Thalamus
thalamus.summary: A pair of egg-shaped gray matter masses on either side of the third ventricle. They relay most sensory and motor information to the cortex.
thalamus.clinical: A thalamic stroke can cause loss of sensation on the opposite side, and later severe burning pain (Dejerine-Roussy syndrome).
thalamus.location: Center of the brain, on both sides of the third ventricle, above the hypothalamus and medial to the internal capsule.
function: Relays sensory input to the cortex (except smell)
Relays motor information from the cerebellum and basal ganglia
Regulates alertness and consciousness
thalamus.connections: Linked to the cortex through the internal capsule. The two thalami are often joined by the interthalamic adhesion.

third-ventricle.name: Third Ventricle
third-ventricle.summary: A narrow, slit-like CSF space in the midline between the two thalami and hypothalamus.
third-ventricle.clinical: A colloid cyst can block the interventricular foramen and cause sudden hydrocephalus with headache.
third-ventricle.location: Midline, between the thalami, with the hypothalamus forming its lower walls.
function: Carries cerebrospinal fluid between the lateral ventricles and the cerebral aqueduct
Holds choroid plexus in its roof
third-ventricle.connections: Receives CSF from the lateral ventricles via the interventricular foramina and drains through the cerebral aqueduct to the fourth ventricle.

transverse-frontopolar-gyrus-and-sulcus.name: Transverse Frontopolar Gyrus and Sulcus
transverse-frontopolar-gyrus-and-sulcus.summary: A small gyrus and sulcus at the front tip of the frontal lobe. They are minor and variable surface features.
transverse-frontopolar-gyrus-and-sulcus.clinical: No specific syndrome. Damage to the frontal pole can cause changes in planning and social behavior.
transverse-frontopolar-gyrus-and-sulcus.location: Frontal pole, the anterior tip of the frontal lobe.
function: Surface landmark of the frontal pole
Part of the anterior prefrontal cortex

transverse-occipital-sulcus.name: Transverse Occipital Sulcus
transverse-occipital-sulcus.summary: A groove on the upper lateral surface of the occipital lobe. It often continues backward from the intraparietal sulcus.
transverse-occipital-sulcus.clinical: No specific syndrome. It is a landmark for the boundary between the parietal and occipital cortex.
transverse-occipital-sulcus.location: Upper lateral surface of the occipital lobe, near the border with the parietal lobe.
function: Surface landmark for parietal and occipital areas
Adds cortical surface area through folding

transverse-temporal-gyri.name: Transverse Temporal Gyri
transverse-temporal-gyri.summary: One or more gyri running diagonally across the temporal plane inside the lateral sulcus. They hold the primary auditory cortex (Brodmann areas 41 and 42).
transverse-temporal-gyri.clinical: Damage on one side reduces sound localization on the opposite side. Damage on both sides can cause cortical deafness.
transverse-temporal-gyri.location: Superior surface of the temporal lobe, buried in the lateral sulcus.
function: Primary auditory cortex
Receives sound information organized by pitch
blood: Middle cerebral artery (inferior division, temporal branches)
transverse-temporal-gyri.connections: Receives input from the medial geniculate body through the acoustic radiation.

triangular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyru.name: Triangular Part of Inferior Frontal Gyrus
triangular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyru.summary: The triangle-shaped middle part of the inferior frontal gyrus (Brodmann area 45). With the opercular part, it forms Broca area.
triangular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyru.clinical: Damage in the dominant hemisphere contributes to Broca aphasia, with slow, effortful speech.
triangular-part-of-inferior-frontal-gyru.location: Lateral frontal lobe, between the ascending and anterior horizontal rami of the lateral sulcus.
function: Language production and word selection
Semantic and grammar processing
blood: Middle cerebral artery (superior division, prefrontal branches)

vestibular-nuclei.name: Vestibular Nuclei
vestibular-nuclei.summary: A group of four nuclei (superior, medial, lateral, inferior) at the pons and medulla border. They process balance and head position.
vestibular-nuclei.clinical: Damage causes vertigo, nystagmus, and unsteadiness. Brainstem stroke can mimic inner ear disease.
vestibular-nuclei.location: Floor of the fourth ventricle at the pontomedullary junction, beneath the vestibular area.
function: Maintain balance and posture
Coordinate eye movements with head movements (vestibulo-ocular reflex)
Adjust muscle tone to keep the body upright
vestibular-nuclei.connections: Send fibers via the medial longitudinal fasciculus to eye muscle nuclei and via the vestibulospinal tracts to the spinal cord. Also connect with the cerebellum.

white-matter-of-telencephalon.name: White Matter of Telencephalon
white-matter-of-telencephalon.summary: The bundles of myelinated nerve fibers beneath the cerebral cortex. They connect cortical areas to each other and to deeper structures.
white-matter-of-telencephalon.clinical: Damage, as in multiple sclerosis or small-vessel disease, disrupts communication between brain regions and appears as white spots on MRI.
white-matter-of-telencephalon.location: Deep to the cerebral cortex in both hemispheres, around the lateral ventricles and basal ganglia.
function: Connects regions within one hemisphere (association fibers)
Connects the two hemispheres (commissural fibers)
Carries fibers to and from the brainstem (projection fibers)

acromioclavicular-joint-s-capsule.name: Acromioclavicular Joint Capsule
acromioclavicular-joint-s-capsule.summary: A thin fibrous sleeve that surrounds the joint between the collarbone and the acromion. Its upper part is thickened by the acromioclavicular ligament.
acromioclavicular-joint-s-capsule.clinical: A fall onto the point of the shoulder can tear the capsule and its ligaments, causing a shoulder separation.
attachments: Margin of the acromial end of the clavicle → margin of the acromion's articular surface
