acromioclavicular-joint-s-capsule.function: Encloses the joint and holds the clavicle and acromion together while allowing small gliding and rotating movements.

acromioclavicular-ligament.name: Acromioclavicular Ligament
acromioclavicular-ligament.summary: A strong band on the top of the joint that reinforces the capsule. It runs from the clavicle to the acromion.
acromioclavicular-ligament.clinical: A mild shoulder separation (grade I) sprains only this ligament. A higher grade also tears the coracoclavicular ligaments.
attachments: Upper surface of the acromial end of the clavicle → upper surface of the acromion
acromioclavicular-ligament.function: Reinforces the top of the capsule and resists forward and backward displacement of the clavicle.

annular-ligament-of-radius.name: Annular Ligament of Radius
annular-ligament-of-radius.summary: A strong fibrous band that wraps around the head of the radius. It forms about four-fifths of a ring, completed by the radial notch of the ulna.
annular-ligament-of-radius.clinical: In young children, a sudden pull on the hand can slip the radial head out of this ligament. This is called nursemaid's elbow.
annular-ligament-of-radius.joint: Proximal radio-ulnar joint (inside the elbow joint capsule)
attachments: Anterior margin of the radial notch of the ulna → around the head and neck of the radius → posterior margin of the radial notch
annular-ligament-of-radius.function: Holds the radial head against the ulna while letting the radius rotate during pronation and supination.

anterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.name: Anterior Sternoclavicular Ligament
anterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.summary: A broad band that reinforces the front of the sternoclavicular joint capsule.
anterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.clinical: Anterior dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint is the more common type. It leaves a visible bump at the medial end of the clavicle.
anterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.joint_type: Saddle-type synovial joint that functions like a ball-and-socket
attachments: Anterior surface of the medial end of the clavicle → anterior surface of the manubrium of the sternum
anterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.function: Reinforces the front of the capsule and helps stop the medial end of the clavicle from moving forward.

articular-capsule-of-elbow-joint.name: Articular Capsule of Elbow Joint
articular-capsule-of-elbow-joint.summary: A fibrous sleeve that encloses the humero-ulnar, humeroradial, and proximal radio-ulnar joints together. It is thin in front and behind and strengthened at the sides by the collateral ligaments.
articular-capsule-of-elbow-joint.clinical: Fluid or blood in the joint swells the capsule and pushes up the elbow fat pads. This can show on an X-ray after injury.
attachments: Humerus above the coronoid, radial, and olecranon fossae → coronoid process and olecranon of the ulna and the annular ligament
articular-capsule-of-elbow-joint.function: Encloses the elbow joint cavity and holds its bones together.

articular-capsule-of-glenohumeral-joint.name: Articular Capsule of Glenohumeral Joint
articular-capsule-of-glenohumeral-joint.summary: A loose, thin fibrous sleeve around the shoulder joint. It is reinforced by the glenohumeral ligaments and the rotator cuff tendons, and it hangs slack below as the axillary pouch.
articular-capsule-of-glenohumeral-joint.clinical: The lower capsule is the weakest part, so the humeral head usually dislocates forward and down. A stiff, thickened capsule causes frozen shoulder.
attachments: Margin of the glenoid cavity and labrum → anatomical neck of the humerus
articular-capsule-of-glenohumeral-joint.function: Encloses the joint. Its looseness allows the wide range of shoulder movement at the cost of stability.

articular-capsule-of-radiocarpal-joint.name: Articular Capsule of Radiocarpal Joint
articular-capsule-of-radiocarpal-joint.summary: A fibrous sleeve that encloses the wrist joint. It is strengthened by the dorsal and palmar radiocarpal ligaments and by the collateral ligaments.
articular-capsule-of-radiocarpal-joint.clinical: Ganglion cysts, often on the back of the wrist, commonly arise from this capsule.
attachments: Distal end of the radius and the articular disc of the distal radio-ulnar joint → proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum)
articular-capsule-of-radiocarpal-joint.function: Encloses the wrist joint and allows flexion, extension, and side-to-side tilting of the hand.

articular-capsule-of-sternoclavicular-jo.name: Articular Capsule of Sternoclavicular Joint
articular-capsule-of-sternoclavicular-jo.summary: A fibrous sleeve around the joint between the clavicle, the manubrium, and the first costal cartilage. The anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments thicken it.
articular-capsule-of-sternoclavicular-jo.clinical: This joint is the only bony link between the upper limb and the trunk. It is strong, so dislocation is uncommon.
articular-capsule-of-sternoclavicular-jo.joint_type: Saddle-type synovial joint that functions like a ball-and-socket
attachments: Margins of the medial end of the clavicle → margins of the manubrium and first costal cartilage
articular-capsule-of-sternoclavicular-jo.function: Encloses the joint and lets the clavicle move in several directions as the shoulder moves.

articular-disc-of-acromioclavicular-join.name: Articular Disc of Acromioclavicular Joint
articular-disc-of-acromioclavicular-join.summary: A small wedge of fibrocartilage between the clavicle and the acromion. It is often incomplete, and it is absent in some people.
articular-disc-of-acromioclavicular-join.clinical: The disc wears down early in life, which contributes to arthritis of this joint.
attachments: Between the acromial end of the clavicle and the acromion, attached to the joint capsule
articular-disc-of-acromioclavicular-join.function: Cushions the joint and helps the surfaces fit together.

articular-disc-of-distal-radio-ulnar-joi.name: Articular Disc of Distal Radio-ulnar Joint
articular-disc-of-distal-radio-ulnar-joi.summary: A triangular fibrocartilage disc that is the central part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex. It separates the head of the ulna from the carpal bones.
articular-disc-of-distal-radio-ulnar-joi.clinical: Tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex follow falls on the outstretched hand or twisting injuries. They cause pain on the little-finger side of the wrist.
attachments: Medial edge of the ulnar notch of the radius → base of the ulnar styloid process and the fovea of the ulnar head
articular-disc-of-distal-radio-ulnar-joi.function: Binds the radius to the ulna, absorbs load across the wrist, and keeps the ulna from contacting the carpus directly.

articular-disc-of-sternoclavicular-joint.name: Articular Disc of Sternoclavicular Joint
articular-disc-of-sternoclavicular-joint.summary: A flat fibrocartilage disc that divides the sternoclavicular joint cavity into two compartments.
articular-disc-of-sternoclavicular-joint.clinical: The disc absorbs force from falls on the shoulder or outstretched arm and helps protect the joint from dislocation.
articular-disc-of-sternoclavicular-joint.joint_type: Saddle-type synovial joint that functions like a ball-and-socket
attachments: Upper part of the medial end of the clavicle → junction of the first costal cartilage and the manubrium
articular-disc-of-sternoclavicular-joint.function: Acts as a shock absorber and prevents the clavicle from sliding medially.

conoid-ligament.name: Conoid Ligament
conoid-ligament.summary: The medial, cone-shaped part of the coracoclavicular ligament. It runs from the coracoid process up to the clavicle.
conoid-ligament.clinical: In a severe shoulder separation (grade III), the conoid and trapezoid ligaments tear and the clavicle rides up.
attachments: Root of the coracoid process of the scapula → conoid tubercle on the underside of the clavicle
conoid-ligament.function: Suspends the scapula from the clavicle and keeps the acromion from being driven below the clavicle.

coracohumeral-ligament.name: Coracohumeral Ligament
coracohumeral-ligament.summary: A broad band that strengthens the top of the shoulder capsule. It runs from the coracoid process to the greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus.
coracohumeral-ligament.clinical: Scarring and tightening of this ligament limits outward rotation of the arm in frozen shoulder.
attachments: Lateral side of the base of the coracoid process → greater and lesser tubercles of the humerus
coracohumeral-ligament.function: Reinforces the upper capsule, helps support the weight of the arm, and limits outward rotation and downward sliding of the humeral head.

dorsal-radiocarpal-ligament.name: Dorsal Radiocarpal Ligament
dorsal-radiocarpal-ligament.summary: A strong band on the back of the wrist that reinforces the joint capsule. It runs obliquely from the radius toward the proximal carpal bones.
dorsal-radiocarpal-ligament.clinical: Forced wrist flexion or a fall can sprain or tear it. It is also a site where ganglion cysts form.
attachments: Dorsal margin of the distal radius → dorsal surfaces of the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum
dorsal-radiocarpal-ligament.function: Strengthens the back of the capsule, links the radius to the carpus, and limits excessive wrist flexion.

glenoid-labrum.name: Glenoid Labrum
glenoid-labrum.summary: A ring of fibrocartilage attached to the rim of the glenoid cavity. It deepens the socket for the humeral head.
glenoid-labrum.clinical: A forward dislocation can tear the labrum from the lower glenoid rim (Bankart lesion). A tear at the top is a SLAP lesion.
attachments: Rim of the glenoid cavity of the scapula → free edge around the humeral head (biceps tendon blends in above)
glenoid-labrum.function: Deepens the socket, increases contact with the humeral head, and adds stability to the shoulder.

inferior-glenohumeral-ligament.name: Inferior Glenohumeral Ligament
inferior-glenohumeral-ligament.summary: The thickest of the glenohumeral ligaments, with anterior and posterior bands joined by a pouch below. It forms a hammock under the humeral head.
inferior-glenohumeral-ligament.clinical: It is the main restraint against forward dislocation when the arm is raised and rotated outward. It is often torn or stretched in dislocations.
attachments: Anterior, inferior, and posterior glenoid rim and labrum → lower part of the anatomical neck and surgical neck of the humerus
inferior-glenohumeral-ligament.function: Supports the humeral head from below and resists forward dislocation with the arm abducted and rotated outward.

interclavicular-ligament.name: Interclavicular Ligament
interclavicular-ligament.summary: A band that crosses the top of the manubrium between the two clavicles. It attaches loosely to the jugular notch.
interclavicular-ligament.clinical: It lies just above the jugular notch, where the trachea can be felt in the neck.
interclavicular-ligament.joint_type: Saddle-type synovial joint that functions like a ball-and-socket
attachments: Superior surface of the sternal end of one clavicle → jugular notch of the manubrium → sternal end of the opposite clavicle
interclavicular-ligament.function: Links the two clavicles and helps stop the shoulders from dropping.

interosseous-membrane-of-forearm.name: Interosseous Membrane of Forearm
interosseous-membrane-of-forearm.summary: A strong fibrous sheet that joins the shafts of the radius and ulna. Most of its fibers run obliquely down and toward the ulna.
interosseous-membrane-of-forearm.clinical: A fall on the outstretched hand drives force up the radius and across this membrane to the ulna. Severe tears with a radial head fracture are called Essex-Lopresti injuries.
attachments: Interosseous border of the radius → interosseous border of the ulna
interosseous-membrane-of-forearm.function: Holds the radius and ulna together, transmits force from the radius to the ulna, and gives origin to deep forearm muscles.

interosseus-membrane-of-forearm.name: Interosseus Membrane of Forearm
interosseus-membrane-of-forearm.summary: A strong fibrous sheet that joins the shafts of the radius and ulna. Most of its fibers run obliquely down and toward the ulna.
interosseus-membrane-of-forearm.clinical: A fall on the outstretched hand drives force up the radius and across this membrane to the ulna. Severe tears with a radial head fracture are called Essex-Lopresti injuries.
attachments: Interosseous border of the radius → interosseous border of the ulna
interosseus-membrane-of-forearm.function: Holds the radius and ulna together, transmits force from the radius to the ulna, and gives origin to deep forearm muscles.

middle-glenohumeral-ligament.name: Middle Glenohumeral Ligament
middle-glenohumeral-ligament.summary: A band on the front of the shoulder capsule, between the superior and inferior glenohumeral ligaments. Its size varies, and it is absent in some people.
middle-glenohumeral-ligament.clinical: It helps resist forward dislocation of the humeral head. Its thickness varies between individuals.
attachments: Anterior part of the glenoid rim and labrum → anterior surface of the anatomical neck of the humerus, near the lesser tubercle
middle-glenohumeral-ligament.function: Limits forward movement of the humeral head and outward rotation when the arm is partly raised.

palmar-radio-ulnar-ligament.name: Palmar Radio-ulnar Ligament
palmar-radio-ulnar-ligament.summary: A band on the palm side of the distal radio-ulnar joint. It joins the front edge of the articular disc and capsule.
palmar-radio-ulnar-ligament.clinical: Injury to the radio-ulnar ligaments with the disc destabilizes the joint and causes wrist pain with forearm rotation.
attachments: Palmar surface of the head and styloid base of the ulna → palmar margin of the ulnar notch of the radius
palmar-radio-ulnar-ligament.function: Stabilizes the distal radio-ulnar joint and keeps the radius and ulna aligned during forearm rotation.

posterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.name: Posterior Sternoclavicular Ligament
posterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.summary: A broad band that reinforces the back of the sternoclavicular joint capsule.
posterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.clinical: Posterior dislocation is rare but dangerous. The clavicle can press on the trachea, esophagus, or great vessels behind the manubrium.
posterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.joint_type: Saddle-type synovial joint that functions like a ball-and-socket
attachments: Posterior surface of the medial end of the clavicle → posterior surface of the manubrium of the sternum
posterior-sternoclavicular-ligament.function: Reinforces the back of the capsule and helps stop the medial end of the clavicle from moving backward.

radial-collateral-ligament.name: Radial Collateral Ligament
radial-collateral-ligament.summary: A fan-shaped band on the outer side of the elbow. It blends with the annular ligament of the radius.
radial-collateral-ligament.clinical: Damage after an elbow dislocation can cause posterolateral instability, where the elbow gives way when the forearm is turned palm up.
attachments: Lateral epicondyle of the humerus → annular ligament of the radius (and the supinator crest of the ulna by its deeper fibers)
radial-collateral-ligament.function: Resists forces that push the elbow into varus and keeps the radial head and ulna stable.

superior-glenohumeral-ligament.name: Superior Glenohumeral Ligament
superior-glenohumeral-ligament.summary: A small band in the upper front of the shoulder capsule. It lies beside the tendon of the long head of biceps.
superior-glenohumeral-ligament.clinical: With the coracohumeral ligament, it forms the rotator interval, which tightens in frozen shoulder.
attachments: Supraglenoid tubercle and upper labrum, near the biceps tendon → top of the lesser tubercle of the humerus (near the anatomical neck)
superior-glenohumeral-ligament.function: Resists downward sliding of the humeral head when the arm hangs at the side.

transverse-humeral-ligament.name: Transverse Humeral Ligament
transverse-humeral-ligament.summary: A thin band of fibers that bridges the intertubercular groove of the humerus. It is a thickening of the shoulder capsule.
transverse-humeral-ligament.clinical: If it is torn or lax, the tendon of the long head of biceps can slip out of its groove.
attachments: Greater tubercle of the humerus → lesser tubercle of the humerus, across the intertubercular groove
transverse-humeral-ligament.function: Holds the tendon of the long head of biceps in the intertubercular groove.

trapezoid-ligament.name: Trapezoid Ligament
trapezoid-ligament.summary: The lateral, flat, four-sided part of the coracoclavicular ligament. It lies in front of and outside the conoid ligament.
trapezoid-ligament.clinical: In a grade III shoulder separation, the trapezoid and conoid ligaments tear and the clavicle rides high.
attachments: Upper surface of the coracoid process of the scapula → trapezoid line on the underside of the clavicle
trapezoid-ligament.function: Works with the conoid ligament to suspend the scapula from the clavicle and resists medial movement of the acromion.

ulnar-collateral-ligament.name: Ulnar Collateral Ligament
ulnar-collateral-ligament.summary: A triangular band on the inner side of the elbow. It has anterior, posterior, and transverse bands, and the anterior band is the strongest.
ulnar-collateral-ligament.clinical: Throwing athletes such as baseball pitchers often tear the anterior band. It is rebuilt with a tendon graft in the Tommy John operation.
attachments: Medial epicondyle of the humerus → coronoid process (anterior band) and olecranon (posterior band) of the ulna
ulnar-collateral-ligament.function: Resists valgus force on the elbow and keeps the humerus and ulna stable.

ulnocapitate-ligament.name: Ulnocapitate Ligament
ulnocapitate-ligament.summary: A palmar ulnocarpal ligament that joins the ulnar side of the wrist to the capitate. It starts from the palmar radio-ulnar ligament and the articular disc.
ulnocapitate-ligament.clinical: Tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex and nearby ligaments cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and instability.
attachments: Palmar radio-ulnar ligament and articular disc → palmar surface of the capitate
ulnocapitate-ligament.function: Links the ulna and disc to the middle of the carpus and stabilizes the wrist.

ulnolunate-ligament.name: Ulnolunate Ligament
ulnolunate-ligament.summary: A palmar ulnocarpal ligament that joins the ulnar side of the wrist to the lunate. It starts from the palmar radio-ulnar ligament and the articular disc.
ulnolunate-ligament.clinical: Tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex and nearby ligaments cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and instability.
attachments: Palmar radio-ulnar ligament and articular disc → palmar surface of the lunate
ulnolunate-ligament.function: Links the ulna and disc to the proximal row of carpal bones and stabilizes the wrist.

ulnotriquetral-ligament.name: Ulnotriquetral Ligament
ulnotriquetral-ligament.summary: A palmar ulnocarpal ligament that joins the ulnar side of the wrist to the triquetrum. It starts from the palmar radio-ulnar ligament and the articular disc.
ulnotriquetral-ligament.clinical: Tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex and nearby ligaments cause ulnar-sided wrist pain and instability.
attachments: Palmar radio-ulnar ligament and articular disc → palmar surface of the triquetrum
ulnotriquetral-ligament.function: Links the ulna and disc to the ulnar side of the carpus and stabilizes the wrist.

anterior-longitudinal-ligament.name: Anterior Longitudinal Ligament
anterior-longitudinal-ligament.summary: A strong, broad band that runs down the front of the vertebral bodies and discs. It is the longest ligament of the spine.
anterior-longitudinal-ligament.clinical: Whiplash and other hyperextension injuries can tear it. It ossifies in diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH).
attachments: Basilar part of the occipital bone and anterior tubercle of the atlas → anterior surface of the sacrum
anterior-longitudinal-ligament.function: Binds the vertebral bodies together, supports the discs from the front, and limits extension of the spine.

intercornual-ligament.name: Intercornual Ligament
intercornual-ligament.summary: A short ligament that joins the sacral cornu to the coccygeal cornu on each side. It helps close the gap for the fifth sacral nerve.
intercornual-ligament.clinical: A hard fall on the buttocks can strain the sacrococcygeal ligaments and cause coccyx pain (coccydynia).
attachments: Sacral cornu → coccygeal cornu
intercornual-ligament.function: Helps hold the coccyx to the sacrum.

interspinous-ligaments.name: Interspinous Ligaments
interspinous-ligaments.summary: Thin, membrane-like ligaments that connect adjacent spinous processes from root to tip. They are best developed in the lumbar region.
interspinous-ligaments.clinical: A lumbar puncture needle passes through the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments. Flexion injuries can sprain or tear them.
attachments: Upper border of one spinous process → lower border of the spinous process above
interspinous-ligaments.function: Limits flexion of the spine and blends with the supraspinous ligament behind and the ligamenta flava in front.

intertransverse-ligaments.name: Intertransverse Ligaments
intertransverse-ligaments.summary: Bands that connect adjacent transverse processes. They are thin in the lumbar region, cord-like in the thoracic region, and often replaced by muscle in the neck.
intertransverse-ligaments.clinical: Sideways bending injuries can strain them, but they are not a common source of problems on their own.
attachments: Transverse process of one vertebra → transverse process of the vertebra below
intertransverse-ligaments.function: Limits bending of the spine to the opposite side.

intervertebral-disc-c6-c7.name: Intervertebral Disc C6-C7
intervertebral-disc-c6-c7.summary: A lower cervical disc. Cervical discs are thicker in front, which helps form the forward curve of the neck. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-c6-c7.clinical: This level and C5-C6 are the most common sites of cervical disc herniation. A side-back herniation here usually presses the C7 root.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the C6 vertebral body → superior endplate of the C7 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-c6-c7.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-c7-t1.name: Intervertebral Disc C7-T1
intervertebral-disc-c7-t1.summary: The lowest disc of the neck, at the junction of the cervical and thoracic spine. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-c7-t1.clinical: A herniation at this level usually presses the C8 root and may cause weakness in the hand.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the C7 vertebral body → superior endplate of the T1 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-c7-t1.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-l1-l2.name: Intervertebral Disc L1-L2
intervertebral-disc-l1-l2.summary: The uppermost lumbar disc. It lies near the lower end of the spinal cord (conus medullaris). Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-l1-l2.clinical: Herniation here is uncommon. When it occurs, it usually presses the L2 root.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the L1 vertebral body → superior endplate of the L2 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-l1-l2.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-l2-l3.name: Intervertebral Disc L2-L3
intervertebral-disc-l2-l3.summary: A thick upper lumbar disc that carries much of the body's weight. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-l2-l3.clinical: Herniation here is uncommon. A side-back herniation usually presses the L3 root.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the L2 vertebral body → superior endplate of the L3 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-l2-l3.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-l3-l4.name: Intervertebral Disc L3-L4
intervertebral-disc-l3-l4.summary: A thick middle lumbar disc. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-l3-l4.clinical: A side-back herniation usually presses the L4 root and can weaken the quadriceps or reduce the knee jerk.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the L3 vertebral body → superior endplate of the L4 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-l3-l4.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-l4-l5.name: Intervertebral Disc L4-L5
intervertebral-disc-l4-l5.summary: A thick lower lumbar disc that bears heavy load and moves a great deal. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-l4-l5.clinical: With L5-S1, this is the most common site of lumbar herniation. A side-back herniation usually presses the L5 root.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the L4 vertebral body → superior endplate of the L5 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-l4-l5.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-l5-s1.name: Intervertebral Disc L5-S1
intervertebral-disc-l5-s1.summary: The lowest mobile disc of the spine. It is wedge-shaped, thicker in front, and sits at the lumbosacral angle. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-l5-s1.clinical: With L4-L5, this is the most common site of lumbar herniation. A side-back herniation usually presses the S1 root.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the L5 vertebral body → superior endplate of the S1 (the base of the sacrum)
intervertebral-disc-l5-s1.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-t1-t2.name: Intervertebral Disc T1-T2
intervertebral-disc-t1-t2.summary: A thin thoracic disc. The head of rib 2 attaches across this level by the costovertebral joint. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-t1-t2.clinical: Thoracic herniation is uncommon because the rib cage limits motion. It can press on the spinal cord because the thoracic canal is narrow.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the T1 vertebral body → superior endplate of the T2 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-t1-t2.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-t9-t10.name: Intervertebral Disc T9-T10
intervertebral-disc-t9-t10.summary: A thin thoracic disc. Rib 10 attaches to the T10 vertebra alone, so no rib head crosses this disc. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-t9-t10.clinical: Thoracic herniation is uncommon because the rib cage limits motion. It can press on the spinal cord because the thoracic canal is narrow.

intervertebral-disc-t10-t11.clinical: Thoracic herniation is uncommon, but the lower thoracic discs are the most often affected. It can press on the spinal cord.

intervertebral-disc-t11-t12.name: Intervertebral Disc T11-T12
intervertebral-disc-t11-t12.summary: A thin thoracic disc just above the thoracolumbar junction. Rib 12 attaches to the T12 vertebra alone. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-t11-t12.clinical: Thoracic herniation is uncommon, but the lower thoracic discs are the most often affected. It can press on the spinal cord.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the T11 vertebral body → superior endplate of the T12 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-t11-t12.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

intervertebral-disc-t12-l1.name: Intervertebral Disc T12-L1
intervertebral-disc-t12-l1.summary: The disc at the thoracolumbar junction, where the stiff thoracic spine meets the mobile lumbar spine. No rib attaches here. Each disc has a tough outer annulus fibrosus around a gel-like nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-t12-l1.clinical: This junction is prone to injury. Herniation here can press on the lowest part of the spinal cord or the cauda equina.
attachments: Inferior endplate of the T12 vertebral body → superior endplate of the L1 vertebral body
intervertebral-disc-t12-l1.function: Joins adjacent vertebral bodies, absorbs compression, and allows small amounts of bending and twisting.

nucleus-pulposus-c5-c6.name: Nucleus Pulposus C5-C6
nucleus-pulposus-c5-c6.summary: The soft, gel-like core of the C5-C6 intervertebral disc. It is a remnant of the embryonic notochord and is mostly water. In the neck it is small and becomes fibrous with age.
nucleus-pulposus-c5-c6.clinical: Cervical nuclei are small. A tear in the annulus can let the nucleus herniate and press on a nerve root.
attachments: Enclosed between the endplates of the two adjacent vertebral bodies and surrounded by the annulus fibrosus
nucleus-pulposus-c5-c6.function: Spreads compression evenly across the disc and acts as a cushion. It loses water with age.

nucleus-pulposus-l1-l2.summary: The soft, gel-like core of the L1-L2 intervertebral disc. It is a remnant of the embryonic notochord and is mostly water. In the lumbar spine it lies slightly behind the center of the disc.

intervertebral-symphysis-sacrum-coccyx.name: Sacrococcygeal Symphysis
intervertebral-symphysis-sacrum-coccyx.summary: The joint between the apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx. It has a small, flat fibrocartilage disc.
intervertebral-symphysis-sacrum-coccyx.clinical: A fall onto the buttocks can injure it and cause coccyx pain. The coccyx moves backward slightly during childbirth.
attachments: Apex of the sacrum → base of the first coccygeal vertebra
intervertebral-symphysis-sacrum-coccyx.function: Joins the coccyx to the sacrum and allows slight movement, with support from the sacrococcygeal ligaments.

ligamenta-flava.name: Ligamenta Flava
ligamenta-flava.summary: Paired yellow, elastic ligaments that join the laminae of adjacent vertebrae. They form part of the back wall of the vertebral canal.
ligamenta-flava.clinical: Thickening of these ligaments narrows the spinal canal (lumbar spinal stenosis). A needle crosses one during lumbar puncture, giving a pop.
attachments: Anterior surface of the lamina above → upper edge and back surface of the lamina below
ligamenta-flava.function: Helps keep the spine upright, assists return to standing after flexion, and limits abrupt flexion that could injure the discs.

posterior-longitudinal-ligament.name: Posterior Longitudinal Ligament
posterior-longitudinal-ligament.summary: A narrow band inside the vertebral canal that runs along the back of the vertebral bodies. It is broader over the discs.
posterior-longitudinal-ligament.clinical: It is narrow at the sides, so disc herniations usually bulge backward and to the side, where nerve roots lie. Ossification can narrow the canal.
attachments: Back of the body of the axis (continuing upward as the tectorial membrane) → back of the sacrum
posterior-longitudinal-ligament.function: Resists flexion of the spine and helps prevent the discs from bulging straight backward.

supraspinous-ligament.name: Supraspinous Ligament
supraspinous-ligament.summary: A strong cord that connects the tips of the spinous processes. Above C7, it continues as the ligamentum nuchae.
supraspinous-ligament.clinical: Flexion injuries can tear it. A lumbar puncture needle passes through it.
attachments: Tip of the C7 spinous process → tips of the spinous processes down to the sacrum
supraspinous-ligament.function: Limits flexion of the spine and keeps the spinous processes aligned.

articular-capsule-of-temporomandibular-j.name: Articular Capsule of the Temporomandibular Joint
articular-capsule-of-temporomandibular-j.summary: A loose fibrous sleeve around the jaw joint. It is lined by synovial membrane and attaches to the margins of the articular disc.
articular-capsule-of-temporomandibular-j.clinical: A loose capsule allows wide mouth opening but also allows the mandibular head to dislocate forward.
attachments: Temporal bone around the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle → neck of the mandible
articular-capsule-of-temporomandibular-j.function: Encloses the joint, holds synovial fluid, and allows gliding and hinge movements.

articular-disc-of-temporomandibular-join.name: Articular Disc of the Temporomandibular Joint
articular-disc-of-temporomandibular-join.summary: An oval fibrocartilage disc that divides the jaw joint into upper and lower compartments. It is thin centrally and thick at the rim.
articular-disc-of-temporomandibular-join.clinical: Anterior displacement of the disc causes clicking, locking, and jaw pain (temporomandibular disorder).
attachments: Periphery fused to the joint capsule
Front attached to the lateral pterygoid tendon
Back blends into a vascular bilaminar zone
articular-disc-of-temporomandibular-join.function: Cushions the joint and moves with the mandibular head. The upper compartment glides and the lower compartment hinges.
articulations: Mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone

intervertebral-disc-c2-c3.name: Intervertebral Disc C2-C3
intervertebral-disc-c2-c3.summary: A fibrocartilage pad between the bodies of C2 and C3. It has an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner nucleus pulposus. It is the first disc below the axis, since no disc lies between the skull, C1, and C2.
intervertebral-disc-c2-c3.clinical: Herniation here is uncommon. It could affect the C3 root, which exits through the C2-C3 foramen.
attachments: Inferior endplate of C2 body → superior endplate of C3 body
intervertebral-disc-c2-c3.function: Absorbs compression, spaces the vertebrae, and permits flexion, extension, and tilting. Cervical discs are thicker in front, which maintains the neck curve.

intervertebral-disc-c3-c4.name: Intervertebral Disc C3-C4
intervertebral-disc-c3-c4.summary: A fibrocartilage pad between the bodies of C3 and C4. It has an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-c3-c4.clinical: Herniation here is uncommon. It could affect the C4 root and cause neck and shoulder pain.
attachments: Inferior endplate of C3 body → superior endplate of C4 body
intervertebral-disc-c3-c4.function: Absorbs compression, spaces the vertebrae, and permits flexion, extension, and tilting. Cervical discs are thicker in front, which maintains the neck curve.

intervertebral-disc-c4-c5.name: Intervertebral Disc C4-C5
intervertebral-disc-c4-c5.summary: A fibrocartilage pad between the bodies of C4 and C5. It has an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-c4-c5.clinical: Herniation can compress the C5 root, causing shoulder pain and deltoid weakness.
attachments: Inferior endplate of C4 body → superior endplate of C5 body
intervertebral-disc-c4-c5.function: Absorbs compression, spaces the vertebrae, and permits flexion, extension, and tilting. Cervical discs are thicker in front, which maintains the neck curve.

intervertebral-disc-c5-c6.name: Intervertebral Disc C5-C6
intervertebral-disc-c5-c6.summary: A fibrocartilage pad between the bodies of C5 and C6. It has an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner nucleus pulposus.
intervertebral-disc-c5-c6.clinical: Among the most common sites of herniation and degeneration. C6 root compression causes thumb numbness and weak elbow flexion.
attachments: Inferior endplate of C5 body → superior endplate of C6 body
intervertebral-disc-c5-c6.function: Absorbs compression, spaces the vertebrae, and permits flexion, extension, and tilting. Cervical discs are thicker in front, which maintains the neck curve.

lateral-temporomandibular-ligament.name: Lateral Temporomandibular Ligament
lateral-temporomandibular-ligament.summary: A strong thickening of the lateral capsule of the jaw joint. Its fibers run downward and backward from the zygomatic arch.
lateral-temporomandibular-ligament.clinical: It limits backward movement of the mandible. Excess strain or trauma can sprain it and cause lateral jaw pain.
attachments: Articular tubercle and zygomatic process of the temporal bone → lateral surface of the neck of the mandible
lateral-temporomandibular-ligament.function: Reinforces the lateral capsule and restrains posterior and downward displacement of the mandible.

lateral-thyrohyoid-ligament.name: Lateral Thyrohyoid Ligament
lateral-thyrohyoid-ligament.summary: A round cord forming the thickened posterior edge of the thyrohyoid membrane. It often contains a small triticeal cartilage.
lateral-thyrohyoid-ligament.clinical: A calcified triticeal cartilage can appear on a neck X-ray and be mistaken for a foreign body.
attachments: Tip of the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage → posterior end of the greater horn of the hyoid bone
lateral-thyrohyoid-ligament.function: Suspends the larynx from the hyoid and lets the larynx rise with the hyoid during swallowing.

median-thyrohyoid-ligament.name: Median Thyrohyoid Ligament
median-thyrohyoid-ligament.summary: The thickened central part of the thyrohyoid membrane. It is a single midline band between the hyoid bone and the thyroid cartilage.
median-thyrohyoid-ligament.clinical: It can be felt between the hyoid bone and the thyroid notch. A bursa separates it from the back of the hyoid body.
attachments: Upper border of the thyroid cartilage → upper posterior margin of the body and greater horns of the hyoid bone
median-thyrohyoid-ligament.function: Connects the larynx to the hyoid bone and keeps the two moving together.

nuchal-ligament.name: Nuchal Ligament
nuchal-ligament.summary: A broad midline sheet in the back of the neck. It continues the supraspinous ligament upward to the skull.
nuchal-ligament.clinical: It forms a relatively bloodless midline plane for posterior neck surgery. It is much thicker in grazing animals.
attachments: External occipital protuberance and median nuchal line → spinous processes of the cervical vertebrae, ending at C7
Posterior tubercle of the atlas
nuchal-ligament.function: Resists neck flexion, helps support the head, and gives attachment to neck and upper back muscles.

nucleus-pulposus-c2-c3.name: Nucleus Pulposus C2-C3
nucleus-pulposus-c2-c3.summary: The soft, gel-like core of the C2-C3 disc. It is rich in water and proteoglycans and sits inside the annulus fibrosus.
nucleus-pulposus-c2-c3.clinical: With age it dries and shrinks. If it herniates through the annulus, it can press on a nerve root.
attachments: Lies between the C2 and C3 endplates, enclosed by the annulus fibrosus
nucleus-pulposus-c2-c3.function: Spreads compressive load evenly across the disc like a fluid cushion.

nucleus-pulposus-c3-c4.name: Nucleus Pulposus C3-C4
nucleus-pulposus-c3-c4.summary: The soft, gel-like core of the C3-C4 disc. It is rich in water and proteoglycans and sits inside the annulus fibrosus.
nucleus-pulposus-c3-c4.clinical: With age it dries and shrinks. If it herniates through the annulus, it can press on a nerve root.
attachments: Lies between the C3 and C4 endplates, enclosed by the annulus fibrosus
nucleus-pulposus-c3-c4.function: Spreads compressive load evenly across the disc like a fluid cushion.

nucleus-pulposus-c4-c5.name: Nucleus Pulposus C4-C5
nucleus-pulposus-c4-c5.summary: The soft, gel-like core of the C4-C5 disc. It is rich in water and proteoglycans and sits inside the annulus fibrosus.
nucleus-pulposus-c4-c5.clinical: With age it dries and shrinks. If it herniates through the annulus, it can press on a nerve root.
attachments: Lies between the C4 and C5 endplates, enclosed by the annulus fibrosus
nucleus-pulposus-c4-c5.function: Spreads compressive load evenly across the disc like a fluid cushion.

quadrangular-membrane.name: Quadrangular Membrane
quadrangular-membrane.summary: A thin elastic sheet in the upper larynx. Its lower free edge forms the vestibular ligament and its upper edge forms the aryepiglottic fold.
quadrangular-membrane.clinical: It helps confine spread of supraglottic tumors and swelling above the vocal folds.
attachments: Lateral margin of the epiglottis → arytenoid cartilage near the corniculate cartilage
quadrangular-membrane.function: Forms the framework of the lateral wall of the laryngeal vestibule.

sphenomandibular-ligament.name: Sphenomandibular Ligament
sphenomandibular-ligament.summary: A thin flat band on the inner side of the jaw joint. It is an accessory ligament of the temporomandibular joint.
sphenomandibular-ligament.clinical: The inferior alveolar nerve and vessels pass between this ligament and the mandibular ramus. It is a landmark for dental nerve block.
attachments: Spine of the sphenoid bone → lingula of the mandible
sphenomandibular-ligament.function: Suspends the mandible and limits its excessive forward movement.

stylohyoid-ligament.name: Stylohyoid Ligament
stylohyoid-ligament.summary: A fibrous cord that hangs from the styloid process to the hyoid bone. It is a remnant of the second pharyngeal arch.
stylohyoid-ligament.clinical: Ossification of this ligament, or an elongated styloid process, can cause throat pain in Eagle syndrome.
attachments: Tip of the styloid process → lesser horn of the hyoid bone
stylohyoid-ligament.function: Suspends the hyoid bone from the skull.

stylomandibular-ligament.name: Stylomandibular Ligament
stylomandibular-ligament.summary: A thickened band of deep cervical fascia. It separates the parotid gland from the submandibular gland.
stylomandibular-ligament.clinical: It tightens when the jaw is thrust forward. It lies behind the joint and is not a major source of injury.
attachments: Apex of the styloid process → angle and posterior border of the mandibular ramus
stylomandibular-ligament.function: Limits excessive forward movement of the mandible.

anterior-cruciate-ligament.name: Anterior Cruciate Ligament
anterior-cruciate-ligament.summary: A strong intra-articular band that crosses inside the knee. It runs upward, backward, and laterally from the tibia to the femur.
anterior-cruciate-ligament.clinical: Tears are common in pivoting sports. The anterior drawer and Lachman tests show excess forward tibial movement.
attachments: Anterior intercondylar area of the tibia → medial surface of the lateral femoral condyle
anterior-cruciate-ligament.function: Prevents forward sliding of the tibia on the femur and limits hyperextension and rotation.

anterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.name: Anterior Ligament of the Fibular Head
anterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.summary: Several flat bands in front of the upper tibiofibular joint. They run obliquely upward from the fibular head to the tibia.
anterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.clinical: Sprain or dislocation of this joint is uncommon. It causes pain on the outer side of the knee.
attachments: Anterior surface of the fibular head → lateral condyle of the tibia
anterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.function: Reinforces the front of the joint capsule and limits movement of the fibular head.

anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral-.name: Anterior Meniscotibial Ligament of the Lateral Meniscus
anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral-.summary: The anterior root of the lateral meniscus. It anchors the front end of the meniscus to the tibia, close to the anterior cruciate ligament.
anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral-.clinical: Root tears let the meniscus extrude from the joint and increase cartilage wear.
attachments: Anterior horn of the lateral meniscus → anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, beside the anterior cruciate ligament
anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral-.function: Holds the front of the lateral meniscus in place on the tibial plateau.

anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-m.name: Anterior Meniscotibial Ligament of the Medial Meniscus
anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-m.summary: The anterior root of the medial meniscus. It anchors the front end of the meniscus to the tibia, in front of the anterior cruciate ligament.
anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-m.clinical: Root tears are less common than posterior root tears. They allow the meniscus to extrude from the joint.
attachments: Anterior horn of the medial meniscus → anterior intercondylar area of the tibia, in front of the lateral meniscus root
anterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-m.function: Holds the front of the medial meniscus in place on the tibial plateau.

anterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.name: Anterior Talocalcaneal Ligament
anterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.summary: A short band on the front of the subtalar joint. It is a thickening of the capsule near the sinus tarsi.
anterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.clinical: It can be injured with the other subtalar ligaments in inversion sprains. This may cause sinus tarsi pain.
attachments: Neck of the talus → anterior part of the upper surface of the calcaneus
anterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.function: Reinforces the front of the subtalar joint and limits excess inversion.

anterior-talofibular-ligament.name: Anterior Talofibular Ligament
anterior-talofibular-ligament.summary: A flat band on the outer side of the ankle. It is the weakest of the three lateral ankle ligaments.
anterior-talofibular-ligament.clinical: It is the most commonly sprained ankle ligament, usually in inversion with the foot pointed down. The anterior drawer test checks it.
attachments: Anterior border of the lateral malleolus → neck of the talus, in front of the malleolar facet
anterior-talofibular-ligament.function: Resists forward sliding of the talus and inversion of the plantar-flexed foot.

anterior-tibiofibular-ligament.name: Anterior Tibiofibular Ligament
anterior-tibiofibular-ligament.summary: A flat band that crosses the front of the lower tibiofibular joint. It runs obliquely downward and outward.
anterior-tibiofibular-ligament.clinical: Injury causes a high ankle sprain, often with forced external rotation. It heals more slowly than a common lateral sprain.
attachments: Anterior tubercle and anterior margin of the distal tibia → anterior surface of the lateral malleolus
anterior-tibiofibular-ligament.function: Holds the fibula against the tibia and keeps the ankle mortise stable.

arcuate-ligament.name: Arcuate Popliteal Ligament
arcuate-ligament.summary: A Y-shaped thickening of the back of the knee capsule. It arches over the popliteus tendon on the outer side.
arcuate-ligament.clinical: It is part of the posterolateral corner of the knee. Injury there causes rotational instability.
attachments: Head of the fibula → posterior capsule of the knee and the lateral femoral condyle
arcuate-ligament.function: Strengthens the posterolateral capsule and helps resist hyperextension and external rotation.

articular-capsule-of-interphalangeal-joi.name: Articular Capsule of the Great Toe Interphalangeal Joint
articular-capsule-of-interphalangeal-joi.summary: A thin fibrous sleeve around the only interphalangeal joint of the great toe. Plantar and collateral ligaments reinforce it.
articular-capsule-of-interphalangeal-joi.clinical: Injury is usually a sprain or a dislocation from stubbing or crushing the toe.
articular-capsule-of-interphalangeal-joi.joint: Interphalangeal joint of the great toe
attachments: Margins of the base of the distal phalanx → margins of the head of the proximal phalanx
articular-capsule-of-interphalangeal-joi.function: Encloses the joint and allows bending and straightening of the tip of the great toe.

articular-capsule-of-knee-joint.name: Articular Capsule of the Knee Joint
articular-capsule-of-knee-joint.summary: The large fibrous sleeve of the knee. It is thin in front, where the quadriceps tendon, patella, and patellar ligament take its place.
articular-capsule-of-knee-joint.clinical: A knee effusion distends the capsule and the suprapatellar bursa, giving a swollen knee and loss of full motion.
attachments: Margins of the femoral condyles and patella → margins of the tibial plateau, with an opening for the popliteus tendon
articular-capsule-of-knee-joint.function: Encloses the joint, holds synovial fluid, and links the surrounding ligaments and menisci.

articular-capsule-of-superior-tibiofibul.name: Articular Capsule of the Superior Tibiofibular Joint
articular-capsule-of-superior-tibiofibul.summary: A fibrous sleeve around the joint between the fibular head and the lateral tibial condyle. Anterior and posterior ligaments strengthen it.
articular-capsule-of-superior-tibiofibul.clinical: In some people the joint cavity connects with the knee joint, so knee disease can spread to it.
attachments: Margins of the fibular head facet → margins of the facet on the lateral tibial condyle
articular-capsule-of-superior-tibiofibul.function: Encloses the joint and allows slight gliding of the fibular head during ankle movement.

articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.name: Articular Capsules of the Distal Interphalangeal Joints of the Foot
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.latin: Capsulae articulares articulationum interphalangealium distalium pedis
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.summary: Thin fibrous sleeves around the distal joints of the second to fifth toes. Plantar and collateral ligaments reinforce them.
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.clinical: Fixed flexion at this joint produces a mallet toe, which often develops painful corns at the tip.
attachments: Base of each distal phalanx → head of the middle phalanx
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.function: Enclose the joints and allow small bending movements of the toe tips.

articular-capsules-of-metatarsophalangea.name: Articular Capsules of the Metatarsophalangeal Joints
articular-capsules-of-metatarsophalangea.summary: Loose fibrous sleeves around the joints at the ball of the foot. They are thin above and thickened below by the plantar ligaments.
articular-capsules-of-metatarsophalangea.clinical: The great toe joint is a common site of gout and of hallux rigidus. Capsule stretching also contributes to bunions.
attachments: Margins of each metatarsal head → margins of the base of the proximal phalanx
articular-capsules-of-metatarsophalangea.function: Enclose the joints and allow toe flexion, extension, and some sideways movement.

articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.name: Articular Capsules of the Proximal Interphalangeal Joints of the Foot
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.latin: Capsulae articulares articulationum interphalangealium proximalium pedis
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.summary: Thin fibrous sleeves around the middle joints of the second to fifth toes. Plantar and collateral ligaments reinforce them.
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.clinical: Fixed flexion at this joint produces a hammer toe, often painful against footwear.
attachments: Base of each middle phalanx → head of the proximal phalanx
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.function: Enclose the joints and allow bending and straightening of the toes.

calcaneocuboid-ligament.name: Calcaneocuboid Ligament
calcaneocuboid-ligament.summary: The calcaneocuboid limb of the bifurcate ligament. It is a short dorsal band between the calcaneus and the cuboid.
calcaneocuboid-ligament.clinical: In inversion injuries it can be torn away with a piece of the calcaneus, which can mimic an ankle sprain.
attachments: Anterior process of the calcaneus → dorsal surface of the cuboid
calcaneocuboid-ligament.function: Stabilizes the calcaneocuboid joint on the outer side of the foot.

calcaneofibular-ligament.name: Calcaneofibular Ligament
calcaneofibular-ligament.summary: A round cord on the outer ankle. It runs down and back from the fibula, deep to the fibularis tendons.
calcaneofibular-ligament.clinical: It is the second most commonly injured lateral ankle ligament, usually torn along with the anterior talofibular ligament.
attachments: Tip and anterior border of the lateral malleolus → lateral surface of the calcaneus
calcaneofibular-ligament.function: Resists inversion, mainly with the foot at neutral or dorsiflexed, and stabilizes the subtalar joint.

calcaneonavicular-ligament.name: Calcaneonavicular Ligament
calcaneonavicular-ligament.summary: The calcaneonavicular limb of the bifurcate ligament. It is a short dorsal band between the calcaneus and the navicular.
calcaneonavicular-ligament.clinical: It can be sprained or avulsed with inversion injuries and cause pain on the outer top of the midfoot.
attachments: Anterior process of the calcaneus → dorsolateral surface of the navicular
calcaneonavicular-ligament.function: Links the calcaneus to the navicular and supports the midtarsal joint.

collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.name: Collateral Interphalangeal Ligaments of the Foot
collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.summary: Paired cords on the inner and outer sides of each toe joint. They are strong and attach to the plantar plates.
collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.clinical: Sprains happen when a toe is bent sideways, as in stubbing the toe.
attachments: Sides of the head of the proximal bone → sides of the base of the next phalanx
collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.function: Prevent sideways bending and keep the toe joints stable.

collateral-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.name: Collateral Metatarsophalangeal Ligaments
collateral-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.summary: Strong cords on each side of the joints at the ball of the foot. They run forward and downward.
collateral-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.clinical: Stretching of the inner ligament and capsule is part of bunion (hallux valgus) deformity.
attachments: Sides of the metatarsal head → sides of the base of the proximal phalanx and plantar plate
collateral-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.function: Give side-to-side stability to the toe joints during push-off.

cuneocuboid-interosseus-ligament.name: Cuneocuboid Interosseous Ligament
cuneocuboid-interosseus-ligament.summary: A strong short band between the lateral cuneiform and the cuboid. It lies deep in the joint between them.
cuneocuboid-interosseus-ligament.clinical: Midfoot sprains involving these joints cause pain and swelling over the middle of the foot.
attachments: Lateral surface of the lateral cuneiform → medial surface of the cuboid
cuneocuboid-interosseus-ligament.function: Binds the lateral cuneiform to the cuboid and supports the transverse arch.

cuneometatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.name: Cuneometatarsal Interosseous Ligaments
cuneometatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.summary: Strong deep bands between the cuneiforms and metatarsal bases. The best known joins the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal.
cuneometatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.clinical: The medial band is the Lisfranc ligament. Its injury causes Lisfranc fracture-dislocation, often missed on X-rays.
attachments: Medial cuneiform (lateral side) → base of the second metatarsal
Lateral cuneiform → adjacent metatarsal bases
cuneometatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.function: Lock the second metatarsal into the tarsus and stabilize the midfoot.

deep-part-of-tibial-collateral-ligament.name: Deep Part of the Tibial Collateral Ligament
deep-part-of-tibial-collateral-ligament.summary: The short deep fibers of the medial collateral ligament. They attach firmly to the medial meniscus.
deep-part-of-tibial-collateral-ligament.clinical: A medial collateral injury can also tear the attached meniscus. Valgus stress at the knee is the usual cause.
attachments: Medial femoral condyle → medial meniscus and the medial tibial condyle below it
deep-part-of-tibial-collateral-ligament.function: Resists valgus stress and anchors the medial meniscus to the femur and tibia.

deep-transverse-metatarsal-ligament.name: Deep Transverse Metatarsal Ligament
deep-transverse-metatarsal-ligament.summary: Four short bands that link the plantar ligaments of neighboring metatarsophalangeal joints. They lie across the heads of the metatarsals.
deep-transverse-metatarsal-ligament.clinical: The interdigital nerves pass below it. Entrapment there can cause Morton neuroma, usually between the third and fourth toes.
attachments: Plantar ligament of one metatarsophalangeal joint → plantar ligament of the next joint, across digits 1 to 5
deep-transverse-metatarsal-ligament.function: Holds the metatarsal heads together and limits spreading of the forefoot.

dorsal-cuneonavicular-ligaments.name: Dorsal Cuneonavicular Ligaments
dorsal-cuneonavicular-ligaments.summary: Three flat bands on top of the foot. Each runs from the navicular to one of the cuneiforms.
dorsal-cuneonavicular-ligaments.clinical: Midfoot sprains here cause pain on top of the arch.
attachments: Dorsal surface of the navicular → dorsal surfaces of the three cuneiforms
dorsal-cuneonavicular-ligaments.function: Bind the navicular to the cuneiforms and support the medial arch.

dorsal-intercuneiform-ligaments.name: Dorsal Intercuneiform Ligaments
dorsal-intercuneiform-ligaments.summary: Transverse bands on top of the foot between neighboring cuneiform bones.
dorsal-intercuneiform-ligaments.clinical: Injury is usually part of a midfoot sprain or a Lisfranc injury.
attachments: Dorsal surface of the medial cuneiform → intermediate cuneiform → lateral cuneiform
dorsal-intercuneiform-ligaments.function: Bind the cuneiforms together and maintain the transverse arch.

dorsal-metatarsal-ligaments.name: Dorsal Metatarsal Ligaments
dorsal-metatarsal-ligaments.summary: Transverse bands across the top of the metatarsal bases. They connect each base to its neighbor.
dorsal-metatarsal-ligaments.clinical: Injury is usually part of a midfoot sprain or a Lisfranc injury.
attachments: Dorsal surface of one metatarsal base → dorsal surface of the adjacent base

dorsal-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.name: Dorsal Tarsometatarsal Ligaments
dorsal-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.summary: Flat bands that join the tarsal bones to the bases of the metatarsals on the top of the foot.
dorsal-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.clinical: A midfoot sprain or Lisfranc injury can tear them and cause swelling and pain over the top of the foot.
attachments: Dorsal surfaces of the cuneiforms and cuboid → dorsal surfaces of the metatarsal bases

fibular-collateral-ligament.name: Fibular Collateral Ligament
fibular-collateral-ligament.summary: A round cord on the outer side of the knee. It lies outside the joint capsule and is separate from it.
fibular-collateral-ligament.clinical: A varus blow can tear it. Look for associated posterolateral corner injury and common fibular nerve damage.
attachments: Lateral epicondyle of the femur → lateral surface of the fibular head
fibular-collateral-ligament.function: Resists varus stress and stabilizes the outer side of the knee.

infrapatellar-fat-pad.name: Infrapatellar Fat Pad
infrapatellar-fat-pad.summary: A pad of fat behind the patellar ligament, inside the capsule but outside the synovial cavity. It fills the space in front of the knee.
infrapatellar-fat-pad.clinical: Pinching or inflammation of the pad (Hoffa syndrome) causes pain below the kneecap.
attachments: Inferior pole of the patella and patellar ligament → front of the tibial plateau, with the infrapatellar fold running to the femoral intercondylar fossa
infrapatellar-fat-pad.function: Cushions the front of the knee and fills gaps as the joint moves.

intercuneiform-interosseus-ligaments.name: Intercuneiform Interosseous Ligaments
intercuneiform-interosseus-ligaments.summary: Strong short bands deep in the joints between the three cuneiform bones.
intercuneiform-interosseus-ligaments.clinical: Injury is usually part of a midfoot sprain or a Lisfranc injury.
attachments: Medial cuneiform → intermediate cuneiform
Intermediate cuneiform → lateral cuneiform
intercuneiform-interosseus-ligaments.function: Bind the cuneiforms together and maintain the transverse arch.

interosseous-membrane-of-leg.name: Interosseous Membrane of the Leg
interosseous-membrane-of-leg.summary: A broad fibrous sheet between the tibia and fibula. Its fibers run downward and outward from the tibia.
interosseous-membrane-of-leg.clinical: A tear can occur with a Maisonneuve fracture, a high fibular fracture with ankle injury.
attachments: Interosseous border of the tibia → interosseous border of the fibula
interosseous-membrane-of-leg.function: Links the two leg bones, transmits force from the fibula to the tibia, and gives muscles an origin.

intersesamoid-ligament.name: Intersesamoid Ligament
intersesamoid-ligament.summary: A band that joins the two sesamoid bones under the head of the first metatarsal. It lies within the plantar plate of the great toe.
intersesamoid-ligament.clinical: Sesamoid injuries cause pain under the ball of the great toe. Sesamoiditis is common in runners and dancers.
attachments: Medial sesamoid bone → lateral sesamoid bone
intersesamoid-ligament.function: Ties the sesamoids together under the first metatarsal head.

lateral-meniscus.name: Lateral Meniscus
lateral-meniscus.summary: A C-shaped, nearly circular pad of fibrocartilage on the lateral tibial plateau. It is smaller and more mobile than the medial meniscus.
lateral-meniscus.clinical: It is often torn together with an acute anterior cruciate ligament injury.
attachments: Anterior horn → anterior intercondylar area of the tibia
Posterior horn → posterior intercondylar area, with meniscofemoral ligaments to the femur
lateral-meniscus.function: Deepens the tibial socket, absorbs shock, spreads load, and stabilizes the knee.

lateral-talocalcaneal-ligament.name: Lateral Talocalcaneal Ligament
lateral-talocalcaneal-ligament.summary: A short band on the outer side of the subtalar joint. It runs parallel to the calcaneofibular ligament.
lateral-talocalcaneal-ligament.clinical: It can be injured in inversion sprains and add to subtalar instability.
attachments: Lateral process of the talus → lateral surface of the calcaneus
lateral-talocalcaneal-ligament.function: Reinforces the lateral capsule and limits inversion of the subtalar joint.

long-plantar-ligament.name: Long Plantar Ligament
long-plantar-ligament.summary: The longest ligament of the foot sole. It spans from the calcaneus to the cuboid and the metatarsal bases.
long-plantar-ligament.clinical: Strain or tear contributes to a flattened outer arch and midfoot pain.
attachments: Plantar surface of the calcaneus → tuberosity of the cuboid, with fibers to the bases of metatarsals 2 to 4 (or 5)
long-plantar-ligament.function: Supports the lateral longitudinal arch and forms a tunnel for the fibularis longus tendon.

medial-meniscus.name: Medial Meniscus
medial-meniscus.summary: A C-shaped pad of fibrocartilage on the medial tibial plateau. It is wider at the back and firmly attached to the medial collateral ligament.
medial-meniscus.clinical: It is torn often, especially with twisting injuries. Its attachment to the collateral ligament limits mobility.
attachments: Anterior horn → anterior intercondylar area of the tibia
Posterior horn → posterior intercondylar area, behind the lateral meniscus root
Outer edge → capsule and deep tibial collateral ligament
medial-meniscus.function: Deepens the tibial socket, absorbs shock, spreads load, and stabilizes the knee.

medial-talocalcaneal-ligament.name: Medial Talocalcaneal Ligament
medial-talocalcaneal-ligament.summary: A short band on the inner side of the subtalar joint. It lies behind the sustentaculum tali.
medial-talocalcaneal-ligament.clinical: It is often involved in eversion injuries and in tarsal tunnel region trauma.
attachments: Medial tubercle of the talus → sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus
medial-talocalcaneal-ligament.function: Reinforces the medial capsule and limits eversion of the subtalar joint.

meniscopatellar-ligament.name: Meniscopatellar Ligament
meniscopatellar-ligament.summary: Thin fibrous bands that link the front of a meniscus to the patella. They are part of the patellar retinacula.
meniscopatellar-ligament.clinical: Tightness or scarring in these bands can limit patellar movement.
attachments: Anterior edge of the meniscus → inferior part of the patella
meniscopatellar-ligament.function: Tie the menisci to the patella so they move forward with extension.

metatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.name: Metatarsal Interosseous Ligaments
metatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.summary: Strong short bands between the bases of neighboring metatarsals. No such strong band joins the first and second.
metatarsal-interosseus-ligaments.clinical: The missing first-second band is why a Lisfranc injury can displace the second metatarsal.
attachments: Side of one metatarsal base → side of the adjacent base, for metatarsals 2 to 5

oblique-popliteal-ligament.name: Oblique Popliteal Ligament
oblique-popliteal-ligament.summary: A broad band on the back of the knee. It is an expansion of the semimembranosus tendon.
oblique-popliteal-ligament.clinical: It resists hyperextension. Injury to the posterior capsule can follow a hyperextension blow.
attachments: Semimembranosus tendon at the medial tibial condyle → intercondylar line and lateral femoral condyle
oblique-popliteal-ligament.function: Strengthens the back of the capsule and resists hyperextension of the knee.

plantar-calcaneocuboid-ligament.name: Plantar Calcaneocuboid Ligament
plantar-calcaneocuboid-ligament.summary: The short plantar ligament. It lies deep to the long plantar ligament and is wide and strong.
plantar-calcaneocuboid-ligament.clinical: It supports the lateral arch. Sprain causes pain under the outer midfoot.
attachments: Anterior tubercle of the calcaneus → plantar surface of the cuboid behind the groove for fibularis longus
plantar-calcaneocuboid-ligament.function: Supports the lateral longitudinal arch and the calcaneocuboid joint.

plantar-calcaneonavivular-ligament.name: Plantar Calcaneonavicular Ligament (Spring Ligament)
plantar-calcaneonavivular-ligament.summary: The spring ligament. A broad band that supports the head of the talus from below.
plantar-calcaneonavivular-ligament.clinical: Weakness or tear, often with tibialis posterior failure, leads to adult acquired flatfoot.
attachments: Sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus → plantar surface of the navicular
plantar-calcaneonavivular-ligament.function: Supports the head of the talus and the medial longitudinal arch.

plantar-cuneocuboid-ligament.name: Plantar Cuneocuboid Ligament
plantar-cuneocuboid-ligament.summary: A strong band under the foot between the cuboid and the lateral cuneiform.
plantar-cuneocuboid-ligament.clinical: Injury is part of a midfoot sprain and causes pain under the arch.
attachments: Plantar surface of the cuboid → plantar surface of the lateral cuneiform
plantar-cuneocuboid-ligament.function: Supports the transverse arch of the foot.

plantar-cuneonavicular-ligaments.name: Plantar Cuneonavicular Ligaments
plantar-cuneonavicular-ligaments.summary: Three bands on the sole that link the navicular to the three cuneiforms. The tibialis posterior tendon strengthens them.
plantar-cuneonavicular-ligaments.clinical: Weakness here is part of flatfoot and arch collapse.
attachments: Plantar surface of the navicular → plantar surfaces of the three cuneiforms

plantar-intercuneiform-ligaments.name: Plantar Intercuneiform Ligaments
plantar-intercuneiform-ligaments.summary: Transverse bands on the sole that connect neighboring cuneiform bones.
plantar-intercuneiform-ligaments.clinical: Injury is usually part of a midfoot sprain or a Lisfranc injury.
attachments: Plantar surface of one cuneiform → plantar surface of the adjacent cuneiform
plantar-intercuneiform-ligaments.function: Support the transverse arch of the foot.

plantar-interphalangeal-ligaments.name: Plantar Interphalangeal Ligaments
plantar-interphalangeal-ligaments.summary: Thick fibrocartilage plates on the sole side of each toe joint. Flexor tendons slide over them.
plantar-interphalangeal-ligaments.clinical: Forced extension of a toe can injure the plate, causing pain under the toe.
attachments: Plantar base of the distal bone of each joint → plantar head of the proximal phalanx
plantar-interphalangeal-ligaments.function: Prevent hyperextension of the toe joints and form a smooth floor for the flexor tendons.

plantar-metatarsal-ligaments.name: Plantar Metatarsal Ligaments
plantar-metatarsal-ligaments.summary: Transverse bands on the sole between the bases of neighboring metatarsals.
plantar-metatarsal-ligaments.clinical: Injury is usually part of a midfoot sprain or a Lisfranc injury.
attachments: Plantar surface of one metatarsal base → plantar surface of the adjacent base
plantar-metatarsal-ligaments.function: Hold the metatarsal bases together and support the transverse arch.

plantar-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.name: Plantar Metatarsophalangeal Ligaments
plantar-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.summary: Thick fibrocartilage plates on the sole side of each toe base joint, also called plantar plates. They are grooved for flexor tendons.
plantar-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.clinical: Tears of the second plate cause forefoot pain and a crossover toe. Turf toe injures the plate of the great toe.
attachments: Plantar neck of the metatarsal → plantar base of the proximal phalanx
plantar-metatarsophalangeal-ligaments.function: Prevent hyperextension of the toe joints, bear load, and link to the deep transverse metatarsal ligament.

plantar-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.name: Plantar Tarsometatarsal Ligaments
plantar-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.summary: A group of fibrous bands on the sole side of the tarsometatarsal joints. They reinforce the joints from below.
plantar-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.clinical: Midfoot (Lisfranc) injuries disrupt these joints and ligaments; they often follow a twisting fall on a planted, plantarflexed foot.
attachments: Plantar surfaces of the cuboid and cuneiforms → plantar surfaces of the bases of the metatarsals
plantar-tarsometatarsal-ligaments.function: Bind the metatarsal bases to the tarsal bones and support the transverse and longitudinal arches.

popliteofibular-ligament.name: Popliteofibular Ligament
popliteofibular-ligament.summary: A strong band that links the popliteus tendon to the fibular head. It is a key stabilizer of the posterolateral corner of the knee.
popliteofibular-ligament.clinical: Often torn together with the posterior cruciate or lateral collateral ligament in posterolateral corner injuries; missed injuries cause chronic instability.
popliteofibular-ligament.joint_type: Not a separate joint; reinforces the knee, a modified hinge
attachments: Popliteus tendon (near the musculotendinous junction) → posterior aspect of the fibular head (styloid process)
popliteofibular-ligament.function: Resists external rotation, varus stress and posterior translation of the tibia, with the lateral collateral ligament.

posterior-cruciate-ligament.name: Posterior Cruciate Ligament
posterior-cruciate-ligament.summary: A thick intracapsular ligament that runs upward, forward and medially from the tibia to the femur. It is the main restraint to posterior tibial translation.
posterior-cruciate-ligament.clinical: Torn by a blow to the front of the flexed knee, such as a dashboard injury; the tibia then sags backward (posterior drawer sign).
attachments: Lateral surface of the medial femoral condyle (intercondylar notch) → posterior intercondylar area of the tibia
posterior-cruciate-ligament.function: Prevents the tibia from sliding backward on the femur (or the femur forward on the tibia), especially in flexion.

posterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.name: Posterior Ligament of Fibular Head
posterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.summary: A band of fibers behind the superior tibiofibular joint. It runs obliquely upward from the fibular head to the tibia.
posterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.clinical: The popliteus tendon crosses close behind it. Joint dislocation is rare and usually follows a twisting injury with the knee flexed.
attachments: Posterior aspect of the fibular head → posterior aspect of the lateral tibial condyle
posterior-ligament-of-fibular-head.function: Reinforces the joint capsule and limits movement of the fibular head.

posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral.name: Posterior Meniscotibial Ligament (Lateral Meniscus)
posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral.summary: A fibrous attachment that anchors the back end of the lateral meniscus to the tibia. The exact structure is named conservatively here.
posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral.clinical: Tears of this root attachment let the meniscus shift outward and weaken its shock-absorbing role.
posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-lateral.bone_type: Fibrocartilage and fibrous tissue (meniscal horn attachment)
landmarks: Posterior horn of the lateral meniscus
Posterior intercondylar area of the tibia
attachments: Posterior horn of the lateral meniscus → posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, in front of the medial meniscal attachment

posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-.name: Posterior Meniscotibial Ligament (Medial Meniscus)
posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-.summary: A fibrous attachment that anchors the back end of the medial meniscus to the tibia. The exact structure is named conservatively here.
posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-.clinical: Medial meniscus posterior root tears are linked to rapid knee osteoarthritis because the meniscus can no longer absorb load.
posterior-meniscotibial-ligament-medial-.bone_type: Fibrocartilage and fibrous tissue (meniscal horn attachment)
landmarks: Posterior horn of the medial meniscus
Posterior intercondylar area of the tibia
attachments: Posterior horn of the medial meniscus → posterior intercondylar area of the tibia, between the posterior cruciate ligament and lateral meniscal attachments

posterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.name: Posterior Talocalcaneal Ligament
posterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.summary: A short band behind the subtalar joint. It joins the talus to the calcaneus.
posterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.clinical: Subtalar sprains often occur with lateral ankle sprains and cause hindfoot pain that feels like an ankle problem.
attachments: Lateral tubercle of the posterior process of the talus → upper surface of the calcaneus
posterior-talocalcaneal-ligament.function: Reinforces the back of the subtalar joint capsule and limits excess motion between talus and calcaneus.

posterior-talofibular-ligament.name: Posterior Talofibular Ligament
posterior-talofibular-ligament.summary: The strongest and deepest of the three lateral ankle ligaments. It runs almost horizontally behind the talus.
posterior-talofibular-ligament.clinical: Rarely injured alone; it tears only in severe inversion sprains or dislocations, after the anterior talofibular and calcaneofibular ligaments.
attachments: Medial surface of the lateral malleolus (malleolar fossa) → lateral tubercle of the posterior process of the talus
posterior-talofibular-ligament.function: Prevents backward slipping of the talus and limits excess inversion, mainly in dorsiflexion.

posterior-tibiofibular-ligament.name: Posterior Tibiofibular Ligament
posterior-tibiofibular-ligament.summary: A strong band behind the distal tibiofibular joint. It is stronger than the anterior ligament.
posterior-tibiofibular-ligament.clinical: Injured in high ankle sprains from forced external rotation or dorsiflexion; a widened mortise on imaging suggests syndesmotic injury.
attachments: Posterior border of the lateral malleolus and distal fibula → posterior tubercle of the distal tibia
posterior-tibiofibular-ligament.function: Holds the lower ends of the tibia and fibula together and keeps the ankle mortise stable.

posterior-tibitalar-ligament.name: Posterior Tibiotalar Ligament
posterior-tibitalar-ligament.parent: Medial collateral ligament of ankle (deltoid ligament)
posterior-tibitalar-ligament.summary: The deepest and strongest part of the medial (deltoid) ligament. It lies close to the talus.
posterior-tibitalar-ligament.clinical: Deltoid injury accompanies lateral malleolus fractures from eversion; deep fibers failing allow the talus to shift outward.
attachments: Medial malleolus (posterior colliculus and intercollicular groove) → medial and posterior surfaces of the talus
posterior-tibitalar-ligament.function: Deep part of the deltoid ligament; resists eversion and lateral shift of the talus.

superficial-part-of-tibial-collateral-li.name: Superficial Part of Tibial Collateral Ligament
superficial-part-of-tibial-collateral-li.summary: A long, flat band on the inner side of the knee. It lies deep to the pes anserinus tendons.
superficial-part-of-tibial-collateral-li.clinical: Sprained or torn by a blow to the outer knee that forces the joint inward; most medial collateral tears heal without surgery.
attachments: Medial epicondyle of the femur → medial surface of the tibia, about 5 to 7 cm below the joint line
superficial-part-of-tibial-collateral-li.function: Main restraint to valgus (knock-knee) stress; also resists external rotation of the tibia.

talocalcaneal-interosseus-ligament.name: Talocalcaneal Interosseous Ligament
talocalcaneal-interosseus-ligament.summary: A strong ligament in the tarsal canal. It separates the subtalar joint from the talocalcaneonavicular joint.
talocalcaneal-interosseus-ligament.clinical: Sprain or scarring here causes sinus tarsi syndrome, with pain on the outer foot just in front of the lateral malleolus.
attachments: Sulcus (groove) of the talus → sulcus of the calcaneus, within the tarsal sinus and canal
talocalcaneal-interosseus-ligament.function: Binds the talus tightly to the calcaneus and resists excess inversion and eversion.

talonavicular-ligament.name: Talonavicular Ligament
talonavicular-ligament.summary: A broad, thin band on the top of the foot. It joins the talar neck to the navicular bone.
talonavicular-ligament.clinical: Sprain here follows forced plantarflexion; this joint is key to the midtarsal motion that stiffens or loosens the foot.
attachments: Dorsal aspect of the neck of the talus → dorsal aspect of the navicular
talonavicular-ligament.function: Supports the top of the talonavicular joint and limits excess plantarflexion.

tibiocalcaneal-ligament.name: Tibiocalcaneal Ligament
tibiocalcaneal-ligament.parent: Medial collateral ligament of ankle (deltoid ligament)
tibiocalcaneal-ligament.summary: A band of the superficial deltoid ligament. It runs straight down from the medial malleolus to the calcaneus.
tibiocalcaneal-ligament.clinical: Part of the deltoid ligament; torn in eversion injuries, which are less common than lateral inversion sprains.
attachments: Anterior colliculus of the medial malleolus → sustentaculum tali of the calcaneus
tibiocalcaneal-ligament.function: Resists eversion and valgus tilt of the heel.

tibionavicular-ligament.name: Tibionavicular Ligament
tibionavicular-ligament.parent: Medial collateral ligament of ankle (deltoid ligament)
tibionavicular-ligament.summary: The front band of the superficial deltoid ligament. It fans from the medial malleolus to the navicular.
tibionavicular-ligament.clinical: Part of the deltoid ligament; may tear with forced eversion or with fractures of the lateral malleolus.
attachments: Anterior colliculus of the medial malleolus → navicular (including the plantar calcaneonavicular ligament)
tibionavicular-ligament.function: Resists eversion and supports the medial side of the ankle and talonavicular joint.
