transverse-ligament-of-knee.name: Transverse Ligament of Knee
transverse-ligament-of-knee.summary: A small band that crosses the front of the tibial plateau. It is not always present.
transverse-ligament-of-knee.clinical: On MRI it can be mistaken for a tear at the front of the lateral meniscus.
attachments: Anterior horn of the medial meniscus → anterior horn of the lateral meniscus
transverse-ligament-of-knee.function: Joins the front of the two menisci so they move together during flexion and extension.

transverse-tibiofibular-ligament.name: Transverse Tibiofibular Ligament
transverse-tibiofibular-ligament.summary: A deep, thick part of the posterior tibiofibular ligament. It forms a lip behind the ankle mortise. It is not always described separately.
transverse-tibiofibular-ligament.clinical: Injury forms part of syndesmotic (high ankle) sprains and can allow the ankle mortise to widen.
attachments: Posterior surface of the lateral malleolus (malleolar fossa) → posterior margin of the distal tibia
transverse-tibiofibular-ligament.function: Deepens the socket for the talus and helps hold the tibia and fibula together.

costotransverse-ligament.name: Costotransverse Ligament
costotransverse-ligament.summary: A short, strong band that fills the gap between the rib neck and the transverse process of the matching vertebra.
costotransverse-ligament.clinical: Along with other costovertebral ligaments, it helps keep the ribs stable; rib subluxation here can cause sharp back pain with breathing.
attachments: Posterior surface of the neck of the rib → anterior surface of the transverse process of the same vertebra
costotransverse-ligament.function: Binds the rib neck to the transverse process and limits rib movement.

cricopharyngeal-ligament.name: Cricopharyngeal Ligament
cricopharyngeal-ligament.summary: A small fibrous band at the back of the larynx. It supports the crico-arytenoid joint. Its exact attachments vary by source.
cricopharyngeal-ligament.clinical: Damage to the crico-arytenoid joint after intubation can limit vocal fold movement and mimic nerve palsy.
attachments: Posterior part of the cricoid cartilage → arytenoid cartilage and pharyngeal wall (fibers blend with the inferior constrictor)
cricopharyngeal-ligament.function: Reinforces the back of the crico-arytenoid joint capsule.

external-intercostal-membrane.name: External Intercostal Membrane
external-intercostal-membrane.summary: A thin fibrous sheet that replaces the external intercostal muscle between the costal cartilages. Its fibers run down and forward.
external-intercostal-membrane.clinical: Surgeons pass chest tubes just above a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle that lies below it.
attachments: Lower border of the rib or costal cartilage above → upper border of the rib or costal cartilage below, near the sternum
external-intercostal-membrane.function: Closes the front of each intercostal space where muscle is absent and helps keep the chest wall intact.

internal-intercostal-membrane.name: Internal Intercostal Membrane
internal-intercostal-membrane.summary: A thin fibrous sheet that replaces the internal intercostal muscle near the spine. Its fibers run down and back.
internal-intercostal-membrane.clinical: The intercostal nerves and vessels pass between this layer and the pleura as they leave the spinal region, so deep stab wounds may injure them.
attachments: Lower border of the rib above → upper border of the rib below, from the rib angle back to the vertebral column
internal-intercostal-membrane.function: Closes the back of each intercostal space where muscle is absent and helps keep the chest wall intact.

intra-articular-ligament-of-head-of-rib.name: Intra-articular Ligament of Head of Rib
intra-articular-ligament-of-head-of-rib.summary: A short band inside the joint of the rib head. It is present on ribs 2 to 9, which meet two vertebrae. Ribs 1 and 10 to 12 lack it.
intra-articular-ligament-of-head-of-rib.clinical: Its attachment to the disc links rib movement with the spine; disc or joint disease can cause pain that spreads around the chest wall.
attachments: Crest of the head of the rib → intervertebral disc between two adjacent vertebrae
intra-articular-ligament-of-head-of-rib.function: Divides the joint into two cavities and anchors the rib head to the disc.

median-cricothyroid-ligament.name: Median Cricothyroid Ligament
median-cricothyroid-ligament.summary: A thick midline band of elastic tissue. It lies just under the skin between the thyroid and cricoid cartilages.
median-cricothyroid-ligament.clinical: Cut in emergency cricothyrotomy to reach the airway below the vocal folds when the upper airway is blocked.
attachments: Upper border of the arch of the cricoid cartilage → lower border of the thyroid cartilage, in the midline
median-cricothyroid-ligament.function: Connects the cricoid and thyroid cartilages in the midline and completes the front of the conus elasticus.

radiate-ligament-of-head-of-rib.name: Radiate Ligament of Head of Rib
radiate-ligament-of-head-of-rib.summary: A fan-shaped band with three parts. It spreads from the rib head to the vertebra above, the vertebra below and the disc.
radiate-ligament-of-head-of-rib.clinical: Damage to this ligament or joint can cause rib head subluxation and pain with deep breathing or twisting.
attachments: Anterior part of the head of the rib → bodies of two adjacent vertebrae and the intervertebral disc between them
radiate-ligament-of-head-of-rib.function: Holds the rib head against the vertebral bodies and reinforces the front of the joint capsule.

acetabular-labrum.name: Acetabular Labrum
acetabular-labrum.summary: A ring of fibrocartilage on the rim of the acetabulum. It deepens the socket and grips the femoral head.
acetabular-labrum.clinical: Labral tears cause groin pain and clicking. They are often linked to femoroacetabular impingement.
landmarks: Acetabular notch (bridged by the transverse acetabular ligament)
attachments: Rim of the acetabulum
Transverse acetabular ligament

anterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.name: Anterior Sacro-iliac Ligament
anterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.summary: A thin band at the front of the sacro-iliac joint. It is a thickening of the joint capsule.
anterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.clinical: It tears in severe pelvic ring injuries such as open-book fractures, which widen the joint.
attachments: Pelvic surface of the sacrum (lateral part) → pelvic surface of the ilium, along the preauricular sulcus
anterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.function: Reinforces the front of the sacro-iliac joint capsule. It is thin and the weakest of the sacro-iliac ligaments.

articular-capsule-of-hip-joint.name: Articular Capsule of Hip Joint
articular-capsule-of-hip-joint.summary: A strong, thick sleeve that surrounds the hip joint from the acetabulum to the femoral neck.
articular-capsule-of-hip-joint.clinical: Femoral neck fractures inside the capsule can tear the retinacular vessels. This may cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
attachments: Acetabular rim, labrum and transverse acetabular ligament → femoral neck (intertrochanteric line in front; neck above the intertrochanteric crest behind)
articular-capsule-of-hip-joint.function: Encloses the joint and holds the femoral head in the socket. Retinacular fibers carry blood vessels to the femoral head.

articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.name: Articular Capsules of Distal Interphalangeal Joints
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.latin: Capsulae articulares articulationum interphalangealium distalium manus
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.summary: Thin capsules around the joints nearest the fingertips. Each covers one distal interphalangeal joint of a finger.
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.clinical: Osteoarthritis here forms bony lumps called Heberden nodes.
attachments: Head of the middle phalanx → base of the distal phalanx
articular-capsules-of-distal-interphalan.function: Encloses each joint and allows flexion and extension of the fingertip. Collateral ligaments and palmar ligaments reinforce it.

articular-capsules-of-metacarpophalangea.name: Articular Capsules of Metacarpophalangeal Joints
articular-capsules-of-metacarpophalangea.summary: Loose capsules around the knuckle joints. They are thin on the back and thickened on the palm side by the palmar ligaments.
articular-capsules-of-metacarpophalangea.clinical: Rheumatoid arthritis often attacks these joints, causing swollen knuckles and ulnar drift of the fingers.
attachments: Metacarpal head → base of the proximal phalanx
articular-capsules-of-metacarpophalangea.function: Encloses each knuckle joint. Allows flexion, extension, abduction, adduction and circumduction.

articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.name: Articular Capsules of Proximal Interphalangeal Joints
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.latin: Capsulae articulares articulationum interphalangealium proximalium manus
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.summary: Capsules around the middle joints of the fingers. Each covers one proximal interphalangeal joint.
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.clinical: Sprains and dislocations are common in ball sports. Osteoarthritis here forms bony lumps called Bouchard nodes.
attachments: Head of the proximal phalanx → base of the middle phalanx
articular-capsules-of-proximal-interphal.function: Encloses each middle finger joint and allows flexion and extension. Collateral ligaments and palmar ligaments reinforce it.

collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.name: Collateral Interphalangeal Ligaments of Hand
collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.summary: Cord-like ligaments on each side of every interphalangeal joint. They run obliquely toward the palm.
collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.clinical: Jamming injuries sprain these ligaments. The joint may stay stiff and swollen for months afterward.
attachments: Side of the head of the proximal bone → side of the base of the distal bone and palmar ligament
collateral-interphalangeal-ligaments-of-.function: Prevent side-to-side bending of the finger joints. They allow only flexion and extension.

collateral-metacarpophalangeal-ligaments.name: Collateral Metacarpophalangeal Ligaments
collateral-metacarpophalangeal-ligaments.summary: Strong cords on each side of the knuckle joints. The cam shape of the metacarpal head tightens them in flexion.
collateral-metacarpophalangeal-ligaments.clinical: A torn ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb knuckle causes gamekeeper thumb, also called skier thumb.
attachments: Side of the metacarpal head (dorsal tubercle) → side of the base of the proximal phalanx and palmar ligament
collateral-metacarpophalangeal-ligaments.function: Stabilize the knuckle against side-to-side force. They are tight in flexion and loose in extension, so fingers spread best when straight.

deep-transverse-metacarpal-ligament.name: Deep Transverse Metacarpal Ligament
deep-transverse-metacarpal-ligament.summary: Three short bands joining the palmar ligaments of the finger knuckles. Lumbrical tendons pass in front of them and interosseous tendons behind them.
deep-transverse-metacarpal-ligament.clinical: It helps hold a fractured metacarpal neck, such as a boxer fracture, from shifting far out of line.
attachments: Palmar ligament of one knuckle joint → palmar ligament of the neighboring knuckle joint
deep-transverse-metacarpal-ligament.function: Binds the heads of metacarpals 2 to 5 together and limits how far they spread apart.

dorsal-carpometacarpal-ligaments.name: Dorsal Carpometacarpal Ligaments
dorsal-carpometacarpal-ligaments.summary: Fibrous bands on the back of the hand linking the distal carpal row to the metacarpal bases.
dorsal-carpometacarpal-ligaments.clinical: Carpometacarpal fracture-dislocations, mostly of the fourth and fifth joints, follow punching or crush injuries. They are often missed on X-ray.
attachments: Distal row carpal bones (trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate) → bases of metacarpals 2 to 5, on the back of the hand
dorsal-carpometacarpal-ligaments.function: Reinforce the back of the carpometacarpal joints. They limit movement, so the second and third joints are almost rigid.

dorsal-intercarpal-ligaments.name: Dorsal Intercarpal Ligaments
dorsal-intercarpal-ligaments.summary: Short transverse bands across the back of the wrist. They connect adjacent carpal bones.
dorsal-intercarpal-ligaments.clinical: Injury contributes to carpal instability. Dorsal wrist ganglion cysts often form near them.
attachments: Dorsal surface of one carpal bone → dorsal surface of the neighboring carpal bone, within and between the two rows
dorsal-intercarpal-ligaments.function: Tie the carpal bones together on the back of the wrist and keep the rows moving as a unit.

dorsal-metacarpal-ligaments.name: Dorsal Metacarpal Ligaments
dorsal-metacarpal-ligaments.summary: Transverse bands that join the bases of metacarpals 2 to 5. They work with the palmar and interosseous metacarpal ligaments.
dorsal-metacarpal-ligaments.clinical: They are torn in carpometacarpal fracture-dislocations. Alone they are rarely injured.
attachments: Dorsal surface of the base of one metacarpal → dorsal surface of the base of the adjacent metacarpal
dorsal-metacarpal-ligaments.function: Bind the metacarpal bases together on the back of the hand. They limit movement between neighboring bases.

dorsal-scaphotriquetral-ligament.name: Dorsal Scaphotriquetral Ligament
dorsal-scaphotriquetral-ligament.summary: A dorsal band that connects the scaphoid to the triquetrum. It is part of the dorsal intercarpal ligament complex.
dorsal-scaphotriquetral-ligament.clinical: Damage to the dorsal intercarpal ligaments can lead to wrist instability.
attachments: Dorsal scaphoid → dorsal triquetrum, passing over the lunate region
dorsal-scaphotriquetral-ligament.function: Links the scaphoid and triquetrum on the back of the wrist and helps hold the proximal carpal row together.

dorsal-ulnocarpal-ligament.name: Dorsal Ulnocarpal Ligament
dorsal-ulnocarpal-ligament.summary: A thin dorsal ligament on the ulnar side of the wrist, joining the distal ulna region to the carpal bones.
dorsal-ulnocarpal-ligament.clinical: Ulnar-sided wrist pain often involves the nearby triangular fibrocartilage complex.
attachments: Distal ulna and its ulnar side → triquetrum (and nearby ulnar carpal bones) on the back of the wrist
dorsal-ulnocarpal-ligament.function: Supports the ulnar side of the back of the wrist and links the ulna to the carpal bones.

frenula-capsulae.name: Retinacula of the Hip Capsule
frenula-capsulae.summary: Longitudinal fibers of the capsule folded back along the femoral neck. They are also called the retinacula of Weitbrecht.
frenula-capsulae.clinical: Femoral neck fractures can tear these fibers and their vessels. This may cut off the blood supply to the femoral head.
attachments: Hip capsule near its femoral attachment → along the femoral neck toward the edge of the femoral head (reflected fibers)
frenula-capsulae.function: Carry retinacular blood vessels along the femoral neck to the femoral head.

iliolumbar-ligament.name: Iliolumbar Ligament
iliolumbar-ligament.summary: A strong, fan-shaped band between the L5 transverse process and the pelvis.
iliolumbar-ligament.clinical: Strain of this ligament can cause low back pain felt over the iliac crest.
iliolumbar-ligament.joint: Lumbosacral junction and sacro-iliac joint region
attachments: Transverse processes of L4 and L5 → iliac crest and ilium (posterior part)
iliolumbar-ligament.function: Anchors the lowest lumbar vertebrae to the ilium. Limits rotation and forward sliding of L5 on the sacrum.

inferior-pubic-ligament.name: Inferior Pubic Ligament
inferior-pubic-ligament.summary: A thick arch of fibers under the pubic symphysis. It is also called the arcuate pubic ligament.
inferior-pubic-ligament.clinical: The deep dorsal vein of the penis or clitoris passes between this ligament and the transverse perineal ligament.
attachments: Inferior pubic ramus (one side) → inferior pubic ramus (other side), arching below the symphysis
inferior-pubic-ligament.function: Strengthens the pubic symphysis from below and rounds the top of the pubic arch.

interosseous-sacro-iliac-ligament.name: Interosseous Sacro-iliac Ligament
interosseous-sacro-iliac-ligament.summary: A very short, thick mass of fibers behind the joint. It is the strongest ligament of the sacro-iliac joint.
interosseous-sacro-iliac-ligament.clinical: Sprain or dysfunction of the sacro-iliac joint causes low back and buttock pain.
attachments: Sacral tuberosity → iliac tuberosity, filling the gap behind the joint
interosseous-sacro-iliac-ligament.function: Is the main bond of the joint. It transfers body weight from the spine to the hip bones.

interosseus-metacarpal-ligaments.name: Interosseous Metacarpal Ligaments
interosseus-metacarpal-ligaments.summary: Short, strong bands between the sides of neighboring metacarpal bases. They lie deeper than the dorsal and palmar ligaments.
interosseus-metacarpal-ligaments.clinical: Together with the other metacarpal ligaments, they make the central metacarpal bases a rigid column.
attachments: Side of the base of one metacarpal → side of the base of the adjacent metacarpal, deep to the joint surfaces
interosseus-metacarpal-ligaments.function: Bind the metacarpal bases together deep within the hand and limit their movement.

interpubic-disc.name: Interpubic Disc
interpubic-disc.summary: A fibrocartilage disc between the two pubic bones. It forms the core of the pubic symphysis.
interpubic-disc.clinical: It softens and widens in pregnancy under the hormone relaxin. Strain can cause pubic pain and a wide gait.
landmarks: Lies between the oval symphysial surfaces of the pubic bodies
attachments: Hyaline cartilage covering each symphysial surface
Superior and inferior pubic ligaments

ischiofemoral-ligament.name: Ischiofemoral Ligament
ischiofemoral-ligament.summary: A spiral band on the back of the hip joint. Its fibers blend with the capsule and the zona orbicularis.
ischiofemoral-ligament.clinical: It tightens when the hip extends. Ischiofemoral impingement can also compress soft tissue between the ischium and femur.
attachments: Ischial part of the acetabular rim → neck of the femur, spiraling up and out toward the base of the greater trochanter
ischiofemoral-ligament.function: Limits hyperextension and, in a flexed hip, internal rotation. It is the weakest of the three hip ligaments.

ligament-of-head-of-femur.name: Ligament of Head of Femur
ligament-of-head-of-femur.summary: A flat band inside the hip joint that runs from the acetabular notch to the pit on the femoral head. Synovium covers it.
ligament-of-head-of-femur.clinical: The artery in this ligament matters in children. The ligament tears in hip dislocation.
attachments: Acetabular notch and transverse acetabular ligament → fovea of the femoral head
ligament-of-head-of-femur.function: Carries a small artery to the femoral head. It adds little to hip stability.

obturator-membrane.name: Obturator Membrane
obturator-membrane.summary: A tough sheet that seals most of the obturator foramen. The obturator canal at its top lets the obturator nerve and vessels pass.
obturator-membrane.clinical: An obturator hernia can pass through the obturator canal and press on the obturator nerve.
obturator-membrane.joint: Obturator foramen of the pelvic girdle
attachments: Margin of the obturator foramen (pubis and ischium) → closes the foramen, leaving an obturator canal above
obturator-membrane.function: Closes the obturator foramen and gives attachment to the obturator internus and externus muscles.

palmar-carpometacarpal-ligaments.name: Palmar Carpometacarpal Ligaments
palmar-carpometacarpal-ligaments.summary: Fibrous bands on the palm side linking the distal carpal row to the metacarpal bases.
palmar-carpometacarpal-ligaments.clinical: Fracture-dislocations of these joints are uncommon but easily missed after high-energy hand trauma.
attachments: Distal row carpal bones → bases of metacarpals 2 to 5, on the palm side
palmar-carpometacarpal-ligaments.function: Reinforce the palm side of the carpometacarpal joints and limit their movement.

palmar-interphalangeal-ligaments.name: Palmar Interphalangeal Ligaments
palmar-interphalangeal-ligaments.summary: Thick fibrocartilage plates on the palm side of each interphalangeal joint, also called volar plates.
palmar-interphalangeal-ligaments.clinical: Hyperextension injuries tear the volar plate of the proximal interphalangeal joint. Chronic laxity can lead to a swan-neck deformity.
attachments: Firmly to the base of the distal bone; loosely to the neck of the proximal bone → form the palm side of the capsule
palmar-interphalangeal-ligaments.function: Prevent hyperextension of the finger joints. Their grooves guide the flexor tendons.

palmar-metacarpal-ligaments.name: Palmar Metacarpal Ligaments
palmar-metacarpal-ligaments.summary: Transverse bands that join the palm sides of the bases of metacarpals 2 to 5.
palmar-metacarpal-ligaments.clinical: Alone they are rarely injured. They tear along with other ligaments in carpometacarpal dislocations.
attachments: Palmar surface of the base of one metacarpal → palmar surface of the base of the adjacent metacarpal
palmar-metacarpal-ligaments.function: Bind the metacarpal bases together on the palm side and limit movement between them.

palmar-scaphotriquetral-ligament.name: Palmar Scaphotriquetral Ligament
palmar-scaphotriquetral-ligament.summary: A palmar band joining the scaphoid and triquetrum. It lies with the other palmar midcarpal ligaments.
palmar-scaphotriquetral-ligament.clinical: Tears of palmar midcarpal ligaments can cause wrist instability.
attachments: Palmar scaphoid → palmar triquetrum, crossing the front of the lunate and capitate region
palmar-scaphotriquetral-ligament.function: Links the scaphoid and triquetrum on the palm side and supports the midcarpal joint.

pisotriquetral-ligament.name: Pisotriquetral Ligament
pisotriquetral-ligament.summary: A short ligament and capsule thickening between the pisiform and the triquetrum.
pisotriquetral-ligament.clinical: Pisotriquetral osteoarthritis causes pain on the ulnar side of the wrist.
attachments: Pisiform → triquetrum, reinforcing the capsule of the pisotriquetral joint
pisotriquetral-ligament.function: Stabilizes the pisiform against the triquetrum. The pisiform acts as a pulley for the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.

posterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.name: Posterior Sacro-iliac Ligament
posterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.summary: A strong sheet of short and long fibers behind the sacro-iliac joint. The long fibers can blend with the sacrotuberous ligament.
posterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.clinical: Sprain causes pain near the dimples over the posterior superior iliac spines.
attachments: Iliac tuberosity and posterior superior iliac spine → sacral crests (short fibers to the S1 to S2 region; long fibers to S3 to S4)
posterior-sacro-iliac-ligament.function: Resists forces that push the sacrum down and forward. It helps transfer body weight to the hip bones.

pubic-symphysis.name: Pubic Symphysis
pubic-symphysis.summary: The midline joint where the two pubic bones meet. A fibrocartilage disc joins them.
pubic-symphysis.clinical: It widens in late pregnancy and childbirth. Separation (diastasis) or injury causes pubic pain and a waddling gait.
landmarks: Symphysial surface of each pubic body
attachments: Interpubic disc
Superior pubic ligament
Inferior (arcuate) pubic ligament
movements: Slight widening and shifting during pregnancy and childbirth

pubofemoral-ligament.name: Pubofemoral Ligament
pubofemoral-ligament.summary: A triangular band on the front and lower side of the hip joint. It blends with the joint capsule.
pubofemoral-ligament.clinical: Forced abduction, as in a split, can strain it.
attachments: Superior pubic ramus and obturator crest → blends with the capsule and the lower part of the iliofemoral ligament on the femoral neck
pubofemoral-ligament.function: Limits excessive abduction and extension of the hip.

radial-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-join.name: Radial Collateral Ligament of Wrist Joint
radial-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-join.summary: A cord on the thumb side of the wrist. It runs from the radial styloid process to the scaphoid.
radial-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-join.clinical: Scaphoid fractures cause tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox next to this ligament.
attachments: Styloid process of the radius → scaphoid (and trapezium)
radial-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-join.function: Stabilizes the radial side of the wrist and limits ulnar deviation.

radiate-carpal-ligament.name: Radiate Carpal Ligament
radiate-carpal-ligament.summary: A palmar ligament whose fibers fan out from the head of the capitate to neighboring carpal bones.
attachments: Head of the capitate → radiating to the scaphoid, trapezoid, lunate and triquetrum on the palm side
radiate-carpal-ligament.function: Binds the capitate to the surrounding carpal bones on the palm side and supports the midcarpal joint.

radioscaphocapitate-ligament.name: Radioscaphocapitate Ligament
radioscaphocapitate-ligament.summary: A palmar radiocarpal ligament running from the radius across the scaphoid to the capitate.
radioscaphocapitate-ligament.clinical: It is torn in severe wrist injuries such as perilunate dislocation.
attachments: Radial styloid process → waist of the scaphoid and body of the capitate (palmar side)
radioscaphocapitate-ligament.function: Supports the scaphoid like a sling and stops the carpus from sliding toward the ulna.

sacrospinous-ligament.name: Sacrospinous Ligament
sacrospinous-ligament.summary: A triangular band in front of the sacrotuberous ligament. With it, the ligament divides the sciatic notches into two foramina.
sacrospinous-ligament.clinical: Surgeons use it to anchor the vaginal vault in sacrospinous fixation for prolapse. The pudendal nerve lies close behind it.
attachments: Lateral margins of the sacrum and coccyx → ischial spine
sacrospinous-ligament.function: Resists forward tilting of the sacrum. Forms the lower border of the greater sciatic foramen.

sacrotuberous-ligament.name: Sacrotuberous Ligament
sacrotuberous-ligament.summary: A strong, broad band behind the pelvis. It gives origin to part of gluteus maximus and may blend with the biceps femoris tendon.
sacrotuberous-ligament.clinical: The pudendal nerve can be compressed between this ligament and the sacrospinous ligament.
attachments: Posterior iliac spines, lower sacrum and coccyx → medial surface of the ischial tuberosity
sacrotuberous-ligament.function: Resists upward tilting of the sacrum and holds the sacrum against the hip bones when standing and sitting.

scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal-ligament.name: Scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal Ligament
scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal-ligament.summary: A palmar ligament binding the scaphoid to the trapezium and trapezoid.
scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal-ligament.clinical: Osteoarthritis of the scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joint is common and causes pain at the base of the thumb.
attachments: Distal pole of the scaphoid → trapezium and trapezoid (palmar side)
scaphotrapeziotrapezoidal-ligament.function: Stabilizes the distal scaphoid against the trapezium and trapezoid.

superior-pubic-ligament.name: Superior Pubic Ligament
superior-pubic-ligament.summary: A thick band along the upper border of the pubic symphysis. It joins the two pubic crests and tubercles.
superior-pubic-ligament.clinical: It may stretch in pregnancy and lets the symphysis widen slightly.
attachments: Pubic crest and tubercle (one side) → pubic crest and tubercle (other side), along the top of the symphysis
superior-pubic-ligament.function: Strengthens the pubic symphysis from above.

transverse-acetabular-ligament.name: Transverse Acetabular Ligament
transverse-acetabular-ligament.summary: A strong band that converts the acetabular notch into a tunnel. It is continuous with the acetabular labrum.
transverse-acetabular-ligament.clinical: The artery of the ligament of the head of the femur passes beneath it.
attachments: One side of the acetabular notch → other side, bridging the notch and joining the labrum
transverse-acetabular-ligament.function: Completes the ring of the acetabular rim. A gap beneath it lets vessels reach the joint.

transverse-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.name: Transverse Part of Iliofemoral Ligament
transverse-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.summary: The upper, more horizontal band of the Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament, on the front of the hip.
transverse-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.clinical: The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament in the body. Hip dislocation needs great force.
attachments: Anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular rim → upper part of the intertrochanteric line of the femur
transverse-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.function: Limits hip hyperextension and external rotation. It is the upper limb of the Y-shaped ligament.

descending-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.name: Descending Part of Iliofemoral Ligament
descending-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.summary: The lower, more vertical band of the Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament, on the front of the hip.
descending-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.clinical: The iliofemoral ligament is the strongest ligament in the body. Hip dislocation needs great force.
attachments: Anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular rim → lower part of the intertrochanteric line of the femur
descending-part-of-iliofemoral-ligament.function: Limits hip hyperextension and lets a person stand upright with little muscle effort.

triradiate-cartilage.name: Triradiate Cartilage
triradiate-cartilage.summary: A Y-shaped plate of hyaline cartilage in the acetabulum. It joins the ilium, ischium and pubis in children.
triradiate-cartilage.clinical: Injury in a child can close the plate early and cause a shallow, deformed hip socket.
landmarks: Y-shaped plate in the floor of the acetabulum
attachments: Joins the three parts of the hip bone at the acetabulum
triradiate-cartilage.ossification: Fuses at about 14 to 16 years; girls usually before boys

ulnar-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-joint.name: Ulnar Collateral Ligament of Wrist Joint
ulnar-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-joint.summary: A cord on the little-finger side of the wrist. It runs from the ulnar styloid process to the triquetrum and pisiform.
ulnar-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-joint.clinical: Ulnar-sided wrist injuries often involve this ligament and the triangular fibrocartilage complex.
attachments: Styloid process of the ulna → triquetrum and pisiform
ulnar-collateral-ligament-of-wrist-joint.function: Stabilizes the ulnar side of the wrist and limits radial deviation.

zona-orbicularis.name: Zona Orbicularis
zona-orbicularis.summary: A ring of circular capsular fibers around the narrowest part of the femoral neck.
zona-orbicularis.clinical: It helps hold the femoral head in place if the capsule is stretched.
attachments: Circular fibers around the neck of the femur, deep within the capsule; no direct bony attachment
zona-orbicularis.function: Forms a collar around the femoral neck that resists pulling the femoral head out of the socket.

triquetrocapitate-ligament.name: Triquetrocapitate Ligament
triquetrocapitate-ligament.summary: A palmar midcarpal ligament running from the triquetrum to the capitate. It forms part of the arcuate ligament with the scaphocapitate ligament.
triquetrocapitate-ligament.clinical: Tears of palmar midcarpal ligaments can cause midcarpal instability and a clunking wrist.
attachments: Palmar triquetrum → capitate (palmar side)
triquetrocapitate-ligament.function: Supports the ulnar side of the midcarpal joint and links the proximal and distal carpal rows.

dorsal-parts-of-lateral-intertransversar.name: Lateral Intertransversarii Lumborum (Dorsal Parts)
dorsal-parts-of-lateral-intertransversar.latin: Musculi intertransversarii laterales lumborum, partes dorsales
dorsal-parts-of-lateral-intertransversar.summary: Small paired slips between adjacent lumbar transverse and accessory processes. Their dorsal parts form the back layer of the lateral lumbar intertransversarii.
dorsal-parts-of-lateral-intertransversar.clinical: They are rich in muscle spindles, so they mainly give position sense to the lumbar spine.
dorsal-parts-of-lateral-intertransversar.origin: Accessory process or transverse process of a lumbar vertebra
dorsal-parts-of-lateral-intertransversar.insertion: Transverse process or accessory process of the vertebra above
action: Lateral flexion of the lumbar spine (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries

iliocostalis-colli-muscle.name: Iliocostalis Cervicis
iliocostalis-colli-muscle.summary: The uppermost part of the iliocostalis column. It links the upper ribs to the lower cervical vertebrae.
iliocostalis-colli-muscle.clinical: It helps extend the neck and is often tight in neck strain and poor posture.
iliocostalis-colli-muscle.insertion: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4 to C6
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

iliocostalis-lumborum-muscle.name: Iliocostalis Lumborum
iliocostalis-lumborum-muscle.summary: The lateral column of the erector spinae in the lower back. It runs from the common tendon to the lower ribs.
iliocostalis-lumborum-muscle.clinical: Strain of the erector spinae is a common cause of low back pain and muscle spasm.
iliocostalis-lumborum-muscle.origin: Common erector spinae tendon (sacrum, iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes and thoracolumbar fascia)
iliocostalis-lumborum-muscle.insertion: Inferior borders of the angles of the lower six or seven ribs
action: Laterally flexes the vertebral column (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries
Dorsal branches of the subcostal and posterior intercostal arteries

iliocostalis-thoracis-muscle.name: Iliocostalis Thoracis
iliocostalis-thoracis-muscle.summary: The middle part of the iliocostalis column. It connects the lower ribs to the upper ribs and C7.
iliocostalis-thoracis-muscle.clinical: It keeps the trunk upright and is part of the erector spinae mass that tightens in back spasm.
iliocostalis-thoracis-muscle.origin: Angles of the lower six ribs
iliocostalis-thoracis-muscle.insertion: Angles of the upper six ribs and the transverse process of C7
action: Laterally flexes the thoracic spine (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

interspinales-lumborum-muscles.name: Interspinales Lumborum
interspinales-lumborum-muscles.summary: Short paired muscles on either side of the interspinous ligament between neighboring lumbar spinous processes. There are about five pairs.
interspinales-lumborum-muscles.clinical: They contain many muscle spindles, so they mainly give position sense to the lumbar spine.
interspinales-lumborum-muscles.origin: Superior surface of a lumbar spinous process
interspinales-lumborum-muscles.insertion: Inferior surface of the spinous process above
action: Assist extension of the lumbar spine
blood: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries

interspinales-thoracis-muscles.name: Interspinales Thoracis
interspinales-thoracis-muscles.summary: Small, inconstant paired muscles between thoracic spinous processes. They occur mainly in the upper and lower thoracic spine.
interspinales-thoracis-muscles.clinical: These tiny muscles have little force. They mainly give position sense to the spine.
interspinales-thoracis-muscles.origin: Spinous process of a thoracic vertebra
interspinales-thoracis-muscles.insertion: Spinous process of the vertebra above
action: Assist extension of the thoracic spine
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

longissimus-colli-muscle.name: Longissimus Cervicis
longissimus-colli-muscle.summary: The neck part of the longissimus column. It joins the upper thoracic transverse processes to the cervical transverse processes.
longissimus-colli-muscle.clinical: It helps extend the neck and is often strained in whiplash and long periods of desk work.
longissimus-colli-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of the upper four or five thoracic vertebrae
longissimus-colli-muscle.insertion: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2 to C6
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

longissimus-thoracis-muscle.name: Longissimus Thoracis
longissimus-thoracis-muscle.summary: The largest column of the erector spinae. It lies between the iliocostalis and spinalis in the back.
longissimus-thoracis-muscle.clinical: It is the muscle most people rub when they have low back ache. Its tightness is common in back strain.
longissimus-thoracis-muscle.origin: Common erector spinae tendon (sacrum, iliac crest, lumbar spinous processes and thoracolumbar fascia) and lumbar transverse processes
longissimus-thoracis-muscle.insertion: Transverse processes of all thoracic vertebrae and the lower nine or ten ribs, between tubercles and angles
action: Laterally flexes the vertebral column (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries
Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal and subcostal arteries

multifidus-lumborum-muscle.name: Multifidus Lumborum
multifidus-lumborum-muscle.summary: Short, thick fascicles on each side of the lumbar spine. Each runs up and in, spanning two to four vertebrae.
multifidus-lumborum-muscle.clinical: Multifidus shrinks and weakens in chronic low back pain. Rehabilitation often targets it to stabilize the spine.
multifidus-lumborum-muscle.origin: Posterior sacrum, posterior superior iliac spine, posterior sacro-iliac ligaments and mammillary processes of the lumbar vertebrae
multifidus-lumborum-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of the vertebrae two to four levels above
action: Rotates the spine to the opposite side
blood: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries

multifidus-thoracis-muscle.name: Multifidus Thoracis
multifidus-thoracis-muscle.summary: Short fascicles on each side of the thoracic spine. Each runs from a transverse process up to a spinous process.
multifidus-thoracis-muscle.clinical: It helps keep the spine steady between vertebrae. Weak or injured multifidus contributes to back pain.
multifidus-thoracis-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of the thoracic vertebrae
multifidus-thoracis-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of the vertebrae two to four levels above
action: Rotates the spine to the opposite side
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

rotatores.name: Rotatores
rotatores.summary: The deepest transversospinalis muscles. Short ones span one level and long ones skip one level. They are best developed in the thoracic region.
rotatores.clinical: They are rich in muscle spindles and give position sense for fine control of the vertebrae.
rotatores.insertion: Lamina and base of the spinous process of the vertebra above (short) or two above (long)
action: Rotate the spine to the opposite side
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries
Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries

semispinalis-colli-muscle.name: Semispinalis Cervicis
semispinalis-colli-muscle.summary: A thick neck muscle deep to the splenius. Its fibers run from the upper thoracic transverse processes to cervical spinous processes.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.clinical: It is a key neck extensor. Strain here follows whiplash or long periods of looking down.
semispinalis-colli-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of T1 to T5 or T6
semispinalis-colli-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of C2 to C5
action: Rotates the neck to the opposite side (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

semispinalis-thoracis-muscle.name: Semispinalis Thoracis
semispinalis-thoracis-muscle.summary: A slim muscle with long tendons that crosses about five or six segments. It runs from the lower thoracic transverse processes up to the cervicothoracic spinous processes.
semispinalis-thoracis-muscle.clinical: It helps hold the upper back upright. It is one of the deep postural muscles that tire in prolonged sitting.
semispinalis-thoracis-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of T6 to T10
semispinalis-thoracis-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of C6 to T4
action: Extends the thoracic and cervical spine (both sides)
Rotates the spine to the opposite side (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

serratus-posterior-inferior-muscle.name: Serratus Posterior Inferior
serratus-posterior-inferior-muscle.summary: A thin, flat muscle at the thoracolumbar junction. It runs from the lower spine to the lower four ribs.
serratus-posterior-inferior-muscle.clinical: Its role in breathing is minor and debated. Surgeons reflect it to reach deeper back muscles.
serratus-posterior-inferior-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of T11 to L2 (through the thoracolumbar fascia)
serratus-posterior-inferior-muscle.insertion: Inferior borders of the lower four ribs (ribs 9 to 12)
action: Pulls the lower ribs down and back
Holds the lower ribs steady during breathing
serratus-posterior-inferior-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of T9 to T12 (intercostal and subcostal nerves)

serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.name: Serratus Posterior Superior
serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.summary: A thin, flat muscle deep to the rhomboids. It runs from the lower neck to the upper ribs.
serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.clinical: Its role in breathing is minor. It may add to upper back pain when strained.
serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 to T3
serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.insertion: Upper borders of ribs 2 to 5, lateral to their angles
serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of upper thoracic nerves (intercostal nerves, T2 to T5)
serratus-posterior-superior-muscle.roots: T2 to T5 (some sources T1 to T4)

spinalis-colli-muscle.name: Spinalis Cervicis
spinalis-colli-muscle.summary: The neck part of the spinalis column, next to the spinous processes. It is small and often absent.
spinalis-colli-muscle.clinical: It is inconstant and small, so it rarely matters clinically on its own.
spinalis-colli-muscle.origin: Ligamentum nuchae and spinous processes of C7 (sometimes T1 and T2)
spinalis-colli-muscle.insertion: Spinous process of C2 (sometimes C3 to C4)

spinalis-thoracis-muscle.name: Spinalis Thoracis
spinalis-thoracis-muscle.summary: The medial column of the erector spinae. It lies next to the spinous processes of the thoracic spine.
spinalis-thoracis-muscle.clinical: It is often tight in back spasm. It blends with the semispinalis, so it is hard to separate in dissection.
spinalis-thoracis-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of the upper lumbar and lower thoracic vertebrae (about T11 to L2)
spinalis-thoracis-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of the upper thoracic vertebrae (about T1 to T8)
blood: Dorsal branches of the posterior intercostal arteries

splenius-colli-muscle.name: Splenius Cervicis
splenius-colli-muscle.summary: A strap-like neck muscle deep to the trapezius. It lies lateral to the midline and runs up from the upper thoracic spine.
splenius-colli-muscle.clinical: Strain causes neck stiffness and pain. It helps rotate the head to the same side.
splenius-colli-muscle.origin: Spinous processes of T3 to T6
splenius-colli-muscle.insertion: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C1 to C3
action: Laterally flexes and rotates the neck to the same side (one side)
splenius-colli-muscle.nerve: Dorsal rami of middle and lower cervical nerves
blood: Dorsal branches of the upper posterior intercostal arteries

ventral-parts-of-lateral-intertransversa.name: Lateral Intertransversarii Lumborum (Ventral Parts)
ventral-parts-of-lateral-intertransversa.latin: Musculi intertransversarii laterales lumborum, partes ventrales
ventral-parts-of-lateral-intertransversa.summary: Small paired slips between adjacent lumbar transverse processes. Their ventral parts lie in front of the dorsal parts.
ventral-parts-of-lateral-intertransversa.clinical: They are rich in muscle spindles, so they mainly give position sense to the lumbar spine.
ventral-parts-of-lateral-intertransversa.origin: Transverse process of a lumbar vertebra
ventral-parts-of-lateral-intertransversa.insertion: Transverse process of the vertebra above
action: Lateral flexion of the lumbar spine (one side)
blood: Dorsal branches of the lumbar arteries

anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.name: Anterior Belly of Digastric
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.summary: The front belly of the digastric muscle runs from the chin region down to the intermediate tendon at the hyoid.
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.origin: Digastric fossa on the inner surface of the lower border of the mandible near the midline
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.insertion: Intermediate tendon of the digastric, which is held to the hyoid bone by a fibrous sling
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.nerve: Nerve to mylohyoid (from the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, CN V3)
blood: Submental artery (branch of the facial artery)
anterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.clinical: It helps open the mouth against resistance. Its nerve supply differs from the posterior belly because of its different embryological origin.

ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.name: Aryepiglottic Part of Oblique Arytenoid
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.summary: This slip continues from the oblique arytenoid muscle up through the aryepiglottic fold to the side of the epiglottis.
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.origin: Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage (continuation of the oblique arytenoid fibers)
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.insertion: Lateral margin of the epiglottis, within the aryepiglottic fold
action: Pulls the epiglottis toward the arytenoid cartilages
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.nerve: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of the vagus nerve)
ary-epiglottic-part-of-oblique-arytenoid.clinical: Along with the oblique arytenoids, it acts as a sphincter that helps close the laryngeal inlet and protect the airway during swallowing.

bucinator.name: Buccinator
bucinator.summary: The main muscle of the cheek. It forms the wall of the mouth and holds the cheek against the teeth.
bucinator.origin: Outer surfaces of the alveolar processes of the maxilla and mandible opposite the molars, and the pterygomandibular raphe
bucinator.insertion: Modiolus at the angle of the mouth, blending with the orbicularis oris
action: Presses the cheek against the teeth
Helps blow air out and suck
Keeps food on the chewing surfaces
bucinator.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
blood: Buccal artery (branch of the maxillary artery)
bucinator.clinical: It keeps food between the teeth while chewing and is used for blowing and sucking. Paralysis causes food to pool in the cheek.

common-tendinous-ring.name: Common Tendinous Ring
common-tendinous-ring.summary: A fibrous ring at the back of the orbit around the optic canal and part of the superior orbital fissure. It anchors the four rectus muscles.
common-tendinous-ring.origin: Sphenoid bone around the optic canal and the medial part of the superior orbital fissure
common-tendinous-ring.insertion: Gives origin to the superior, inferior, medial, and lateral rectus muscles
action: Anchors the origins of the four rectus muscles
common-tendinous-ring.clinical: Inflammation or tumors at this orbital apex can pinch the optic and oculomotor nerves, causing vision loss and double vision.

corrugator-supercilii.name: Corrugator Supercilii
corrugator-supercilii.summary: A small muscle deep to the eyebrow. It pulls the eyebrows together and down.
corrugator-supercilii.origin: Medial end of the superciliary arch of the frontal bone
corrugator-supercilii.insertion: Skin of the medial half of the eyebrow, above the middle of the supraorbital margin
action: Draws the eyebrows medially and downward (frowning)
corrugator-supercilii.nerve: Temporal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
corrugator-supercilii.clinical: It makes the vertical frown lines between the eyebrows. Botulinum toxin is often injected here to soften these lines.

deep-part-of-masseter.name: Deep Part of Masseter
deep-part-of-masseter.summary: The deeper, more vertical layer of the masseter. It lies close to the temporomandibular joint.
deep-part-of-masseter.origin: Deep surface of the zygomatic arch (posterior part)
deep-part-of-masseter.insertion: Upper part of the ramus of the mandible and its coronoid process
deep-part-of-masseter.nerve: Masseteric nerve (from the mandibular nerve, CN V3)
deep-part-of-masseter.clinical: Overuse from teeth grinding (bruxism) can enlarge the masseter and cause jaw pain and headaches.

depressor-anguli-oris.name: Depressor Anguli Oris
depressor-anguli-oris.summary: A triangular muscle that runs from the lower jaw to the corner of the mouth.
depressor-anguli-oris.origin: Oblique line of the mandible, below the canine and premolar teeth
depressor-anguli-oris.insertion: Skin at the angle of the mouth, blending with the orbicularis oris
action: Pulls the corner of the mouth down and laterally
depressor-anguli-oris.nerve: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
depressor-anguli-oris.clinical: It pulls the mouth corners down in a frown or sad expression. Weakness from facial nerve injury makes the mouth corner droop.

depressor-labii-inferioris.name: Depressor Labii Inferioris
depressor-labii-inferioris.summary: A quadrangular muscle of the lower lip. It lies deep to the depressor anguli oris.
depressor-labii-inferioris.origin: Oblique line of the mandible, between the symphysis and the mental foramen
depressor-labii-inferioris.insertion: Skin and mucosa of the lower lip, blending with the orbicularis oris
action: Pulls the lower lip down and slightly outward
depressor-labii-inferioris.nerve: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
depressor-labii-inferioris.clinical: The marginal mandibular nerve that supplies it can be injured in surgery near the jaw, which leaves the lower lip lopsided when smiling.

depressor-septi-nasi.name: Depressor Septi Nasi
depressor-septi-nasi.summary: A small slip of the nasalis region that runs from the upper lip area to the base of the nasal septum.
depressor-septi-nasi.origin: Incisive fossa of the maxilla, above the central incisor
depressor-septi-nasi.insertion: Mobile part of the nasal septum and the back of the ala of the nose
action: Pulls the nasal septum and nostril wing down
depressor-septi-nasi.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
depressor-septi-nasi.clinical: It pulls the nasal tip down when smiling. Some plastic surgeons treat a drooping nasal tip by weakening or releasing this muscle.

epicranial-aponeurosis.name: Epicranial Aponeurosis
epicranial-aponeurosis.summary: A tough tendon sheet over the top of the skull. It links the frontalis in front with the occipitalis behind.
epicranial-aponeurosis.origin: Frontal belly (frontalis) in front and occipital belly (occipitalis) behind
epicranial-aponeurosis.insertion: Blends laterally with the temporoparietalis and the temporal fascia
action: Transmits the pull of the frontalis and occipitalis
Moves the scalp over the skull
epicranial-aponeurosis.clinical: It forms the galea layer of the scalp. Deep cuts through it gape open, and bleeding under it can spread widely.

external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.name: External Part of Thyroarytenoid
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.summary: The outer, lateral part of the thyroarytenoid muscle. It lies beside the vocal fold.
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Lower half of the angle of the thyroid cartilage and the cricothyroid ligament
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Anterolateral surface of the arytenoid cartilage
action: Relaxes the vocal folds by shortening them
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.nerve: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of the vagus nerve)
external-part-of-thyro-arytenoid-muscle.clinical: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve weakens the vocal fold and causes a hoarse or breathy voice.

frontalis-muscle.name: Frontalis
frontalis-muscle.summary: The front belly of the epicranius. It forms the muscle of the forehead and has no bony attachment.
frontalis-muscle.origin: Epicranial aponeurosis (galea), in front of the coronal suture
frontalis-muscle.insertion: Skin of the eyebrows and forehead, blending with the orbicularis oculi and procerus
action: Wrinkles the skin of the forehead
frontalis-muscle.nerve: Temporal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
frontalis-muscle.clinical: It raises the eyebrows and wrinkles the forehead. Facial nerve injury flattens the forehead on the affected side.

genioglossus-muscle.name: Genioglossus
genioglossus-muscle.summary: The largest extrinsic tongue muscle. It makes up most of the bulk of the tongue and fans out from the chin.
genioglossus-muscle.origin: Superior mental spine on the inner surface of the mandible near the midline
genioglossus-muscle.insertion: Ventral surface of the tongue from root to tip, and the body of the hyoid bone
action: Depresses the center of the tongue
genioglossus-muscle.clinical: It keeps the airway open by pulling the tongue forward. With hypoglossal nerve injury the protruded tongue deviates toward the weak side.

geniohyoid-muscle.name: Geniohyoid
geniohyoid-muscle.summary: A short, narrow muscle above the mylohyoid. It runs from the chin to the hyoid bone.
geniohyoid-muscle.origin: Inferior mental spine on the inner surface of the mandible
geniohyoid-muscle.insertion: Anterior surface of the body of the hyoid bone
action: Pulls the hyoid bone up and forward
Depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed
geniohyoid-muscle.nerve: C1 fibers carried by the hypoglossal nerve
geniohyoid-muscle.clinical: It helps pull the hyoid forward during swallowing. It is supplied by C1 fibers that travel with the hypoglossal nerve.

hyoglossus-muscle.name: Hyoglossus
hyoglossus-muscle.summary: A flat, quadrangular extrinsic muscle that rises from the hyoid bone into the side of the tongue.
hyoglossus-muscle.origin: Body and greater horn of the hyoid bone
hyoglossus-muscle.insertion: Side and underside of the tongue
hyoglossus-muscle.clinical: It is a surgical landmark. The hypoglossal nerve runs on its outer surface, and the lingual artery passes deep to it.

inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.name: Inferior Head of Lateral Pterygoid
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.summary: The larger lower head of the lateral pterygoid. It runs backward from the lateral pterygoid plate to the neck of the mandible.
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.origin: Lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.insertion: Pterygoid fovea on the neck of the mandible
action: Depresses the chin (opens the mouth) with the other side
Moves the jaw side to side when one side acts
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.nerve: Nerve to lateral pterygoid (anterior trunk of the mandibular nerve, CN V3)
blood: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
inferior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.clinical: It pulls the jaw forward to open the mouth. Overactivity or injury can contribute to jaw dislocation and clicking of the temporomandibular joint.

inferior-oblique-muscle.name: Inferior Oblique
inferior-oblique-muscle.summary: The only extra-ocular muscle that arises from the front of the orbit. It runs under the eye to the outer back of the eyeball.
inferior-oblique-muscle.origin: Orbital surface of the maxilla, near the front of the orbital floor
inferior-oblique-muscle.insertion: Lateral sclera behind the equator of the eyeball, deep to the lateral rectus
action: Elevates the eye, especially when adducted
Extorts the eye (rotates the top outward)
inferior-oblique-muscle.nerve: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
blood: Inferior muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
inferior-oblique-muscle.clinical: It is tested by looking up and in. Oculomotor nerve palsy or an orbital floor fracture can limit upward gaze.

inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.name: Inferior Pharyngeal Constrictor
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.summary: The thickest and lowest of the three constrictors. It has an upper thyropharyngeus part and a lower cricopharyngeus part.
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.origin: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage (thyropharyngeus) and the side of the cricoid cartilage (cricopharyngeus)
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe at the back of the pharynx
action: Constricts the lower pharynx during swallowing
Cricopharyngeus closes the upper esophageal opening at rest
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.nerve: Pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve), with the external and recurrent laryngeal nerves
blood: Pharyngeal branches of the superior thyroid artery
inferior-pharyngeal-constrictor.clinical: A weak spot between its two parts can form a Zenker diverticulum. The cricopharyngeus acts as the upper esophageal sphincter.

inferior-rectus-muscle.name: Inferior Rectus
inferior-rectus-muscle.summary: The extra-ocular muscle along the floor of the orbit. It pulls the eye downward.
inferior-rectus-muscle.origin: Inferior part of the common tendinous ring
inferior-rectus-muscle.insertion: Inferior sclera, about 6 mm behind the corneal edge
action: Depresses the eye, especially when abducted
inferior-rectus-muscle.nerve: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
blood: Inferior muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
inferior-rectus-muscle.clinical: In an orbital floor blowout fracture it can become trapped, which limits upward gaze and causes double vision.

inferior-tarsus.name: Inferior Tarsal Muscle
inferior-tarsus.summary: A thin smooth muscle in the lower eyelid. The model group lists it with the extra-ocular muscles, so this may also represent the lower tarsal plate.
inferior-tarsus.origin: Capsulopalpebral fascia extending from the inferior rectus muscle
inferior-tarsus.insertion: Inferior border of the inferior tarsal plate
inferior-tarsus.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion
blood: Palpebral branches of the ophthalmic artery
inferior-tarsus.clinical: Its sympathetic supply is lost in Horner syndrome, which can slightly raise the lower lid and narrow the eye opening.

intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.name: Intermediate Tendon of Digastric
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.summary: The central tendon that joins the posterior and anterior bellies of the digastric muscle.
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.origin: Continues from the posterior belly of the digastric
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.insertion: Continues into the anterior belly; held to the hyoid body and greater horn by a fibrous sling
action: Changes the direction of pull between the two bellies
intermediate-tendon-of-digastric-muscle.clinical: It is held to the hyoid bone by a fibrous sling and often passes through the stylohyoid muscle.

interspinales-colli-muscles.name: Cervical Interspinales
interspinales-colli-muscles.summary: Short paired muscles that connect the spinous processes of adjacent cervical vertebrae.
interspinales-colli-muscles.origin: Spinous process of one cervical vertebra
interspinales-colli-muscles.insertion: Spinous process of the vertebra directly above
interspinales-colli-muscles.nerve: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
interspinales-colli-muscles.clinical: They are rich in sensory receptors and help the brain sense neck position. They are sometimes weakened after whiplash injuries.

lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.name: Lateral Cricoarytenoid
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.summary: A small laryngeal muscle that runs from the side of the cricoid cartilage to the arytenoid cartilage.
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Superior border of the arch of the cricoid cartilage
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage (front)
action: Adducts the vocal folds by rotating the arytenoids medially
Closes the front part of the glottis
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.nerve: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of the vagus nerve)
lateral-crico-arytenoid-muscle.clinical: It closes the vocal folds for speech and coughing. Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury leaves the fold weak and the voice hoarse.

lateral-rectus-muscle.name: Lateral Rectus
lateral-rectus-muscle.summary: The extra-ocular muscle on the outer side of the eyeball. It turns the eye outward.
lateral-rectus-muscle.origin: Lateral part of the common tendinous ring and the greater wing of the sphenoid
lateral-rectus-muscle.insertion: Lateral sclera, about 7 mm behind the corneal edge
blood: Lateral muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
lateral-rectus-muscle.clinical: Abducens nerve palsy stops the eye from moving outward. The eye drifts inward and the person sees double side by side.

levator-anguli-oris.name: Levator Anguli Oris
levator-anguli-oris.summary: A muscle deep to the zygomaticus muscles. It raises the corner of the mouth.
levator-anguli-oris.origin: Canine fossa of the maxilla, below the infraorbital foramen
levator-anguli-oris.insertion: Skin at the angle of the mouth, blending with the orbicularis oris
action: Raises the corner of the mouth
levator-anguli-oris.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
levator-anguli-oris.clinical: It helps form a smile. Facial nerve palsy leaves the mouth corner drooping on the affected side.

levator-labii-superioris.name: Levator Labii Superioris
levator-labii-superioris.summary: A broad sheet that rises from below the eye to the upper lip.
levator-labii-superioris.origin: Infraorbital margin of the maxilla, above the infraorbital foramen
levator-labii-superioris.insertion: Skin of the upper lip, blending with the orbicularis oris
levator-labii-superioris.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
levator-labii-superioris.clinical: It lifts the upper lip to show the teeth. In a facial palsy the nasolabial fold flattens on the affected side.

levator-nasolabialis.name: Levator Labii Superioris Alaeque Nasi
levator-nasolabialis.latin: Musculus levator labii superioris alaeque nasi
levator-nasolabialis.summary: The label "levator nasolabialis" is not a standard human term. It most likely represents the levator labii superioris alaeque nasi, a slip beside the nose.
levator-nasolabialis.insertion: Alar cartilage of the nose and the skin of the upper lip
levator-nasolabialis.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
levator-nasolabialis.clinical: It lifts the upper lip and flares the nostril, as in a sneer. Facial nerve palsy weakens this movement.

levator-palpebrae-superioris.name: Levator Palpebrae Superioris
levator-palpebrae-superioris.summary: The muscle that lifts the upper eyelid. It runs above the superior rectus along the roof of the orbit.
levator-palpebrae-superioris.origin: Lesser wing of the sphenoid, above and in front of the optic canal
levator-palpebrae-superioris.insertion: Skin of the upper eyelid and the front of the superior tarsal plate
levator-palpebrae-superioris.nerve: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
blood: Ophthalmic artery branches (supraorbital and lacrimal arteries)
levator-palpebrae-superioris.clinical: Oculomotor nerve palsy causes complete ptosis, a drooping upper eyelid. Horner syndrome causes mild ptosis from loss of the superior tarsal muscle.

longissimus-capitis-muscle.name: Longissimus Capitis
longissimus-capitis-muscle.summary: The part of the longissimus muscle that reaches the skull. It lies deep to the splenius capitis.
longissimus-capitis-muscle.origin: Transverse processes of the upper four or five thoracic vertebrae and articular processes of the lower three or four cervical vertebrae
longissimus-capitis-muscle.insertion: Posterior margin of the mastoid process of the temporal bone
action: Bends and rotates the head to the same side
longissimus-capitis-muscle.nerve: Dorsal rami of the middle and lower cervical spinal nerves
longissimus-capitis-muscle.clinical: It is a common site of neck strain and muscle tension headaches.

longus-capitis-muscle.name: Longus Capitis
longus-capitis-muscle.summary: A broad prevertebral muscle in front of the upper cervical spine. It runs from the cervical vertebrae to the base of the skull.
longus-capitis-muscle.origin: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6
longus-capitis-muscle.insertion: Inferior surface of the basilar part of the occipital bone
longus-capitis-muscle.nerve: Anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves
longus-capitis-muscle.clinical: It is the main head flexor of the neck. Whiplash injuries can strain it and cause neck pain and stiffness.

longus-cervicis-muscle.name: Longus Colli
longus-cervicis-muscle.summary: A long prevertebral muscle on the front of the vertebral column. It has vertical, superior oblique, and inferior oblique parts.
longus-cervicis-muscle.origin: Bodies of C5 to T3 and the anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6
longus-cervicis-muscle.insertion: Anterior tubercle of the atlas, bodies of C2 to C4, and anterior tubercles of C5 and C6
action: Bends the neck to the same side
Rotates the neck slightly to the opposite side
longus-cervicis-muscle.nerve: Anterior rami of the cervical spinal nerves
longus-cervicis-muscle.clinical: It flexes the neck. Swelling in the retropharyngeal space in front of it can show on lateral neck X-rays.

medial-pterygoid-muscle.name: Medial Pterygoid
medial-pterygoid-muscle.summary: A thick, four-sided muscle on the inner side of the mandibular ramus. It mirrors the masseter on the outside.
medial-pterygoid-muscle.origin: Medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and the pyramidal process of the palatine bone (deep head); maxillary tuberosity (superficial head)
medial-pterygoid-muscle.insertion: Medial surface of the mandibular ramus and angle (pterygoid tuberosity)
action: Moves the jaw side to side for grinding
medial-pterygoid-muscle.nerve: Nerve to medial pterygoid (mandibular nerve, CN V3)
blood: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
medial-pterygoid-muscle.clinical: Together with the masseter it forms a muscular sling around the mandibular angle. Spasm here can cause trismus, a limited mouth opening.

medial-rectus-muscle.name: Medial Rectus
medial-rectus-muscle.summary: The extra-ocular muscle on the inner side of the eyeball. It is the thickest rectus and turns the eye inward.
medial-rectus-muscle.origin: Medial part of the common tendinous ring
medial-rectus-muscle.insertion: Medial sclera, about 5.5 mm behind the corneal edge
medial-rectus-muscle.nerve: Inferior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
blood: Medial muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
medial-rectus-muscle.clinical: Oculomotor nerve palsy leaves the eye pointing down and out. A medial orbital wall fracture can trap this muscle.

mentalis-muscle.name: Mentalis
mentalis-muscle.summary: A small cone-shaped muscle at the chin. It lies deep to the lower lip.
mentalis-muscle.origin: Incisive fossa of the mandible, below the lower incisors
action: Raises and protrudes the lower lip
Wrinkles the skin of the chin
mentalis-muscle.nerve: Marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
mentalis-muscle.clinical: It wrinkles the chin when pouting or showing doubt. Spasm can cause a dimpled, quivering chin.

middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.name: Middle Pharyngeal Constrictor
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.summary: The fan-shaped middle constrictor of the pharynx. It overlaps the lower part of the superior constrictor.
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.origin: Stylohyoid ligament and the lesser and greater horns of the hyoid bone
action: Constricts the middle pharynx during swallowing
middle-pharyngeal-constrictor.clinical: The constrictors contract in order from top to bottom to push food down. Weakness after stroke can cause swallowing problems.

multifidus-colli-muscle.name: Cervical Multifidus
multifidus-colli-muscle.summary: The cervical part of the multifidus. Short muscle bundles span two to four vertebrae in the deep groove beside the spine.
multifidus-colli-muscle.origin: Articular processes of the lower cervical vertebrae (about C4 to C7)
multifidus-colli-muscle.insertion: Spinous processes of vertebrae two to four levels above
action: Rotates the neck to the opposite side
multifidus-colli-muscle.nerve: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
multifidus-colli-muscle.clinical: It stabilizes the cervical joints. Poor activation of this muscle is linked with chronic neck pain.

mylohyoid-muscle.name: Mylohyoid
mylohyoid-muscle.summary: A flat triangular muscle that forms the muscular floor of the mouth. The two sides meet at a midline raphe.
mylohyoid-muscle.origin: Mylohyoid line on the inner surface of the mandible
mylohyoid-muscle.insertion: Median raphe and the body of the hyoid bone
action: Elevates the floor of the mouth and the tongue
Depresses the mandible when the hyoid is fixed
mylohyoid-muscle.nerve: Nerve to mylohyoid (mandibular nerve, CN V3)
blood: Mylohyoid branch of the inferior alveolar artery
mylohyoid-muscle.clinical: Infection of the submandibular space can spread above and below this muscle, causing Ludwig angina with a swollen floor of mouth.

nasalis-muscle.name: Nasalis
nasalis-muscle.summary: A small muscle of the nose with a transverse part that compresses and an alar part that dilates the nostril.
nasalis-muscle.origin: Maxilla, lateral to the nasal notch (transverse part) and above the lateral incisor (alar part)
nasalis-muscle.insertion: Nasal aponeurosis over the bridge of the nose (transverse part) and the alar cartilage (alar part)
nasalis-muscle.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
nasalis-muscle.clinical: The alar part flares the nostrils during heavy breathing. Facial palsy can narrow the nostril on the affected side.

obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.name: Obliquus Capitis Inferior
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.summary: The larger of the two oblique suboccipital muscles. It runs from the axis to the atlas, and does not reach the skull.
action: Rotates the head and atlas to the same side
obliquus-inferior-capitis-muscle.clinical: It forms a border of the suboccipital triangle, where the vertebral artery and suboccipital nerve run. It rotates the atlas.

obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.name: Obliquus Capitis Superior
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.summary: A short suboccipital muscle that runs from the atlas up to the occipital bone.
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.insertion: Occipital bone, between the superior and inferior nuchal lines
action: Bends the head to the same side
obliquus-superior-capitis-muscle.clinical: It forms the upper-outer border of the suboccipital triangle. Strain of the suboccipital group is linked to tension headache.

occipitalis-muscle.name: Occipitalis
occipitalis-muscle.summary: The back belly of the epicranius. It lies over the back of the skull.
occipitalis-muscle.origin: Lateral two-thirds of the highest nuchal line and the mastoid process
action: Fixes the aponeurosis for the frontalis
occipitalis-muscle.nerve: Posterior auricular nerve (branch of the facial nerve, CN VII)
occipitalis-muscle.clinical: It pulls the scalp backward. Tight occipitalis and nearby nerves can contribute to occipital headaches.

orbicularis-oris-muscle.name: Orbicularis Oris
orbicularis-oris-muscle.summary: A ring-shaped sphincter around the mouth. It is made of many fibers that blend in from nearby muscles.
orbicularis-oris-muscle.origin: Maxilla and mandible near the midline, and the modiolus at the angle of the mouth
orbicularis-oris-muscle.insertion: Skin and mucous membrane of the lips
orbicularis-oris-muscle.nerve: Buccal and marginal mandibular branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
orbicularis-oris-muscle.clinical: It closes and purses the lips for speech, eating, and kissing. Weakness causes drooling and trouble whistling or blowing.

orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.name: Orbital Part of Orbicularis Oculi
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.summary: The thick outer ring of the orbicularis oculi. It circles the margin of the orbit.
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.origin: Nasal part of the frontal bone, frontal process of the maxilla, and the medial palpebral ligament
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.insertion: Loops around the orbit and returns to its medial origin
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.nerve: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
orbital-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.clinical: It closes the eyelids tightly, as in squinting. In Bell palsy the eye cannot close, which risks drying and damage of the cornea.

palatopharyngeus-muscle.name: Palatopharyngeus
palatopharyngeus-muscle.summary: A thin muscle that forms the palatopharyngeal arch, also called the posterior tonsillar pillar.
palatopharyngeus-muscle.origin: Hard palate and the palatine aponeurosis of the soft palate
palatopharyngeus-muscle.insertion: Posterior border of the thyroid cartilage and the side wall of the pharynx
action: Pulls the palatopharyngeal arch toward the midline
blood: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
palatopharyngeus-muscle.clinical: It helps close off the throat from the nose during swallowing. It is a landmark during tonsillectomy.

palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.name: Palpebral Part of Orbicularis Oculi
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.summary: The thin inner part of the orbicularis oculi. It lies within the eyelids themselves.
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.origin: Medial palpebral ligament and the nearby bone
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.nerve: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
palpebral-part-of-orbicularis-oculi.clinical: It produces blinking and gentle eye closure, which spreads tears across the eye. Weakness causes a dry, exposed eye.

posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.name: Posterior Belly of Digastric
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.summary: The back belly of the digastric muscle. It runs forward and down from the skull to the hyoid bone region.
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.origin: Mastoid notch of the temporal bone
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.insertion: Intermediate tendon of the digastric, held to the hyoid bone by a fibrous sling
action: Elevates and retracts the hyoid bone
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.nerve: Digastric branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
posterior-belly-of-digastric-muscle.clinical: It is a landmark in the neck, because the facial nerve and several arteries pass deep to it. It is supplied by the facial nerve.

posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.name: Posterior Cricoarytenoid
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.summary: A fan-shaped muscle on the back of the cricoid cartilage. It is the only muscle that opens the vocal folds.
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the lamina of the cricoid cartilage
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Muscular process of the arytenoid cartilage (back)
action: Abducts the vocal folds (opens the glottis)
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.nerve: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of the vagus nerve)
posterior-crico-arytenoid-muscle.clinical: Damage to both recurrent laryngeal nerves can paralyze it on both sides, which closes the airway and may require an emergency tracheostomy.

procerus-muscle.name: Procerus
procerus-muscle.summary: A small pyramid-shaped muscle over the bridge of the nose.
procerus-muscle.origin: Nasal bone and the upper lateral nasal cartilage
procerus-muscle.insertion: Skin of the lower forehead between the eyebrows
action: Pulls the medial ends of the eyebrows down
Wrinkles the skin over the bridge of the nose
procerus-muscle.nerve: Temporal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
procerus-muscle.clinical: It makes the horizontal wrinkles at the root of the nose and a frown. Botulinum toxin is often used here with the corrugator.

rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus Capitis Anterior
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.summary: A short, flat muscle in front of the atlanto-occipital joint. It lies deep to the longus capitis.
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.origin: Anterior surface of the lateral mass of the atlas (C1) and the base of its transverse process
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.insertion: Basilar part of the occipital bone, just in front of the occipital condyle
action: Flexes the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.nerve: Loop between the anterior rami of C1 and C2
rectus-anterior-capitis-muscle.clinical: It flexes and stabilizes the head on the atlas. Whiplash can strain it and cause upper neck pain.

rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus Capitis Lateralis
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.summary: A short muscle that runs from the transverse process of the atlas to the skull, lateral to the rectus capitis anterior.
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.insertion: Jugular process of the occipital bone
action: Bends the head to the same side at the atlanto-occipital joint
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.nerve: Anterior ramus of C1 (with a contribution from C2)
rectus-lateralis-capitis-muscle.clinical: It bends the head sideways and helps hold the head steady on the atlas.

rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus Capitis Posterior Major
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.summary: A triangular suboccipital muscle that runs from the axis up to the occipital bone.
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.insertion: Lateral part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone
action: Rotates the head to the same side
rectus-posterior-major-capitis-muscle.clinical: It forms the medial border of the suboccipital triangle. Its strain can contribute to cervicogenic headache.

rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.name: Rectus Capitis Posterior Minor
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.summary: A small triangular suboccipital muscle next to the midline. It lies deep to the rectus capitis posterior major.
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.insertion: Medial part of the inferior nuchal line of the occipital bone
rectus-posterior-minor-capitis-muscle.clinical: A fibrous link joins it to the spinal dura mater. This link may be involved in some cervicogenic headaches.

risorius-muscle.name: Risorius
risorius-muscle.summary: A thin, variable muscle band that runs sideways from the cheek to the corner of the mouth.
risorius-muscle.insertion: Skin at the angle of the mouth
action: Retracts the angle of the mouth (grin)
risorius-muscle.nerve: Buccal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
risorius-muscle.clinical: It pulls the mouth corners sideways in a grin. It is absent in some people.

spinalis-capitis-muscle.name: Spinalis Capitis
spinalis-capitis-muscle.summary: The small head part of the spinalis muscle. It is often fused with the semispinalis capitis.
spinalis-capitis-muscle.origin: Spinous and transverse processes of the lower cervical and upper thoracic vertebrae
spinalis-capitis-muscle.insertion: Occipital bone between the superior and inferior nuchal lines
spinalis-capitis-muscle.nerve: Dorsal rami of cervical spinal nerves
spinalis-capitis-muscle.clinical: It is inconstant and often described as part of the semispinalis capitis. It helps hold the head upright.

splenius-capitis-muscle.name: Splenius Capitis
splenius-capitis-muscle.summary: A broad strap muscle on the back of the neck. It wraps around the deeper neck muscles like a bandage.
splenius-capitis-muscle.origin: Lower half of the nuchal ligament and the spinous processes of C7 to T3 (or T4)
splenius-capitis-muscle.insertion: Mastoid process and the lateral part of the superior nuchal line
action: Extends the head and neck (both sides)
Bends and rotates the head to the same side (one side)
