splenius-capitis-muscle.nerve: Dorsal rami of the middle cervical spinal nerves
splenius-capitis-muscle.clinical: Together the two sides extend the head. It forms part of the floor of the posterior triangle of the neck.

stylohyoid-muscle.name: Stylohyoid
stylohyoid-muscle.summary: A slender muscle that runs from the styloid process to the hyoid bone. It splits near its end to let the digastric tendon pass.
stylohyoid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the styloid process of the temporal bone
stylohyoid-muscle.insertion: Body of the hyoid bone, at its junction with the greater horn
stylohyoid-muscle.nerve: Stylohyoid branch of the facial nerve (CN VII)
stylohyoid-muscle.clinical: It lifts the hyoid during swallowing. Facial nerve injury in the neck can weaken it.

stylopharyngeus-muscle.name: Stylopharyngeus
stylopharyngeus-muscle.summary: A long, thin muscle that descends from the styloid process into the pharynx between the superior and middle constrictors.
stylopharyngeus-muscle.origin: Medial side of the base of the styloid process
stylopharyngeus-muscle.insertion: Posterior and superior borders of the thyroid cartilage, blending with the pharyngeal wall
action: Elevates the pharynx and larynx during swallowing and speech
blood: Pharyngeal branches of the maxillary artery
stylopharyngeus-muscle.clinical: It is the only muscle supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve. A weak gag reflex can be a sign of glossopharyngeal injury.

superficial-part-of-masseter.name: Superficial Part of Masseter
superficial-part-of-masseter.summary: The larger, outer layer of the masseter. Its fibers run downward and backward over the side of the jaw.
superficial-part-of-masseter.origin: Maxillary process of the zygomatic bone and the front two-thirds of the lower border of the zygomatic arch
superficial-part-of-masseter.insertion: Angle and lower half of the lateral surface of the mandibular ramus
superficial-part-of-masseter.clinical: It is the strongest chewing muscle and is easily felt when clenching the teeth. The parotid duct crosses its surface.

superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.name: Superior Head of Lateral Pterygoid
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.summary: The smaller upper head of the lateral pterygoid. It attaches to the articular disc of the temporomandibular joint.
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.origin: Infratemporal surface and crest of the greater wing of the sphenoid
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.insertion: Articular disc and capsule of the temporomandibular joint, and the pterygoid fovea of the mandible
action: Stabilizes the condyle and disc during closing
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.nerve: Nerve to lateral pterygoid (mandibular nerve, CN V3)
blood: Pterygoid branches of the maxillary artery
superior-head-of-lateral-pterygoid-muscl.clinical: It steadies the disc and condyle during jaw closing. Disc displacement can cause clicking and pain in the jaw joint.

superior-oblique-muscle.name: Superior Oblique
superior-oblique-muscle.summary: A long extra-ocular muscle whose tendon loops through a pulley called the trochlea before reaching the eyeball.
superior-oblique-muscle.origin: Body of the sphenoid bone, above and medial to the optic canal
superior-oblique-muscle.insertion: Upper outer sclera behind the equator, deep to the superior rectus
action: Intorts the eye (rotates the top inward)
Depresses the eye, especially when adducted
blood: Superior muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
superior-oblique-muscle.clinical: Trochlear nerve palsy causes vertical double vision, worst when looking down, such as on stairs. The head tilts away from the affected side.

superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.name: Superior Pharyngeal Constrictor
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.summary: The uppermost and thinnest of the three constrictors. It wraps around the nasopharynx and upper oropharynx.
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.origin: Pterygoid hamulus, pterygomandibular raphe, the mylohyoid line of the mandible, and the side of the tongue
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.insertion: Median pharyngeal raphe and the pharyngeal tubercle of the occipital bone
action: Constricts the upper pharynx during swallowing
blood: Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
superior-pharyngeal-constrictor.clinical: It helps seal the nasopharynx from the mouth during swallowing. Weakness can cause food or fluid to enter the nose.

superior-rectus-muscle.name: Superior Rectus
superior-rectus-muscle.summary: The extra-ocular muscle along the roof of the orbit. It lies beneath the levator palpebrae superioris.
superior-rectus-muscle.origin: Superior part of the common tendinous ring
superior-rectus-muscle.insertion: Upper sclera, about 7 mm behind the corneal edge
action: Elevates the eye, especially when abducted
superior-rectus-muscle.nerve: Superior division of the oculomotor nerve (CN III)
blood: Lateral muscular branch of the ophthalmic artery
superior-rectus-muscle.clinical: Oculomotor nerve palsy weakens upward gaze. Test it by asking the person to look up and out.

superior-tarsus.name: Superior Tarsal Muscle
superior-tarsus.summary: A thin smooth muscle beneath the levator palpebrae superioris, also called Muller muscle. The model group lists it with the extra-ocular muscles, so this may also represent the upper tarsal plate.
superior-tarsus.origin: Underside of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle
superior-tarsus.insertion: Upper border of the superior tarsal plate
action: Elevates the upper eyelid slightly (about 2 mm)
superior-tarsus.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion
blood: Palpebral arcade of the ophthalmic artery
superior-tarsus.clinical: Loss of its sympathetic supply in Horner syndrome causes a mild droop of the upper eyelid.

temporalis-muscle.name: Temporalis
temporalis-muscle.summary: A large fan-shaped muscle that fills the temporal fossa. Its tendon passes under the zygomatic arch.
temporalis-muscle.origin: Temporal fossa and the deep surface of the temporal fascia
temporalis-muscle.insertion: Tip and medial surface of the coronoid process and the front border of the mandibular ramus
temporalis-muscle.nerve: Deep temporal nerves (mandibular nerve, CN V3)
temporalis-muscle.clinical: Its strong tendon can be felt moving at the temple when chewing. Pain here is common in tension headaches and jaw clenching.

temporoparietalis-muscle.name: Temporoparietalis
temporoparietalis-muscle.summary: A thin, variable sheet of muscle above the ear. It is a lateral extension of the epicranius.
temporoparietalis-muscle.insertion: Lateral edge of the epicranial aponeurosis
action: Slightly raises the ear and eyebrow
temporoparietalis-muscle.nerve: Temporal branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
temporoparietalis-muscle.clinical: It is part of the superficial muscular layer of the scalp. It is thin and often poorly developed.

thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.name: Thyroepiglottic Part of Thyroarytenoid
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.summary: A thin slip of the thyroarytenoid muscle that extends into the aryepiglottic fold to the edge of the epiglottis.
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.origin: Inner surface of the thyroid cartilage near the angle
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.insertion: Lateral margin of the epiglottis, within the aryepiglottic fold
action: Draws the epiglottis forward and down
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.nerve: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (branch of the vagus nerve)
thyro-epiglottic-part-of-thyro-arytenoid.clinical: It widens the laryngeal inlet. Loss of laryngeal muscle control can allow food to enter the airway.

thyrohyoid-muscle.name: Thyrohyoid
thyrohyoid-muscle.summary: A small, flat, quadrangular muscle that looks like an upward continuation of the sternothyroid.
thyrohyoid-muscle.origin: Oblique line of the thyroid cartilage
thyrohyoid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the greater horn and body of the hyoid bone
action: Elevates the larynx when the hyoid is fixed
thyrohyoid-muscle.nerve: C1 fibers carried by the hypoglossal nerve
thyrohyoid-muscle.clinical: It brings the larynx and hyoid closer during swallowing. It receives C1 fibers carried by the hypoglossal nerve.

transverse-arytenoid-muscle.name: Transverse Arytenoid
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.summary: An unpaired muscle that spans the back of the two arytenoid cartilages.
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.origin: Posterior surface and lateral border of one arytenoid cartilage
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.insertion: Same surfaces of the opposite arytenoid cartilage
action: Closes the posterior (cartilaginous) part of the glottis
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.nerve: Recurrent laryngeal nerve (the internal laryngeal nerve may also contribute)
transverse-arytenoid-muscle.clinical: It closes the back part of the glottis. This is the only unpaired intrinsic laryngeal muscle.

trochlea-of-superior-oblique-muscle.name: Trochlea of Superior Oblique
trochlea-of-superior-oblique-muscle.summary: A small fibrocartilage pulley attached to the frontal bone at the upper inner corner of the orbit. It is not a muscle itself.
trochlea-of-superior-oblique-muscle.origin: Trochlear fovea (fossa) of the frontal bone
trochlea-of-superior-oblique-muscle.insertion: Loops around the tendon of the superior oblique
action: Redirects the pull of the superior oblique tendon toward the back and side of the eyeball
trochlea-of-superior-oblique-muscle.clinical: The tendon of the superior oblique slides through it. Inflammation or scarring here can cause Brown syndrome, with limited upward gaze when looking inward.

zygomaticus-major-muscle.name: Zygomaticus Major
zygomaticus-major-muscle.summary: A long, narrow muscle that runs from the cheekbone to the corner of the mouth. It is the main smiling muscle.
zygomaticus-major-muscle.origin: Lateral surface of the zygomatic bone, near the zygomaticotemporal suture
zygomaticus-major-muscle.insertion: Skin at the angle of the mouth, blending with the orbicularis oris and levator anguli oris
action: Draws the angle of the mouth up and back (smiling)
zygomaticus-major-muscle.nerve: Buccal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
zygomaticus-major-muscle.clinical: Facial nerve palsy makes the smile asymmetric because the mouth corner does not lift on the weak side.

zygomaticus-minor-muscle.name: Zygomaticus Minor
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.summary: A slender muscle that lies in front of the zygomaticus major. It runs from the cheekbone to the upper lip.
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.origin: Lateral surface of the zygomatic bone, in front of the zygomaticus major
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.insertion: Muscle and skin of the upper lip, lateral to the levator labii superioris
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.nerve: Buccal and zygomatic branches of the facial nerve (CN VII)
zygomaticus-minor-muscle.clinical: It deepens the nasolabial fold and raises the upper lip. Its fold flattens in facial nerve palsy.

adductor-minimus.name: Adductor Minimus
adductor-minimus.summary: The upper, front fibers of the adductor magnus, sometimes described as a separate small muscle. It lies just above the adductor brevis.
adductor-minimus.origin: Inferior ramus of the pubis and adjacent ischial ramus.
adductor-minimus.insertion: Upper part of the linea aspera and the femoral shaft just below the lesser trochanter.
action: Assists lateral rotation of the thigh
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
adductor-minimus.clinical: Many texts do not separate it from adductor magnus. It can be strained with the other adductors in sports groin injuries.

opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.name: Opponens Digiti Minimi of Foot
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (fourth layer area)
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.parent: Flexor digiti minimi brevis of foot
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.summary: A small, inconstant slip of the flexor digiti minimi brevis that runs to the fifth metatarsal. It is much less developed than the hand muscle of the same name.
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.origin: Long plantar ligament and sheath of the fibularis longus tendon.
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.insertion: Lateral part of the fifth metatarsal.
action: Draws the fifth metatarsal plantarly and medially
Assists the flexor digiti minimi brevis
opponens-digiti-minimi-muscle-of-foot.clinical: It is often absent or fused with the flexor digiti minimi brevis, so it is rarely identified in surgery.

abductor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.name: Abductor Digiti Minimi of Foot
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (first layer)
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.summary: A superficial muscle along the lateral border of the sole. It forms the lateral edge of the sole contour.
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.origin: Lateral and medial processes of the calcaneal tuberosity and the plantar aponeurosis.
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe.
action: Flexes the fifth toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
abductor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.clinical: Entrapment of its nerve branch (the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve, or Baxter nerve) can cause chronic heel pain.

abductor-hallucis.name: Abductor Hallucis
abductor-hallucis.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (first layer)
abductor-hallucis.summary: A superficial muscle along the medial border of the sole. It helps support the medial longitudinal arch.
abductor-hallucis.origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity, flexor retinaculum, and plantar aponeurosis.
abductor-hallucis.insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe.
action: Flexes the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
abductor-hallucis.clinical: Overstretching or weakness is linked to bunion (hallux valgus) deformity.

adductor-brevis.name: Adductor Brevis
adductor-brevis.summary: A short, triangular adductor lying behind the pectineus and adductor longus. It lies in front of the adductor magnus.
adductor-brevis.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
adductor-brevis.insertion: Pectineal line and upper part of the linea aspera of the femur.
adductor-brevis.nerve: Obturator nerve (anterior division; sometimes also posterior)
adductor-brevis.clinical: The anterior branch of the obturator nerve runs on its anterior surface, so the muscle guides surgeons to that nerve.

adductor-longus.name: Adductor Longus
adductor-longus.summary: The most superficial and anterior adductor. It forms the medial wall of the femoral triangle.
adductor-longus.origin: Anterior surface of the body of the pubis, below the pubic crest.
adductor-longus.insertion: Middle third of the linea aspera of the femur.
adductor-longus.clinical: It is the adductor most often strained or torn, a common cause of groin pain in kicking and skating sports.

adductor-magnus.name: Adductor Magnus
adductor-magnus.summary: The largest adductor, with an adductor part and a hamstring part. It has two nerve supplies because of this dual origin.
adductor-magnus.origin: Adductor part: inferior pubic ramus and ischial ramus. Hamstring part: ischial tuberosity.
adductor-magnus.insertion: Adductor part: gluteal tuberosity, linea aspera, and medial supracondylar line. Hamstring part: adductor tubercle of the femur.
adductor-magnus.nerve: Obturator nerve (adductor part) and tibial part of the sciatic nerve (hamstring part)
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
adductor-magnus.clinical: The adductor hiatus between its two parts lets the femoral vessels pass to the popliteal fossa.

calcaneal-tendon.name: Calcaneal Tendon (Achilles Tendon)
calcaneal-tendon.group: Superficial posterior compartment of the leg
calcaneal-tendon.summary: The thick tendon formed by the gastrocnemius and soleus, the strongest and thickest tendon in the body. It runs to the back of the heel.
calcaneal-tendon.origin: Formed in the lower leg by the tendons of the gastrocnemius and soleus.
calcaneal-tendon.insertion: Middle part of the posterior surface of the calcaneus.
action: Plantar flexes the ankle (transmits the pull of the triceps surae)
Raises the heel during walking and running
calcaneal-tendon.nerve: Tibial nerve (through the gastrocnemius and soleus)
calcaneal-tendon.clinical: Rupture is common in middle-aged athletes. A squeeze of the calf (Thompson test) then fails to plantar flex the foot.

dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-foot.name: Dorsal Interossei of Foot
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-foot.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (fourth layer)
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-foot.summary: Four bipennate muscles between the metatarsals. They abduct the toes away from the second toe, which is the axis of the foot.
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-foot.origin: Adjacent sides of two neighboring metatarsals (each muscle has two heads).
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-foot.insertion: Bases of the proximal phalanges and extensor expansions: first on the medial side of toe 2, others on the lateral sides of toes 2–4.
action: Abduct toes 2–4 from the axis of the second toe
dorsal-interossei-muscles-of-foot.clinical: Weakness of the interossei contributes to claw toe deformity.

extensor-digitorum-brevis.name: Extensor Digitorum Brevis
extensor-digitorum-brevis.group: Muscles of the dorsum of the foot
extensor-digitorum-brevis.summary: A small muscle on the top of the foot, in front of the lateral malleolus. Its tendons join those of the extensor digitorum longus.
extensor-digitorum-brevis.origin: Anterior part of the superior and lateral surfaces of the calcaneus.
extensor-digitorum-brevis.insertion: Lateral sides of the extensor digitorum longus tendons to toes 2–4.
action: Extends toes 2–4 at the metatarsophalangeal joints
extensor-digitorum-brevis.clinical: A bruise or swelling of its belly on the lateral foot can be mistaken for an ankle sprain.

extensor-digitorum-longus-tendon.name: Extensor Digitorum Longus Tendon
extensor-digitorum-longus-tendon.summary: The long tendons of the extensor digitorum longus. They pass under the extensor retinacula and divide to serve toes 2–5.
extensor-digitorum-longus-tendon.origin: Muscle belly of the extensor digitorum longus on the fibula, tibia, and interosseous membrane.
extensor-digitorum-longus-tendon.insertion: Extensor expansions of toes 2–5, ending on the middle and distal phalanges.
extensor-digitorum-longus-tendon.clinical: Tendons lie just under the skin on the top of the foot and can be cut by a laceration there.

extensor-digitorum-longus.name: Extensor Digitorum Longus
extensor-digitorum-longus.summary: A long muscle on the front of the leg, lateral to the tibialis anterior. It splits into four tendons for the lateral four toes.
extensor-digitorum-longus.origin: Lateral condyle of the tibia, upper three quarters of the anterior fibula, and interosseous membrane.
extensor-digitorum-longus.insertion: Middle and distal phalanges of toes 2–5, through the extensor expansions.
extensor-digitorum-longus.clinical: Deep fibular nerve injury weakens this muscle and causes foot drop with the other anterior leg muscles.

extensor-hallucis-brevis.name: Extensor Hallucis Brevis
extensor-hallucis-brevis.group: Muscles of the dorsum of the foot
extensor-hallucis-brevis.summary: The medial part of the extensor digitorum brevis, serving the great toe. It is often treated as a separate muscle.
extensor-hallucis-brevis.origin: Anterior part of the superior and lateral surfaces of the calcaneus.
extensor-hallucis-brevis.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe.
action: Extends the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
extensor-hallucis-brevis.clinical: Its belly is a palpable bulge on the top of the foot and can be bruised by trauma.

extensor-hallucis-longus.name: Extensor Hallucis Longus
extensor-hallucis-longus.summary: A thin muscle that lies deep between the tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum longus. Its tendon runs to the great toe.
extensor-hallucis-longus.origin: Middle part of the anterior surface of the fibula and the interosseous membrane.
extensor-hallucis-longus.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the distal phalanx of the great toe.
extensor-hallucis-longus.clinical: Resisted great toe extension tests the L5 nerve root. Weakness suggests an L5 radiculopathy.

fibularis-brevis-muscle.name: Fibularis Brevis
fibularis-brevis-muscle.summary: The shorter, deeper muscle of the lateral compartment. Its tendon passes behind the lateral malleolus to the fifth metatarsal.
fibularis-brevis-muscle.origin: Distal two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula.
fibularis-brevis-muscle.insertion: Tuberosity at the base of the fifth metatarsal.
fibularis-brevis-muscle.clinical: Avulsion fracture of the fifth metatarsal base is caused by sudden inversion pulling on this tendon.

fibularis-longus-muscle.name: Fibularis Longus
fibularis-longus-muscle.summary: A long, superficial lateral muscle. Its tendon crosses the sole to anchor the first metatarsal and helps hold the arches.
fibularis-longus-muscle.origin: Head and upper two thirds of the lateral surface of the fibula.
fibularis-longus-muscle.insertion: Medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal.
action: Supports the transverse and lateral longitudinal arches
fibularis-longus-muscle.clinical: Injury to the common fibular nerve near the fibular neck weakens eversion and can cause foot drop.

fibularis-tertius-muscle.name: Fibularis Tertius
fibularis-tertius-muscle.summary: A small slip of the extensor digitorum longus that continues to the fifth metatarsal. It is absent in some people.
fibularis-tertius-muscle.origin: Distal third of the anterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane.
fibularis-tertius-muscle.insertion: Dorsal surface of the base of the fifth metatarsal.
fibularis-tertius-muscle.clinical: It is absent in a minority of people, which has no functional importance.

flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.name: Flexor Digiti Minimi Brevis of Foot
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.latin: Musculus flexor digiti minimi brevis pedis
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (third layer)
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.summary: A small muscle on the lateral side of the sole, deep to the abductor digiti minimi.
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.origin: Base of the fifth metatarsal and sheath of the fibularis longus tendon.
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.insertion: Base of the proximal phalanx of the fifth toe.
action: Flexes the fifth toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
flexor-digiti-minimi-of-foot.clinical: It is a minor muscle with little clinical importance on its own.

flexor-digitorum-brevis.name: Flexor Digitorum Brevis
flexor-digitorum-brevis.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (first layer)
flexor-digitorum-brevis.summary: A central superficial muscle of the sole. Its four tendons split to let the long flexor tendons pass through.
flexor-digitorum-brevis.origin: Medial process of the calcaneal tuberosity and the plantar aponeurosis.
flexor-digitorum-brevis.insertion: Sides of the middle phalanges of toes 2–5.
action: Flexes toes 2–5 at the proximal interphalangeal joints
flexor-digitorum-brevis.clinical: The plantar aponeurosis, which gives it origin, is the structure inflamed in plantar fasciitis.

flexor-digitorum-longus.name: Flexor Digitorum Longus
flexor-digitorum-longus.group: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
flexor-digitorum-longus.summary: A deep muscle of the posterior leg. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and divides into four tendons in the sole.
flexor-digitorum-longus.origin: Medial part of the posterior surface of the tibia, below the soleal line.
flexor-digitorum-longus.insertion: Bases of the distal phalanges of toes 2–5.
flexor-digitorum-longus.clinical: Its tendon crosses the flexor hallucis longus tendon in the sole at the knot of Henry, a landmark in tendon transfers.

flexor-hallucis-longus.name: Flexor Hallucis Longus
flexor-hallucis-longus.group: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
flexor-hallucis-longus.summary: A powerful deep muscle of the posterior leg. Its tendon passes under the sustentaculum tali and along the sole to the great toe.
flexor-hallucis-longus.origin: Inferior two thirds of the posterior surface of the fibula and interosseous membrane.
flexor-hallucis-longus.insertion: Base of the distal phalanx of the great toe.
flexor-hallucis-longus.clinical: Tendinitis in this tendon is common in ballet dancers, who push off from the great toe.

gracilis-muscle.name: Gracilis
gracilis-muscle.summary: A long, thin strap muscle on the medial thigh. It is the only adductor that crosses the knee.
gracilis-muscle.origin: Body and inferior ramus of the pubis.
gracilis-muscle.insertion: Superior part of the medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
gracilis-muscle.clinical: Surgeons use its tendon for grafts and as a free muscle flap, since its loss causes little weakness.

lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.name: Lateral Head of Flexor Hallucis Brevis
lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.latin: Caput laterale musculi flexoris hallucis brevis
lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (first layer area)
lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.summary: The lateral part of the two-headed flexor hallucis brevis. Its tendon holds the lateral sesamoid bone under the first metatarsal head.
lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.origin: Plantar surfaces of the cuboid and lateral cuneiform.
lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, through the lateral sesamoid.
action: Flexes the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
lateral-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.clinical: Sesamoid bones in its tendons can fracture or become inflamed (sesamoiditis), causing pain under the ball of the foot.

lateral-head-of-gastrocnemius.name: Lateral Head of Gastrocnemius
lateral-head-of-gastrocnemius.group: Superficial posterior compartment of the leg
lateral-head-of-gastrocnemius.summary: The lateral of the two heads of the calf muscle. It lies above and behind the knee on the outer side.
lateral-head-of-gastrocnemius.origin: Lateral surface of the lateral condyle of the femur.
lateral-head-of-gastrocnemius.insertion: Posterior surface of the calcaneus, through the calcaneal tendon.
lateral-head-of-gastrocnemius.clinical: A small sesamoid bone, the fabella, sometimes lies in the tendon of this head behind the knee.

long-head-of-biceps-femoris.name: Long Head of Biceps Femoris
long-head-of-biceps-femoris.summary: The long head is a true hamstring, crossing both hip and knee. It forms the lateral border of the popliteal fossa with the short head.
long-head-of-biceps-femoris.origin: Inferomedial impression on the ischial tuberosity.
long-head-of-biceps-femoris.nerve: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
long-head-of-biceps-femoris.clinical: Hamstring strains most often involve this head near its proximal attachment during sprinting.

lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.name: Lumbricals of Foot
lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (second layer)
lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.summary: Four small muscles that arise from the flexor digitorum longus tendons. They run to the medial sides of toes 2–5.
lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.origin: Tendons of the flexor digitorum longus (first from the medial side of the tendon to toe 2; others from adjacent sides).
lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.insertion: Medial side of the extensor expansions of toes 2–5.
lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.nerve: First lumbrical: medial plantar nerve. Second to fourth: lateral plantar nerve (deep branch)
lumbrical-muscles-of-foot.clinical: Weakness of the lumbricals and interossei lets the toes claw, a common deformity in neuropathy.

medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.name: Medial Head of Flexor Hallucis Brevis
medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.latin: Caput mediale musculi flexoris hallucis brevis
medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (first layer area)
medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.summary: The medial part of the two-headed flexor hallucis brevis. Its tendon holds the medial sesamoid bone under the first metatarsal head.
medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.origin: Medial cuneiform and the tibialis posterior tendon.
medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.insertion: Medial side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, through the medial sesamoid.
action: Flexes the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
medial-head-of-flexor-hallucis-brevis.clinical: The medial sesamoid is the one most often injured, causing pain under the ball of the foot.

medial-head-of-gastrocnemius.name: Medial Head of Gastrocnemius
medial-head-of-gastrocnemius.group: Superficial posterior compartment of the leg
medial-head-of-gastrocnemius.summary: The medial of the two heads of the calf muscle. It is larger than the lateral head and reaches lower down the leg.
medial-head-of-gastrocnemius.origin: Popliteal surface of the femur, just above the medial condyle.
medial-head-of-gastrocnemius.insertion: Posterior surface of the calcaneus, through the calcaneal tendon.
medial-head-of-gastrocnemius.clinical: A tear at its musculotendinous junction is called tennis leg, with sudden calf pain during push-off.

oblique-head-of-adductor-hallucis.name: Oblique Head of Adductor Hallucis
oblique-head-of-adductor-hallucis.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (third layer)
oblique-head-of-adductor-hallucis.summary: The larger head of the adductor hallucis. It runs obliquely across the deep sole toward the great toe.
oblique-head-of-adductor-hallucis.origin: Bases of metatarsals 2–4, the cuboid, lateral cuneiform, and sheath of the fibularis longus tendon.
oblique-head-of-adductor-hallucis.insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, with the transverse head.
action: Flexes the great toe at the metatarsophalangeal joint
oblique-head-of-adductor-hallucis.clinical: Its tendon is released in some bunion operations to correct great toe drift.

obturator-externus.name: Obturator Externus
obturator-externus.group: Deep gluteal and lateral rotator muscles
obturator-externus.summary: A flat, fan-shaped muscle covering the outside of the obturator foramen. Its tendon passes behind the femoral neck.
obturator-externus.origin: External surface of the obturator membrane and the margins of the obturator foramen.
action: Stabilizes the head of the femur in the acetabulum
obturator-externus.clinical: Its tendon lies close to the medial circumflex femoral artery, which is the main supply to the femoral head.

pectineus-muscle.name: Pectineus
pectineus-muscle.summary: A flat, quadrangular muscle forming part of the floor of the femoral triangle. It lies between the psoas and adductor longus.
pectineus-muscle.insertion: Pectineal line of the femur, running from the lesser trochanter to the linea aspera.
action: Assists medial rotation of the thigh
pectineus-muscle.nerve: Femoral nerve; often also the obturator nerve or accessory obturator nerve
pectineus-muscle.clinical: Its dual nerve supply reflects its mixed anterior and medial compartment origin.

plantar-interossei-muscles.name: Plantar Interossei
plantar-interossei-muscles.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (fourth layer)
plantar-interossei-muscles.summary: Three unipennate muscles on the plantar side of the metatarsals. They draw toes 3–5 toward the second toe.
plantar-interossei-muscles.origin: Bases and medial sides of metatarsals 3–5.
plantar-interossei-muscles.insertion: Medial sides of the bases of the proximal phalanges of toes 3–5, and extensor expansions.
action: Adduct toes 3–5 toward the second toe
plantar-interossei-muscles.clinical: The mnemonic PAD and DAB recalls that plantar interossei adduct and dorsal interossei abduct.

plantaris-muscle.name: Plantaris
plantaris-muscle.group: Superficial posterior compartment of the leg
plantaris-muscle.summary: A small muscle with a short belly and a very long, thin tendon. The tendon runs between the gastrocnemius and soleus.
plantaris-muscle.origin: Inferior part of the lateral supracondylar line of the femur and the oblique popliteal ligament.
plantaris-muscle.insertion: Posterior surface of the calcaneus, medial to the calcaneal tendon.
action: Weakly assists plantar flexion of the ankle
plantaris-muscle.clinical: It is absent in roughly one in ten people. Surgeons use its long tendon as a graft.

popliteus-muscle.name: Popliteus
popliteus-muscle.group: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
popliteus-muscle.summary: A small triangular muscle forming part of the floor of the popliteal fossa. It lies deep to the gastrocnemius.
popliteus-muscle.origin: Lateral surface of the lateral femoral condyle and the lateral meniscus.
popliteus-muscle.insertion: Posterior surface of the tibia, above the soleal line.
action: Unlocks the extended knee by rotating the femur laterally on the tibia
popliteus-muscle.clinical: It initiates knee flexion by unlocking the joint. Its injury is part of posterolateral corner damage.

quadratus-femoris-muscle.name: Quadratus Femoris
quadratus-femoris-muscle.group: Deep gluteal and lateral rotator muscles
quadratus-femoris-muscle.summary: A flat, rectangular muscle below the inferior gemellus. It is the lowest of the deep lateral rotators of the hip.
quadratus-femoris-muscle.origin: Lateral border of the ischial tuberosity.
quadratus-femoris-muscle.insertion: Quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest of the femur.
quadratus-femoris-muscle.clinical: The medial circumflex femoral artery runs along its upper border, so it is a landmark in hip surgery.

quadratus-plantae-muscle.name: Quadratus Plantae
quadratus-plantae-muscle.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (second layer)
quadratus-plantae-muscle.summary: A flat, two-headed muscle in the middle layer of the sole. It is also called the flexor accessorius.
quadratus-plantae-muscle.origin: Medial head: medial surface of the calcaneus. Lateral head: lateral border of the plantar calcaneus.
quadratus-plantae-muscle.insertion: Posterolateral margin of the flexor digitorum longus tendon.
action: Assists the flexor digitorum longus in flexing toes 2–5
Corrects the oblique pull of the long tendon
quadratus-plantae-muscle.clinical: Its straight pull cancels the oblique pull of the long flexor tendon, so the toes flex directly toward the heel.

rectus-femoris-muscle.name: Rectus Femoris
rectus-femoris-muscle.summary: The straight, bipennate part of the quadriceps. It is the only quadriceps muscle that crosses the hip joint.
rectus-femoris-muscle.origin: Straight head: anterior inferior iliac spine. Reflected head: ilium just above the acetabulum.
rectus-femoris-muscle.insertion: Base of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.
action: Extends the leg at the knee
Flexes the thigh at the hip
rectus-femoris-muscle.clinical: The anterior inferior iliac spine can be avulsed in adolescents by forceful kicking.

sartorius-muscle.name: Sartorius
sartorius-muscle.summary: The longest muscle in the body, a thin strap running obliquely across the front of the thigh. It crosses both hip and knee.
sartorius-muscle.origin: Anterior superior iliac spine and the upper part of the notch below it.
sartorius-muscle.insertion: Superior part of the medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
action: Flexes, abducts, and laterally rotates the thigh
Flexes the knee and medially rotates the flexed leg
sartorius-muscle.clinical: It forms the lateral border of the femoral triangle and the roof of the adductor canal.

semimembranosus-muscle.name: Semimembranosus
semimembranosus-muscle.summary: A hamstring with a flat membranous upper tendon. It lies deep to the semitendinosus on the medial side.
semimembranosus-muscle.origin: Superolateral impression on the ischial tuberosity.
semimembranosus-muscle.insertion: Posterior part of the medial condyle of the tibia, with expansions to the oblique popliteal ligament.
semimembranosus-muscle.nerve: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
semimembranosus-muscle.clinical: A bursa beneath its tendon can swell and form a popliteal (Baker) cyst.

semitendinosus-muscle.name: Semitendinosus
semitendinosus-muscle.summary: A hamstring with a long, cord-like tendon in its lower half. It lies superficial to the semimembranosus.
semitendinosus-muscle.origin: Inferomedial impression on the ischial tuberosity, with the long head of biceps femoris.
semitendinosus-muscle.insertion: Superior part of the medial surface of the tibia (pes anserinus).
semitendinosus-muscle.nerve: Tibial division of the sciatic nerve
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
semitendinosus-muscle.clinical: Its tendon is commonly harvested as a graft to rebuild the anterior cruciate ligament.

short-head-of-biceps-femoris.name: Short Head of Biceps Femoris
short-head-of-biceps-femoris.summary: The short head arises from the femur, so it crosses only the knee. It is the only biceps femoris head supplied by the common fibular nerve.
short-head-of-biceps-femoris.origin: Lateral lip of the linea aspera and the lateral supracondylar line of the femur.
short-head-of-biceps-femoris.insertion: Head of the fibula, with the long head.
short-head-of-biceps-femoris.nerve: Common fibular division of the sciatic nerve
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
short-head-of-biceps-femoris.clinical: In injuries of the sciatic nerve, the common fibular part is often more affected than the tibial part.

soleus-muscle.name: Soleus
soleus-muscle.group: Superficial posterior compartment of the leg
soleus-muscle.summary: A broad, flat muscle lying deep to the gastrocnemius. It is the main postural muscle of the calf.
soleus-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the fibular head and upper fibula, soleal line and middle third of the medial border of the tibia, and tendinous arch.
soleus-muscle.insertion: Posterior surface of the calcaneus, through the calcaneal tendon.
action: Prevents the body from tipping forward when standing
soleus-muscle.clinical: It acts as a muscle pump for leg veins. Blood clots often start in its venous sinuses.

tibialis-anterior-muscle.name: Tibialis Anterior
tibialis-anterior-muscle.summary: The most medial muscle of the anterior compartment. It lies against the lateral surface of the tibia and is easily felt.
tibialis-anterior-muscle.origin: Lateral condyle and upper half of the lateral surface of the tibia, and interosseous membrane.
tibialis-anterior-muscle.insertion: Medial and plantar surfaces of the medial cuneiform and base of the first metatarsal.
tibialis-anterior-muscle.clinical: Weakness causes foot drop. Overuse can cause shin splints along the front of the shin.

tibialis-posterior-muscle.name: Tibialis Posterior
tibialis-posterior-muscle.group: Deep posterior compartment of the leg
tibialis-posterior-muscle.summary: The deepest muscle of the posterior compartment. Its tendon passes behind the medial malleolus and fans out under the foot.
tibialis-posterior-muscle.origin: Interosseous membrane and adjacent posterior surfaces of the tibia and fibula.
tibialis-posterior-muscle.insertion: Tuberosity of the navicular, the cuneiforms, the cuboid, and the bases of metatarsals 2–4.
tibialis-posterior-muscle.clinical: Tendon failure leads to a progressive flatfoot deformity in adults.

transverse-head-of-adductor-hallucis.name: Transverse Head of Adductor Hallucis
transverse-head-of-adductor-hallucis.group: Muscles of the sole of the foot (third layer)
transverse-head-of-adductor-hallucis.summary: The smaller head of the adductor hallucis. It runs transversely across the heads of the metatarsals.
transverse-head-of-adductor-hallucis.origin: Plantar ligaments of the metatarsophalangeal joints of toes 3–5 and the deep transverse metatarsal ligament.
transverse-head-of-adductor-hallucis.insertion: Lateral side of the base of the proximal phalanx of the great toe, with the oblique head.
action: Supports the transverse arch of the foot
transverse-head-of-adductor-hallucis.clinical: Its tendon is released in some bunion surgeries to correct great toe drift.

vastus-intermedius-muscle.name: Vastus Intermedius
vastus-intermedius-muscle.summary: The deepest quadriceps muscle, lying directly on the femur beneath the rectus femoris.
vastus-intermedius-muscle.origin: Anterior and lateral surfaces of the upper two thirds of the femoral shaft.
vastus-intermedius-muscle.insertion: Base of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity through the patellar ligament.
action: Extends the leg at the knee
vastus-intermedius-muscle.clinical: Its deepest fibers form the articularis genus, which pulls the synovial capsule of the knee upward during extension.

vastus-lateralis-muscle.name: Vastus Lateralis
vastus-lateralis-muscle.summary: The largest quadriceps muscle, on the lateral side of the thigh. Its lower fibers blend with the iliotibial tract.
vastus-lateralis-muscle.origin: Greater trochanter, intertrochanteric line, gluteal tuberosity, and lateral lip of the linea aspera.
vastus-lateralis-muscle.insertion: Base and lateral border of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity.
action: Extends the leg at the knee
blood: Perforating branches of the deep femoral artery
vastus-lateralis-muscle.clinical: It is a preferred site for intramuscular injections in infants because it is large and away from major nerves.

vastus-medialis-muscle.name: Vastus Medialis
vastus-medialis-muscle.summary: The medial quadriceps muscle, with low fibers that run obliquely to the patella. These oblique fibers are called the vastus medialis obliquus.
vastus-medialis-muscle.origin: Intertrochanteric line, medial lip of the linea aspera, medial supracondylar line, and adductor tendons.
vastus-medialis-muscle.insertion: Base and medial border of the patella through the quadriceps tendon, then the tibial tuberosity.
action: Extends the leg at the knee
Oblique fibers keep the patella from sliding laterally
vastus-medialis-muscle.clinical: Weakness of its oblique fibers is linked to patellofemoral pain and lateral patellar tracking.

diaphragm.name: Diaphragm
diaphragm.summary: A dome-shaped sheet of muscle and tendon separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities. It is the main muscle of quiet inspiration.
diaphragm.origin: Sternal part: back of the xiphoid process. Costal part: inner surfaces of ribs 7–12 and their cartilages. Lumbar part: lumbar vertebrae L1–L3 through the crura and arcuate ligaments.
action: Contracts and flattens to enlarge the thorax for inspiration
Raises abdominal pressure to assist coughing, vomiting, and defecation
diaphragm.nerve: Phrenic nerve (motor and most sensory); lower intercostal and subcostal nerves for edge sensation
diaphragm.clinical: Irritation of the central part can cause pain referred to the shoulder tip. Openings for the vena cava, esophagus, and aorta lie at T8, T10, and T12.

external-abdominal-oblique-muscle.name: External Abdominal Oblique
external-abdominal-oblique-muscle.summary: The largest and most superficial of the three flat abdominal muscles. Its fibers run downward and forward, as when putting hands in pockets.
external-abdominal-oblique-muscle.insertion: Linea alba, pubic tubercle, and anterior half of the iliac crest, through a broad aponeurosis.
action: Bends the trunk to the same side and rotates it to the opposite side (one side)
external-abdominal-oblique-muscle.nerve: Lower six thoracic nerves (intercostal and subcostal)
external-abdominal-oblique-muscle.clinical: Its aponeurosis forms the inguinal ligament and the superficial inguinal ring, a common site of inguinal hernia.

internal-abdominal-oblique-muscle.name: Internal Abdominal Oblique
internal-abdominal-oblique-muscle.summary: The middle flat abdominal muscle, lying deep to the external oblique. Its fibers run upward and forward, at right angles to the external oblique.
internal-abdominal-oblique-muscle.origin: Thoracolumbar fascia, anterior two thirds of the iliac crest, and lateral two thirds of the inguinal ligament.
internal-abdominal-oblique-muscle.insertion: Inferior borders of ribs 10–12, linea alba, and pubic crest and pectineal line through the conjoint tendon.
action: Bends and rotates the trunk to the same side (one side)
internal-abdominal-oblique-muscle.nerve: Lower thoracic nerves, iliohypogastric nerve, and ilioinguinal nerve
internal-abdominal-oblique-muscle.clinical: Its lowest fibers form the cremaster muscle in men and help make up the conjoint tendon and the inguinal canal wall.

linea-alba.name: Linea Alba
linea-alba.summary: A tough fibrous band in the midline of the abdomen, formed by the interwoven aponeuroses of the three flat muscles. It is not a muscle.
linea-alba.origin: Above: xiphoid process and costal cartilages.
linea-alba.insertion: Below: pubic symphysis and pubic crest.
action: Anchors the abdominal wall muscles in the midline
Separates the right and left rectus abdominis muscles
linea-alba.clinical: It is relatively bloodless, so surgeons use it for midline incisions. It can stretch or split, causing diastasis recti or an epigastric hernia.

quadratus-lumborum-muscle.name: Quadratus Lumborum
quadratus-lumborum-muscle.summary: A thick, quadrilateral muscle on the back wall of the abdomen. It lies lateral to the psoas major and behind the kidney.
quadratus-lumborum-muscle.origin: Iliolumbar ligament and posterior part of the iliac crest.
quadratus-lumborum-muscle.insertion: Medial half of the inferior border of the 12th rib and the transverse processes of lumbar vertebrae L1–L4.
action: Bends the trunk to the same side (lateral flexion)
quadratus-lumborum-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of T12 and L1–L4
quadratus-lumborum-muscle.clinical: Spasm of this muscle is a frequent source of low back pain and lateral trunk stiffness.

rectus-abdominis-muscle.name: Rectus Abdominis
rectus-abdominis-muscle.summary: A long, paired strap muscle running vertically on each side of the linea alba. It lies inside the rectus sheath.
rectus-abdominis-muscle.insertion: Xiphoid process and costal cartilages of ribs 5–7.
rectus-abdominis-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of the lower six thoracic nerves
rectus-abdominis-muscle.clinical: Tendinous intersections create the six-pack look. The two halves can separate in pregnancy, called diastasis recti.

transversus-abdominis-muscle.name: Transversus Abdominis
transversus-abdominis-muscle.summary: The deepest of the three flat abdominal muscles, with fibers running horizontally. It acts like a corset around the abdomen.
transversus-abdominis-muscle.origin: Internal surfaces of costal cartilages 7–12, thoracolumbar fascia, iliac crest, and lateral third of the inguinal ligament.
transversus-abdominis-muscle.insertion: Linea alba, and the pubic crest and pectineal line through the conjoint tendon.
transversus-abdominis-muscle.nerve: Lower thoracic nerves, iliohypogastric nerve, and ilioinguinal nerve
transversus-abdominis-muscle.clinical: Regional nerve blocks are often placed in the plane between it and the internal oblique, called a TAP block.

coccygeus-muscle.name: Coccygeus Muscle
coccygeus-muscle.summary: A small triangular muscle that forms the posterior part of the pelvic diaphragm. It lies on the sacrospinous ligament.
coccygeus-muscle.clinical: Weakness of the pelvic floor, often after childbirth, can contribute to pelvic organ prolapse.
coccygeus-muscle.origin: Ischial spine and the adjacent sacrospinous ligament
coccygeus-muscle.insertion: Lateral margins of the coccyx and the lowest part of the sacrum
coccygeus-muscle.nerve: Branches of the ventral rami of S3 to S4 (nerve to levator ani and coccygeus)
coccygeus-muscle.roots: S4 to S5 (variant S3 to S4)

external-anal-sphincter.name: External Anal Sphincter
external-anal-sphincter.summary: A ring of voluntary skeletal muscle around the lower anal canal. It lies outside the internal anal sphincter.
external-anal-sphincter.clinical: Tears of this muscle during childbirth can cause fecal incontinence.
external-anal-sphincter.origin: Perineal body and the anococcygeal ligament, with fibers attaching to the coccyx
external-anal-sphincter.insertion: Encircles the anal canal and blends with the perineal body in front
action: Provides voluntary control of defecation and continence
external-anal-sphincter.nerve: Inferior rectal nerve (from the pudendal nerve) and the perineal branch of S4

gluteus-maximus-muscle.name: Gluteus Maximus Muscle
gluteus-maximus-muscle.summary: The largest and most superficial gluteal muscle. It forms the bulk of the buttock.
gluteus-maximus-muscle.clinical: Injury to the inferior gluteal nerve makes it hard to rise from a seated position or to climb stairs.
gluteus-maximus-muscle.origin: Ilium behind the posterior gluteal line, dorsal sacrum and coccyx, sacrotuberous ligament, and thoracolumbar fascia
gluteus-maximus-muscle.insertion: Iliotibial tract (most fibers) and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur
action: Extends the thigh at the hip
Upper fibers abduct and lower fibers adduct
Stabilizes the extended knee through the iliotibial tract

gluteus-medius-muscle.name: Gluteus Medius Muscle
gluteus-medius-muscle.summary: A fan-shaped muscle on the outer ilium, lying mostly under gluteus maximus. It is the main stabilizer of the pelvis during walking.
gluteus-medius-muscle.clinical: Weakness or superior gluteal nerve injury causes a positive Trendelenburg sign, with the pelvis dropping on the unsupported side.
gluteus-medius-muscle.origin: External surface of the ilium between the anterior and posterior gluteal lines
gluteus-medius-muscle.insertion: Lateral surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
action: Anterior fibers medially rotate the thigh
Keeps the pelvis level during single-leg stance

gluteus-minimus-muscle.name: Gluteus Minimus Muscle
gluteus-minimus-muscle.summary: The smallest and deepest of the three gluteal muscles. It lies directly under gluteus medius.
gluteus-minimus-muscle.clinical: Together with gluteus medius, its weakness causes a Trendelenburg gait.
gluteus-minimus-muscle.origin: External surface of the ilium between the anterior and inferior gluteal lines
gluteus-minimus-muscle.insertion: Anterior surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
action: Keeps the pelvis level during single-leg stance

iliacus-muscle.name: Iliacus Muscle
iliacus-muscle.summary: A fan-shaped muscle that fills the iliac fossa. It joins psoas major to form the iliopsoas.
iliacus-muscle.clinical: A hematoma in the iliacus can compress the femoral nerve and cause weakness of knee extension.
iliacus-muscle.origin: Iliac fossa, the ala of the sacrum, and the anterior sacroiliac ligaments
iliacus-muscle.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur, by the common iliopsoas tendon
action: Flexes the thigh at the hip
Flexes the trunk on the thigh when the leg is fixed
blood: Iliac branch of the iliolumbar artery

iliococcygeus-muscle.name: Iliococcygeus Muscle
iliococcygeus-muscle.summary: The thin posterior and lateral part of levator ani. It forms a sling that supports the pelvic floor.
iliococcygeus-muscle.clinical: Weakness of the levator ani group contributes to pelvic organ prolapse and urinary incontinence.
iliococcygeus-muscle.origin: Posterior part of the tendinous arch of levator ani and the ischial spine
action: Pulls the anococcygeal body forward and upward
iliococcygeus-muscle.nerve: Nerve to levator ani (from S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve

inferior-gemellus-muscle.name: Inferior Gemellus Muscle
inferior-gemellus-muscle.summary: A small muscle that lies along the lower edge of the obturator internus tendon. It is one of the lateral rotators of the hip.
inferior-gemellus-muscle.clinical: It is a landmark below piriformis; the sciatic nerve usually passes over it deep to gluteus maximus.
inferior-gemellus-muscle.origin: Upper part of the ischial tuberosity
inferior-gemellus-muscle.insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter, with the obturator internus tendon
action: Holds the femoral head in the acetabulum

inguinal-ligament.name: Inguinal Ligament
inguinal-ligament.summary: A thick band that is the folded lower edge of the external oblique aponeurosis. It runs from the hip bone to the pubis. This is a ligament, not a muscle.
inguinal-ligament.clinical: It is the landmark that separates inguinal hernias (above) from femoral hernias (below).
action: Forms the floor of the inguinal canal
Gives attachment to the internal oblique and transversus abdominis
Forms the roof of the muscular and vascular compartments of the thigh

obturator-internus.name: Obturator Internus Muscle
obturator-internus.summary: A fan-shaped muscle on the inner wall of the lesser pelvis. Its tendon turns around the ischium to reach the femur.
obturator-internus.clinical: Its fascia forms the pudendal canal, which carries the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels.
obturator-internus.origin: Inner surface of the obturator membrane and the surrounding pubis and ischium
obturator-internus.insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter of the femur
action: Steadies the femoral head in the acetabulum

piriformis-muscle.name: Piriformis Muscle
piriformis-muscle.summary: A pear-shaped muscle that leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen. It is a key landmark of the gluteal region.
piriformis-muscle.clinical: Piriformis syndrome occurs when this muscle irritates the sciatic nerve, causing buttock pain and sciatica-like symptoms.
piriformis-muscle.origin: Anterior surface of the sacrum (S2 to S4), the sacrotuberous ligament, and the ilium near the greater sciatic notch
piriformis-muscle.insertion: Superior border of the greater trochanter of the femur
action: Steadies the femoral head in the acetabulum
piriformis-muscle.nerve: Nerve to piriformis (ventral rami of S1 and S2)

psoas-major.name: Psoas Major Muscle
psoas-major.summary: A long muscle on the posterior abdominal wall that runs down into the thigh. It joins iliacus to form the iliopsoas.
psoas-major.clinical: A psoas abscess, often from spinal infection, can track down to the thigh; pain on hip extension is the psoas sign.
psoas-major.origin: Transverse processes of the lumbar vertebrae, and the sides of T12 to L5 with their intervening discs
psoas-major.insertion: Lesser trochanter of the femur, by the common iliopsoas tendon
action: Flexes the thigh at the hip
Flexes the trunk on the thigh when the leg is fixed
Bends the lumbar spine to the same side
psoas-major.roots: L1 to L3 (variant L2 to L4)

pubo-analis-muscle.name: Puboanalis Muscle
pubo-analis-muscle.summary: The part of levator ani that runs from the pubis to the wall of the anal canal. Some sources describe it as part of pubococcygeus.
pubo-analis-muscle.clinical: Damage to levator ani fibers during childbirth is linked to pelvic floor weakness and anal incontinence.
pubo-analis-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the body of the pubis
pubo-analis-muscle.insertion: Wall of the anal canal, near the groove between the internal and external anal sphincters
action: Lifts and supports the anal canal
pubo-analis-muscle.nerve: Nerve to levator ani (from S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve

pubococcygeus-muscle.name: Pubococcygeus Muscle
pubococcygeus-muscle.summary: The middle and main part of levator ani. It runs backward from the pubis alongside the pelvic organs.
pubococcygeus-muscle.clinical: Kegel exercises strengthen this muscle to help prevent stress urinary incontinence.
pubococcygeus-muscle.origin: Posterior surface of the body of the pubis and the anterior part of the tendinous arch
pubococcygeus-muscle.nerve: Nerve to levator ani (from S4) and branches of the pudendal nerve

pyramidalis-muscle.name: Pyramidalis Muscle
pyramidalis-muscle.summary: A small triangular muscle in front of the lower rectus abdominis. It is absent in roughly 20 percent of people.
pyramidalis-muscle.clinical: Surgeons sometimes use it as a midline landmark when entering the lower abdomen.
pyramidalis-muscle.origin: Anterior surface of the pubis and the pubic symphysis
pyramidalis-muscle.insertion: Linea alba, a short distance above the pubis

superior-gemellus-muscle.name: Superior Gemellus Muscle
superior-gemellus-muscle.summary: A small muscle that lies along the upper edge of the obturator internus tendon. It is one of the lateral rotators of the hip.
superior-gemellus-muscle.clinical: It marks the upper border of the obturator internus tendon in the deep gluteal region.
superior-gemellus-muscle.origin: Outer surface of the ischial spine
superior-gemellus-muscle.insertion: Medial surface of the greater trochanter, with the obturator internus tendon
action: Holds the femoral head in the acetabulum

tendinous-arch-of-levator-ani.name: Tendinous Arch of Levator Ani
tendinous-arch-of-levator-ani.summary: A thickened band of fascia on the obturator internus. It gives origin to much of levator ani. This is fascia, not true muscle.
tendinous-arch-of-levator-ani.clinical: Detachment of this arch from the pelvic wall is a recognized cause of pelvic organ prolapse.
tendinous-arch-of-levator-ani.origin: Back of the body of the pubis, near the pubic symphysis
action: Gives origin to the levator ani muscle
Anchors the pelvic diaphragm to the side wall of the pelvis

external-intercostal-muscles.name: External Intercostal Muscles
external-intercostal-muscles.summary: The outermost layer of muscle between the ribs. Fibers run downward and forward, like the direction of hands in pockets.
external-intercostal-muscles.clinical: For chest tube or needle insertion, pass just above the top of a rib to avoid the neurovascular bundle under the rib above.
external-intercostal-muscles.origin: Lower border of the rib above
external-intercostal-muscles.insertion: Upper border of the rib below
action: Hold the intercostal space firm against pressure changes
external-intercostal-muscles.nerve: Intercostal nerves (ventral rami of T1 to T11)
blood: Anterior intercostal arteries (from the internal thoracic artery)

internal-intercostal-muscles.name: Internal Intercostal Muscles
internal-intercostal-muscles.summary: The middle layer of muscle between the ribs. Fibers run downward and backward, at right angles to the external layer.
internal-intercostal-muscles.clinical: The intercostal neurovascular bundle lies between this layer and the innermost layer.
internal-intercostal-muscles.origin: Floor of the costal groove and lower border of the rib above
internal-intercostal-muscles.insertion: Upper border of the rib below
action: Depress the ribs during forced expiration
internal-intercostal-muscles.nerve: Intercostal nerves (ventral rami of T1 to T11)
blood: Anterior intercostal arteries (from the internal thoracic artery)

innermost-intercostal-muscles.name: Innermost Intercostal Muscles
innermost-intercostal-muscles.summary: The deepest layer of intercostal muscle. It is separated from the internal layer by the intercostal vessels and nerve.
innermost-intercostal-muscles.clinical: It is thin and incomplete; the pleura lies directly behind it, so deep needle punctures can enter the pleural cavity.
innermost-intercostal-muscles.insertion: Inner surface of the next rib below, or the one after
action: Depress the ribs during forced expiration
innermost-intercostal-muscles.nerve: Intercostal nerves (ventral rami of T1 to T11)
blood: Anterior intercostal arteries (from the internal thoracic artery)

levatores-breves-costarum.name: Levatores Breves Costarum
levatores-breves-costarum.summary: Small muscles on the back of the chest wall. Each runs from a transverse process to the rib just below.
levatores-breves-costarum.clinical: These muscles are small and seldom matter alone, but they contribute to back stiffness with rib or thoracic spine injury.
levatores-breves-costarum.origin: Tips of the transverse processes of C7 to T11
levatores-breves-costarum.insertion: Upper border of the rib immediately below, between the tubercle and the angle
action: Assist extension and lateral bending of the vertebral column
levatores-breves-costarum.nerve: Dorsal rami of spinal nerves C8 to T11

levatores-longi-costarum.name: Levatores Longi Costarum
levatores-longi-costarum.summary: The longer set of levator muscles on the back of the chest wall. Each spans two ribs, skipping the nearest one.
levatores-longi-costarum.clinical: These are mainly lower thoracic muscles and help support the posterior chest wall.
levatores-longi-costarum.origin: Tips of the transverse processes of the lower thoracic vertebrae (about T7 to T10)
levatores-longi-costarum.insertion: Upper border of the second rib below, between the tubercle and the angle
action: Assist extension and lateral bending of the vertebral column
levatores-longi-costarum.nerve: Dorsal rami of spinal nerves C8 to T11

oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.name: Oblique Part of Cricothyroid Muscle
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.summary: The posterior, more horizontal fibers of the cricothyroid muscle on the outside of the larynx. The cricothyroid is the only intrinsic laryngeal muscle outside the larynx.
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.clinical: Injury to the external laryngeal nerve during thyroid surgery causes a weak voice and loss of high pitch.
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.origin: Anterolateral surface of the cricoid cartilage
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.insertion: Inferior horn and lower margin of the thyroid cartilage
action: Tilts the thyroid cartilage forward and slides it
Tenses and lengthens the vocal folds to raise pitch
oblique-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.nerve: External laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve)
blood: Cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery

omohyoid-muscle.name: Omohyoid Muscle
omohyoid-muscle.summary: A thin two-bellied strap muscle with an intermediate tendon. It runs from the scapula to the hyoid bone.
omohyoid-muscle.clinical: The inferior belly crosses the posterior triangle and divides it into the occipital and omoclavicular (subclavian) triangles.
omohyoid-muscle.origin: Inferior belly: upper border of the scapula near the suprascapular notch
omohyoid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the body of the hyoid bone
action: Depresses and retracts the hyoid bone

platysma.name: Platysma
platysma.summary: A thin, broad sheet of muscle in the superficial fascia of the neck. It is a muscle of facial expression.
platysma.clinical: Facial nerve palsy can weaken it, and it must be carefully closed in neck surgery to limit scarring.
platysma.origin: Fascia over the upper pectoralis major and deltoid
platysma.insertion: Lower border of the mandible, skin of the lower face, and the angle of the mouth
action: Tenses the skin of the neck
Depresses the mandible and corner of the mouth
Shows tension and fear in the face
platysma.nerve: Cervical branch of the facial nerve

scalenus-anterior-muscle.name: Anterior Scalene Muscle
scalenus-anterior-muscle.summary: A deep neck muscle that runs from the cervical spine to the first rib. It lies in front of the brachial plexus roots.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.clinical: Tightness can compress the subclavian artery and brachial plexus, causing thoracic outlet syndrome. The phrenic nerve crosses its front.
scalenus-anterior-muscle.origin: Anterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C3 to C6
scalenus-anterior-muscle.insertion: Scalene tubercle on the inner border of the first rib
action: Elevates the first rib in inspiration
Bends the neck to the same side
Rotates the neck to the opposite side
scalenus-anterior-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of cervical spinal nerves

scalenus-medius-muscle.name: Middle Scalene Muscle
scalenus-medius-muscle.summary: The largest and longest scalene muscle. It lies behind the anterior scalene and the brachial plexus roots.
scalenus-medius-muscle.clinical: The long thoracic nerve pierces it, and the brachial plexus emerges between it and the anterior scalene. This gap is the interscalene block site.
scalenus-medius-muscle.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C2 to C7
scalenus-medius-muscle.insertion: Upper surface of the first rib, behind the groove for the subclavian artery
action: Bends the neck to the same side
scalenus-medius-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of cervical spinal nerves

scalenus-posterior-muscle.name: Posterior Scalene Muscle
scalenus-posterior-muscle.summary: The smallest and deepest scalene muscle. It lies behind the middle scalene and attaches to the second rib.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.clinical: It is sometimes fused with the middle scalene and can add to thoracic outlet compression.
scalenus-posterior-muscle.origin: Posterior tubercles of the transverse processes of C4 to C6
scalenus-posterior-muscle.insertion: Outer surface of the second rib
action: Bends the neck to the same side
scalenus-posterior-muscle.nerve: Ventral rami of cervical spinal nerves

sternocleidomastoid-muscle.name: Sternocleidomastoid Muscle
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.summary: A thick, two-headed muscle that crosses the side of the neck obliquely. It divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.clinical: Shortening or fibrosis causes congenital muscular torticollis, with the head tilted to one side and the face turned the other way.
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.origin: Sternal head: front of the manubrium. Clavicular head: upper surface of the medial third of the clavicle
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.insertion: Lateral surface of the mastoid process and the lateral half of the superior nuchal line
action: One side tilts the head to the same side and turns the face to the opposite side
Both sides together flex the neck
Both sides extend the head at the atlanto-occipital joint
sternocleidomastoid-muscle.nerve: Accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor; C2 and C3 for pain and position sense

sternohyoid-muscle.name: Sternohyoid Muscle
sternohyoid-muscle.summary: A thin strap muscle in the front of the neck. It runs from the sternum and clavicle to the hyoid bone.
sternohyoid-muscle.clinical: It lies in front of the thyroid gland and is split in the midline during thyroid surgery.
sternohyoid-muscle.origin: Back of the manubrium, medial end of the clavicle, and the posterior sternoclavicular ligament
sternohyoid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the body of the hyoid bone
action: Depresses the hyoid bone after swallowing

sternothyroid-muscle.name: Sternothyroid Muscle
sternothyroid-muscle.summary: A strap muscle in the front of the neck, deep to sternohyoid. It lies directly on the thyroid gland.
sternothyroid-muscle.clinical: Its attachment to the thyroid cartilage limits upward spread of a swollen thyroid gland.
sternothyroid-muscle.origin: Back of the manubrium and the edge of the first costal cartilage
sternothyroid-muscle.insertion: Oblique line on the lamina of the thyroid cartilage
action: Depresses the larynx and hyoid bone after swallowing

straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.name: Straight Part of Cricothyroid Muscle
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.summary: The anterior, more vertical fibers of the cricothyroid muscle on the outside of the larynx.
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.clinical: Loss of this muscle from external laryngeal nerve injury weakens the voice and limits pitch range.
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.insertion: Lower border of the lamina of the thyroid cartilage
action: Tenses and lengthens the vocal folds to raise pitch
straight-part-of-cricothyroid-muscle.nerve: External laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve)
blood: Cricothyroid branch of the superior thyroid artery

subclavius-muscle.name: Subclavius Muscle
subclavius-muscle.group: Muscles of the anterior thoracic wall
subclavius-muscle.summary: A small muscle that lies between the clavicle and the first rib. It runs under the clavicle.
subclavius-muscle.clinical: It cushions the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus from a broken clavicle. It lies close to the route for subclavian vein catheters.
subclavius-muscle.origin: Junction of the first rib and its costal cartilage
subclavius-muscle.insertion: Subclavian groove on the underside of the middle third of the clavicle
subclavius-muscle.nerve: Nerve to subclavius (from the upper trunk of the brachial plexus)
blood: Clavicular branch of the thoracoacromial artery

transversus-thoracis-muscle.name: Transversus Thoracis Muscle
transversus-thoracis-muscle.group: Muscles of the anterior thoracic wall
transversus-thoracis-muscle.summary: A thin, fan-shaped muscle on the inner surface of the front chest wall. It lies behind the sternum.
transversus-thoracis-muscle.clinical: The internal thoracic artery runs on its surface, which matters when raising a sternal bypass graft.
transversus-thoracis-muscle.origin: Inner surface of the lower body of the sternum and the xiphoid process
transversus-thoracis-muscle.insertion: Inner surfaces of costal cartilages 2 to 6
transversus-thoracis-muscle.nerve: Intercostal nerves (ventral rami of T2 to T6)
blood: Anterior intercostal arteries (from the internal thoracic artery)

abducens-nerve-vi.name: Abducens Nerve (VI)
abducens-nerve-vi.summary: Cranial nerve VI supplies only the lateral rectus muscle, which turns the eye outward.
abducens-nerve-vi.roots: CN VI; abducens nucleus in the lower pons
abducens-nerve-vi.from: Pontomedullary junction, between the pons and the medullary pyramid
abducens-nerve-vi.course: It climbs the clivus, pierces the dura, and runs through the cavernous sinus beside the internal carotid artery. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
abducens-nerve-vi.injury: The eye drifts inward and the person sees double side by side. The double vision is worse when looking toward the injured side.
abducens-nerve-vi.clinical: Its long course makes it prone to stretch in raised intracranial pressure, a classic false-localizing sign.

accessory-nerve-xi.name: Accessory Nerve (XI)
accessory-nerve-xi.summary: Cranial nerve XI is a motor nerve for the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles.
accessory-nerve-xi.roots: CN XI; spinal accessory nucleus in the upper cervical cord (C1-C5, or C6)
accessory-nerve-xi.from: Spinal roots from the upper cervical cord rise through the foramen magnum and join into one trunk
accessory-nerve-xi.course: It leaves the skull through the jugular foramen and passes deep to sternocleidomastoid. It then crosses the posterior triangle of the neck to reach trapezius.
accessory-nerve-xi.sensory: No true skin supply; it carries proprioceptive fibers from the muscles it supplies.
accessory-nerve-xi.injury: Injury causes a drooping shoulder, weak shoulder shrug, and difficulty raising the arm above horizontal.
accessory-nerve-xi.clinical: The nerve lies superficially in the posterior triangle, so lymph node biopsy or neck surgery can injure it.

ampulla-of-lacrimal-canaliculus.name: Ampulla of Lacrimal Canaliculus
ampulla-of-lacrimal-canaliculus.summary: The ampulla is a small swelling in each lacrimal canaliculus where the vertical part turns into the horizontal part.
ampulla-of-lacrimal-canaliculus.location: Medial eyelid margin, about 2 mm from the lacrimal punctum, at the bend of each canaliculus
function: Collects tears from the punctum
Passes tears on to the horizontal canaliculus and then the lacrimal sac
blood: Palpebral branches of the ophthalmic artery
ampulla-of-lacrimal-canaliculus.nerve: Sensory supply from the infratrochlear nerve (V1) and the infraorbital nerve (V2)
ampulla-of-lacrimal-canaliculus.clinical: Narrowing or scarring of the canaliculus blocks tear drainage and causes a watery eye (epiphora).

anterior-chamber-of-eyeball.name: Anterior Chamber of Eyeball
anterior-chamber-of-eyeball.summary: The anterior chamber is the fluid-filled space between the cornea and the iris.
anterior-chamber-of-eyeball.location: Between the back of the cornea in front and the iris and pupil behind
function: Holds aqueous humor
Lets aqueous humor drain at the iridocorneal angle
anterior-chamber-of-eyeball.clinical: Blocked drainage at the angle raises eye pressure and causes glaucoma. Blood in this chamber is called hyphema.

anterior-segment-of-eyeball.name: Anterior Segment of Eyeball
anterior-segment-of-eyeball.summary: The anterior segment is the front part of the eye, in front of the vitreous body.
anterior-segment-of-eyeball.location: Front third of the eyeball, from the cornea back to the lens
function: Bends and focuses incoming light
Controls light entry through the pupil
Makes and drains aqueous humor
blood: Long posterior ciliary arteries (both from the ophthalmic artery)
anterior-segment-of-eyeball.nerve: Sensation from the long ciliary nerves (V1); autonomic fibers to the iris and ciliary muscle
anterior-segment-of-eyeball.clinical: Cataract and angle-closure glaucoma both arise in this part of the eye.

anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.name: Anterior Division of Mandibular Nerve
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.summary: The smaller anterior division of V3 is mostly motor to the chewing muscles and also gives the buccal nerve.
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.roots: CN V3 (trigeminal motor nucleus and main sensory nucleus)
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.from: Mandibular nerve trunk, just below the foramen ovale
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.course: It runs forward in the infratemporal fossa. It gives masseteric and deep temporal nerves, a nerve to lateral pterygoid, and the buccal nerve.
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.sensory: Cheek skin and lining through the buccal nerve
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.injury: Injury weakens chewing on that side and the jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening.
anterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.clinical: Medial pterygoid is not in this group; it comes directly from the main mandibular trunk.

buccal-nerve.name: Buccal Nerve
buccal-nerve.summary: The buccal nerve is a sensory branch of V3 for the cheek. It does not supply the buccinator muscle.
buccal-nerve.from: Anterior division of the mandibular nerve, in the infratemporal fossa
buccal-nerve.course: It passes between the two heads of lateral pterygoid and runs down deep to the temporalis tendon. It ends on the surface of buccinator.
buccal-nerve.sensory: Skin and inner lining of the cheek, and the gum next to the lower molars
buccal-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness of the cheek lining. It may be affected by lower molar dental procedures.
buccal-nerve.clinical: Despite its name, buccinator is moved by the facial nerve. The buccal nerve only carries sensation.

chorda-tympani.name: Chorda Tympani
chorda-tympani.summary: The chorda tympani carries taste from the front of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to two salivary glands.
chorda-tympani.roots: CN VII (nervus intermedius); solitary nucleus for taste, superior salivatory nucleus for secretion
chorda-tympani.from: Facial nerve in the facial canal, just above the stylomastoid foramen
chorda-tympani.course: It crosses the middle ear over the handle of the malleus. It leaves through the petrotympanic fissure and joins the lingual nerve.
motor: Parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual glands, through the submandibular ganglion
chorda-tympani.sensory: Taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue
chorda-tympani.injury: Injury causes loss of taste on the front of the tongue on that side and reduced saliva from the two glands.
chorda-tympani.clinical: Middle ear infection or ear surgery can damage it because it passes through the middle ear.

cochlea.name: Cochlea
cochlea.summary: The cochlea is a spiral chamber in the inner ear that changes sound vibrations into nerve signals.
cochlea.location: Petrous part of the temporal bone, in front of the vestibule; it makes about 2.5 turns
function: Converts sound vibrations into nerve impulses
Sorts sounds by pitch along the basilar membrane
blood: Labyrinthine artery (usually from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery)
cochlea.clinical: Loss of hair cells in the organ of Corti causes sensorineural deafness. A cochlear implant stimulates the nerve directly.

cochlear-nerve.name: Cochlear Nerve
cochlear-nerve.summary: The cochlear nerve is the hearing part of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
cochlear-nerve.roots: CN VIII; dorsal and ventral cochlear nuclei at the pontomedullary junction
cochlear-nerve.from: Spiral ganglion in the modiolus of the cochlea
cochlear-nerve.course: It runs through the internal acoustic meatus with the vestibular and facial nerves. It enters the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction.
cochlear-nerve.sensory: Hearing, from the hair cells of the organ of Corti
cochlear-nerve.injury: Injury causes sensorineural hearing loss and often ringing in the ear (tinnitus).
cochlear-nerve.clinical: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) can press on this nerve and cause one-sided hearing loss.

cornea.name: Cornea
cornea.summary: The cornea is the clear front window of the eye. It provides most of the focusing power of the eye.
cornea.location: Front of the eyeball, continuous with the sclera at the limbus
function: Bends light onto the lens (about two thirds of eye focusing power)
Protects the front of the eye
blood: None; it is avascular and takes nutrients from tears, aqueous humor, and limbal capillaries
cornea.nerve: Long ciliary nerves from the ophthalmic nerve (V1); very dense pain fibers
cornea.clinical: A corneal scratch is very painful. Because the cornea has no vessels, transplants are rarely rejected.

facial-nerve-vii.name: Facial Nerve (VII)
facial-nerve-vii.summary: Cranial nerve VII moves the muscles of facial expression. It also carries taste and gland secretion fibers.
facial-nerve-vii.roots: CN VII; facial motor nucleus, superior salivatory nucleus, solitary nucleus
facial-nerve-vii.from: Pontomedullary junction, lateral to the abducens nerve
facial-nerve-vii.course: It enters the internal acoustic meatus and runs in the facial canal. It leaves at the stylomastoid foramen and splits in the parotid gland.
motor: Parasympathetic fibers to the lacrimal, submandibular, sublingual, and nasal glands
facial-nerve-vii.sensory: Taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue; a small patch of skin at the ear
facial-nerve-vii.injury: Bell palsy causes weakness of the whole half of the face, including the forehead. A brain lesion above the nucleus spares the forehead.
facial-nerve-vii.clinical: Terminal branches in the parotid gland are temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular, and cervical.

glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.name: Glossopharyngeal Nerve (IX)
glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.summary: Cranial nerve IX supplies the back of the tongue and throat. It moves stylopharyngeus and drives the parotid gland.
glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.roots: CN IX; nucleus ambiguus, inferior salivatory nucleus, solitary nucleus
glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.from: Lateral medulla, in the postolivary sulcus above the vagus nerve
glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.course: It leaves through the jugular foramen and descends with stylopharyngeus. It passes between the internal and external carotid arteries to the pharynx and tongue.
motor: Parasympathetic fibers to the parotid gland, through the otic ganglion
glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.sensory: Taste and general sensation from the posterior third of the tongue; pharynx; tonsil; middle ear; carotid sinus and carotid body
glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.injury: Injury causes loss of taste at the back of the tongue, a weak gag reflex, and trouble swallowing.
