glossopharyngeal-nerve-ix.clinical: Glossopharyngeal neuralgia causes sharp throat pain on swallowing. Touching the pharynx tests its sensory side in the gag reflex.

hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.name: Hypoglossal Nerve (XII)
hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.summary: Cranial nerve XII is the motor nerve of the tongue.
hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.roots: CN XII; hypoglossal nucleus in the medulla
hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.from: Rootlets in the preolivary sulcus on the front of the medulla
hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.course: It leaves through the hypoglossal canal and descends deep to the posterior belly of digastric. It then arches forward over the hyoid region into the tongue.
hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.injury: On sticking out the tongue, it deviates toward the injured side. Later the tongue wastes on that side.
hyppoglossal-nerve-xii.clinical: Palatoglossus is not supplied by this nerve; it comes from the vagus. Neck surgery near the carotid artery can injure the nerve.

inferior-alveolar-nerve.name: Inferior Alveolar Nerve
inferior-alveolar-nerve.summary: The inferior alveolar nerve supplies the lower teeth and gum. Its end branch, the mental nerve, supplies the chin and lower lip.
inferior-alveolar-nerve.roots: CN V3 (sensory); motor fibers only in the nerve to mylohyoid
inferior-alveolar-nerve.from: Posterior division of the mandibular nerve, in the infratemporal fossa
inferior-alveolar-nerve.course: It descends between the ramus of the mandible and the sphenomandibular ligament. It enters the mandibular foramen and runs in the mandibular canal.
motor: Mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric, through the nerve to mylohyoid
inferior-alveolar-nerve.sensory: All lower teeth and gum; chin and lower lip through the mental nerve
inferior-alveolar-nerve.injury: Injury during jaw surgery or lower third molar removal causes numbness of the lower lip and chin on that side.
inferior-alveolar-nerve.clinical: A dental inferior alveolar nerve block numbs the lower teeth, lip, and chin on one side.

iris.name: Iris
iris.summary: The iris is the colored ring of tissue with a central hole, the pupil. It controls how much light enters the eye.
iris.location: In front of the lens, between the anterior and posterior chambers
function: Changes pupil size to control light entering the eye
Sphincter pupillae narrows the pupil
Dilator pupillae widens the pupil
blood: Long posterior ciliary arteries and anterior ciliary arteries, forming the major arterial circle of the iris
iris.nerve: Parasympathetic from the oculomotor nerve (sphincter); sympathetic from the superior cervical ganglion (dilator)
iris.clinical: A fixed, widened pupil can signal compression of the oculomotor nerve, for example from brain herniation.

lacrimal-canaliculus.name: Lacrimal Canaliculus
lacrimal-canaliculus.summary: The lacrimal canaliculi are two small tubes that carry tears from the eyelid openings to the lacrimal sac.
lacrimal-canaliculus.location: Medial margin of each eyelid, from the lacrimal punctum to the lacrimal sac; one upper and one lower
function: Drain tears from the lacrimal lake
Carry tears to the lacrimal sac
blood: Palpebral branches of the ophthalmic artery
lacrimal-canaliculus.nerve: Sensory supply from the infratrochlear nerve (V1) and the infraorbital nerve (V2)
lacrimal-canaliculus.clinical: A cut through the medial lower eyelid can sever the canaliculus and cause constant tearing unless repaired.

lacrimal-gland.name: Lacrimal Gland
lacrimal-gland.summary: The lacrimal gland makes the watery part of tears. It lies in the upper outer corner of the orbit.
lacrimal-gland.location: Lacrimal fossa in the superolateral orbit; a smaller part extends into the upper eyelid
function: Secretes the watery layer of tears
Adds lysozyme and other protective proteins
blood: Lacrimal artery (branch of the ophthalmic artery)
lacrimal-gland.nerve: Parasympathetic secretion from the facial nerve via the greater petrosal nerve and pterygopalatine ganglion; sensation from the lacrimal nerve (V1)
lacrimal-gland.clinical: Sjögren syndrome damages the gland and causes dry eyes.

lacrimal-sac.name: Lacrimal Sac
lacrimal-sac.summary: The lacrimal sac is the upper widened end of the nasolacrimal duct. It receives tears from both canaliculi.
lacrimal-sac.location: Lacrimal fossa on the medial wall of the orbit, behind the medial palpebral ligament
function: Receives tears from the canaliculi
Passes tears down to the nasolacrimal duct
blood: Branches of the ophthalmic, facial (angular), and maxillary arteries
lacrimal-sac.nerve: Sensory supply from the infratrochlear nerve (V1) and the infraorbital nerve (V2)
lacrimal-sac.clinical: Infection of the sac (dacryocystitis) causes a red, painful swelling just below the medial corner of the eye.

lens.name: Lens
lens.summary: The lens is a clear, flexible disc behind the iris. It fine-tunes focus by changing shape.
lens.location: Behind the iris and pupil and in front of the vitreous body, held by zonular fibres
function: Focuses light on the retina
Changes shape to focus near and far objects (accommodation)
lens.clinical: A clouded lens is a cataract. Surgery replaces it with an artificial lens. The lens has no blood vessels or nerves.

lingual-nerve.name: Lingual Nerve
lingual-nerve.summary: The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the front of the tongue. It also carries taste fibers from the chorda tympani.
lingual-nerve.roots: CN V3 (sensory); chorda tympani joins it from CN VII
lingual-nerve.from: Posterior division of the mandibular nerve, in the infratemporal fossa
lingual-nerve.course: It runs down in front of the inferior alveolar nerve and is joined by the chorda tympani. It passes near the third lower molar into the tongue.
motor: Carries parasympathetic fibers from the chorda tympani to the submandibular and sublingual glands
lingual-nerve.sensory: General sensation from the anterior two thirds of the tongue, floor of mouth, and inner gum; taste through the chorda tympani
lingual-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness and loss of taste on that side of the tongue.
lingual-nerve.clinical: It lies close to the lower third molar, so wisdom tooth surgery can injure it.

mental-nerve.name: Mental Nerve
mental-nerve.summary: The mental nerve is the end branch of the inferior alveolar nerve. It supplies the chin and lower lip.
mental-nerve.from: Inferior alveolar nerve, in the mandibular canal
mental-nerve.course: It leaves the mandible through the mental foramen, near the second premolar. It then divides into branches for the chin, lower lip, and gum.
mental-nerve.sensory: Skin of the chin; skin and lining of the lower lip; front gum of the lower jaw
mental-nerve.injury: Injury during jaw fracture or implant surgery causes numbness of the chin and lower lip.
mental-nerve.clinical: Numb chin syndrome can be an early sign of disease affecting the jaw, including some cancers.

motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.name: Motor Root of Trigeminal Nerve
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.summary: The motor root of the trigeminal nerve is a small root that supplies the chewing muscles.
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.roots: CN V; motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve in the mid pons
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.from: Lateral pons, beside the larger sensory root
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.course: It passes under the trigeminal ganglion and leaves through the foramen ovale. There it joins the mandibular nerve (V3).
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.injury: Injury weakens chewing and the jaw deviates toward the injured side when opened.
motor-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.clinical: Only the mandibular division (V3) carries these motor fibers.

nasolacrimal-duct.name: Nasolacrimal Duct
nasolacrimal-duct.summary: The nasolacrimal duct carries tears from the lacrimal sac into the nose.
nasolacrimal-duct.location: Runs down in the nasolacrimal canal, from the lacrimal sac to the inferior nasal meatus
function: Drains tears into the inferior nasal meatus
blood: Branches of the sphenopalatine and infraorbital arteries
nasolacrimal-duct.nerve: Sensory supply from the infraorbital nerve (V2) and the anterior superior alveolar nerve
nasolacrimal-duct.clinical: A blocked duct is common in newborns and causes a watery eye. Crying makes the nose run because tears drain into it.

nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.name: Nerve to Mylohyoid
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.summary: This small motor nerve supplies the mylohyoid muscle and the anterior belly of digastric.
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.roots: CN V3 (motor fibers from the trigeminal motor nucleus)
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.from: Inferior alveolar nerve, just before the mandibular foramen
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.course: It pierces the sphenomandibular ligament and runs in the mylohyoid groove of the mandible. It ends on the underside of mylohyoid.
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.sensory: A small, variable patch of skin under the chin
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.injury: Injury causes weak elevation of the floor of the mouth and hyoid bone.
nerve-to-mylohyoid-muscle.clinical: It leaves the inferior alveolar nerve before the mandibular foramen, so a nerve block may also numb the floor of the mouth.

oculomotor-nerve-iii.name: Oculomotor Nerve (III)
oculomotor-nerve-iii.summary: Cranial nerve III moves the eye in most directions and lifts the upper eyelid. It also narrows the pupil.
oculomotor-nerve-iii.roots: CN III; oculomotor nucleus and Edinger-Westphal nucleus in the midbrain
oculomotor-nerve-iii.from: Interpeduncular fossa on the front of the midbrain
oculomotor-nerve-iii.course: It passes between the posterior cerebral and superior cerebellar arteries and runs in the wall of the cavernous sinus. It enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
motor: Parasympathetic fibers to the sphincter pupillae and ciliary muscle, through the ciliary ganglion
oculomotor-nerve-iii.injury: The eye points down and out, the upper lid droops (ptosis), and the pupil is widened.
oculomotor-nerve-iii.clinical: An aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery can press on this nerve and widen the pupil first.

olfactory-nerve-i.name: Olfactory Nerve (I)
olfactory-nerve-i.summary: Cranial nerve I carries the sense of smell. It is made of many small bundles, not one trunk.
olfactory-nerve-i.roots: CN I; olfactory receptor cells, synapsing in the olfactory bulb
olfactory-nerve-i.from: Olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity
olfactory-nerve-i.course: About twenty small bundles pass up through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone. They end in the olfactory bulb.
olfactory-nerve-i.injury: Fracture of the cribriform plate can tear the nerve bundles and cause loss of smell (anosmia).
olfactory-nerve-i.clinical: Such a fracture can also tear the meninges and let cerebrospinal fluid leak from the nose.

ophtalmic-nerve.name: Ophthalmic Nerve (V1)
ophtalmic-nerve.summary: The ophthalmic nerve is the first and smallest division of the trigeminal nerve. It is purely sensory.
ophtalmic-nerve.roots: CN V1; trigeminal ganglion, with main sensory and spinal trigeminal nuclei
ophtalmic-nerve.course: It runs forward in the wall of the cavernous sinus. It divides into frontal, lacrimal, and nasociliary nerves and enters the orbit by the superior orbital fissure.
ophtalmic-nerve.sensory: Forehead and scalp to the vertex, upper eyelid, cornea, nose and its tip, and the roof of the nasal cavity
ophtalmic-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness of the forehead and cornea, and the corneal blink reflex is lost.
ophtalmic-nerve.clinical: Shingles of this division (herpes zoster ophthalmicus) can threaten vision, especially when the tip of the nose is involved.

optic-nerve-ii.name: Optic Nerve (II)
optic-nerve-ii.summary: Cranial nerve II carries vision from the retina to the brain. It is really a brain tract, wrapped in meninges.
optic-nerve-ii.roots: CN II; retinal ganglion cells, projecting mainly to the lateral geniculate nucleus
optic-nerve-ii.course: It leaves the orbit through the optic canal with the ophthalmic artery. It meets the other nerve at the optic chiasm.
optic-nerve-ii.injury: Injury causes loss of vision in that eye and loss of the pupil light reflex on stimulating it.
optic-nerve-ii.clinical: Raised intracranial pressure swells the optic disc (papilledema), because the nerve sheath is continuous with the meninges.

posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.name: Posterior Division of Mandibular Nerve
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.summary: The posterior division of V3 is mainly sensory. It gives the auriculotemporal, lingual, and inferior alveolar nerves.
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.from: Mandibular nerve trunk, below the foramen ovale
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.course: It runs down in the infratemporal fossa. It splits into the auriculotemporal, lingual, and inferior alveolar nerves.
motor: Mylohyoid and anterior belly of digastric, through the inferior alveolar nerve
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.sensory: Skin of the temple and ear; tongue and floor of mouth; lower teeth, lip, and chin
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness of the lower jaw region, tongue, and lower lip on that side.
posterior-division-of-mandibular-nerve.clinical: Lower jaw dental procedures target this division. A mandibular block numbs the inferior alveolar and lingual nerves.

posterior-segment-of-eyeball.name: Posterior Segment of Eyeball
posterior-segment-of-eyeball.summary: The posterior segment is the back part of the eye, behind the lens. It holds the vitreous body and the retina.
posterior-segment-of-eyeball.location: Back two thirds of the eyeball, behind the lens
function: Holds the vitreous body, which keeps the eye shape
Houses the retina that detects light
blood: Short posterior ciliary arteries (choroid and outer retina)
posterior-segment-of-eyeball.nerve: Optic nerve (II) carries vision out; short ciliary nerves carry sensation and autonomic fibers
posterior-segment-of-eyeball.clinical: Retinal detachment and diabetic eye disease affect this part of the eye.

retina.name: Retina
retina.summary: The retina is the light-sensitive layer lining the back of the eye. It sends visual signals to the brain through the optic nerve.
retina.location: Inner lining of the back of the eyeball, between the vitreous body and the choroid
function: Detects light with rods and cones
Starts processing of the image
Sends signals out through the optic nerve
retina.clinical: Retinal detachment causes a curtain-like loss of vision. Blockage of the central retinal artery causes sudden painless blindness.

sclera.name: Sclera
sclera.summary: The sclera is the tough white outer coat of the eyeball. It gives the eye its shape and protects it.
sclera.location: Back five sixths of the outer wall of the eyeball, continuous with the cornea in front
function: Keeps the shape of the eyeball
Protects the inner eye
Gives attachment to the eye muscles
blood: Anterior ciliary arteries (episcleral vessels); the sclera itself has few vessels
sclera.clinical: The sclera turns yellow in jaundice. Inflammation of it (scleritis) is deep and painful.

sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.name: Sensory Root of Trigeminal Nerve
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.summary: The sensory root is the large root that carries facial sensation from the trigeminal ganglion to the brainstem.
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.roots: CN V; central processes end in the main sensory, spinal trigeminal, and mesencephalic nuclei
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.course: It runs back in the posterior cranial fossa and enters the lateral pons through the middle cerebellar peduncle region.
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.sensory: Touch, pain, temperature, and position sense from the face, scalp, mouth, teeth, and dura
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.injury: Injury causes loss of facial sensation on that side, including the corneal reflex.
sensory-root-of-trigeminal-nerve.clinical: Pressure from a looping blood vessel on this root is a common cause of trigeminal neuralgia.

suspensory-ligament-of-eyeball.name: Suspensory Ligament of Eyeball
suspensory-ligament-of-eyeball.summary: This hammock-like sling under the eyeball supports it. It is also called the suspensory ligament of Lockwood.
suspensory-ligament-of-eyeball.location: Below the eyeball, formed by the fascial sheaths of inferior rectus and inferior oblique, with the medial and lateral check ligaments
function: Supports the eyeball from below
Holds its position even if the orbital floor is damaged
suspensory-ligament-of-eyeball.clinical: It keeps the eye from sinking much in an orbital floor fracture.

trigeminal-nerve-v.name: Trigeminal Nerve (V)
trigeminal-nerve-v.summary: Cranial nerve V is the main sensory nerve of the face. It also moves the chewing muscles.
trigeminal-nerve-v.roots: CN V; motor nucleus, main sensory nucleus, spinal trigeminal nucleus, mesencephalic nucleus
trigeminal-nerve-v.from: Lateral pons, as a large sensory root and a small motor root
trigeminal-nerve-v.course: The sensory root forms the trigeminal ganglion. Its three divisions leave the skull: V1 by the superior orbital fissure, V2 by foramen rotundum, V3 by foramen ovale.
trigeminal-nerve-v.sensory: Skin of the face and front scalp, nasal and oral cavities, teeth, front two thirds of the tongue, and most of the dura
trigeminal-nerve-v.injury: Sensory loss in the face and weak chewing. The jaw deviates toward the injured side when opened.
trigeminal-nerve-v.clinical: Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, severe, shock-like facial pain, often triggered by touch or chewing.

trochlear-nerve-iv.name: Trochlear Nerve (IV)
trochlear-nerve-iv.summary: Cranial nerve IV supplies only the superior oblique muscle. It is the thinnest cranial nerve.
trochlear-nerve-iv.roots: CN IV; trochlear nucleus in the midbrain
trochlear-nerve-iv.from: Back of the midbrain, just below the inferior colliculus; it is the only cranial nerve to leave from the back of the brainstem
trochlear-nerve-iv.course: Its fibers cross to the other side before leaving. It wraps around the brainstem, runs in the cavernous sinus, and enters the orbit by the superior orbital fissure.
motor: Superior oblique (turns the eye down when looking inward)
trochlear-nerve-iv.injury: The eye cannot look down well when turned inward. This causes vertical double vision, often noticed when reading or on stairs.
trochlear-nerve-iv.clinical: People often tilt the head away from the affected side to reduce the double vision.

tympanic-membrane.name: Tympanic Membrane
tympanic-membrane.summary: The tympanic membrane is the eardrum. It vibrates with sound and passes the vibrations to the ear bones.
tympanic-membrane.location: Between the external acoustic meatus and the middle ear; tilted so it faces downward and forward
function: Vibrates in response to sound
Passes vibrations to the malleus
blood: Anterior tympanic artery (both from the maxillary artery)
tympanic-membrane.nerve: Outer surface: auriculotemporal nerve (V3) and vagus nerve; inner surface: glossopharyngeal nerve (IX)
tympanic-membrane.clinical: A ruptured eardrum causes pain and conductive hearing loss. An otoscope shows a bright cone of light in the lower front area of a healthy drum.

vagus-nerve-x.name: Vagus Nerve (X)
vagus-nerve-x.summary: Cranial nerve X is the longest cranial nerve. It supplies the throat and voice box and gives parasympathetic fibers to the chest and abdomen.
vagus-nerve-x.roots: CN X; nucleus ambiguus, dorsal motor nucleus of vagus, solitary nucleus, spinal trigeminal nucleus
vagus-nerve-x.from: Lateral medulla, in the postolivary sulcus below the glossopharyngeal nerve
vagus-nerve-x.course: It leaves through the jugular foramen and descends in the carotid sheath. It passes through the chest and enters the abdomen with the esophagus.
motor: Muscles of the pharynx and soft palate (except stylopharyngeus and tensor veli palatini)
Parasympathetic fibers to the heart, lungs, and gut up to the left colic flexure
vagus-nerve-x.sensory: Pharynx, larynx, viscera of the chest and abdomen, a small area of the external ear, and the dura
vagus-nerve-x.injury: Injury of the recurrent laryngeal branch causes hoarseness. A lesion on one side makes the uvula deviate to the opposite side.
vagus-nerve-x.clinical: Strong vagal activation can slow the heart and cause fainting (vasovagal syncope).

vestibular-nerve.name: Vestibular Nerve
vestibular-nerve.summary: The vestibular nerve is the balance part of the vestibulocochlear nerve.
vestibular-nerve.roots: CN VIII; vestibular nuclei in the pons and medulla
vestibular-nerve.from: Vestibular ganglion, connected to the utricle, saccule, and semicircular ducts
vestibular-nerve.course: It runs through the internal acoustic meatus with the cochlear and facial nerves. It enters the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction.
vestibular-nerve.sensory: Balance, head position, and head movement
vestibular-nerve.injury: Injury causes vertigo, unsteadiness, and involuntary eye movements (nystagmus).
vestibular-nerve.clinical: Vestibular neuritis causes sudden severe vertigo. A vestibular schwannoma can also arise from this nerve.

vestibule.name: Vestibule
vestibule.summary: The vestibule is the central chamber of the inner ear. It holds the organs that sense head tilt and straight-line motion.
vestibule.location: Middle of the bony labyrinth in the petrous temporal bone, between the cochlea and the semicircular canals
function: Houses the utricle and saccule that sense head position and straight-line acceleration
Receives vibrations from the stapes at the oval window
blood: Labyrinthine artery (usually from the anterior inferior cerebellar artery)
vestibule.clinical: Disease of the inner ear balance organs causes vertigo, nausea, and unsteadiness.

vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.name: Vestibulocochlear Nerve (VIII)
vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.summary: Cranial nerve VIII carries hearing and balance signals from the inner ear to the brainstem.
vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.roots: CN VIII; cochlear nuclei and vestibular nuclei at the pontomedullary junction
vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.from: Cochlea and vestibular organs of the inner ear
vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.course: It runs through the internal acoustic meatus with the facial nerve. It enters the brainstem at the pontomedullary junction.
vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.injury: Injury causes hearing loss, ringing in the ear, vertigo, and unsteadiness.
vestibulocochlear-nerve-viii.clinical: A vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) grows on this nerve and may also press on the facial nerve.

vitreous-body.name: Vitreous Body
vitreous-body.summary: The vitreous body is the clear jelly that fills the large chamber behind the lens.
vitreous-body.location: Between the lens in front and the retina behind, filling most of the eyeball
function: Maintains the shape of the eyeball
Holds the retina against the choroid
Transmits light to the retina
vitreous-body.clinical: Age-related vitreous shrinkage causes floaters and flashes. Pulling on the retina can cause a retinal tear.

zonular-fibres.name: Zonular Fibres
zonular-fibres.summary: The zonular fibres are thin strands that hang the lens from the ciliary body.
zonular-fibres.location: Between the ciliary processes and the equator of the lens
function: Suspend the lens in position
Pass ciliary muscle tension to the lens to change its shape
zonular-fibres.clinical: Weak zonular fibres, as in Marfan syndrome, let the lens shift out of place.

anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.name: Anterior Branch of Obturator Nerve
anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.summary: The anterior branch of the obturator nerve supplies most of the adductor muscles and a patch of medial thigh skin.
anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.from: Obturator nerve, as it leaves the obturator canal
anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.course: It descends in front of obturator externus and adductor brevis. It lies behind pectineus and adductor longus.
anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial thigh (cutaneous branch); hip joint (articular branch)
anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.injury: Injury weakens thigh adduction and causes numbness of a small area of the medial thigh.
anterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.clinical: Pain from an obturator hernia or pelvic disease can be felt along the medial thigh.

anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.name: Anterior Cutaneous Branches of Femoral Nerve
anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.summary: The anterior cutaneous branches of the femoral nerve are the medial and intermediate femoral cutaneous nerves. They give sensation to the front of the thigh.
anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.from: Femoral nerve, in the femoral triangle
anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.course: They pierce the fascia lata (the intermediate branch often goes through sartorius). They run down the front of the thigh toward the knee.
anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.sensory: Skin of the anterior and anteromedial thigh down to the knee
anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.injury: Injury or surgical cuts cause patchy numbness over the front of the thigh.
anterior-cutaneous-branches-of-femoral-n.clinical: They help form the patellar plexus near the knee.

common-fibular-nerve.name: Common Fibular Nerve
common-fibular-nerve.summary: The common fibular nerve is the smaller branch of the sciatic nerve. It supplies the front and outer leg and the top of the foot.
common-fibular-nerve.roots: L4-S2 (posterior divisions of the sacral plexus)
common-fibular-nerve.from: Sciatic nerve, near the top of the popliteal fossa
common-fibular-nerve.course: It runs along the biceps femoris tendon and winds around the neck of the fibula. It divides there into superficial and deep fibular nerves.
common-fibular-nerve.sensory: Skin of the upper lateral leg, through the lateral sural cutaneous nerve
common-fibular-nerve.injury: Injury causes foot drop, weak eversion, and numbness of the outer lower leg and top of the foot.
common-fibular-nerve.clinical: It is the most commonly injured nerve of the leg because it lies just under the skin at the fibular neck.

common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.name: Common Plantar Digital Branches of Lateral Plantar Nerve
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.latin: Nervi digitales plantares communes nervi plantaris lateralis
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.summary: This branch comes from the superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve. It passes to the fourth web space of the sole.
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.from: Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.course: It runs toward the fourth web space between the toes and divides into proper plantar digital nerves.
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.sensory: Plantar skin of the adjacent sides of the fourth and fifth toes
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.injury: Injury causes numbness on the sole side of the outer two toes.
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.clinical: Compression of the plantar nerves in the tarsal tunnel causes burning pain and numbness in the sole.

common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.name: Common Plantar Digital Branches of Medial Plantar Nerve
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.latin: Nervi digitales plantares communes nervi plantaris medialis
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.summary: There are three common plantar digital nerves from the medial plantar nerve. They run to the first, second, and third web spaces.
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.from: Medial plantar nerve, in the sole
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.course: They run forward between the long flexor tendons toward the web spaces. Each divides into two proper plantar digital nerves.
motor: First lumbrical (from the first common digital nerve)
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.sensory: Plantar skin of the adjacent sides of toes 1-2, 2-3, and 3-4
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.injury: Injury causes numbness of the toe undersurfaces. Weakness of the first lumbrical is hard to detect.
common-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.clinical: Morton neuroma usually forms on the third common plantar digital nerve, between the third and fourth toes.

deep-fibular-nerve.name: Deep Fibular Nerve
deep-fibular-nerve.summary: The deep fibular nerve supplies the muscles of the front of the leg. It lifts the foot and toes.
deep-fibular-nerve.from: Common fibular nerve, at the neck of the fibula
deep-fibular-nerve.course: It runs down the front of the leg beside the anterior tibial artery. It crosses the ankle and ends on the top of the foot.
deep-fibular-nerve.sensory: Skin of the first web space between the great toe and second toe
deep-fibular-nerve.injury: Injury causes foot drop with a high-stepping gait and loss of toe extension.
deep-fibular-nerve.clinical: Anterior compartment syndrome can compress this nerve. Testing the first web space checks its sensation.

dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.name: Dorsal Digital Branches of Deep Fibular Nerve
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.latin: Nervi digitales dorsales hallucis lateralis et digiti secundi medialis
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.summary: These are the end branches of the deep fibular nerve. They supply skin of the first web space.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.from: Medial terminal branch of the deep fibular nerve, on the top of the foot
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.course: They run in the first space between the metatarsals and split to reach the adjacent sides of the great and second toes.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.sensory: Skin on the adjacent sides of the great toe and second toe
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.injury: Injury causes numbness in the first web space only.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-deep-fibular-.clinical: This small patch is the only skin area supplied by the deep fibular nerve, so it is used to test the nerve.

dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.name: Dorsal Digital Branches of Superficial Fibular Nerve
dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.summary: These branches carry sensation from the top of most of the toes. They come from the medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.from: Medial and intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerves of the foot
dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.course: They run forward over the top of the foot and along the sides of the toes.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.sensory: Skin on the top of the toes, except the first web space and the outer edge of the little toe
dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.injury: Injury causes numbness on the top of the toes.
dorsal-digital-branches-of-superficial-f.clinical: The deep fibular nerve supplies the first web space and the sural nerve supplies the little toe edge.

infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.name: Infrapatellar Branch of Saphenous Nerve
infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.summary: The infrapatellar branch is a skin nerve that curves below the patella. It supplies the front and inner side of the knee.
infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.from: Saphenous nerve, near the medial side of the knee
infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.course: It pierces sartorius and the fascia lata and curves forward below the patella. It joins the patellar plexus.
infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.sensory: Skin over the front and inner side of the knee, below the patella
infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.injury: Surgical cuts near the knee can injure it. This causes numbness or a painful scar nerve below the patella.
infrapatellar-branch-of-saphenous-nerve.clinical: Knee replacement, ACL repair with hamstring graft, and knee scopes can all injure it.

intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.name: Intermediate Dorsal Cutaneous Nerve of Foot
intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.summary: This skin nerve supplies the outer part of the top of the foot and the adjacent sides of the outer toes.
intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.from: Superficial fibular nerve, after it pierces the deep fascia of the lower leg
intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.course: It crosses the front of the ankle, lateral to the medial dorsal cutaneous nerve. It divides into dorsal digital nerves.
intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.sensory: Skin of the outer part of the top of the foot; adjacent sides of toes 3-4 and 4-5
intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.injury: Injury causes numbness over the outer top of the foot and outer toes.
intermediate-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-f.clinical: It can be injured in ankle sprains or by surgery at the front of the ankle.

lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.name: Lateral Femoral Cutaneous Nerve
lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.summary: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is a purely sensory nerve of the outer thigh.
lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.from: Lumbar plexus, from the posterior divisions of L2 and L3
lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.course: It emerges at the outer edge of psoas major and crosses iliacus. It passes under or through the inguinal ligament near the anterior superior iliac spine.
lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the anterolateral thigh, down to the knee
lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.injury: Compression causes burning pain and numbness on the outer thigh.
lateral-femoral-cutaneous-nerve.clinical: Meralgia paresthetica is compression at the inguinal ligament, linked to tight belts, obesity, and pregnancy.

lateral-plantar-nerve.name: Lateral Plantar Nerve
lateral-plantar-nerve.summary: The lateral plantar nerve is a branch of the tibial nerve. It supplies most of the small muscles of the sole and the outer sole skin.
lateral-plantar-nerve.from: Tibial nerve, under the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel
lateral-plantar-nerve.course: It runs forward between flexor digitorum brevis and quadratus plantae. Near the fifth metatarsal base it divides into superficial and deep branches.
lateral-plantar-nerve.sensory: Skin of the lateral sole and the outer one and a half toes
lateral-plantar-nerve.injury: Injury causes weakness of toe spreading and clawing of the toes, with numbness of the outer sole.
lateral-plantar-nerve.clinical: It is the foot counterpart of the ulnar nerve in the hand. Tarsal tunnel syndrome can compress it.

medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.name: Medial Crural Cutaneous Branches of Saphenous Nerve
medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.latin: Rami cutanei cruris mediales nervi sapheni
medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.summary: These skin branches of the saphenous nerve supply the inner side of the leg.
medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.course: They run down with the great saphenous vein along the inner leg. They pass to the ankle and the inner edge of the foot.
medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.sensory: Skin of the medial leg, medial ankle, and medial border of the foot
medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.injury: Injury causes numbness or burning pain along the inner leg.
medial-crural-cutaneous-branches-of-saph.clinical: Stripping or harvesting the great saphenous vein can injure them.

medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.name: Medial Dorsal Cutaneous Nerve of Foot
medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.summary: This skin nerve supplies the inner part of the top of the foot and the inner toes.
medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.from: Superficial fibular nerve, after it pierces the deep fascia of the lower leg
medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.course: It crosses the front of the ankle and divides into dorsal digital nerves. It also joins the saphenous nerve.
medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.sensory: Skin of the medial top of the foot; medial side of the great toe; adjacent sides of toes 2-3
medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.injury: Injury causes numbness on the inner top of the foot and the great toe.
medial-dorsal-cutaneous-nerve-of-foot.clinical: It can be trapped or cut near the front of the ankle, causing tingling that radiates to the toes.

medial-plantar-nerve.name: Medial Plantar Nerve
medial-plantar-nerve.summary: The medial plantar nerve is the larger branch of the tibial nerve in the foot. It supplies the inner sole and inner toes.
medial-plantar-nerve.from: Tibial nerve, under the flexor retinaculum in the tarsal tunnel
medial-plantar-nerve.course: It runs forward deep to abductor hallucis. It divides into a proper digital nerve to the great toe and three common plantar digital nerves.
medial-plantar-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial two thirds of the sole and the plantar side of the inner three and a half toes
medial-plantar-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness of the inner sole and toes and weak flexion of the great toe.
medial-plantar-nerve.clinical: It is the foot counterpart of the median nerve in the hand. Tarsal tunnel syndrome can compress it.

medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.name: Medial Sural Cutaneous Nerve
medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.summary: The medial sural cutaneous nerve is a skin branch of the tibial nerve. It joins another branch to form the sural nerve.
medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.from: Tibial nerve, in the popliteal fossa
medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.course: It runs down between the two heads of gastrocnemius and pierces the deep fascia about mid-calf. It joins the sural communicating branch.
medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the back of the lower leg
medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness on the back of the calf.
medial-sural-cutaneous-nerve.clinical: It runs with the small saphenous vein, so varicose vein surgery can injure it.

muscular-branches-of-deep-fibular-nerve.name: Muscular Branches of Deep Fibular Nerve
muscular-branches-of-deep-fibular-nerve.summary: These short branches supply the muscles in the front compartment of the leg.
muscular-branches-of-deep-fibular-nerve.from: Deep fibular nerve, in the anterior compartment of the leg
muscular-branches-of-deep-fibular-nerve.course: They arise along the nerve as it runs down between the extensor muscles. Each enters its muscle.
muscular-branches-of-deep-fibular-nerve.injury: Injury causes weak lifting of the foot and toes, and foot drop.
muscular-branches-of-deep-fibular-nerve.clinical: Anterior compartment syndrome can compress these branches and cause foot drop.

posterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.name: Posterior Branch of Obturator Nerve
posterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.summary: The posterior branch of the obturator nerve supplies obturator externus and part of adductor magnus. It also supplies the knee joint.
posterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.from: Obturator nerve, as it leaves the obturator canal
posterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.course: It pierces obturator externus and runs between adductor brevis and adductor magnus. A slender branch follows the femoral and popliteal arteries to the knee.
posterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.injury: Injury weakens adduction and causes vague knee pain.
posterior-branch-of-obturator-nerve.clinical: Hip disease can cause knee pain because the hip and knee share obturator nerve supply.

proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.name: Proper Plantar Digital Branches of Lateral Plantar Nerve
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.latin: Nervi digitales plantares proprii nervi plantaris lateralis
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.summary: These are the final skin nerves to the outer toes on the sole side.
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.from: Superficial branch of the lateral plantar nerve, directly or through the common plantar digital nerve
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.course: They run along the sides of the toes on the sole side. One goes to the outer side of the little toe.
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.sensory: Plantar skin of the little toe and the outer half of the fourth toe, including the toe tips and nail beds
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.injury: Injury causes numbness of the outer toes.
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-later.clinical: A toe nerve block placed at the base of the toe numbs these nerves for toenail surgery.

proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.name: Proper Plantar Digital Branches of Medial Plantar Nerve
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.latin: Nervi digitales plantares proprii nervi plantaris medialis
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.summary: These are the final skin nerves to the inner toes on the sole side.
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.from: Medial plantar nerve, directly for the great toe, and common plantar digital nerves for the other toes
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.course: They run along the sides of the inner toes on the sole side. They also reach the toe tips and nail beds.
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.sensory: Plantar skin of the inner three and a half toes, including toe tips and nail beds
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.injury: Injury causes numbness of the great toe and neighboring toes.
proper-plantar-digital-branches-of-media.clinical: A toe nerve block at the base of the toe numbs these nerves for toenail surgery.

saphenous-nerve.name: Saphenous Nerve
saphenous-nerve.summary: The saphenous nerve is the longest branch of the femoral nerve. It is purely sensory and reaches the inner foot.
saphenous-nerve.from: Femoral nerve, in the femoral triangle
saphenous-nerve.course: It passes through the adductor canal and leaves between sartorius and gracilis at the knee. It then follows the great saphenous vein down the leg.
saphenous-nerve.sensory: Skin of the medial knee, medial leg, and medial border of the foot as far as the ball of the big toe
saphenous-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness or burning pain along the inner leg and foot.
saphenous-nerve.clinical: It can be compressed in the adductor canal. Saphenous vein harvest and stripping can also injure it.

sciatic-nerve.name: Sciatic Nerve
sciatic-nerve.summary: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body. It supplies the back of the thigh and, through its two divisions, all muscles below the knee.
sciatic-nerve.from: Sacral plexus; it leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen, below piriformis
sciatic-nerve.course: It passes deep to gluteus maximus and descends the back of the thigh. Near the popliteal fossa it divides into the tibial and common fibular nerves.
motor: Hamstring muscles: semitendinosus, semimembranosus, long head of biceps femoris
All muscles below the knee, through its two divisions
sciatic-nerve.sensory: No skin branches in the thigh; its divisions supply most of the leg and foot skin
sciatic-nerve.injury: Injury causes weak knee flexion and loss of all movement below the knee. Foot drop is common because the fibular part is more exposed.
sciatic-nerve.clinical: Posterior hip dislocation and badly placed gluteal injections can injure it. Sciatica is pain from irritation of its roots.

superficial-fibular-nerve.name: Superficial Fibular Nerve
superficial-fibular-nerve.summary: The superficial fibular nerve supplies the muscles that evert the foot. It also gives sensation to most of the top of the foot.
superficial-fibular-nerve.from: Common fibular nerve, near the neck of the fibula
superficial-fibular-nerve.course: It descends in the lateral compartment between fibularis longus and brevis. In the lower leg it pierces the fascia and divides into dorsal cutaneous nerves.
superficial-fibular-nerve.sensory: Skin of the lower outer leg and most of the top of the foot and toes, except the first web space
superficial-fibular-nerve.injury: Injury weakens foot eversion and causes numbness of the lower outer leg and top of the foot.
superficial-fibular-nerve.clinical: It can be trapped where it pierces the fascia, causing pain and tingling on the outer lower leg.

sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.name: Sural Communicating Branch of Common Fibular Nerve
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.latin: Ramus communicans fibularis nervi fibularis communis
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.summary: This small skin branch of the common fibular nerve joins the medial sural cutaneous nerve to help form the sural nerve.
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.from: Common fibular nerve, in the popliteal fossa
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.course: It runs down the outer calf and joins the medial sural cutaneous nerve in the lower calf.
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.sensory: Skin of the lateral calf and outer foot, through the sural nerve
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.injury: Injury causes numbness on the outer calf and ankle edge.
sural-communicating-branch-of-common-fib.clinical: Its size varies from person to person, and the sural nerve may be formed in different ways.

sural-nerve.name: Sural Nerve
sural-nerve.summary: The sural nerve is a purely sensory nerve of the outer lower leg and foot.
sural-nerve.from: Formed by the medial sural cutaneous nerve and the sural communicating branch of the common fibular nerve
sural-nerve.course: It descends beside the small saphenous vein and passes behind the lateral malleolus. It continues along the outer border of the foot.
sural-nerve.sensory: Skin of the back and outer lower leg, outer ankle, outer border of the foot, and the outer side of the little toe
sural-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness along the outer foot and ankle.
sural-nerve.clinical: Surgeons often use it as a nerve graft donor. It is at risk in Achilles tendon surgery and small saphenous vein surgery.

tibial-nerve.name: Tibial Nerve
tibial-nerve.summary: The tibial nerve is the larger branch of the sciatic nerve. It supplies the back of the leg and the sole of the foot.
tibial-nerve.from: Sciatic nerve, near the top of the popliteal fossa
tibial-nerve.course: It runs through the popliteal fossa and down the deep back of the leg. It passes behind the medial malleolus and splits into the plantar nerves.
motor: Muscles of the sole, through the plantar nerves
tibial-nerve.sensory: Skin of the back of the calf, the heel, and the sole of the foot
tibial-nerve.injury: Injury weakens plantarflexion and inversion, so the person cannot stand on tiptoe. The sole becomes numb.
tibial-nerve.clinical: Tarsal tunnel syndrome is compression of the tibial nerve behind the medial malleolus and causes burning pain in the sole.

iliohypogastric-nerve.name: Iliohypogastric Nerve
iliohypogastric-nerve.summary: A branch of the lumbar plexus that supplies the lower abdominal wall muscles and the skin over the suprapubic region and upper buttock.
iliohypogastric-nerve.clinical: It can be cut or trapped during lower abdominal incisions or hernia repair, causing groin or suprapubic pain.
iliohypogastric-nerve.from: Anterior ramus of L1 (with a contribution from T12).
iliohypogastric-nerve.course: Emerges from the upper lateral border of psoas major and crosses quadratus lumborum. It pierces transversus abdominis near the iliac crest and runs between the two deep abdominal muscles.
iliohypogastric-nerve.sensory: Skin of the suprapubic region (anterior cutaneous branch) and the skin over the upper lateral buttock (lateral cutaneous branch).
iliohypogastric-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness over the suprapubic skin and chronic neuralgia. Weakness of the lower abdominal wall may add to the risk of inguinal hernia.

ilio-inguinal-nerve.name: Ilio-inguinal Nerve
ilio-inguinal-nerve.summary: A small lumbar plexus branch that runs through the inguinal canal and supplies the skin of the groin and upper genital region.
ilio-inguinal-nerve.clinical: It is easily injured during hernia repair, which can leave lasting groin pain or numbness.
ilio-inguinal-nerve.course: Runs just below and parallel to the iliohypogastric nerve across quadratus lumborum. It pierces the deep abdominal muscles, enters the inguinal canal and leaves through the superficial inguinal ring.
ilio-inguinal-nerve.sensory: Skin of the upper medial thigh, the root of the penis and anterior scrotum in men, or the mons pubis and labium majus in women.
ilio-inguinal-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness and burning pain in the groin and upper genitals. It is a common complication of inguinal hernia surgery.

intercostal-nerves.name: Intercostal Nerves
intercostal-nerves.summary: The anterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves T1 to T11. They supply the chest wall muscles and skin, and the lower ones continue onto the abdominal wall.
intercostal-nerves.clinical: Shingles (herpes zoster) often appears as a painful band of rash along one intercostal nerve.
intercostal-nerves.from: Anterior rami of thoracic spinal nerves T1–T11.
intercostal-nerves.course: Run in the intercostal space between the innermost and internal intercostal muscles, below the vein and artery. Nerves T7–T11 continue into the anterior abdominal wall.
intercostal-nerves.sensory: Skin of the chest and abdominal wall through lateral and anterior cutaneous branches. Also the parietal pleura and parietal peritoneum.
intercostal-nerves.injury: Injury or irritation causes band-like pain or numbness along one dermatome. Intercostal nerve blocks are used for rib fractures and chest surgery.

femoral-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.name: Femoral Branch of Genitofemoral Nerve
femoral-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.summary: The sensory branch of the genitofemoral nerve. It passes under the inguinal ligament and supplies the skin over the upper front of the thigh.
femoral-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.clinical: It forms the sensory limb of the cremasteric reflex, so stroking the upper inner thigh in males can raise the testis.
femoral-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.course: Descends lateral to the genital branch and passes behind the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery. It pierces the femoral sheath and fascia lata to reach the skin.
femoral-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.sensory: Skin of the upper anterior thigh over the femoral triangle.
femoral-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.injury: Injury causes numbness in a small patch of upper anterior thigh skin. It can occur after hernia repair or pelvic surgery.

femoral-nerve.name: Femoral Nerve
femoral-nerve.summary: The largest branch of the lumbar plexus. It extends the knee and flexes the hip, and supplies the skin of the front of the thigh and medial leg.
femoral-nerve.clinical: Femoral nerve injury makes the knee buckle and abolishes the patellar reflex. Bleeding into iliacus or psoas can compress it.
femoral-nerve.from: Posterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2–L4.
femoral-nerve.course: Descends between psoas major and iliacus, then passes under the inguinal ligament lateral to the femoral artery. It enters the femoral triangle and splits into many branches.
motor: Quadriceps femoris (rectus femoris and the three vasti)
femoral-nerve.sensory: Skin of the anterior thigh through anterior cutaneous branches, and the medial leg and foot through the saphenous nerve.
femoral-nerve.injury: Injury weakens knee extension and hip flexion and causes sensory loss over the front of the thigh and medial leg. Pelvic surgery and retractors are common causes.

genital-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.name: Genital Branch of Genitofemoral Nerve
genital-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.summary: The branch of the genitofemoral nerve that enters the inguinal canal. It supplies the cremaster muscle and a small area of genital skin.
genital-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.clinical: It is the motor limb of the cremasteric reflex. Loss of the reflex can suggest nerve injury or testicular torsion.
genital-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.course: Passes through the deep inguinal ring and runs within the spermatic cord in men, or with the round ligament of the uterus in women.
genital-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.sensory: Skin of the anterior scrotum in men or of the labium majus in women.
genital-branch-of-genitofemoral-nerve.injury: Injury can cause loss of the cremasteric reflex and numbness of the anterior scrotum or labium majus. It may be damaged during hernia repair.

genitofemoral-nerve.name: Genitofemoral Nerve
genitofemoral-nerve.summary: A lumbar plexus nerve that pierces psoas major and divides into a genital branch and a femoral branch near the inguinal ligament.
genitofemoral-nerve.clinical: Entrapment after hernia repair or pelvic surgery can cause chronic groin pain. The cremasteric reflex tests this nerve.
genitofemoral-nerve.from: Anterior rami of L1 and L2.
genitofemoral-nerve.course: Pierces psoas major and runs down on its anterior surface beneath the fascia. It divides above the inguinal ligament into the genital and femoral branches.
genitofemoral-nerve.sensory: Skin of the upper anterior thigh (femoral branch) and the anterior scrotum or labium majus (genital branch).
genitofemoral-nerve.injury: Injury causes groin and upper thigh pain or numbness and loss of the cremasteric reflex.

obturator-nerve.name: Obturator Nerve
obturator-nerve.summary: A lumbar plexus nerve that passes through the pelvis and the obturator canal to supply the adductor muscles and the skin of the medial thigh.
obturator-nerve.clinical: Pain down the medial thigh can signal an obturator hernia (Howship-Romberg sign) or pelvic disease pressing on the nerve.
obturator-nerve.from: Anterior divisions of the anterior rami of L2–L4.
obturator-nerve.course: Descends through psoas major, emerges at its medial border and runs along the lateral pelvic wall. It enters the obturator canal and divides into anterior and posterior branches.
obturator-nerve.injury: Injury weakens thigh adduction and causes numbness of the medial thigh. Pelvic surgery, childbirth and pelvic fractures are common causes.

maxillary-nerve.name: Maxillary Nerve
maxillary-nerve.summary: The second division of the trigeminal nerve (V2). It is purely sensory and supplies the midface, upper teeth, palate and nasal cavity.
maxillary-nerve.clinical: V2 is often involved in trigeminal neuralgia. An infraorbital nerve block numbs the upper lip and cheek for dental or facial procedures.
maxillary-nerve.roots: Cranial nerve V (trigeminal); sensory nuclei in the brainstem
maxillary-nerve.course: Leaves the middle cranial fossa through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa. It enters the orbit as the infraorbital nerve and emerges at the infraorbital foramen.
maxillary-nerve.sensory: Skin of the lower eyelid, cheek, side of the nose and upper lip. Also the upper teeth and gums, palate, nasal cavity, maxillary sinus and dura of the middle cranial fossa.
maxillary-nerve.injury: Injury or irritation causes facial pain or numbness over the midface. Orbital floor fractures can damage the infraorbital nerve and numb the cheek.

meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.name: Meningeal Branch of Maxillary Nerve
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.summary: A small sensory branch of the maxillary nerve that supplies the dura mater of the middle cranial fossa.
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.clinical: The dura is sensitive to pain, and irritation of its nerves may contribute to some headaches.
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.from: Maxillary nerve, given off in the middle cranial fossa.
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.course: Arises before the maxillary nerve reaches the foramen rotundum. It runs with the middle meningeal artery in the dura of the anterior middle cranial fossa.
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.sensory: Dura mater of the middle cranial fossa.
meningeal-branch-of-maxillary-nerve.injury: Irritation of the dura, for example from bleeding or inflammation, can cause headache through this nerve.

ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.name: Ganglia of Sympathetic Trunk
ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.summary: Clusters of sympathetic nerve cell bodies strung along the sympathetic trunk beside the vertebral column, from the neck to the coccyx.
ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.clinical: Damage to the cervical ganglia causes Horner syndrome. Sympathetic ganglion procedures can treat excessive sweating or poor blood flow.
ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.from: Preganglionic fibers from the lateral horn of the spinal cord at T1–L2.
ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.course: Lie in a chain on each side of the vertebral column: about 3 cervical, 11 or 12 thoracic, 4 lumbar and 4 or 5 sacral. They link to spinal nerves by rami communicantes.
motor: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers to smooth muscle, blood vessels and sweat glands
Postganglionic fibers to the heart and viscera through cardiac and splanchnic branches
ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.sensory: Carries no sensory fibers of its own, but visceral pain fibers pass through without synapsing.
ganglia-of-sympathetic-trunk.injury: Injury or interruption causes loss of sweating and vasodilation in the supplied area. In the neck it causes Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).

sympathetic-nerves.name: Sympathetic Nerves
sympathetic-nerves.summary: The sympathetic fibers of the thoracolumbar autonomic system. They carry signals from the spinal cord to organs, vessels and glands for the fight-or-flight response.
sympathetic-nerves.clinical: Sympathetic overactivity raises heart rate and blood pressure. Blocking these nerves can relieve some chronic pain syndromes.
sympathetic-nerves.from: Lateral horn of the spinal cord at T1–L2.
sympathetic-nerves.course: Preganglionic fibers leave in the ventral roots and enter the sympathetic trunk. They synapse there, or pass on as splanchnic nerves to prevertebral ganglia.
motor: Smooth muscle of vessels and viscera
Sweat glands and arrector pili muscles
sympathetic-nerves.sensory: Visceral pain fibers travel along these nerves to the spinal cord.
sympathetic-nerves.injury: Interruption causes loss of sweating and vessel tone in the supplied region.

sympathetic-trunk.name: Sympathetic Trunk
sympathetic-trunk.summary: A paired chain of sympathetic ganglia and connecting nerve fibers that runs beside the vertebral column from the skull base to the coccyx.
sympathetic-trunk.clinical: The cervical part contains the stellate ganglion, which is blocked to treat some pain and circulation problems of the arm and face.
sympathetic-trunk.from: Preganglionic fibers from the lateral horn of the spinal cord at T1–L2.
sympathetic-trunk.course: Runs in front of the neck vertebrae, over the heads of the ribs, beside the lumbar vertebrae and in front of the sacrum. The two trunks join at the ganglion impar.
motor: Postganglionic sympathetic fibers to the head, limbs, thoracic wall and viscera
sympathetic-trunk.sensory: Visceral pain fibers pass through it without synapsing.
sympathetic-trunk.injury: Injury of the cervical part causes Horner syndrome. Lumbar sympathectomy can be used to treat severe leg ischemia.

accessory-pancreatic-duct.name: Accessory Pancreatic Duct
accessory-pancreatic-duct.summary: A small duct that drains the upper part of the pancreatic head. It opens into the duodenum at the minor duodenal papilla.
accessory-pancreatic-duct.clinical: In pancreas divisum the main and accessory ducts fail to fuse, so most juice drains through the small minor papilla. This can cause pancreatitis.
accessory-pancreatic-duct.location: In the pancreatic head. It opens at the minor duodenal papilla in the second part of the duodenum, about 2 cm above the major papilla.
function: Carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum
accessory-pancreatic-duct.nerve: Vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers from the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses.

anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vi.name: Anterior Lateral Segment of Liver (VI)
anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vi.summary: Couinaud segment VI, the inferior lateral part of the right lobe. It lies below the right hepatic vein.
anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vi.clinical: Each segment has its own blood supply and bile duct, so surgeons can remove segment VI alone (segmentectomy).
anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vi.location: Inferior part of the right lobe, lateral to the gallbladder fossa and next to the right kidney and right colic flexure.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the right hepatic vein
anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vi.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

anterior-medial-segment-of-liver-v.name: Anterior Medial Segment of Liver (V)
anterior-medial-segment-of-liver-v.summary: Couinaud segment V, the inferior medial part of the right lobe. It lies beside the gallbladder fossa.
anterior-medial-segment-of-liver-v.clinical: The gallbladder bed lies on this segment, so gallbladder cancer often invades segments IV and V first.
anterior-medial-segment-of-liver-v.location: Inferior part of the right lobe, next to the gallbladder fossa and the plane of the middle hepatic vein.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the middle hepatic vein
anterior-medial-segment-of-liver-v.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

left-anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-i.name: Left Anterior Lateral Segment of Liver (III)
left-anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-i.summary: Couinaud segment III, the anterior lower part of the left lateral section. It lies to the left of the falciform ligament.
left-anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-i.clinical: Segments II and III together are removed in a left lateral sectionectomy, and are often used for living-donor transplants in children.
left-anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-i.location: Anterior part of the left lateral section, to the left of the falciform ligament and fissure for the ligamentum teres.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the left hepatic vein
left-anterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-i.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

left-medial-segment-of-liver.name: Left Medial Segment of Liver (IV)
left-medial-segment-of-liver.summary: Couinaud segment IV, the part of the left liver between the falciform ligament and the middle hepatic vein. It includes the quadrate lobe.
left-medial-segment-of-liver.clinical: Segment IV is split into IVa (upper) and IVb (lower, the quadrate lobe). Both parts are removed in a left hepatectomy.
left-medial-segment-of-liver.location: Between the falciform ligament on the left and the gallbladder fossa and middle hepatic vein plane on the right.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the middle hepatic vein
left-medial-segment-of-liver.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

left-posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-.name: Left Posterior Lateral Segment of Liver (II)
left-posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-.summary: Couinaud segment II, the upper posterior part of the left lateral section. It lies to the left of the falciform ligament.
left-posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-.clinical: Segment II lies against the diaphragm and can be injured by chest or upper abdominal trauma on the left.
left-posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-.location: Upper posterior part of the left lateral section, near the diaphragm and the stomach.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the left hepatic vein
left-posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vii.name: Posterior Lateral Segment of Liver (VII)
posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vii.summary: Couinaud segment VII, the superior lateral part of the right lobe, against the diaphragm. It lies above the right hepatic vein.
posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vii.clinical: Segment VII is hard to reach in surgery because of its deep position beneath the diaphragm and ribs.
posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vii.location: Upper posterior part of the right lobe, next to the diaphragm and the bare area of the liver.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the right hepatic vein
posterior-lateral-segment-of-liver-vii.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

posterior-medial-segment-of-liver-viii.name: Posterior Medial Segment of Liver (VIII)
posterior-medial-segment-of-liver-viii.summary: Couinaud segment VIII, the superior medial part of the right lobe, just under the dome of the diaphragm.
posterior-medial-segment-of-liver-viii.clinical: Liver abscesses and tumors in segment VIII can irritate the diaphragm and cause right shoulder pain.
posterior-medial-segment-of-liver-viii.location: Upper anterior part of the right lobe, beneath the dome of the diaphragm, next to the middle hepatic vein plane.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
Stores glycogen
blood: Segmental branches of the hepatic artery proper
Segmental branches of the portal vein
Drains by the middle hepatic vein (and right hepatic vein)
posterior-medial-segment-of-liver-viii.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

posterior-segment-of-liver-i.name: Posterior Segment of Liver (I)
posterior-segment-of-liver-i.summary: Couinaud segment I, the caudate lobe. It lies between the inferior vena cava and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum.
posterior-segment-of-liver-i.clinical: In Budd-Chiari syndrome the caudate lobe often enlarges, because its short veins drain directly into the inferior vena cava.
posterior-segment-of-liver-i.location: Posterior surface of the liver, between the inferior vena cava and the fissure for the ligamentum venosum.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes nutrients and drugs
blood: Branches of both right and left hepatic arteries
Branches of both right and left portal veins
Drains by short hepatic veins directly into the inferior vena cava
posterior-segment-of-liver-i.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

ascending-colon.name: Ascending Colon
ascending-colon.summary: The part of the large intestine that rises on the right side of the abdomen from the cecum to the right colic flexure.
ascending-colon.clinical: Right-sided colon cancers can grow silently and often present with iron-deficiency anemia from slow bleeding.
ascending-colon.location: Right flank, from the cecum at the ileocecal junction up to the right colic (hepatic) flexure below the liver. It is secondarily retroperitoneal.
function: Absorbs water and electrolytes
Forms and moves stool
blood: Drained by the superior mesenteric vein
ascending-colon.nerve: Sympathetic fibers through the superior mesenteric plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve.

bile-duct.name: Bile Duct
bile-duct.summary: The common bile duct. It carries bile from the liver and gallbladder to the duodenum.
bile-duct.clinical: A gallstone stuck in the bile duct causes obstructive jaundice and can trigger pancreatitis.
bile-duct.location: Forms in the hepatoduodenal ligament, passes behind the first part of the duodenum and the pancreatic head, and opens at the major duodenal papilla.
function: Conveys bile to the duodenum
bile-duct.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from the celiac plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve.

descending-colon.name: Descending Colon
descending-colon.summary: The part of the large intestine that runs down the left side of the abdomen from the left colic flexure to the sigmoid colon.
descending-colon.clinical: It is narrower than the ascending colon, so tumors here more often cause obstruction. It is a common site for a colostomy.
descending-colon.location: Left flank, from the left colic (splenic) flexure down to the pelvic brim. It is secondarily retroperitoneal, lying on the left kidney, quadratus lumborum and iliacus.
function: Stores stool
Absorbs remaining water
blood: Drained by the inferior mesenteric vein
descending-colon.nerve: Sympathetic fibers through the inferior mesenteric plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).

duodenum.name: Duodenum
duodenum.summary: The first and shortest part of the small intestine. It is a C-shaped tube about 25 cm long that curves around the head of the pancreas.
duodenum.clinical: A duodenal ulcer on the back wall of the first part can erode the gastroduodenal artery and cause serious bleeding.
duodenum.location: Retroperitoneal at vertebral levels L1 to L3, wrapped around the pancreatic head. Only the first 2 cm is intraperitoneal.
function: Receives chyme from the stomach
Receives bile and pancreatic juice
Neutralizes acid and begins absorption
blood: Drained by the portal vein system
duodenum.nerve: Vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers from the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses.

free-taenia.name: Free Taenia
free-taenia.summary: One of the three bands of longitudinal muscle on the colon. It has no mesentery or omentum attached to it.
free-taenia.clinical: Following the taeniae down to where they meet leads to the base of the appendix during surgery.
free-taenia.location: On the anterior or anterolateral surface of the colon, running from the base of the appendix to the rectosigmoid junction.
function: Its tone gathers the colon wall into haustra
blood: Colic branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries
free-taenia.nerve: Enteric nervous system with sympathetic and parasympathetic input.

gallbladder.name: Gallbladder
gallbladder.summary: A pear-shaped sac under the liver that stores and concentrates bile. It holds about 30 to 50 mL.
gallbladder.clinical: Gallstones can cause biliary colic or cholecystitis. Pain over the gallbladder on deep inspiration is Murphy sign.
gallbladder.location: In the gallbladder fossa on the underside of the liver, between segments IV and V, at the right ninth costal cartilage.
function: Stores and concentrates bile
Contracts after fatty meals in response to cholecystokinin
blood: Cystic artery (from the right hepatic artery)
Cystic veins to the portal vein
gallbladder.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from the celiac plexus, vagus nerve and right phrenic nerve (referred pain to the right shoulder).

greater-omentum.name: Greater Omentum
greater-omentum.summary: A large apron of peritoneum that hangs from the greater curvature of the stomach and covers the intestines.
greater-omentum.clinical: It can wrap around inflamed organs and limit the spread of infection. Surgeons also use it as a flap to repair tissues.
greater-omentum.location: Hangs from the greater curvature of the stomach and first part of the duodenum, in front of the transverse colon and small intestine.
function: Cushions and insulates the abdominal organs
Stores fat
Walls off infection and helps immune defense
greater-omentum.nerve: Sympathetic fibers running with its blood vessels.

jejunum.name: Jejunum
jejunum.summary: The middle part of the small intestine, about 2.5 m long. It has a thick wall with prominent circular folds.
jejunum.clinical: Crohn disease and extensive resection of the jejunum can impair absorption and cause short bowel syndrome.
jejunum.location: Left upper abdomen, from the duodenojejunal flexure. It is suspended from the posterior abdominal wall by the mesentery.
function: Main site of nutrient absorption
Continues chemical digestion
blood: Jejunal arteries (from the superior mesenteric artery)
Drained by the superior mesenteric vein
jejunum.nerve: Sympathetic fibers (T9–T10) through the superior mesenteric plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the vagus nerve.

kidney.name: Kidney
kidney.summary: A bean-shaped organ that filters blood, makes urine and regulates fluid, salts and blood pressure. There is one on each side.
kidney.clinical: Kidney stones cause severe colicky pain that runs from the loin to the groin.
kidney.location: Retroperitoneal on each side of the spine, from T12 to L3. The right kidney sits slightly lower than the left because of the liver.
function: Filters blood and forms urine
Balances fluid, electrolytes and acid-base
Produces renin and erythropoietin
Activates vitamin D
blood: Renal vein to the inferior vena cava
kidney.nerve: Renal plexus (sympathetic fibers from T10–L1 and vagal fibers).

lesser-omentum.name: Lesser Omentum
lesser-omentum.summary: A double fold of peritoneum that connects the liver to the lesser curvature of the stomach and the first part of the duodenum.
lesser-omentum.clinical: Squeezing its free edge (the Pringle maneuver) controls liver bleeding by compressing the hepatic artery and portal vein.
lesser-omentum.location: Between the liver (porta hepatis and fissure for the ligamentum venosum) and the lesser curvature of the stomach and duodenum.
function: Supports the stomach and liver
Carries vessels, nerves and bile duct
blood: Right and left gastric arteries along the lesser curvature
lesser-omentum.nerve: Sympathetic and vagal fibers running with its vessels.

liver.name: Liver
liver.summary: The largest internal organ. It makes bile, processes nutrients and drugs, stores glycogen and makes many blood proteins.
liver.clinical: Cirrhosis scars the liver and raises pressure in the portal vein, causing varices, ascites and jaundice.
liver.location: Right upper quadrant under the diaphragm, extending across the midline into the left upper abdomen. It is protected by the lower ribs.
function: Produces bile
Metabolizes carbohydrates, fats and proteins
Detoxifies drugs and toxins
Makes clotting factors and albumin
Stores glycogen, iron and vitamins
blood: Hepatic artery proper (right and left branches)
Hepatic veins drain to the inferior vena cava
liver.nerve: Hepatic plexus (sympathetic from the celiac plexus, parasympathetic from the vagus); the capsule senses pain through the right phrenic nerve.

meso-appendix.name: Meso-appendix
meso-appendix.summary: A triangular fold of peritoneum that attaches the appendix to the lower end of the ileal mesentery.
meso-appendix.clinical: Surgeons tie off the appendicular artery in the meso-appendix during appendectomy.
meso-appendix.location: Connects the vermiform appendix to the terminal ileal mesentery near the ileocecal junction.
function: Suspends the appendix
Carries its blood vessels, nerves and lymphatics
blood: Appendicular artery (branch of the ileocolic artery)
meso-appendix.nerve: Sympathetic fibers (T10) and vagal fibers running with the appendicular artery.

mesocolic-taenia.name: Mesocolic Taenia
mesocolic-taenia.summary: One of the three bands of longitudinal muscle on the colon. The mesocolon attaches along this band.
mesocolic-taenia.clinical: The three taeniae converge on the base of the appendix, which helps surgeons find it.
mesocolic-taenia.location: Along the colon where the transverse or sigmoid mesocolon attaches, on the posterior or inferior side in the transverse colon.
function: Its tone gathers the colon wall into haustra
blood: Colic branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries
mesocolic-taenia.nerve: Enteric nervous system with sympathetic and parasympathetic input.

mesocolon.name: Mesocolon
mesocolon.summary: Folds of peritoneum that attach parts of the colon to the posterior abdominal wall. The transverse and sigmoid colon have a mesocolon.
mesocolon.clinical: The sigmoid colon can twist on its mesocolon, causing sigmoid volvulus and bowel obstruction.
mesocolon.location: The transverse mesocolon crosses the pancreas and duodenum. The sigmoid mesocolon is in the left iliac fossa and pelvis.
function: Suspends the colon
Carries vessels, nerves and lymphatics
mesocolon.nerve: Sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers running with the vessels.

omental-taenia.name: Omental Taenia
omental-taenia.summary: One of the three bands of longitudinal muscle on the colon. The greater omentum attaches along this band on the transverse colon.
omental-taenia.clinical: The taeniae are used as a guide to tell colon from small intestine on imaging and in surgery.
omental-taenia.location: On the posterosuperior surface of the transverse colon, where the greater omentum attaches. On the other colon parts it lies posterolaterally.
function: Its tone gathers the colon wall into haustra
blood: Colic branches of the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries
omental-taenia.nerve: Enteric nervous system with sympathetic and parasympathetic input.

pancreas.name: Pancreas
pancreas.summary: A soft gland behind the stomach. It makes digestive enzymes (exocrine) and hormones such as insulin and glucagon (endocrine).
pancreas.clinical: Cancer of the pancreatic head can block the bile duct and cause painless jaundice. Pancreatitis causes pain that radiates to the back.
pancreas.location: Retroperitoneal at L1–L2, from the C-loop of the duodenum to the splenic hilum, behind the stomach.
function: Secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate
Secretes insulin and glucagon from the islets
pancreas.nerve: Vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers from the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses.

pancreatic-duct.name: Pancreatic Duct
pancreatic-duct.summary: The main duct of the pancreas. It runs the length of the gland and carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum.
pancreatic-duct.clinical: A gallstone lodged at the ampulla can block this duct and cause gallstone pancreatitis.
pancreatic-duct.location: Runs from the tail through the body to the head of the pancreas. It joins the bile duct and opens at the major duodenal papilla.
function: Carries pancreatic juice to the duodenum
blood: Pancreatic branches of the splenic and pancreaticoduodenal arteries
pancreatic-duct.nerve: Vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers from the celiac and superior mesenteric plexuses.

renal-pelvis.name: Renal Pelvis
renal-pelvis.summary: The funnel-shaped upper end of the ureter, formed by the union of the major calyces inside the kidney.
renal-pelvis.clinical: Blockage at the ureteropelvic junction causes hydronephrosis. Kidney stones often lodge here.
renal-pelvis.location: Inside the renal sinus of the kidney. It narrows into the ureter at the ureteropelvic junction.
function: Collects urine from the calyces
Passes urine into the ureter
renal-pelvis.nerve: Renal plexus; pain travels through T10–L1.

sigmoid-colon.name: Sigmoid Colon
sigmoid-colon.summary: The S-shaped part of the large intestine between the descending colon and the rectum. It is about 40 cm long but varies.
sigmoid-colon.clinical: Diverticulitis and volvulus are common here, and it is a frequent site of colorectal cancer.
sigmoid-colon.location: From the pelvic brim in the left iliac fossa to the rectosigmoid junction at S3. It is suspended by the sigmoid mesocolon.
function: Stores stool
Absorbs remaining water
blood: Drained by the inferior mesenteric vein
