sigmoid-colon.nerve: Sympathetic fibers through the inferior mesenteric plexus and parasympathetic fibers from the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4).

spleen.name: Spleen
spleen.summary: The largest lymphoid organ. It filters blood, removes old red blood cells and supports immune defense.
spleen.clinical: The spleen is easily injured by blunt trauma or lower left rib fractures. Removal raises the risk of infection.
spleen.location: Left upper quadrant under the 9th to 11th ribs, behind the stomach and above the left colic flexure.
function: Filters blood and removes old red cells
Mounts immune responses
Stores platelets
blood: Splenic vein joins the superior mesenteric vein to form the portal vein
spleen.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from the celiac plexus; capsule pain may refer to the left shoulder.

stomach.name: Stomach
stomach.summary: A J-shaped, muscular sac that stores food, mixes it with acid and enzymes and releases it slowly into the duodenum.
stomach.clinical: Peptic ulcers often result from Helicobacter pylori infection or anti-inflammatory drugs. Gastric cancer can spread to nearby nodes.
stomach.location: Upper left abdomen under the diaphragm, between the esophagus and the duodenum. The pylorus lies near the transpyloric plane (L1).
function: Stores and mixes food
Secretes acid, pepsin and intrinsic factor
Empties chyme into the duodenum
stomach.nerve: Vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T6–T9) through the celiac plexus.

suprarenal-gland.name: Suprarenal Gland
suprarenal-gland.summary: The adrenal gland. A small gland sits on top of each kidney and makes steroid hormones and adrenaline.
suprarenal-gland.clinical: Tumors such as pheochromocytoma release excess adrenaline and cause severe high blood pressure. Adrenal failure causes Addison disease.
suprarenal-gland.location: Retroperitoneal, on the upper pole of each kidney. The right is pyramid-shaped and the left is crescent-shaped.
function: Cortex makes cortisol, aldosterone and androgens
Medulla makes adrenaline and noradrenaline
suprarenal-gland.nerve: Preganglionic sympathetic fibers (T10–L1) that go directly to the medulla.

transverse-colon.name: Transverse Colon
transverse-colon.summary: The longest and most mobile part of the colon. It crosses the abdomen from the right to the left colic flexure.
transverse-colon.clinical: The splenic flexure is a watershed between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries and is prone to ischemic colitis.
transverse-colon.location: Upper abdomen, hanging from the transverse mesocolon below the stomach and covered by the greater omentum.
function: Absorbs water and electrolytes
Moves and stores stool
transverse-colon.nerve: Vagus nerve for the proximal two-thirds and pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2–S4) for the distal third, with sympathetic fibers.

ureter.name: Ureter
ureter.summary: A muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries urine from the renal pelvis to the bladder. There is one on each side.
ureter.clinical: Stones tend to lodge at three narrow points: the ureteropelvic junction, the pelvic brim and the bladder entry. Surgeons can injure the ureter near the uterine artery.
ureter.location: Retroperitoneal on the psoas major, crossing the pelvic brim near the common iliac artery bifurcation, then running to the bladder.
function: Carries urine by peristalsis
blood: Common iliac and internal iliac branches
ureter.nerve: Renal, aortic and hypogastric plexuses; pain travels through T11–L2 and refers from loin to groin.

vermiform-appendix.name: Vermiform Appendix
vermiform-appendix.summary: A narrow blind tube, 6 to 10 cm long, that arises from the cecum. It contains abundant lymphoid tissue.
vermiform-appendix.clinical: Appendicitis begins as vague pain around the navel and then moves to the right lower abdomen near McBurney point.
vermiform-appendix.location: Right iliac fossa, from the posteromedial cecum below the ileocecal valve where the taeniae converge. Its tip is often retrocecal.
function: Contains lymphoid tissue for immune defense
May act as a reservoir for gut bacteria
blood: Appendicular artery (branch of the ileocolic artery)
vermiform-appendix.nerve: Sympathetic fibers (T10) and vagal fibers; early pain is felt near the navel.

accessory-parotid-gland.name: Accessory Parotid Gland
accessory-parotid-gland.summary: A small detached piece of parotid tissue. It lies on the masseter just above the parotid duct and empties into that duct.
accessory-parotid-gland.clinical: Present in about 20% of people. It can be mistaken for a mass or can develop its own tumor.
accessory-parotid-gland.location: On the masseter muscle, between the zygomatic arch and the parotid duct, in front of the main gland.
function: Secretes serous saliva into the parotid duct
blood: Transverse facial artery (from the superficial temporal artery)
accessory-parotid-gland.nerve: Parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve; sympathetic fibers from the external carotid plexus

adenohypophysis.name: Anterior Pituitary (Adenohypophysis)
adenohypophysis.summary: The glandular front part of the pituitary gland. It makes and releases several hormones under control of hypothalamic releasing hormones.
adenohypophysis.clinical: Pituitary adenomas are common. Large ones press on the optic chiasm and cause bitemporal hemianopia.
adenohypophysis.location: In the hypophyseal fossa of the sella turcica of the sphenoid bone, below the optic chiasm, anterior to the neurohypophysis.
function: Secretes growth hormone, prolactin, ACTH, TSH, FSH and LH
blood: Superior hypophyseal arteries (from the internal carotid artery) via the hypophyseal portal system
adenohypophysis.nerve: No direct nerve supply to the gland cells; controlled by hypothalamic hormones carried in portal veins

epiglottis.name: Epiglottis
epiglottis.summary: A leaf-shaped plate of elastic cartilage covered by mucosa. It tips backward during swallowing to help guard the laryngeal inlet.
epiglottis.clinical: Epiglottitis is infection and swelling of the epiglottis. It can block the airway and is an emergency.
epiglottis.location: Behind the tongue root and hyoid bone, at the upper end of the larynx. Its stalk attaches to the thyroid cartilage.
function: Helps cover the laryngeal inlet during swallowing
Directs food toward the esophagus
blood: Superior laryngeal artery (from the superior thyroid artery)
epiglottis.nerve: Internal laryngeal branch of the vagus nerve (CN X), sensory

gingiva.name: Gingiva (Gums)
gingiva.summary: The gums. This firm mucous membrane covers the alveolar processes of the jaws and surrounds the necks of the teeth.
gingiva.clinical: Gingivitis is inflammation of the gums. If untreated it can progress to periodontitis and tooth loss.
gingiva.location: Covers the alveolar bone of the maxilla and mandible and encircles the neck of each tooth.
function: Seals and protects the tooth sockets
Supports the teeth
blood: Greater palatine, lingual and buccal branches
gingiva.nerve: Maxillary nerve (V2) branches for the upper gums; mandibular nerve (V3) branches for the lower gums (sensory)

neurohypophysis.name: Posterior Pituitary (Neurohypophysis)
neurohypophysis.summary: The neural back part of the pituitary gland. It stores and releases oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone made in the hypothalamus.
neurohypophysis.clinical: Damage to this region can cause diabetes insipidus, with large volumes of dilute urine from too little antidiuretic hormone.
neurohypophysis.location: In the hypophyseal fossa behind the adenohypophysis. It is continuous with the hypothalamus through the infundibulum.
function: Releases antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin)
Releases oxytocin
blood: Inferior hypophyseal arteries (from the internal carotid artery)
neurohypophysis.nerve: Hypothalamohypophyseal tract axons from the supraoptic and paraventricular nuclei

parotid-duct.name: Parotid Duct
parotid-duct.summary: The duct of the parotid gland, about 5 cm long. It crosses the masseter, pierces the buccinator and opens opposite the upper second molar.
parotid-duct.clinical: Stones can block the duct and cause painful swelling while eating. The duct can be felt over the clenched masseter.
parotid-duct.location: Leaves the front of the parotid gland, runs over the masseter and opens into the vestibule of the mouth.
function: Carries saliva from the parotid gland to the mouth
parotid-duct.nerve: Parasympathetic fibers from the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the otic ganglion control the gland

parotid-gland.name: Parotid Gland
parotid-gland.summary: The largest salivary gland. It fills the space in front of and below the ear, and the facial nerve passes through it.
parotid-gland.clinical: Mumps causes painful swelling. Surgery on the gland risks injury to the facial nerve and facial weakness.
parotid-gland.location: In the retromandibular fossa, in front of and below the ear, covering the ramus of the mandible and the masseter.
function: Secretes watery, serous saliva rich in amylase
blood: Branches of the external carotid artery
Transverse facial and superficial temporal arteries
parotid-gland.nerve: Parasympathetic: glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) via the lesser petrosal nerve, otic ganglion and auriculotemporal nerve; sympathetic: external carotid plexus

pineal-gland.name: Pineal Gland
pineal-gland.summary: A small cone-shaped gland in the midline of the brain. It makes melatonin, which helps set the sleep and wake cycle.
pineal-gland.clinical: It often calcifies with age and shows as a midline marker on imaging. Tumors can press on the midbrain tectum and affect upward gaze.
pineal-gland.location: In the midline, attached by a stalk to the back of the third ventricle roof, above the superior colliculi (epithalamus).
function: Secretes melatonin
Helps regulate day and night rhythms
blood: Posterior choroidal arteries (from the posterior cerebral artery)
pineal-gland.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from the superior cervical ganglion

soft-palate.name: Soft Palate
soft-palate.summary: The muscular back part of the palate, behind the hard palate. It rises during swallowing to close off the nasopharynx.
soft-palate.clinical: Vagus nerve injury makes one side of the palate droop. The uvula then deviates away from the injured side.
soft-palate.location: Hangs from the posterior edge of the hard palate, between the oral cavity and the nasopharynx.
function: Closes the nasopharynx during swallowing and speech
Helps push food into the pharynx
blood: Ascending palatine artery (from the facial artery)
soft-palate.nerve: Pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve, CN X) for most muscles; tensor veli palatini by the mandibular nerve (V3); sensation by lesser palatine nerves (V2)

sublingual-gland.name: Sublingual Gland
sublingual-gland.summary: The smallest of the three major salivary glands. It lies under the tongue and makes mostly mucous saliva.
sublingual-gland.clinical: A blocked duct can form a ranula, a mucus-filled cyst on the floor of the mouth.
sublingual-gland.location: In the floor of the mouth, above the mylohyoid muscle and under the sublingual fold of the tongue.
function: Secretes mucous saliva through many small ducts
sublingual-gland.nerve: Parasympathetic: facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani, lingual nerve and submandibular ganglion

submandibular-duct.name: Submandibular Duct
submandibular-duct.summary: The duct of the submandibular gland, about 5 cm long. It runs forward in the floor of the mouth to open beside the tongue frenulum.
submandibular-duct.clinical: It is the most common site of salivary stones. The lingual nerve loops under the duct, so surgery here risks that nerve.
submandibular-duct.location: Leaves the deep part of the gland, passes forward above the mylohyoid and opens at the sublingual papilla.
function: Carries saliva from the submandibular gland to the mouth
submandibular-duct.nerve: Parasympathetic fibers from the facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani control the gland

submandibular-gland.name: Submandibular Gland
submandibular-gland.summary: A walnut-sized salivary gland below the jaw. It wraps around the back edge of the mylohyoid muscle and makes mixed saliva, mostly serous.
submandibular-gland.clinical: Stones can block the duct and cause painful swelling at meals. Surgery risks the marginal mandibular branch of the facial nerve.
submandibular-gland.location: In the submandibular triangle, below the body of the mandible, with a superficial part and a deep part.
function: Secretes mixed serous and mucous saliva
submandibular-gland.nerve: Parasympathetic: facial nerve (CN VII) via the chorda tympani, lingual nerve and submandibular ganglion

superior-parathyroid-gland.name: Superior Parathyroid Gland
superior-parathyroid-gland.summary: A small pea-sized gland on the back of the thyroid lobe. Usually there are two superior and two inferior glands.
superior-parathyroid-gland.clinical: Accidental removal in thyroid surgery can cause low blood calcium. Overactive glands cause high blood calcium and kidney stones.
superior-parathyroid-gland.location: On the posterior surface of the thyroid lobe, usually near the level of the cricoid cartilage. Its position is more constant than the inferior gland.
function: Secretes parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium
blood: Inferior thyroid artery (sometimes with the superior thyroid artery)
superior-parathyroid-gland.nerve: Sympathetic fibers from cervical ganglia supply the vessels; hormone release depends on blood calcium, not nerves

tongue.name: Tongue
tongue.summary: A muscular organ in the floor of the mouth. It helps with taste, chewing, swallowing and speech.
tongue.clinical: Hypoglossal nerve injury makes the tongue point toward the injured side when it is stuck out.
tongue.location: In the floor of the mouth and oropharynx. A V-shaped terminal sulcus separates the oral part from the pharyngeal part.
function: Tastes and senses touch and temperature
Moves food during chewing and swallowing
Shapes speech sounds
blood: Lingual artery (from the external carotid artery)
Tonsillar branch of the facial artery
tongue.nerve: Motor: hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), except palatoglossus (vagus). Anterior two thirds: lingual (touch) and chorda tympani (taste). Posterior third: glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX)

uvula-of-palate.name: Uvula of Palate
uvula-of-palate.summary: A small cone-shaped projection from the back edge of the soft palate. It contains the musculus uvulae and helps seal the nasopharynx.
uvula-of-palate.clinical: A bifid uvula can signal a hidden cleft of the soft palate. In vagus nerve injury it deviates away from the injured side.
uvula-of-palate.location: Hangs from the middle of the free posterior edge of the soft palate, above the root of the tongue.
function: Helps close the nasopharynx during swallowing
Assists speech
uvula-of-palate.nerve: Pharyngeal plexus (vagus nerve, CN X) for the musculus uvulae; sensation from the lesser palatine nerves (V2)

corpus-cavernosum-of-penis.name: Corpus Cavernosum of Penis
corpus-cavernosum-of-penis.summary: One of a pair of erectile columns on the upper side of the penis. They fill with blood to make the penis rigid.
corpus-cavernosum-of-penis.clinical: A tear of the tunica albuginea during erection is a penile fracture. Peyronie disease causes scarring and curvature.
corpus-cavernosum-of-penis.location: Paired columns side by side on the dorsum of the penis. Their back ends form the crura, attached to the ischiopubic rami.
function: Fills with blood to produce erection
blood: Deep artery of the penis (from the internal pudendal artery)
corpus-cavernosum-of-penis.nerve: Cavernous nerves (parasympathetic, S2-S4) cause erection; pudendal nerve (S2-S4) gives sensation

corpus-spongiosum-of-penis.name: Corpus Spongiosum of Penis
corpus-spongiosum-of-penis.summary: A single midline column of erectile tissue below the corpora cavernosa. It surrounds the spongy urethra and keeps it open during erection.
corpus-spongiosum-of-penis.clinical: Straddle injuries can crush the bulb against the pubic bone and tear the urethra.
corpus-spongiosum-of-penis.location: On the underside of the penis, between the corpora cavernosa. It swells into the bulb at the root and the glans at the tip.
function: Keeps the urethra open during erection
Forms the bulb and the glans penis
blood: Artery of the bulb of the penis (from the internal pudendal artery)
corpus-spongiosum-of-penis.nerve: Cavernous nerves (parasympathetic, S2-S4); pudendal nerve (S2-S4) gives sensation

ductus-deferens.name: Ductus Deferens (Vas Deferens)
ductus-deferens.summary: A thick-walled muscular tube about 45 cm long. It carries sperm from the epididymis to the ejaculatory duct.
ductus-deferens.clinical: A vasectomy cuts and ties this duct in the scrotum to prevent sperm from reaching the semen.
ductus-deferens.location: Runs from the epididymis up the spermatic cord, through the inguinal canal, over the ureter and behind the bladder.
function: Carries sperm from the epididymis
Moves sperm forward by muscle contraction during emission
blood: Artery of the ductus deferens (from the umbilical or inferior vesical artery)
ductus-deferens.nerve: Sympathetic fibers via the inferior hypogastric plexus

ejaculatory-duct.name: Ejaculatory Duct
ejaculatory-duct.summary: A short duct about 2 cm long. It forms where the ductus deferens joins the duct of the seminal gland.
ejaculatory-duct.clinical: Blockage of the ducts, for example by cysts or prostate swelling, can cause low sperm count and infertility.
ejaculatory-duct.location: Passes through the prostate and opens into the prostatic urethra on the seminal colliculus.
function: Delivers sperm and seminal fluid into the urethra at ejaculation
ejaculatory-duct.nerve: Sympathetic fibers via the inferior hypogastric plexus

epididymis.name: Epididymis
epididymis.summary: A comma-shaped, tightly coiled duct on the back of the testis. Sperm mature and are stored here.
epididymis.clinical: Epididymitis is inflammation of this structure. It causes scrotal pain and swelling, often from infection.
epididymis.location: In the scrotum, along the posterior border of the testis, with a head, body and tail.
function: Matures sperm
Stores sperm
Moves sperm toward the ductus deferens
epididymis.nerve: Sympathetic fibers via the testicular plexus; sensory fibers from T10-L1

glans-penis.name: Glans Penis
glans-penis.summary: The cone-shaped tip of the penis. It is the expanded end of the corpus spongiosum and contains the external urethral opening.
glans-penis.clinical: Balanitis is inflammation of the glans. In hypospadias the urethra opens on the underside instead of at the tip.
glans-penis.location: At the distal end of the penis, covered in life by the prepuce (foreskin) unless circumcised.
function: Covers the ends of the corpora cavernosa
Provides sensation
Carries the external urethral orifice
blood: Artery of the bulb of the penis
glans-penis.nerve: Dorsal nerve of the penis (pudendal nerve, S2-S4), sensory

prostate.name: Prostate
prostate.summary: A chestnut-sized gland that surrounds the first part of the urethra just below the bladder. It makes part of the seminal fluid.
prostate.clinical: Benign enlargement narrows the urethra and slows urine flow. Cancer is usually in the back and can be felt by rectal exam.
prostate.location: Below the bladder neck, above the pelvic floor, behind the pubic symphysis and in front of the rectum.
function: Secretes an alkaline fluid for semen
Helps close the bladder neck during ejaculation
prostate.nerve: Inferior hypogastric (prostatic) plexus: sympathetic (T10-L2) and parasympathetic (S2-S4)

seminal-gland.name: Seminal Gland (Seminal Vesicle)
seminal-gland.summary: A coiled gland about 5 cm long behind the bladder. It makes most of the fluid in semen, but it does not store sperm.
seminal-gland.clinical: Infection or enlargement may be felt on rectal exam. Its duct is a site of ejaculatory duct blockage.
seminal-gland.location: On the back of the bladder, beside the ductus deferens ampulla and in front of the rectum.
function: Secretes thick alkaline fluid rich in fructose
Contributes about 60 to 70% of semen volume
seminal-gland.nerve: Inferior hypogastric plexus; sympathetic fibers cause contraction at emission

testis.name: Testis
testis.summary: The male gonad. It makes sperm in the seminiferous tubules and testosterone in the interstitial cells.
testis.clinical: Testicular torsion is a surgical emergency. Lymph drains to lumbar nodes, so testicular cancer spreads to the abdomen first.
testis.location: In the scrotum, wrapped in the tunica vaginalis and tunica albuginea. One lies on each side.
function: Produces sperm
Produces testosterone
blood: Testicular artery (from the abdominal aorta at about L2)
testis.nerve: Testicular plexus (sympathetic, T10-L1); pain is referred to the umbilical region

urethra.name: Urethra
urethra.summary: The tube that carries urine from the bladder to the outside. In males it is about 20 cm long and also carries semen; in females it is about 4 cm.
urethra.clinical: A short female urethra makes urinary infections more common. In males, pelvic fracture can tear the membranous part.
urethra.location: Starts at the internal urethral orifice of the bladder, passes through the pelvic floor and ends at the external urethral orifice.
function: Carries urine out of the body
Carries semen in males
blood: Inferior vesical and middle rectal arteries (prostatic part)
Artery of the bulb of the penis (spongy part)
urethra.nerve: Inferior hypogastric plexus; pudendal nerve (S2-S4) supplies the external urethral sphincter

urinary-bladder.name: Urinary Bladder
urinary-bladder.summary: A hollow muscular organ that stores urine. When empty it lies in the pelvis, and when full it rises into the abdomen.
urinary-bladder.clinical: When full, it can be reached above the pubic bone without entering the peritoneum, as in suprapubic catheter placement.
urinary-bladder.location: Behind the pubic symphysis, in front of the rectum in males, below the peritoneum.
function: Stores urine
Empties urine through the urethra by detrusor contraction
blood: Superior vesical arteries (from the umbilical artery)
Inferior vesical artery (or vaginal artery in females)
urinary-bladder.nerve: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) contract the detrusor; sympathetic fibers (T11-L2) via the hypogastric plexus

anterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.name: Anterior Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BVIII)
anterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis anterior [B VIII] pulmonis sinistri
anterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.summary: This segmental bronchus (BVIII) carries air to the anterior basal segment of the left inferior lobe. Many sources fuse it with the medial basal segment.
anterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the left inferior lobar bronchus and runs downward and forward.
function: Ventilates the anterior basal bronchopulmonary segment of the left lung
anterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
anterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.clinical: Naming differs between sources: some list separate BVII and BVIII on the left, others use a combined BVII+VIII.

anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.name: Anterior Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BIII)
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.latin: Bronchus segmentalis anterior [B III] pulmonis sinistri
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.summary: This segmental bronchus (BIII) carries air to the anterior segment of the left superior lobe.
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.location: Arises from the upper division of the left superior lobar bronchus and runs forward.
function: Ventilates the anterior bronchopulmonary segment of the left superior lobe
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.clinical: Lung cancer in the upper lobe often involves these segmental bronchi. Bronchoscopy can sample them directly.

anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.name: Anterior Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.latin: Bronchus segmentalis anterior [B III] pulmonis dextri
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.summary: In standard anatomy this branch (BIII) arises from the right superior lobar bronchus and supplies the anterior segment of the upper lobe. The model files it under the inferior lobar bronchus, so it may represent the anterior basal bronchus (BVIII).
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.location: Standard position: branch of the right superior lobar bronchus, running forward. Model group: right inferior lobar bronchus.
function: Ventilates one anterior bronchopulmonary segment of the right lung
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
anterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.clinical: Segmental bronchi allow a surgeon to remove a single diseased segment (segmentectomy) and spare the rest of the lobe.

anteromedial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of.name: Anteromedial Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BVII+VIII)
anteromedial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis anteromedialis [B VII+VIII] pulmonis sinistri
anteromedial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of.summary: This segmental bronchus (BVII+VIII) combines the medial and anterior basal segments of the left inferior lobe. Many textbooks treat them as one segment.
anteromedial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the left inferior lobar bronchus and runs downward and forward.
function: Ventilates the anteromedial basal bronchopulmonary segment of the left lung
anteromedial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
anteromedial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of.clinical: The model also shows separate anterior basal and medial basal branches, so this label may overlap them.

apical-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung-.name: Apical Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BI)
apical-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung-.latin: Bronchus segmentalis apicalis [B I] pulmonis dextri
apical-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung-.summary: This segmental bronchus (BI) carries air to the apical segment at the top of the right superior lobe.
apical-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung-.location: Arises from the right superior lobar bronchus and runs upward toward the lung apex.
function: Ventilates the apical bronchopulmonary segment of the right lung
apical-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung-.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
apical-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung-.clinical: A tumor at the lung apex (Pancoast tumor) can invade the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain, causing arm pain and Horner syndrome.

apicoposterior-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.name: Apicoposterior Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BI+BII)
apicoposterior-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.latin: Bronchus segmentalis apicoposterior [B I+II] pulmonis sinistri
apicoposterior-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.summary: This segmental bronchus (BI+BII) serves the combined apical and posterior segment of the left superior lobe.
apicoposterior-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.location: Arises from the upper division of the left superior lobar bronchus and passes upward and backward.
function: Ventilates the apicoposterior bronchopulmonary segment of the left lung
apicoposterior-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
apicoposterior-segmental-bronchus-of-lef.clinical: The left lung has one apicoposterior segment where the right lung has separate apical and posterior segments.

inferior-lingular-segmental-bronchus-of-.name: Inferior Lingular Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BV)
inferior-lingular-segmental-bronchus-of-.latin: Bronchus lingularis inferior [B V] pulmonis sinistri
inferior-lingular-segmental-bronchus-of-.summary: This segmental bronchus (BV) carries air to the inferior lingular segment, which lies next to the heart.
inferior-lingular-segmental-bronchus-of-.location: Arises from the lingular bronchus and runs downward and forward.
function: Ventilates the inferior lingular segment of the left superior lobe
inferior-lingular-segmental-bronchus-of-.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
inferior-lingular-segmental-bronchus-of-.clinical: Bronchiectasis and chronic infection commonly involve the lingula, which drains poorly against gravity.

inferior-lobe-of-left-lung.name: Inferior Lobe of Left Lung
inferior-lobe-of-left-lung.summary: The inferior lobe is the lower lobe of the left lung. It lies below and behind the oblique fissure.
inferior-lobe-of-left-lung.location: Fills the lower back of the left chest and rests on the left dome of the diaphragm.
function: Gas exchange
Contains the superior segment and the basal segments
inferior-lobe-of-left-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
inferior-lobe-of-left-lung.clinical: Collapse of this lobe can hide behind the heart shadow on a chest X-ray.

inferior-lobe-of-right-lung.name: Inferior Lobe of Right Lung
inferior-lobe-of-right-lung.summary: The inferior lobe is the largest lobe of the right lung. It lies below and behind the oblique fissure.
inferior-lobe-of-right-lung.location: Fills most of the lower back of the chest and rests on the right dome of the diaphragm.
function: Gas exchange
Contains the superior segment and four basal segments
inferior-lobe-of-right-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
inferior-lobe-of-right-lung.clinical: Pneumonia and aspirated material most often involve this lobe, especially the superior and posterior basal segments.

inferior-parathyroid-gland.name: Inferior Parathyroid Gland
inferior-parathyroid-gland.summary: The inferior parathyroid is a small endocrine gland, usually one on each side. It lies behind the lower part of the thyroid lobe.
inferior-parathyroid-gland.location: Sits near the lower pole of the thyroid on its back surface. Its position varies, and it may lie low in the neck or near the thymus.
function: Makes parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium
inferior-parathyroid-gland.clinical: Removal or damage during thyroid surgery can cause low blood calcium (hypocalcemia).

intermediate-bronchus.name: Intermediate Bronchus
intermediate-bronchus.summary: The intermediate bronchus is the continuation of the right main bronchus after the superior lobar bronchus branches off. It is about 3 cm long.
intermediate-bronchus.location: Runs downward behind the right pulmonary artery and divides into the middle and inferior lobar bronchi.
function: Carries air to the right middle and inferior lobes
intermediate-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
intermediate-bronchus.clinical: Lymph nodes around it can compress the middle lobe bronchus. The intermediate bronchus is easy to identify on bronchoscopy.

lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left.name: Lateral Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BIX)
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis lateralis [B IX] pulmonis sinistri
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left.summary: This segmental bronchus (BIX) carries air to the lateral basal segment of the left inferior lobe.
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the left inferior lobar bronchus and runs downward and laterally.
function: Ventilates the lateral basal bronchopulmonary segment of the left lung
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left.clinical: Aspirated material tends to settle in the basal segments in a person who is upright.

lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-righ.name: Lateral Basal Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BIX)
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-righ.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis lateralis [B IX] pulmonis dextri
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-righ.summary: This segmental bronchus (BIX) carries air to the lateral basal segment of the right inferior lobe.
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-righ.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the right inferior lobar bronchus and runs downward and laterally.
function: Ventilates the lateral basal bronchopulmonary segment of the right lung
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-righ.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
lateral-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-righ.clinical: Aspirated material tends to settle in the basal segments of the right lung in a person who is upright.

lateral-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.name: Lateral Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BIV)
lateral-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.latin: Bronchus segmentalis lateralis [B IV] pulmonis dextri
lateral-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.summary: This segmental bronchus (BIV) carries air to the lateral segment of the right middle lobe.
lateral-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.location: Arises from the middle lobar bronchus and runs forward and laterally.
function: Ventilates the lateral bronchopulmonary segment of the right middle lobe
lateral-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
lateral-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.clinical: The narrow middle lobe bronchus is easily compressed by lymph nodes, which can cause right middle lobe collapse.

left-inferior-lobar-bronchus.name: Left Inferior Lobar Bronchus
left-inferior-lobar-bronchus.summary: This bronchus supplies the left inferior lobe. It is the lower continuation of the left main bronchus after the superior lobar bronchus branches off.
left-inferior-lobar-bronchus.location: Descends behind and below the pulmonary artery. It gives off the superior segmental bronchus, then a basal trunk.
function: Ventilates the left inferior lobe
left-inferior-lobar-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
left-inferior-lobar-bronchus.clinical: Aspirated material often reaches the left lower lobe, although less often than the right.

left-lobe-of-thymus.name: Left Lobe of Thymus
left-lobe-of-thymus.summary: The left lobe is one of the two lobes of the thymus. It is a soft lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature.
left-lobe-of-thymus.location: Lies in the superior mediastinum, behind the manubrium and in front of the great vessels.
function: Matures T lymphocytes
Removes T cells that would attack normal body tissue
left-lobe-of-thymus.clinical: A large thymus shadow in an infant is normal. A mass in this area in an adult can be a thymoma.

left-main-bronchus.name: Left Main Bronchus
left-main-bronchus.summary: The left main bronchus is longer, narrower and more horizontal than the right. It runs from the carina to the left lung root.
left-main-bronchus.location: Begins at the carina and passes below the aortic arch, in front of the oesophagus and descending aorta. It is about 5 cm long.
function: Carries air from the trachea to the left lung
Divides into the superior and inferior lobar bronchi
left-main-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
left-main-bronchus.clinical: An enlarged left atrium or aortic arch aneurysm can compress the left main bronchus.

left-superior-lobar-bronchus.name: Left Superior Lobar Bronchus
left-superior-lobar-bronchus.summary: This bronchus supplies the left superior lobe, including the lingula. It arises from the left main bronchus at the lung root.
left-superior-lobar-bronchus.location: Divides into an upper division (apicoposterior and anterior segments) and a lower lingular division.
function: Ventilates the left superior lobe and lingula
left-superior-lobar-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
left-superior-lobar-bronchus.clinical: Its lingular division matches the right middle lobe, though the left lung has no separate middle lobe.

medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left-.name: Medial Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BVII)
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left-.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis medialis [B VII] pulmonis sinistri
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left-.summary: This segmental bronchus (BVII) is the medial basal branch of the left inferior lobar bronchus. It is often absent as a separate branch because it fuses with the anterior basal bronchus.
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left-.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the left inferior lobar bronchus and runs downward on the medial side.
function: Ventilates the medial basal part of the left inferior lobe, next to the heart
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left-.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-left-.clinical: Terminologia Anatomica lists it separately, but most clinical texts combine it with the anterior basal segment.

medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-right.name: Medial Basal Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BVII)
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-right.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis medialis [B VII] pulmonis dextri
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-right.summary: This segmental bronchus (BVII) carries air to the medial basal segment of the right inferior lobe, next to the heart and diaphragm.
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-right.location: Arises from the right inferior lobar bronchus and runs downward on the medial side.
function: Ventilates the medial basal bronchopulmonary segment of the right lung
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-right.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
medial-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-right.clinical: Disease here can blur the right heart border and the right side of the diaphragm on chest X-ray.

medial-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.name: Medial Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BV)
medial-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.latin: Bronchus segmentalis medialis [B V] pulmonis dextri
medial-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.summary: This segmental bronchus (BV) carries air to the medial segment of the right middle lobe, next to the heart.
medial-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.location: Arises from the middle lobar bronchus and runs forward and medially.
function: Ventilates the medial bronchopulmonary segment of the right middle lobe
medial-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
medial-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lung.clinical: Chronic infection or collapse here is called right middle lobe syndrome and appears next to the right heart border on chest X-ray.

middle-lobar-bronchus.name: Middle Lobar Bronchus
middle-lobar-bronchus.summary: This bronchus supplies the right middle lobe. It arises from the front of the intermediate bronchus.
middle-lobar-bronchus.location: Passes forward, downward and laterally, then divides into lateral and medial segmental bronchi.
function: Ventilates the right middle lobe
middle-lobar-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
middle-lobar-bronchus.clinical: It is long, narrow and surrounded by lymph nodes, so it often collapses in right middle lobe syndrome.

middle-lobe-of-right-lung.name: Middle Lobe of Right Lung
middle-lobe-of-right-lung.summary: The middle lobe is the smallest lobe of the right lung. It is wedge-shaped and found only on the right side.
middle-lobe-of-right-lung.location: Lies between the horizontal and oblique fissures, mostly on the front of the lung beside the right heart border.
function: Gas exchange
Contains the lateral and medial bronchopulmonary segments
middle-lobe-of-right-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
middle-lobe-of-right-lung.clinical: Right middle lobe syndrome is collapse of this lobe, often from compression of its narrow bronchus.

oesophagus.name: Oesophagus
oesophagus.summary: The oesophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries food from the pharynx to the stomach.
oesophagus.location: Begins at the level of C6, runs behind the trachea and heart, passes through the diaphragm at T10, and joins the stomach at T11.
function: Moves food and liquid to the stomach by peristalsis
Upper and lower sphincters help prevent reflux
blood: Oesophageal branches of the thoracic aorta
oesophagus.nerve: Vagus nerve (oesophageal plexus) and sympathetic trunk
oesophagus.clinical: Reflux can cause Barrett oesophagus. Dilated lower oesophageal veins (varices) can bleed in portal hypertension.

posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-le.name: Posterior Basal Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BX)
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-le.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis posterior [B X] pulmonis sinistri
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-le.summary: This segmental bronchus (BX) carries air to the posterior basal segment, the lowest and most posterior part of the left lung.
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-le.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the left inferior lobar bronchus and runs straight down toward the back.
function: Ventilates the posterior basal bronchopulmonary segment of the left lung
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-le.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-le.clinical: Fluid and pneumonia often collect in this dependent segment in a person lying on the back.

posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-ri.name: Posterior Basal Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BX)
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-ri.latin: Bronchus segmentalis basalis posterior [B X] pulmonis dextri
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-ri.summary: This segmental bronchus (BX) carries air to the posterior basal segment, the lowest and most posterior part of the right lung.
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-ri.location: Arises from the basal trunk of the right inferior lobar bronchus and runs straight down toward the back.
function: Ventilates the posterior basal bronchopulmonary segment of the right lung
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-ri.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
posterior-basal-segmental-bronchus-of-ri.clinical: This segment lies low and behind, so fluid and aspirated material often collect here. Pleural effusion is tapped in this area.

posterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lu.name: Posterior Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BII)
posterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lu.latin: Bronchus segmentalis posterior [B II] pulmonis dextri
posterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lu.summary: This segmental bronchus (BII) carries air to the posterior segment of the right superior lobe.
posterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lu.location: Arises from the right superior lobar bronchus and passes backward and laterally.
function: Ventilates the posterior bronchopulmonary segment of the right superior lobe
posterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lu.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
posterior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lu.clinical: Aspirated material often enters this segment when a person lies on the right side or face down.

right-inferior-lobar-bronchus.name: Right Inferior Lobar Bronchus
right-inferior-lobar-bronchus.summary: This bronchus supplies the right inferior lobe. It is the continuation of the intermediate bronchus below the middle lobar bronchus.
right-inferior-lobar-bronchus.location: Descends into the lower lobe and gives off the superior segmental bronchus, then a basal trunk with four basal branches.
function: Ventilates the right inferior lobe
right-inferior-lobar-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
right-inferior-lobar-bronchus.clinical: Because it is the most direct downward path, inhaled objects and aspirated fluid often end up in the right lower lobe.

right-lobe-of-thymus.name: Right Lobe of Thymus
right-lobe-of-thymus.summary: The right lobe is one of the two lobes of the thymus. It is a soft lymphoid organ where T lymphocytes mature.
right-lobe-of-thymus.location: Lies in the superior mediastinum, behind the manubrium and in front of the great vessels.
function: Matures T lymphocytes
Removes T cells that would attack normal body tissue
right-lobe-of-thymus.clinical: The thymus is large in children and shrinks after puberty as fat replaces it. Thymoma is linked to myasthenia gravis.

right-main-bronchus.name: Right Main Bronchus
right-main-bronchus.summary: The right main bronchus is the shorter, wider and more vertical of the two main bronchi. It runs from the carina to the right lung root.
right-main-bronchus.location: Begins at the carina behind the sternal angle (T4-T5) and passes under the azygos vein arch to the hilum. It is about 2.5 cm long.
function: Carries air from the trachea to the right lung
Divides into the superior lobar bronchus and the intermediate bronchus
right-main-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
right-main-bronchus.clinical: Inhaled foreign bodies enter the right main bronchus more often than the left because it is wider and more vertical.

right-superior-lobar-bronchus.name: Right Superior Lobar Bronchus
right-superior-lobar-bronchus.summary: This bronchus supplies the right superior lobe. It arises from the right main bronchus above the pulmonary artery, so it is called the eparterial bronchus.
right-superior-lobar-bronchus.location: Arises about 2.5 cm from the carina, just before the right main bronchus enters the lung.
function: Ventilates the right superior lobe
Divides into apical, posterior and anterior segmental bronchi
right-superior-lobar-bronchus.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
right-superior-lobar-bronchus.clinical: Its early, high origin explains why a tumor near the right hilum can block the upper lobe first.

superior-lingular-segmental-broncus-of-l.name: Superior Lingular Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BIV)
superior-lingular-segmental-broncus-of-l.latin: Bronchus lingularis superior [B IV] pulmonis sinistri
superior-lingular-segmental-broncus-of-l.summary: This segmental bronchus (BIV) carries air to the superior lingular segment. The lingula is the left counterpart of the right middle lobe.
superior-lingular-segmental-broncus-of-l.location: Arises from the lingular bronchus, the lower division of the left superior lobar bronchus, and runs forward.
function: Ventilates the superior lingular segment of the left superior lobe
superior-lingular-segmental-broncus-of-l.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
superior-lingular-segmental-broncus-of-l.clinical: Lingular infection can blur the left heart border on chest X-ray.

superior-lobe-of-left-lung.name: Superior Lobe of Left Lung
superior-lobe-of-left-lung.summary: The superior lobe is the upper lobe of the left lung. It includes the lingula, a tongue-shaped part that matches the right middle lobe.
superior-lobe-of-left-lung.location: Lies above the oblique fissure, from the apex to the front of the lung. Its lower front edge forms the cardiac notch and lingula.
function: Gas exchange
Contains the apicoposterior, anterior, superior lingular and inferior lingular segments
superior-lobe-of-left-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
superior-lobe-of-left-lung.clinical: Lingular disease can blur the left heart border on chest X-ray.

superior-lobe-of-right-lung.name: Superior Lobe of Right Lung
superior-lobe-of-right-lung.summary: The superior lobe is the highest of the three right lung lobes. It is separated from the middle lobe by the horizontal fissure.
superior-lobe-of-right-lung.location: Lies above the horizontal fissure, from the lung apex down to about the fourth rib in front. It rests behind the upper anterior chest wall.
function: Gas exchange
Contains the apical, posterior and anterior bronchopulmonary segments
superior-lobe-of-right-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
superior-lobe-of-right-lung.clinical: Apical tumors can invade the brachial plexus and sympathetic chain. Tuberculosis often settles in the upper lobes.

superior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.name: Superior Segmental Bronchus of Left Lung (BVI)
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.latin: Bronchus segmentalis superior [B VI] pulmonis sinistri
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.summary: This segmental bronchus (BVI) is the first branch of the left inferior lobar bronchus and supplies the top of the lower lobe.
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.location: Arises from the back of the left inferior lobar bronchus and passes backward.
function: Ventilates the superior bronchopulmonary segment of the left inferior lobe
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-left-lung.clinical: Aspirated material from a person lying on the back often enters this segment, as on the right.

superior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.name: Superior Segmental Bronchus of Right Lung (BVI)
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.latin: Bronchus segmentalis superior [B VI] pulmonis dextri
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.summary: This segmental bronchus (BVI) is the first branch of the right inferior lobar bronchus and supplies the top of the lower lobe.
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.location: Arises from the back of the right inferior lobar bronchus and passes backward.
function: Ventilates the superior bronchopulmonary segment of the right inferior lobe
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.nerve: Pulmonary plexus: vagus nerve (parasympathetic) and sympathetic fibers (T1-T5)
superior-segmental-bronchus-of-right-lun.clinical: This is the most common site for aspirated material and lung abscess in a person lying on the back.

thyroid-gland.name: Thyroid Gland
thyroid-gland.summary: The thyroid is a butterfly-shaped endocrine gland in the front of the neck. It has two lobes joined by a narrow isthmus.
thyroid-gland.location: Lies in front of the trachea at about C5 to T1. The isthmus crosses the second to fourth tracheal rings.
function: Makes thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) that set metabolic rate
Makes calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium
thyroid-gland.clinical: The recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to the gland, so it can be injured during thyroid surgery.

trachea.name: Trachea
trachea.summary: The trachea is a flexible tube about 10 to 12 cm long that carries air between the larynx and the main bronchi. C-shaped cartilage rings keep it open.
trachea.location: Begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage (C6), runs in the midline through the neck and mediastinum, and ends at the carina (T4-T5).
function: Conducts air to and from the lungs
Warms, humidifies and cleans air with ciliated mucous lining
Divides into the right and left main bronchi
trachea.nerve: Vagus nerve (recurrent laryngeal branches) and sympathetic fibers
trachea.clinical: Tracheostomy is usually made through the second to fourth tracheal rings, below the thyroid isthmus.

abdominal-aorta.name: Abdominal Aorta
abdominal-aorta.summary: The abdominal aorta is the continuation of the thoracic aorta below the diaphragm. It supplies the abdominal wall and organs and ends by dividing into the common iliac arteries.
abdominal-aorta.from: Thoracic aorta, at the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm (T12)
abdominal-aorta.course: Descends in front of the lumbar vertebrae, slightly left of the midline, to its bifurcation at L4.
supplies: Gastrointestinal tract, liver, spleen and pancreas
Posterior abdominal wall and pelvis via iliac arteries
abdominal-aorta.clinical: An abdominal aortic aneurysm is a widening of this artery, most often below the renal arteries. Rupture is life-threatening.

anterior-branch-of-renal-artery.name: Anterior Branch of Renal Artery
anterior-branch-of-renal-artery.summary: The anterior branch (anterior division) of the renal artery is the larger of the two divisions. It passes in front of the renal pelvis.
anterior-branch-of-renal-artery.from: Renal artery, near the renal hilum
anterior-branch-of-renal-artery.course: Passes in front of the renal pelvis and divides into segmental arteries.
supplies: Most of the kidney by tissue volume
anterior-branch-of-renal-artery.clinical: Segmental arteries are end arteries, so a blocked branch causes infarction of one kidney segment.

anterior-inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-ar.name: Anterior Inferior Pancreaticoduodenal Artery
anterior-inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-ar.summary: This is the anterior branch of the inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery. It runs along the front of the pancreatic head.
anterior-inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-ar.from: Inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery (from the superior mesenteric artery)
anterior-inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-ar.course: Passes to the right along the front of the pancreatic head, next to the duodenum. It joins the anterior superior pancreaticoduodenal artery.
supplies: Second to fourth parts of the duodenum
anterior-inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-ar.clinical: These arcades link the coeliac and superior mesenteric territories, so blood flow can continue if one trunk narrows.

appendicular-artery.name: Appendicular Artery
appendicular-artery.summary: The appendicular artery is the only artery to the appendix. It runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix.
appendicular-artery.from: Ileocolic artery (or one of its caecal branches)
appendicular-artery.course: Passes behind the terminal ileum and enters the mesoappendix, running toward the tip of the appendix.
appendicular-artery.clinical: It is an end artery. Swelling in appendicitis can cut off its flow and cause gangrene and perforation.

ascending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.name: Ascending Branch of Left Colic Artery
ascending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.summary: The ascending branch of the left colic artery supplies the upper descending colon and the splenic flexure.
ascending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.course: Runs upward toward the splenic flexure and joins the left branch of the middle colic artery.
ascending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.clinical: This join is a main link between the superior and inferior mesenteric territories.

coeliac-trunk.name: Coeliac Trunk
coeliac-trunk.summary: The coeliac trunk is a short, wide, unpaired artery that supplies the foregut. It divides into three branches.
coeliac-trunk.from: Abdominal aorta, just below the aortic hiatus (T12)
coeliac-trunk.course: Passes forward about 1 to 2 cm above the pancreas, behind the lesser sac, and splits into three branches.
supplies: Upper duodenum and part of the pancreas
coeliac-trunk.clinical: The median arcuate ligament of the diaphragm can compress this artery, causing abdominal pain after meals.

colic-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.name: Colic Branch of Ileocolic Artery
colic-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.summary: The colic branch is the ascending branch of the ileocolic artery. It supplies the lower ascending colon.
colic-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.course: Runs up along the medial side of the ascending colon and joins the descending branch of the right colic artery.
colic-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.clinical: It forms part of the marginal artery, which keeps the colon supplied if one artery is blocked.

common-hepatic-artery.name: Common Hepatic Artery
common-hepatic-artery.summary: The common hepatic artery is a branch of the coeliac trunk. It supplies the liver, stomach, duodenum and pancreas through its two terminal branches.
common-hepatic-artery.course: Runs to the right along the upper border of the pancreas, then gives off the gastroduodenal artery and continues as the proper hepatic artery.
common-hepatic-artery.clinical: Variants are common. In some people the right or left hepatic artery arises from the superior mesenteric or left gastric artery, which matters in liver surgery.

descending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.name: Descending Branch of Left Colic Artery
descending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.summary: The descending branch of the left colic artery supplies the lower descending colon.
descending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.course: Runs downward along the colon and joins the first sigmoid artery.
descending-branch-of-left-colic-artery.clinical: It joins the marginal artery, which keeps the sigmoid colon supplied if the inferior mesenteric artery is tied.

gastroduodenal-artery.name: Gastroduodenal Artery
gastroduodenal-artery.summary: The gastroduodenal artery arises from the common hepatic artery and descends behind the first part of the duodenum.
gastroduodenal-artery.course: Passes behind the first part of the duodenum and divides at its lower border into two terminal branches.
gastroduodenal-artery.clinical: A posterior duodenal ulcer can erode this artery and cause severe bleeding.

hepatic-portal-vein.name: Hepatic Portal Vein
hepatic-portal-vein.summary: The hepatic portal vein carries nutrient-rich blood from the digestive tract, pancreas and spleen to the liver. It has no valves.
drains: Splenic vein (with the inferior mesenteric vein)
hepatic-portal-vein.into: Liver sinusoids, then the hepatic veins and the inferior vena cava
hepatic-portal-vein.course: Forms behind the neck of the pancreas (L1-L2). It ascends about 8 cm in the hepatoduodenal ligament, behind the bile duct and hepatic artery, and divides at the porta hepatis.
hepatic-portal-vein.clinical: In portal hypertension, blood backs up and flows through collateral veins, causing oesophageal varices and a caput medusae.

hepatic-veins.name: Hepatic Veins
hepatic-veins.summary: The hepatic veins drain blood out of the liver. They carry mixed blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery to the inferior vena cava.
hepatic-veins.into: Inferior vena cava, just below the diaphragm
hepatic-veins.course: Three main veins (right, middle and left) run inside the liver and open into the inferior vena cava directly below the diaphragm.
hepatic-veins.clinical: Blockage of the hepatic veins causes Budd-Chiari syndrome, with a swollen painful liver and ascites.

ileal-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.name: Ileal Branch of Ileocolic Artery
ileal-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.summary: The ileal branch of the ileocolic artery supplies the end of the ileum.
ileal-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.course: Runs upward and to the left along the terminal ileum and joins the ileal branches of the superior mesenteric artery.
ileal-branch-of-ileocolic-artery.clinical: Loss of this supply can cause ischemia of the terminal ileum.

ileocolic-artery.name: Ileocolic Artery
ileocolic-artery.summary: The ileocolic artery is the lowest right-sided branch of the superior mesenteric artery. It supplies the terminal ileum, caecum and appendix.
ileocolic-artery.course: Runs down and to the right in the root of the mesentery toward the ileocaecal junction and divides into several branches.
ileocolic-artery.clinical: Poor flow in this artery can cause ischemia of the caecum and terminal ileum.

iliolumbar-artery.name: Iliolumbar Artery
iliolumbar-artery.summary: The iliolumbar artery is a branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery. It supplies the iliacus and the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall.
iliolumbar-artery.from: Posterior division of the internal iliac artery
iliolumbar-artery.course: Ascends behind the obturator nerve and external iliac vessels, then behind the psoas major, and divides into lumbar and iliac branches.
iliolumbar-artery.clinical: It anastomoses with the fourth lumbar, circumflex iliac and obturator arteries, forming collateral routes.

iliolumbar-vein.name: Iliolumbar Vein
iliolumbar-vein.summary: The iliolumbar vein drains the iliacus, psoas major and quadratus lumborum, and the structures supplied by the iliolumbar artery.
drains: Muscles of the posterior abdominal wall
iliolumbar-vein.into: Common iliac vein (sometimes the internal iliac vein)
iliolumbar-vein.course: Accompanies the iliolumbar artery, passes behind the psoas major, and joins the common iliac vein.
iliolumbar-vein.clinical: It links the lumbar and vertebral venous systems with the common iliac vein, giving an alternate route when the vena cava is blocked.

inferior-epigastric-artery.name: Inferior Epigastric Artery
inferior-epigastric-artery.summary: The inferior epigastric artery supplies the lower anterior abdominal wall. It passes along the medial edge of the deep inguinal ring.
inferior-epigastric-artery.from: External iliac artery, just above the inguinal ligament
inferior-epigastric-artery.course: Runs up and medially along the medial side of the deep inguinal ring, enters the rectus sheath, and joins the superior epigastric artery.
inferior-epigastric-artery.clinical: Surgeons use it as a landmark to separate direct inguinal hernias (medial to it) from indirect hernias (lateral to it).

inferior-epigastric-vein.name: Inferior Epigastric Vein
inferior-epigastric-vein.summary: The inferior epigastric vein drains the lower anterior abdominal wall. It accompanies the inferior epigastric artery.
inferior-epigastric-vein.into: External iliac vein, just above the inguinal ligament
inferior-epigastric-vein.course: Runs up inside the rectus sheath and joins the superior epigastric vein, forming a link between the caval systems.
inferior-epigastric-vein.clinical: It forms a collateral route between the inferior and superior vena cava when either is blocked.

inferior-mesenteric-artery.name: Inferior Mesenteric Artery
inferior-mesenteric-artery.summary: The inferior mesenteric artery supplies the hindgut. It is smaller than the superior mesenteric artery.
inferior-mesenteric-artery.from: Abdominal aorta, at about L3, in front of the aorta
inferior-mesenteric-artery.course: Descends to the left behind the peritoneum, crosses the left common iliac vessels, and continues as the superior rectal artery.
supplies: Distal third of the transverse colon
inferior-mesenteric-artery.clinical: It is often tied during aneurysm repair or colon surgery. The marginal artery usually keeps the colon alive.

inferior-mesenteric-vein.name: Inferior Mesenteric Vein
inferior-mesenteric-vein.summary: The inferior mesenteric vein drains the hindgut. It is a tributary of the portal system.
inferior-mesenteric-vein.into: Splenic vein (sometimes the superior mesenteric vein or their junction)
inferior-mesenteric-vein.course: Ascends to the left of the duodenojejunal flexure, behind the body of the pancreas, and joins the splenic vein.
inferior-mesenteric-vein.clinical: It links the portal system with the rectal veins, so it contributes to portosystemic anastomoses in portal hypertension.

inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-artery.name: Inferior Pancreaticoduodenal Artery
inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-artery.summary: The inferior pancreaticoduodenal artery arises low on the pancreatic head and divides into an anterior and a posterior branch.
inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-artery.from: Superior mesenteric artery (sometimes from its first jejunal branch)
inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-artery.course: Passes to the right, above the third part of the duodenum, and divides into anterior and posterior branches that meet the superior arcades.
inferior-pancreaticoduodenal-artery.clinical: The shared arcades make the head of the pancreas and duodenum hard to separate surgically.

inferior-suprarenal-artery.name: Inferior Suprarenal Artery
inferior-suprarenal-artery.summary: The inferior suprarenal artery supplies the lower part of the suprarenal gland.
inferior-suprarenal-artery.course: Passes upward from the renal artery to the lower part of the suprarenal gland.
inferior-suprarenal-artery.clinical: The gland also receives superior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery and a middle one from the aorta.

inferior-vena-cava-ab.name: Inferior Vena Cava (Abdominal Part)
inferior-vena-cava-ab.summary: The abdominal part of the inferior vena cava returns blood from the lower limbs, pelvis and abdomen to the heart.
inferior-vena-cava-ab.course: Forms where the common iliac veins join at L5. It ascends to the right of the aorta, passes behind the liver, and pierces the diaphragm at T8.
inferior-vena-cava-ab.clinical: Large clots can reach the lungs from leg veins through the vena cava. A pregnant uterus can compress it when lying on the back.

intrarenal-arteries-of-left-kidney.name: Intrarenal Arteries of Left Kidney
intrarenal-arteries-of-left-kidney.summary: The intrarenal arteries are the branches of the renal artery inside the left kidney. They run from the hilum into the cortex.
intrarenal-arteries-of-left-kidney.from: Segmental arteries from the left renal artery
intrarenal-arteries-of-left-kidney.course: Segmental arteries divide into interlobar arteries in the renal columns, then arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary border, then interlobular arteries in the cortex.
supplies: Renal cortex and medulla of the left kidney
intrarenal-arteries-of-left-kidney.clinical: These vessels are end arteries, so a blocked branch infarcts the tissue it supplies.

intrarenal-arteries-of-right-kidney.name: Intrarenal Arteries of Right Kidney
intrarenal-arteries-of-right-kidney.summary: The intrarenal arteries are the branches of the renal artery inside the right kidney. They run from the hilum into the cortex.
intrarenal-arteries-of-right-kidney.from: Segmental arteries from the right renal artery
intrarenal-arteries-of-right-kidney.course: Segmental arteries divide into interlobar arteries in the renal columns, then arcuate arteries at the corticomedullary border, then interlobular arteries in the cortex.
supplies: Renal cortex and medulla of the right kidney
intrarenal-arteries-of-right-kidney.clinical: These vessels are end arteries, so a blocked branch infarcts the tissue it supplies.

intrarenal-veins-of-left-kidney.name: Intrarenal Veins of Left Kidney
intrarenal-veins-of-left-kidney.summary: The intrarenal veins drain the left kidney. They follow the arteries but join freely with each other.
drains: Renal cortex and medulla of the left kidney
intrarenal-veins-of-left-kidney.course: Blood passes from interlobular veins to arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and then segmental veins that unite into the renal vein.
intrarenal-veins-of-left-kidney.clinical: Unlike the arteries, these veins form many connections, so a blockage in one is usually tolerated.

intrarenal-veins-of-right-kidney.name: Intrarenal Veins of Right Kidney
intrarenal-veins-of-right-kidney.summary: The intrarenal veins drain the right kidney. They follow the arteries but join freely with each other.
drains: Renal cortex and medulla of the right kidney
intrarenal-veins-of-right-kidney.course: Blood passes from interlobular veins to arcuate veins, then interlobar veins, and then segmental veins that unite into the renal vein.
intrarenal-veins-of-right-kidney.clinical: Unlike the arteries, these veins form many connections, so a blockage in one is usually tolerated.

left-ascending-lumbal-vein.name: Left Ascending Lumbar Vein
left-ascending-lumbal-vein.summary: The left ascending lumbar vein is a long vertical vein that joins the lumbar veins on the left. It continues upward as the hemi-azygos vein.
left-ascending-lumbal-vein.into: Hemi-azygos vein (after joining the left subcostal vein)
left-ascending-lumbal-vein.course: Ascends beside the lumbar vertebrae behind the psoas major and joins the left subcostal vein behind the diaphragm.
left-ascending-lumbal-vein.clinical: It forms a collateral path linking the vena cava with the azygos system when the vena cava is blocked.

left-colic-artery.name: Left Colic Artery
left-colic-artery.summary: The left colic artery supplies the descending colon and the left part of the transverse colon.
left-colic-artery.course: Passes to the left behind the peritoneum toward the descending colon and divides into ascending and descending branches.
supplies: Left part of the transverse colon
left-colic-artery.clinical: The splenic flexure lies between the superior and inferior mesenteric supplies and is prone to ischemia.

left-gastric-artery.name: Left Gastric Artery
left-gastric-artery.summary: The left gastric artery is the smallest branch of the coeliac trunk. It supplies the lower oesophagus and the lesser curvature of the stomach.
left-gastric-artery.course: Ascends to the oesophageal hiatus, gives oesophageal branches, then turns down along the lesser curvature and joins the right gastric artery.
branches: Gastric branches (anastomose with right gastric artery)
left-gastric-artery.clinical: Oesophageal veins that accompany it connect the portal and systemic systems and can form varices.

left-gastro-omental-vein.name: Left Gastro-omental Vein
left-gastro-omental-vein.summary: The left gastro-omental vein drains the left part of the greater curvature of the stomach and the greater omentum.
drains: Left part of the greater curvature of the stomach
left-gastro-omental-vein.course: Runs along the greater curvature in the gastrosplenic ligament and ends in the splenic vein.
left-gastro-omental-vein.clinical: Gastric veins connect to the portal system, so they can enlarge as gastric varices in portal hypertension.

left-renal-artery.name: Left Renal Artery
left-renal-artery.summary: The left renal artery carries blood to the left kidney. It is shorter than the right and lies behind the left renal vein.
left-renal-artery.from: Abdominal aorta, just below the superior mesenteric artery (L1-L2)
left-renal-artery.course: Passes laterally behind the left renal vein and the pancreas to the renal hilum, where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
left-renal-artery.clinical: Accessory renal arteries are common and should be spotted before a donor kidney is removed.

left-renal-vein.name: Left Renal Vein
left-renal-vein.summary: The left renal vein drains the left kidney. It is longer than the right and crosses in front of the aorta.
left-renal-vein.into: Inferior vena cava, at about L1-L2
left-renal-vein.course: Leaves the hilum in front of the left renal artery. It passes in front of the aorta, below the superior mesenteric artery, and enters the vena cava.
left-renal-vein.clinical: Compression between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery is called nutcracker syndrome. It can cause blood in the urine.

left-subcostal-vein.name: Left Subcostal Vein
left-subcostal-vein.summary: The left subcostal vein runs below the twelfth rib with the subcostal artery. It helps form the hemi-azygos vein.
drains: Muscles and skin of the upper lumbar wall
left-subcostal-vein.course: Passes behind the diaphragm, joins the left ascending lumbar vein, and continues as the hemi-azygos vein.
left-subcostal-vein.clinical: It is part of the azygos system, which gives an alternative route back to the heart if the vena cava is blocked.

lumbar-arteries.name: Lumbar Arteries
lumbar-arteries.summary: The lumbar arteries are paired segmental arteries that supply the back and walls of the abdomen. They are the lumbar version of the posterior intercostal arteries.
lumbar-arteries.from: Posterior surface of the abdominal aorta (usually four pairs at L1-L4; a fifth pair may arise from the median sacral artery)
lumbar-arteries.course: Run laterally around the vertebral bodies, behind the psoas major, and pass between the muscle layers of the abdominal wall.
branches: Dorsal branch (supplies back muscles, skin and spinal canal contents)
Spinal branch (to spinal cord and meninges)
lumbar-arteries.clinical: Lumbar arteries can bleed during spinal or retroperitoneal surgery. They can also be involved in aortic aneurysm repair.

lumbar-branch-of-iliolumbar-artery.name: Lumbar Branch of Iliolumbar Artery
lumbar-branch-of-iliolumbar-artery.summary: The lumbar branch of the iliolumbar artery goes to the muscles of the posterior abdominal wall and sends a branch to the cauda equina.
lumbar-branch-of-iliolumbar-artery.course: Ascends behind the psoas major, supplies psoas major and quadratus lumborum, and sends a spinal branch through the intervertebral foramen.
lumbar-branch-of-iliolumbar-artery.clinical: It links the internal iliac system with the lumbar arteries, giving a collateral route if the aorta is blocked.

lumbar-veins.name: Lumbar Veins
lumbar-veins.summary: The lumbar veins drain the posterior abdominal wall. Usually four pairs run beside the lumbar arteries.
drains: Posterior abdominal wall muscles and skin
lumbar-veins.into: Inferior vena cava (the upper ones may reach the azygos system through the ascending lumbar veins)
lumbar-veins.course: Run around the vertebral bodies behind the psoas major and enter the back of the vena cava. They connect with the ascending lumbar veins.
lumbar-veins.clinical: They give a route for blood to bypass a blocked inferior vena cava, and for spread of cancer to the spine.

marginal-artery.name: Marginal Artery
marginal-artery.summary: The marginal artery is a continuous arterial chain along the inner border of the colon. It links the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries.
marginal-artery.from: Formed by anastomosis between branches of the ileocolic, right colic, middle colic and left colic arteries
marginal-artery.course: Runs close to the colon wall from the ileocaecal junction to the sigmoid colon and gives off short vasa recta.
branches: Vasa recta (straight arteries to the colon wall)
supplies: Colon from the ascending to the descending part
marginal-artery.clinical: Weak points of this chain, such as at the splenic flexure, can lead to colon ischemia.

middle-colic-vein.name: Middle Colic Vein
middle-colic-vein.summary: The middle colic vein drains the transverse colon. It travels with the middle colic artery.
middle-colic-vein.course: Runs in the transverse mesocolon and joins the superior mesenteric vein near the lower border of the pancreas.
middle-colic-vein.clinical: It is often tied during transverse colon surgery. It lies close to the pancreas, so tearing it during surgery can cause heavy bleeding.

musculophrenic-artery.name: Musculophrenic Artery
musculophrenic-artery.summary: The musculophrenic artery is a terminal branch of the internal thoracic artery. It runs behind the costal margin to the diaphragm.
musculophrenic-artery.from: Internal thoracic artery (one of its two terminal branches)
musculophrenic-artery.course: Passes laterally and downward behind the costal cartilages of the seventh to ninth ribs, pierces the diaphragm and ends near the last intercostal space.
branches: Anterior intercostal arteries (seventh to ninth spaces)
musculophrenic-artery.clinical: It is a collateral link between the internal thoracic and the lower intercostal and epigastric vessels.

posterior-branch-of-renal-artery.name: Posterior Branch of Renal Artery
posterior-branch-of-renal-artery.summary: The posterior branch (posterior division) of the renal artery supplies the back of the kidney. It passes behind the renal pelvis.
posterior-branch-of-renal-artery.from: Renal artery, near the renal hilum
posterior-branch-of-renal-artery.course: Passes behind the renal pelvis and continues as the posterior segmental artery.
posterior-branch-of-renal-artery.clinical: A relatively bloodless line (Brodel line) lies between the anterior and posterior territories, and surgeons use it for kidney incisions.

proper-hepatic-artery.name: Proper Hepatic Artery
proper-hepatic-artery.summary: The proper hepatic artery carries blood to the liver. It lies in the free edge of the lesser omentum in front of the portal vein.
proper-hepatic-artery.from: Common hepatic artery, after the gastroduodenal artery arises
proper-hepatic-artery.course: Ascends in the hepatoduodenal ligament, to the left of the bile duct and in front of the portal vein, and divides at the porta hepatis.
branches: Right hepatic artery (gives the cystic artery)
supplies: Lesser curvature of the stomach (via right gastric)
proper-hepatic-artery.clinical: A surgeon can clamp the hepatoduodenal ligament (Pringle maneuver) to control liver bleeding.

right-ascending-lumbar-vein.name: Right Ascending Lumbar Vein
right-ascending-lumbar-vein.summary: The right ascending lumbar vein is a long vertical vein that joins the lumbar veins on the right. It continues upward as the azygos vein.
right-ascending-lumbar-vein.into: Azygos vein (after joining the right subcostal vein)
right-ascending-lumbar-vein.course: Ascends beside the lumbar vertebrae behind the psoas major, passes through the diaphragm, and joins the right subcostal vein.
right-ascending-lumbar-vein.clinical: It forms a collateral path linking the vena cava with the azygos system when the vena cava is blocked.

right-colic-artery.name: Right Colic Artery
right-colic-artery.summary: The right colic artery supplies the ascending colon. It often arises from the ileocolic artery rather than directly from the superior mesenteric artery.
right-colic-artery.from: Superior mesenteric artery (or the ileocolic artery)
right-colic-artery.course: Runs to the right behind the peritoneum toward the ascending colon, then divides into ascending and descending branches.
right-colic-artery.clinical: Ligation of this artery during a right hemicolectomy must preserve the marginal artery to keep the remaining bowel alive.

right-colic-vein.name: Right Colic Vein
right-colic-vein.summary: The right colic vein drains the ascending colon. It travels with the right colic artery.
right-colic-vein.course: Runs behind the peritoneum toward the root of the mesentery and joins the superior mesenteric vein.
right-colic-vein.clinical: In a right hemicolectomy, it is tied along with the other right-sided mesenteric vessels.

right-gastro-omental-vein.name: Right Gastro-omental Vein
right-gastro-omental-vein.summary: The right gastro-omental vein drains the right part of the greater curvature of the stomach and the greater omentum.
drains: Right part of the greater curvature of the stomach
right-gastro-omental-vein.into: Superior mesenteric vein, usually through the gastrocolic trunk
right-gastro-omental-vein.course: Runs along the greater curvature and passes behind the pylorus to join the superior mesenteric vein.
right-gastro-omental-vein.clinical: It is tied near the pylorus during surgical removal of the stomach.

right-renal-artery.name: Right Renal Artery
right-renal-artery.summary: The right renal artery carries blood to the right kidney. It is longer than the left and passes behind the inferior vena cava.
right-renal-artery.from: Abdominal aorta, just below the superior mesenteric artery (L1-L2)
right-renal-artery.course: Passes laterally behind the inferior vena cava and the right renal vein to the renal hilum, where it divides into anterior and posterior divisions.
right-renal-artery.clinical: Renal artery stenosis can cause high blood pressure. About 30 percent of people have an extra renal artery.

right-renal-vein.name: Right Renal Vein
right-renal-vein.summary: The right renal vein drains the right kidney. It is short, about 2.5 cm, and goes straight into the inferior vena cava.
