right-renal-vein.into: Inferior vena cava, at about L1-L2
right-renal-vein.course: Leaves the renal hilum in front of the right renal artery and passes behind the descending part of the duodenum to enter the vena cava.
right-renal-vein.clinical: The short right renal vein makes the right kidney harder to remove for donation than the left.

cards.name: Unidentified Vessel (Pterygoid Canal Area)
cards.summary: The model label for this mesh is only a placeholder. It sits under the artery of the pterygoid canal in the maxillary artery tree.
cards.clinical: No specific clinical note. Identify the mesh in the 3D model before studying it.
cards.from: Not identified (grouped under the artery of the pterygoid canal in the model)
cards.course: Not identified. It lies in the deep face near the pterygopalatine fossa.

x.name: Unidentified Vessel (Pterygoid Canal Area, Paired)
x.summary: The model label for this mesh is only a placeholder. It sits under the artery of the pterygoid canal in the maxillary artery tree.
x.clinical: No specific clinical note. Identify the mesh in the 3D model before studying it.
x.from: Not identified (grouped under the artery of the pterygoid canal in the model)
x.course: Not identified. It lies in the deep face near the pterygopalatine fossa.

accessory-branch-of-middle-meningeal-art.name: Accessory Branch of Middle Meningeal Artery
accessory-branch-of-middle-meningeal-art.summary: A small, variable branch of the middle meningeal artery. It enters the skull through the foramen ovale.
accessory-branch-of-middle-meningeal-art.clinical: It can contribute to supply of the trigeminal ganglion and may be involved in meningioma blood supply.
accessory-branch-of-middle-meningeal-art.from: Middle meningeal artery (or directly from the maxillary artery)
accessory-branch-of-middle-meningeal-art.course: Passes upward medial to the mandibular nerve and enters the middle cranial fossa through the foramen ovale.

anterior-deep-temporal-artery.name: Anterior Deep Temporal Artery
anterior-deep-temporal-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that ascends deep to the temporalis muscle. It supplies the front part of that muscle.
anterior-deep-temporal-artery.clinical: It can bleed during surgical approaches to the temporal region or when temporalis is detached.
anterior-deep-temporal-artery.course: Ascends between the temporalis muscle and the temporal bone in the infratemporal and temporal fossae.
supplies: Adjacent periosteum of the temporal fossa

artery-of-pterygoid-canal.name: Artery of Pterygoid Canal
artery-of-pterygoid-canal.summary: A small branch of the maxillary artery in the pterygopalatine fossa. It runs backward through the pterygoid (Vidian) canal.
artery-of-pterygoid-canal.clinical: It can anastomose with internal carotid branches, giving a route for collateral flow to the middle ear region.
artery-of-pterygoid-canal.from: Maxillary artery (third part, in the pterygopalatine fossa); sometimes the descending palatine artery
artery-of-pterygoid-canal.course: Runs backward through the pterygoid canal with the nerve of the pterygoid canal toward the foramen lacerum.

buccal-artery.name: Buccal Artery
buccal-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that runs forward to the cheek. It travels with the buccal nerve.
buccal-artery.clinical: It anastomoses with facial artery branches, so cheek bleeding can persist unless both sources are controlled.
buccal-artery.course: Passes forward between the medial pterygoid muscle and the ramus of the mandible, then onto the buccinator.
supplies: Gingiva of the upper and lower jaw (buccal side)

descending-palatine-artery.name: Descending Palatine Artery
descending-palatine-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that descends from the pterygopalatine fossa. It divides into the greater and lesser palatine arteries.
descending-palatine-artery.clinical: Injury during maxillary surgery, such as Le Fort osteotomy, can cause heavy bleeding from the palate.
descending-palatine-artery.from: Maxillary artery (third part, in the pterygopalatine fossa)
descending-palatine-artery.course: Descends through the greater palatine canal and splits into the greater and lesser palatine arteries.

greater-palatine-artery.name: Greater Palatine Artery
greater-palatine-artery.summary: The larger terminal branch of the descending palatine artery. It supplies the hard palate.
greater-palatine-artery.clinical: It is at risk in palatal incisions and grafts; the greater palatine foramen is a key landmark for nerve blocks.
greater-palatine-artery.course: Emerges from the greater palatine foramen and runs forward on the hard palate. It ends by passing up the incisive canal to meet the sphenopalatine artery.

inferior-alveolar-artery.name: Inferior Alveolar Artery
inferior-alveolar-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that supplies the lower teeth and chin. It travels with the inferior alveolar nerve.
inferior-alveolar-artery.clinical: It can be injured during inferior alveolar nerve blocks or third molar surgery, causing hematoma or bleeding.
inferior-alveolar-artery.course: Descends to the mandibular foramen and runs in the mandibular canal with the nerve. It ends at the mental foramen.

infra-orbital-artery.name: Infra-orbital Artery
infra-orbital-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that travels through the floor of the orbit. It emerges on the face below the eye.
infra-orbital-artery.clinical: It is at risk in orbital floor fractures and in infra-orbital nerve blocks or midface surgery.
infra-orbital-artery.from: Maxillary artery (third part, in the pterygopalatine fossa)
infra-orbital-artery.course: Enters the orbit through the inferior orbital fissure, runs in the infra-orbital groove and canal, and exits at the infra-orbital foramen.
supplies: Maxillary incisors, canine and anterior sinus wall

maxillary-artery.name: Maxillary Artery
maxillary-artery.summary: The larger terminal branch of the external carotid artery. It supplies the deep face, jaws, teeth, nose and dura mater.
maxillary-artery.clinical: Its middle meningeal branch is the usual source of epidural hematoma. Sphenopalatine branches are a common source of severe nosebleed.
maxillary-artery.from: External carotid artery, behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland
maxillary-artery.course: Passes forward deep to the mandibular neck in three parts: mandibular, pterygoid and pterygopalatine. It ends in the pterygopalatine fossa as the sphenopalatine artery.

maxillary-veins.name: Maxillary Veins
maxillary-veins.group: Veins of the face and deep face
maxillary-veins.summary: Short veins that accompany the first part of the maxillary artery. They carry blood from the pterygoid venous plexus.
maxillary-veins.clinical: The pterygoid plexus links to the cavernous sinus, so deep facial infections can spread toward the brain.
maxillary-veins.into: Retromandibular vein (by joining the superficial temporal vein)
maxillary-veins.course: Pass backward behind the neck of the mandible within the parotid gland and unite with the superficial temporal vein.

mental-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-arter.name: Mental Branch of Inferior Alveolar Artery
mental-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-arter.summary: A terminal branch of the inferior alveolar artery. It leaves the mandible through the mental foramen to supply the chin.
mental-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-arter.clinical: It can bleed in procedures near the mental foramen, such as implant placement in the premolar region.
mental-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-arter.course: Exits the mental foramen with the mental nerve and passes to the chin and lower lip.
supplies: Skin and soft tissue of the chin
Lower lip (anastomoses with the inferior labial artery)

middle-meningeal-artery.name: Middle Meningeal Artery
middle-meningeal-artery.summary: The largest artery of the dura mater. It runs in grooves on the inner surface of the skull.
middle-meningeal-artery.clinical: Tearing after a blow to the pterion causes an epidural hematoma, a neurosurgical emergency.
middle-meningeal-artery.course: Passes between the two roots of the auriculotemporal nerve, enters the skull via the foramen spinosum, and divides into frontal and parietal branches.

mylohyoid-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-ar.name: Mylohyoid Branch of Inferior Alveolar Artery
mylohyoid-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-ar.summary: A small branch that leaves the inferior alveolar artery just before the mandibular foramen. It runs along the mylohyoid groove.
mylohyoid-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-ar.clinical: It can bleed or form a hematoma in the floor of the mouth during mandibular surgery.
mylohyoid-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-ar.from: Inferior alveolar artery, just before it enters the mandibular foramen
mylohyoid-branch-of-inferior-alveolar-ar.course: Runs forward in the mylohyoid groove of the mandible with the nerve to mylohyoid, then along the underside of the mylohyoid muscle.

posterior-deep-temporal-artery.name: Posterior Deep Temporal Artery
posterior-deep-temporal-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that ascends deep to the temporalis muscle. It supplies the back part of that muscle.
posterior-deep-temporal-artery.clinical: It can bleed when the temporalis muscle is elevated in surgical approaches to the skull.
posterior-deep-temporal-artery.course: Ascends between the temporalis muscle and the temporal bone, behind the anterior deep temporal artery.
supplies: Adjacent periosteum of the temporal fossa

posterior-lateral-nasal-branches-of-sphe.name: Posterior Lateral Nasal Branches of Sphenopalatine Artery
posterior-lateral-nasal-branches-of-sphe.latin: Rami nasales posteriores laterales arteriae sphenopalatinae
posterior-lateral-nasal-branches-of-sphe.summary: Branches of the sphenopalatine artery that supply the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, including the conchae.
posterior-lateral-nasal-branches-of-sphe.clinical: They are a common source of posterior nosebleeds, which may need packing or artery ligation.
posterior-lateral-nasal-branches-of-sphe.from: Sphenopalatine artery, after it passes through the sphenopalatine foramen
posterior-lateral-nasal-branches-of-sphe.course: Enter the nasal cavity through the sphenopalatine foramen and spread over the conchae and meatuses.

posterior-septal-branches-of-sphenopalat.name: Posterior Septal Branches of Sphenopalatine Artery
posterior-septal-branches-of-sphenopalat.summary: Branches of the sphenopalatine artery that supply the nasal septum. The longest runs forward and down the septum.
posterior-septal-branches-of-sphenopalat.clinical: They join Kiesselbach plexus, the usual site of anterior nosebleeds.
posterior-septal-branches-of-sphenopalat.from: Sphenopalatine artery, after it passes through the sphenopalatine foramen
posterior-septal-branches-of-sphenopalat.course: Cross the roof of the nasal cavity to the septum. The longest branch (nasopalatine artery) runs down to the incisive canal.
supplies: Anterior hard palate (via the incisive canal)

posterior-superior-alveolar-artery.name: Posterior Superior Alveolar Artery
posterior-superior-alveolar-artery.summary: A branch of the maxillary artery that descends on the back of the maxilla. It supplies the upper molar and premolar teeth.
posterior-superior-alveolar-artery.clinical: A hematoma can form during posterior superior alveolar nerve block because of the nearby pterygoid venous plexus.
posterior-superior-alveolar-artery.from: Maxillary artery (third part, near the pterygopalatine fossa)
posterior-superior-alveolar-artery.course: Descends over the maxillary tuberosity. Branches enter the posterior alveolar foramina and run in the maxilla.

angular-artery.name: Angular Artery
angular-artery.summary: The terminal branch of the facial artery. It ends at the medial corner of the eye.
angular-artery.clinical: It links the external and internal carotid systems by joining the dorsal nasal branch of the ophthalmic artery.
angular-artery.course: Ascends along the side of the nose to the medial angle (canthus) of the eye.
supplies: Lower eyelid and medial eye region

angular-vein.name: Angular Vein
angular-vein.summary: A short vein at the medial corner of the eye. It forms where the supratrochlear and supraorbital veins meet and continues as the facial vein.
angular-vein.clinical: It has no valves and connects to the ophthalmic veins. Infections near the nose and eye can reach the cavernous sinus.
angular-vein.course: Runs obliquely down along the side of the nose from the medial angle of the eye, then continues as the facial vein.

anterior-cerebral-artery.name: Anterior Cerebral Artery
anterior-cerebral-artery.summary: One of the two terminal branches of the internal carotid artery. It supplies the medial surface of the cerebral hemisphere.
anterior-cerebral-artery.clinical: Occlusion causes weakness and sensory loss of the opposite leg more than the arm, with possible abulia.
anterior-cerebral-artery.course: Runs forward and medially above the optic nerve, joins its partner by the anterior communicating artery, then arches around the corpus callosum.
branches: Medial striate artery (recurrent artery of Heubner)
supplies: Upper edge of the lateral hemisphere

anterior-communicating-artery.name: Anterior Communicating Artery
anterior-communicating-artery.summary: A short vessel that joins the two anterior cerebral arteries. It closes the front of the cerebral arterial circle (circle of Willis).
anterior-communicating-artery.clinical: It is the most common site of berry aneurysm; rupture causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.
anterior-communicating-artery.from: Joins the left and right anterior cerebral arteries (A1 and A2 junction)
anterior-communicating-artery.course: Crosses the midline in front of the optic chiasm, in the interhemispheric fissure.
supplies: Small perforating branches to the hypothalamus and anterior optic chiasm region

anterior-division-of-retromandibular-vei.name: Anterior Division of Retromandibular Vein
anterior-division-of-retromandibular-vei.summary: The front branch of the retromandibular vein. It joins the facial vein to form the common facial vein.
anterior-division-of-retromandibular-vei.clinical: It is a landmark during parotid and neck surgery and is often ligated with the facial vein.
drains: Maxillary vein territory (scalp, parotid and deep face)
anterior-division-of-retromandibular-vei.into: Common facial vein (by joining the facial vein)
anterior-division-of-retromandibular-vei.course: Leaves the retromandibular vein near the lower parotid gland and runs downward and forward to meet the facial vein.

anterior-ethmoidal-artery.name: Anterior Ethmoidal Artery
anterior-ethmoidal-artery.summary: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that leaves the orbit through the anterior ethmoidal canal. It supplies the front of the nose and the dura of the anterior cranial fossa.
anterior-ethmoidal-artery.clinical: It is a source of nosebleed, and injury in orbital surgery can cause a retro-orbital hematoma.
anterior-ethmoidal-artery.course: Passes through the anterior ethmoidal foramen, crosses the anterior cranial fossa beside the cribriform plate, and descends into the nose.
supplies: Anterior nasal septum and lateral wall
Dura of the anterior cranial fossa

anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.name: Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery
anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.summary: A branch of the basilar artery near its start. It supplies the front and underside of the cerebellum and the lower lateral pons.
anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.clinical: Occlusion causes vertigo, hearing loss, facial weakness and ataxia on the same side (lateral pontine syndrome).
anterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.course: Runs backward and laterally across the pons toward the cerebellopontine angle, near the facial and vestibulocochlear nerves.
branches: Labyrinthine (internal auditory) artery in most people

anterior-intercavernous-sinus.name: Anterior Intercavernous Sinus
anterior-intercavernous-sinus.summary: A small venous channel that links the two cavernous sinuses. It lies in front of the pituitary stalk.
anterior-intercavernous-sinus.clinical: It can bleed during transsphenoidal pituitary surgery.
anterior-intercavernous-sinus.course: Crosses the midline in the diaphragma sellae, anterior to the pituitary gland. With the posterior channel it forms the circular sinus.

anterior-parietal-artery.name: Anterior Parietal Artery
anterior-parietal-artery.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the lateral surface of the front part of the parietal lobe.
anterior-parietal-artery.clinical: Occlusion can cause sensory loss and neglect of the opposite side of the body.
anterior-parietal-artery.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs upward and backward over the surface of the parietal lobe.
supplies: Parts of the postcentral gyrus and superior parietal lobule

anterior-septal-branches-of-anterior-eth.name: Anterior Septal Branches of Anterior Ethmoidal Artery
anterior-septal-branches-of-anterior-eth.latin: Rami septales anteriores arteriae ethmoidalis anterioris
anterior-septal-branches-of-anterior-eth.summary: Small branches of the anterior ethmoidal artery that supply the upper front part of the nasal septum.
anterior-septal-branches-of-anterior-eth.clinical: They help form Kiesselbach plexus, the usual site of anterior nosebleeds.
anterior-septal-branches-of-anterior-eth.from: Anterior ethmoidal artery, after it enters the nasal cavity
anterior-septal-branches-of-anterior-eth.course: Descend on the nasal septum from the roof of the nose.

anterior-spinal-artery.name: Anterior Spinal Artery
anterior-spinal-artery.summary: A single artery formed by two small branches of the vertebral arteries. It runs down the front of the spinal cord and supplies most of its cross-section.
anterior-spinal-artery.clinical: Occlusion causes anterior spinal artery syndrome: paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sense, with vibration sense preserved.
anterior-spinal-artery.from: Vertebral arteries (two small branches that unite near the foramen magnum)
anterior-spinal-artery.course: Descends in the anterior median fissure of the spinal cord. Radicular arteries reinforce it, including the artery of Adamkiewicz.
supplies: Anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord

anterior-temporal-branch.name: Anterior Temporal Branch
anterior-temporal-branch.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that supplies the front of the temporal lobe.
anterior-temporal-branch.clinical: Temporal lobe infarcts can cause language problems (dominant side) or memory and behavior changes.
anterior-temporal-branch.from: Middle cerebral artery (insular and opercular branches)
anterior-temporal-branch.course: Runs downward and forward over the lateral surface of the temporal lobe.
supplies: Anterior superior and middle temporal gyri

artery-of-central-sulcus.name: Artery of Central Sulcus
artery-of-central-sulcus.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs in the central sulcus. It supplies cortex on both sides of that sulcus.
artery-of-central-sulcus.clinical: Occlusion causes weakness and sensory loss of the opposite face and hand.
artery-of-central-sulcus.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and follows the central sulcus upward.
supplies: Lower parts of the precentral and postcentral gyri (motor and sensory cortex)

artery-of-postcentral-sulcus.name: Artery of Postcentral Sulcus
artery-of-postcentral-sulcus.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs in the postcentral sulcus. It supplies the sensory cortex area.
artery-of-postcentral-sulcus.clinical: Occlusion causes loss of touch and position sense on the opposite side of the body.
artery-of-postcentral-sulcus.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs upward and backward along the postcentral sulcus.
supplies: Postcentral gyrus (primary somatosensory cortex), lateral part

artery-of-precentral-sulcus.name: Artery of Precentral Sulcus
artery-of-precentral-sulcus.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery that runs in the precentral sulcus. It supplies the premotor and motor cortex areas.
artery-of-precentral-sulcus.clinical: Occlusion causes weakness of the opposite face and arm and, in the dominant hemisphere, speech problems.
artery-of-precentral-sulcus.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs upward along the precentral sulcus.

ascending-pharyngeal-artery.name: Ascending Pharyngeal Artery
ascending-pharyngeal-artery.summary: The smallest branch of the external carotid artery. It ascends beside the pharynx to the base of the skull.
ascending-pharyngeal-artery.clinical: It can be a source of bleeding after tonsil surgery and can feed some skull base tumors.
ascending-pharyngeal-artery.course: Ascends between the internal carotid artery and the side wall of the pharynx to the base of the skull.
supplies: Meninges of the posterior cranial fossa

basilar-artery.name: Basilar Artery
basilar-artery.summary: An unpaired artery formed by the union of the two vertebral arteries. It runs along the front of the pons.
basilar-artery.clinical: Occlusion can cause locked-in syndrome or coma. A top-of-basilar embolus affects the midbrain and thalamus.
basilar-artery.from: Union of the left and right vertebral arteries at the pontomedullary junction
basilar-artery.course: Ascends in the basilar groove of the pons and ends at the top of the pons by dividing into the two posterior cerebral arteries.

basilar-venous-plexus.name: Basilar Venous Plexus
basilar-venous-plexus.summary: A network of venous channels on the clivus, between layers of dura. It links nearby sinuses.
basilar-venous-plexus.clinical: It provides a route between the cranial sinuses and the vertebral venous plexus; bleeding can occur in clival surgery.
basilar-venous-plexus.into: Internal vertebral venous plexus (via the foramen magnum), and the inferior petrosal sinuses
basilar-venous-plexus.course: Lies on the clivus and connects the two inferior petrosal sinuses and the cavernous sinuses. It continues through the foramen magnum.

branch-to-angular-gyrus.name: Branch to Angular Gyrus
branch-to-angular-gyrus.summary: A terminal cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the angular gyrus.
branch-to-angular-gyrus.clinical: Damage in the dominant hemisphere can cause alexia, agraphia and Gerstmann syndrome.
branch-to-angular-gyrus.from: Middle cerebral artery (terminal cortical branch, M4)
branch-to-angular-gyrus.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs backward over the inferior parietal lobule.

callosomarginal-artery.name: Callosomarginal Artery
callosomarginal-artery.summary: A branch of the anterior cerebral artery that runs in the cingulate sulcus. It supplies the medial surface of the frontal lobe.
callosomarginal-artery.clinical: It is variable and may be absent. Occlusion causes weakness of the opposite leg.
callosomarginal-artery.from: Anterior cerebral artery (pericallosal part, in the interhemispheric fissure)
callosomarginal-artery.course: Runs backward in the cingulate sulcus above the cingulate gyrus, parallel to the pericallosal artery.
branches: Anterior, middle and posterior internal frontal arteries

cavernous-sinus.name: Cavernous Sinus
cavernous-sinus.summary: A paired venous space on each side of the sphenoid body and pituitary gland. It contains the internal carotid artery and the abducens nerve.
cavernous-sinus.clinical: Face infections can cause cavernous sinus thrombosis, with eye movement palsy, proptosis and facial numbness.
cavernous-sinus.into: Superior petrosal sinus and inferior petrosal sinus (also emissary veins to the pterygoid plexus)
cavernous-sinus.course: Lies beside the sella turcica. The oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves run in its lateral wall.

central-retinal-artery.name: Central Retinal Artery
central-retinal-artery.summary: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that enters the optic nerve. It supplies the inner layers of the retina.
central-retinal-artery.clinical: Occlusion causes sudden painless loss of vision in one eye, with a cherry-red spot on the macula.
central-retinal-artery.course: Pierces the optic nerve sheath about 1 cm behind the eyeball and runs inside the nerve to the optic disc, where it divides.
branches: Superior and inferior nasal retinal arterioles
Superior and inferior temporal retinal arterioles

common-facial-vein.name: Common Facial Vein
common-facial-vein.group: Veins of the face and neck
common-facial-vein.summary: A short vein formed by the facial vein and the anterior division of the retromandibular vein. It drains into the internal jugular vein.
common-facial-vein.clinical: It is often tied off during neck dissection or submandibular gland surgery.
drains: Parotid region and deep face (via the retromandibular vein)
common-facial-vein.course: Forms near the angle of the mandible and runs down and back to enter the internal jugular vein near the level of the hyoid bone.

distal-lateral-striate-branches.name: Distal Lateral Striate Branches
distal-lateral-striate-branches.summary: Small perforating branches of the middle cerebral artery that enter the brain through the anterior perforated substance. They supply deep structures near the internal capsule.
distal-lateral-striate-branches.clinical: These small vessels are prone to hypertensive rupture and lacunar infarcts, causing weakness of the opposite side.
distal-lateral-striate-branches.course: Arise along the M1 segment, then turn upward into the anterior perforated substance and the base of the forebrain.
supplies: Parts of the caudate nucleus and globus pallidus
Internal capsule (upper anterior limb and genu)

external-carotid-artery.name: External Carotid Artery
external-carotid-artery.summary: One of the two terminal branches of the common carotid artery. It supplies the neck, face, scalp and jaws.
external-carotid-artery.clinical: Its branches can be ligated or embolized to control severe nosebleed or facial hemorrhage.
external-carotid-artery.from: Common carotid artery, at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (about C3-C4)
external-carotid-artery.course: Ascends toward the neck of the mandible and ends within the parotid gland by dividing into the maxillary and superficial temporal arteries.

external-jugular-vein.name: External Jugular Vein
external-jugular-vein.summary: A superficial vein of the neck that crosses the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It drains the scalp and side of the face.
external-jugular-vein.clinical: It becomes visibly distended in right heart failure or raised venous pressure, and it is sometimes used for IV access.
external-jugular-vein.course: Forms near the angle of the mandible from the posterior auricular vein and the posterior division of the retromandibular vein. It descends over the sternocleidomastoid and pierces the deep fascia above the clavicle.

facial-artery.name: Facial Artery
facial-artery.summary: A branch of the external carotid artery that winds over the lower jaw and crosses the face to the eye.
facial-artery.clinical: Its pulse can be felt where it crosses the mandible at the front edge of the masseter.
facial-artery.from: External carotid artery, in the carotid triangle
facial-artery.course: Passes deep to the submandibular gland and hooks over the mandible. It then ascends across the cheek to the medial angle of the eye.

facial-vein.name: Facial Vein
facial-vein.summary: The main vein of the face. It begins as the angular vein and runs down the face behind the facial artery.
facial-vein.clinical: It has no valves and connects to the cavernous sinus, so infections of the upper lip and nose can spread intracranially.
facial-vein.into: Common facial vein (by joining the anterior division of the retromandibular vein)
facial-vein.course: Descends obliquely across the cheek, crosses the lower border of the mandible, and passes toward the angle of the jaw.

frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.name: Frontal Branch of Superficial Temporal Artery
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.summary: The front terminal branch of the superficial temporal artery. It runs up over the forehead and scalp.
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.clinical: It is a common site for biopsy in suspected temporal arteritis. Its pulse is palpable in front of the ear.
frontal-branch-of-superficial-temporal-a.course: Runs upward and forward over the temple to the forehead.
supplies: Scalp of the forehead and temple

frontal-branches-of-callosomarginal-arte.name: Frontal Branches of Callosomarginal Artery
frontal-branches-of-callosomarginal-arte.summary: Branches of the callosomarginal artery that supply the medial surface of the frontal lobe.
frontal-branches-of-callosomarginal-arte.clinical: Occlusion causes weakness and sensory loss of the opposite lower limb.
frontal-branches-of-callosomarginal-arte.course: Pass upward and forward from the cingulate sulcus onto the medial frontal lobe.

inferior-labial-artery.name: Inferior Labial Artery
inferior-labial-artery.summary: A branch of the facial artery that supplies the lower lip. It runs between the orbicularis oris muscle and the mucosa.
inferior-labial-artery.clinical: A cut lip bleeds heavily because of anastomoses between left and right arteries.
inferior-labial-artery.from: Facial artery, near the corner of the mouth
inferior-labial-artery.course: Runs medially in the lower lip. It joins the opposite artery and the mental branch of the inferior alveolar artery.

inferior-labial-veins.name: Inferior Labial Veins
inferior-labial-veins.summary: Small veins that drain the lower lip. They empty into the facial vein.
inferior-labial-veins.clinical: Lip infections can spread through the valveless facial vein system.
inferior-labial-veins.course: Run laterally from the lower lip, alongside the inferior labial artery.

inferior-ophthalmic-vein.name: Inferior Ophthalmic Vein
inferior-ophthalmic-vein.summary: A vein that begins in the floor of the orbit. It drains into the cavernous sinus or the superior ophthalmic vein.
inferior-ophthalmic-vein.clinical: It links the orbit to the pterygoid venous plexus, so face and sinus infections may spread to the cavernous sinus.
drains: Inferior rectus and inferior oblique muscles
inferior-ophthalmic-vein.into: Cavernous sinus (directly, or via the superior ophthalmic vein); a branch also joins the pterygoid venous plexus
inferior-ophthalmic-vein.course: Runs backward in the orbit floor, then passes through the superior orbital fissure or the inferior orbital fissure.

inferior-petrosal-sinus.name: Inferior Petrosal Sinus
inferior-petrosal-sinus.summary: A paired dural venous sinus that drains the cavernous sinus. It runs along the groove between the petrous temporal bone and the occipital bone.
inferior-petrosal-sinus.clinical: Sampling blood from this sinus helps find the source of ACTH in Cushing disease.
drains: Veins of the medulla and pons
inferior-petrosal-sinus.course: Runs in the petro-occipital groove to the jugular foramen and drains into the superior bulb of the internal jugular vein.

inferior-sagittal-sinus.name: Inferior Sagittal Sinus
inferior-sagittal-sinus.summary: A small midline sinus in the lower edge of the falx cerebri. It joins the great cerebral vein to form the straight sinus.
inferior-sagittal-sinus.clinical: Falx cerebri tumors or thrombosis can impair venous drainage of the medial hemispheres.
drains: Medial surface of the cerebral hemispheres
inferior-sagittal-sinus.into: Straight sinus (by joining the great cerebral vein)
inferior-sagittal-sinus.course: Runs backward in the free lower edge of the falx cerebri and ends at the tentorium, where it joins the great cerebral vein.

insular-branches-of-middle-cerebral-arte.name: Insular Branches of Middle Cerebral Artery (M2)
insular-branches-of-middle-cerebral-arte.summary: The M2 segment of the middle cerebral artery. It runs over the insula inside the lateral sulcus.
insular-branches-of-middle-cerebral-arte.clinical: M2 occlusion can cause aphasia (dominant hemisphere) or neglect, with face and arm weakness.
insular-branches-of-middle-cerebral-arte.from: Middle cerebral artery (M1 segment), usually at the limen insulae by dividing into superior and inferior trunks
insular-branches-of-middle-cerebral-arte.course: Loops over the insula within the lateral sulcus and gives branches that pass to the surface of the brain.

internal-carotid-artery.name: Internal Carotid Artery
internal-carotid-artery.summary: One of the two terminal branches of the common carotid artery. It carries blood to the brain and eye and has no branches in the neck.
internal-carotid-artery.clinical: Stenosis at its origin causes transient ischemic attack or stroke. Carotid endarterectomy treats it.
internal-carotid-artery.from: Common carotid artery, at about the C3-C4 level
internal-carotid-artery.course: Ascends in the neck, enters the carotid canal, passes through the cavernous sinus, and ends by dividing into the anterior and middle cerebral arteries.
supplies: Anterior and middle regions of the brain

internal-jugular-vein.name: Internal Jugular Vein
internal-jugular-vein.summary: The main vein draining the brain, face and neck. It lies in the carotid sheath.
internal-jugular-vein.clinical: It is used for central venous catheters, and its pressure waves reflect right heart filling pressure.
internal-jugular-vein.into: Brachiocephalic vein (by joining the subclavian vein)
internal-jugular-vein.course: Starts at the jugular foramen and descends beside the carotid arteries in the carotid sheath. It joins the subclavian vein behind the sternal end of the clavicle.

lacrimal-artery.name: Lacrimal Artery
lacrimal-artery.summary: A branch of the ophthalmic artery that supplies the lacrimal gland.
lacrimal-artery.clinical: A recurrent branch links it with the middle meningeal artery, a collateral route between the internal and external carotid systems.
lacrimal-artery.course: Runs forward along the upper edge of the lateral rectus with the lacrimal nerve to the lacrimal gland.

lateral-frontobasal-artery.name: Lateral Frontobasal Artery
lateral-frontobasal-artery.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the lower lateral surface of the frontal lobe.
lateral-frontobasal-artery.clinical: Occlusion can affect speech production in the dominant hemisphere and behavior.
lateral-frontobasal-artery.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs forward over the orbital and inferior frontal surface.

lateral-occipital-artery.name: Lateral Occipital Artery
lateral-occipital-artery.summary: A branch of the posterior cerebral artery that supplies the lower lateral surface of the occipital and temporal lobes.
lateral-occipital-artery.clinical: Occlusion of posterior cerebral branches can cause visual field loss or visual agnosia.
lateral-occipital-artery.course: Runs backward and laterally around the base of the brain to the lateral occipital surface.

lateral-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arte.name: Lateral Pontine Branches of Basilar Artery
lateral-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arte.summary: Short and long circumferential branches that wrap around the pons. They supply the lateral pons and middle cerebellar peduncle.
lateral-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arte.clinical: Occlusion causes lateral pontine syndromes, with facial weakness, ataxia and loss of pain and temperature sense.
lateral-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arte.course: Wind around the side of the pons and enter its lateral surface.

lingual-vein.name: Lingual Vein
lingual-vein.summary: Veins that drain the tongue. They include the dorsal lingual, deep lingual and sublingual veins.
lingual-vein.clinical: The deep lingual veins under the tongue absorb medicines placed under the tongue.
lingual-vein.into: Internal jugular vein (directly, or via the facial or common facial vein)
lingual-vein.course: Accompany the lingual artery and hypoglossal nerve, pass backward to the neck, and drain into the internal jugular vein.

long-posterior-ciliary-arteries.name: Long Posterior Ciliary Arteries
long-posterior-ciliary-arteries.summary: Two small arteries, medial and lateral, that supply the front part of the eye. They help form the major arterial circle of the iris.
long-posterior-ciliary-arteries.clinical: Together with the anterior ciliary arteries, they can be disrupted by eye surgery, causing anterior segment ischemia.
long-posterior-ciliary-arteries.course: Pierce the sclera beside the optic nerve and run forward between the sclera and choroid to the ciliary body.

medial-occipital-artery.name: Medial Occipital Artery
medial-occipital-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It supplies the medial occipital lobe, including the primary visual cortex.
medial-occipital-artery.clinical: Occlusion causes loss of vision in the opposite half of the visual field, often sparing the macula.
medial-occipital-artery.course: Runs backward along the medial surface of the occipital lobe and divides into the calcarine and parieto-occipital arteries.

medial-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arter.name: Medial Pontine Branches of Basilar Artery
medial-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arter.summary: Small paramedian branches that arise directly from the basilar artery. They enter the pons from its front surface.
medial-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arter.clinical: Occlusion causes medial pontine infarcts, with weakness of the opposite limbs and sometimes abducens nerve palsy.
medial-pontine-branches-of-basilar-arter.course: Penetrate the pons directly from the basilar artery along the midline.

middle-cerebral-artery-m1-segment.name: Middle Cerebral Artery (M1 Segment)
middle-cerebral-artery-m1-segment.summary: The first part of the middle cerebral artery. It runs sideways from the internal carotid artery toward the lateral sulcus.
middle-cerebral-artery-m1-segment.clinical: M1 occlusion causes a large stroke with opposite face and arm weakness and aphasia or neglect.
middle-cerebral-artery-m1-segment.course: Runs laterally in the lateral sulcus (sphenoidal segment) and divides near the insula into the M2 trunks.
supplies: Basal ganglia and internal capsule (via lateral striate arteries)

middle-cerebral-artery-m3-segment.name: Middle Cerebral Artery (M3 Segment)
middle-cerebral-artery-m3-segment.summary: The opercular part of the middle cerebral artery. Its branches run over the opercula to the surface of the lateral sulcus.
middle-cerebral-artery-m3-segment.clinical: Occlusion of M3 branches causes smaller cortical strokes, with deficits tied to the region involved.
middle-cerebral-artery-m3-segment.course: Turn out of the insula over the frontal, parietal and temporal opercula, and exit the lateral sulcus onto the cortical surface.
branches: Cortical (M4) branches to the lateral hemisphere
supplies: Opercula of the frontal, parietal and temporal lobes

middle-temporal-branch.name: Middle Temporal Branch
middle-temporal-branch.latin: Ramus temporalis medius arteriae cerebri mediae
middle-temporal-branch.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the middle part of the lateral temporal lobe.
middle-temporal-branch.clinical: Blockage of a middle cerebral artery branch can damage temporal lobe function, including hearing and language.
middle-temporal-branch.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs over the lateral surface of the temporal lobe.
supplies: Lateral surface of the temporal lobe (middle part)

occipital-artery.name: Occipital Artery
occipital-artery.summary: A branch of the external carotid artery that supplies the back of the scalp and deep neck muscles.
occipital-artery.clinical: It can bleed heavily in scalp wounds of the back of the head. The hypoglossal nerve loops around its origin.
occipital-artery.course: Passes deep to the posterior belly of digastric and the mastoid process, then runs in the scalp of the back of the head.
supplies: Scalp of the back of the head

occipital-vein.name: Occipital Vein
occipital-vein.summary: A vein that drains the scalp at the back of the head. It joins deep veins at the base of the skull.
occipital-vein.clinical: Scalp veins can carry infection into the skull through emissary veins, which have no valves.
occipital-vein.into: Suboccipital venous plexus and vertebral vein (variably the internal jugular or posterior auricular vein)
occipital-vein.course: Begins in a scalp network, pierces the trapezius, and descends to the suboccipital region.

occiptal-sinus.name: Occipital Sinus
occiptal-sinus.summary: The smallest dural venous sinus. It lies in the attached edge of the falx cerebelli.
occiptal-sinus.clinical: It is usually small, but it can be large and may cause bleeding in posterior fossa surgery.
occiptal-sinus.course: Runs in the falx cerebelli from the foramen magnum up to the confluence of sinuses. It connects with the marginal sinuses.

ophthalmic-artery.name: Ophthalmic Artery
ophthalmic-artery.summary: A branch of the internal carotid artery that supplies the eye, orbit, and parts of the forehead and nose.
ophthalmic-artery.clinical: Occlusion of its central retinal branch causes sudden painless loss of vision. Brief blockage causes amaurosis fugax.
ophthalmic-artery.from: Internal carotid artery, just after it leaves the cavernous sinus
ophthalmic-artery.course: Passes through the optic canal below and lateral to the optic nerve, then crosses the nerve in the orbit.
branches: Short and long posterior ciliary arteries
supplies: Ethmoid air cells and nasal cavity

orbitofrontal-branches-of-anterior-cereb.name: Orbitofrontal Branches of Anterior Cerebral Artery
orbitofrontal-branches-of-anterior-cereb.summary: Cortical branches of the anterior cerebral artery. They supply the orbital (undersurface) part of the frontal lobe.
orbitofrontal-branches-of-anterior-cereb.clinical: Anterior cerebral artery stroke can cause weakness of the opposite leg and changes in behavior.
orbitofrontal-branches-of-anterior-cereb.course: Run forward and downward from the anterior cerebral artery to the orbital surface of the frontal lobe.
supplies: Medial orbital surface of the frontal lobe

parieto-occipital-artery.name: Parieto-occipital Artery
parieto-occipital-artery.summary: A cortical branch of the posterior cerebral artery. It runs in the parieto-occipital sulcus on the medial brain surface.
parieto-occipital-artery.clinical: Posterior cerebral artery stroke causes loss of vision in the opposite visual field, often sparing central vision.
parieto-occipital-artery.course: Runs along the parieto-occipital sulcus on the medial surface of the hemisphere.

pericallosal-artery.name: Pericallosal Artery
pericallosal-artery.summary: The part of the anterior cerebral artery that curves around the corpus callosum. It supplies the medial brain surface.
pericallosal-artery.clinical: Aneurysms of the anterior cerebral artery can occur here. Stroke causes opposite leg weakness.
pericallosal-artery.from: Anterior cerebral artery (beyond the anterior communicating artery)
pericallosal-artery.course: Runs in the callosal sulcus above the corpus callosum, back toward the splenium.

posterior-auricular-vein.name: Posterior Auricular Vein
posterior-auricular-vein.summary: A small vein behind the ear. It joins the posterior division of the retromandibular vein to form the external jugular vein.
posterior-auricular-vein.clinical: It is a landmark for the start of the external jugular vein, which is useful for emergency IV access.
drains: Scalp behind and above the ear
posterior-auricular-vein.into: External jugular vein (with the posterior division of the retromandibular vein)
posterior-auricular-vein.course: Begins in a scalp network behind the ear and descends in front of the mastoid process.

posterior-cerebral-artery.name: Posterior Cerebral Artery
posterior-cerebral-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the basilar artery. It supplies the occipital lobe, the inferior temporal lobe, and parts of the thalamus.
posterior-cerebral-artery.clinical: Stroke here causes loss of vision in the opposite visual field, often sparing central vision.
posterior-cerebral-artery.course: Passes around the midbrain, joined by the posterior communicating artery, then runs above the tentorium to the occipital lobe.

posterior-communicating-artery.name: Posterior Communicating Artery
posterior-communicating-artery.summary: A short artery that joins the internal carotid artery to the posterior cerebral artery. It is part of the cerebral arterial circle.
posterior-communicating-artery.clinical: Aneurysms at its origin can press on the oculomotor nerve, causing a drooping eyelid and a dilated pupil.
posterior-communicating-artery.course: Runs backward above the oculomotor nerve to join the posterior cerebral artery.

posterior-division-of-retromandibular-ve.name: Posterior Division of Retromandibular Vein
posterior-division-of-retromandibular-ve.summary: The rear branch of the retromandibular vein. It joins the posterior auricular vein to form the external jugular vein.
posterior-division-of-retromandibular-ve.clinical: The external jugular vein it forms is visible in the neck and is used for IV access.
drains: Superficial temporal and maxillary territory (via the parent vein)
posterior-division-of-retromandibular-ve.into: External jugular vein (with the posterior auricular vein)
posterior-division-of-retromandibular-ve.course: Leaves the retromandibular vein near the lower parotid gland and descends over the sternocleidomastoid.

posterior-ethmoidal-artery.name: Posterior Ethmoidal Artery
posterior-ethmoidal-artery.summary: A small branch of the ophthalmic artery. It supplies the posterior ethmoid air cells and the upper nasal cavity.
posterior-ethmoidal-artery.clinical: It is smaller than the anterior ethmoidal artery and is a less common source of nosebleeds.
posterior-ethmoidal-artery.course: Passes through the posterior ethmoidal foramen between the orbit and the ethmoid sinuses.
supplies: Dura of the anterior cranial fossa
Upper nasal septum and lateral nasal wall

posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.name: Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery
posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.summary: The largest branch of the vertebral artery. It supplies the underside of the cerebellum and the lateral medulla.
posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.clinical: Blockage can cause lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome, with vertigo, hoarseness, and loss of pain and temperature sense.
posterior-inferior-cerebellar-artery.course: Loops around the medulla, then runs to the underside of the cerebellum.
branches: Choroidal branch to the fourth ventricle
supplies: Choroid plexus of the fourth ventricle

posterior-intercavernous-sinus.name: Posterior Intercavernous Sinus
posterior-intercavernous-sinus.summary: A small dural venous channel that links the two cavernous sinuses behind the pituitary gland.
posterior-intercavernous-sinus.clinical: It can bleed during pituitary surgery through the sphenoid sinus.
posterior-intercavernous-sinus.course: Crosses the midline in the dura behind the pituitary stalk. With the anterior channel it forms the circular sinus.

posterior-parietal-artery.name: Posterior Parietal Artery
posterior-parietal-artery.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the posterior part of the lateral parietal lobe.
posterior-parietal-artery.clinical: Stroke here can cause problems with spatial awareness and body image.
posterior-parietal-artery.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs over the posterior parietal surface.

posterior-temporal-branch.name: Posterior Temporal Branch
posterior-temporal-branch.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the posterior part of the lateral temporal lobe.
posterior-temporal-branch.clinical: Blockage can cause fluent aphasia, because the nearby posterior temporal cortex is involved in understanding speech.
posterior-temporal-branch.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs backward over the lateral temporal lobe.
supplies: Posterior superior and middle temporal gyri

prefrontal-artery.name: Prefrontal Artery
prefrontal-artery.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the lateral frontal lobe in front of the motor cortex.
prefrontal-artery.clinical: Stroke in this area can impair speech output, planning, and judgment.
prefrontal-artery.course: Emerges from the lateral sulcus and runs forward over the lateral surface of the frontal lobe.
supplies: Inferior and middle frontal gyri (prefrontal cortex)

proximal-lateral-striate-branches.name: Proximal Lateral Striate (Lenticulostriate) Branches
proximal-lateral-striate-branches.summary: Small penetrating branches from the first part of the middle cerebral artery. They supply deep structures of the brain.
proximal-lateral-striate-branches.clinical: These thin arteries often rupture or block in hypertension, causing deep brain hemorrhage or small lacunar strokes.
proximal-lateral-striate-branches.course: Arise from the first segment and pass upward through the anterior perforated substance.
supplies: Head and body of the caudate nucleus

retromandibular-vein.name: Retromandibular Vein
retromandibular-vein.summary: A vein within the parotid gland formed by the superficial temporal and maxillary veins. It divides into two branches below the gland.
retromandibular-vein.clinical: It lies within the parotid gland, so it is a landmark during parotid surgery.
retromandibular-vein.into: Splits into anterior division (to the facial vein) and posterior division (to the external jugular vein)
retromandibular-vein.course: Descends through the parotid gland, deep to the facial nerve and superficial to the external carotid artery.

septal-branches-of-posterior-ethmoidal-a.name: Septal Branches of Posterior Ethmoidal Artery
septal-branches-of-posterior-ethmoidal-a.summary: Small branches of the posterior ethmoidal artery that supply the upper part of the nasal septum.
septal-branches-of-posterior-ethmoidal-a.clinical: They contribute to the blood supply of the nasal septum and can be a source of upper nosebleeds.
septal-branches-of-posterior-ethmoidal-a.course: Enter the nasal cavity through the roof and descend on the nasal septum.

short-posterior-ciliary-arteries.name: Short Posterior Ciliary Arteries
short-posterior-ciliary-arteries.summary: Several small arteries that pierce the back of the eyeball around the optic nerve. They supply the choroid.
short-posterior-ciliary-arteries.clinical: Poor flow here can cause optic nerve ischemia. Giant cell arteritis can cause sudden vision loss this way.
short-posterior-ciliary-arteries.course: Run forward along the optic nerve and pierce the sclera near its entry.

sigmoid-sinus.name: Sigmoid Sinus
sigmoid-sinus.summary: An S-shaped dural sinus that continues from the transverse sinus. It ends at the jugular foramen as the internal jugular vein.
sigmoid-sinus.clinical: Middle ear or mastoid infection can spread to the sinus and cause thrombosis.
sigmoid-sinus.course: Runs in a groove on the inner surface of the mastoid part of the temporal bone to the jugular foramen.

straight-sinus.name: Straight Sinus
straight-sinus.summary: An unpaired dural sinus that runs where the falx cerebri meets the tentorium cerebelli. It drains deep brain veins.
straight-sinus.clinical: It is a deep, midline sinus that can be affected by thrombosis, causing deep brain swelling.
straight-sinus.into: Confluence of sinuses (usually the left transverse sinus)
straight-sinus.course: Runs backward and downward along the midline junction of the falx and tentorium.

submental-artery.name: Submental Artery
submental-artery.summary: A branch of the facial artery in the neck. It runs along the underside of the jaw to supply the chin.
submental-artery.clinical: Surgeons use it as a blood supply for a submental skin flap.
submental-artery.course: Runs forward on the mylohyoid muscle below the mandible to the chin.

submental-vein.name: Submental Vein
submental-vein.summary: A vein that drains the chin and the area under the jaw. It joins the facial vein.
submental-vein.clinical: It is a tributary of the facial vein and may be involved in spread of infection from the lower face.
submental-vein.course: Runs backward beneath the chin and below the mandible.

superficial-temporal-artery.name: Superficial Temporal Artery
superficial-temporal-artery.summary: The smaller terminal branch of the external carotid artery. It supplies the scalp of the temple and side of the head.
superficial-temporal-artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt in front of the ear. It is inflamed in giant cell arteritis and used for biopsy.
superficial-temporal-artery.from: External carotid artery (terminal branch, in the parotid gland)
superficial-temporal-artery.course: Passes behind the mandibular neck, climbs in front of the ear, and divides into frontal and parietal branches.
supplies: Scalp of the temple and top of the head

superficial-temporal-veins.name: Superficial Temporal Veins
superficial-temporal-veins.summary: Veins that drain the scalp over the temple and forehead. They join the maxillary vein to form the retromandibular vein.
superficial-temporal-veins.clinical: Scalp veins have no valves, so infection can spread inward through emissary veins.
drains: Scalp of the temple and top of the head
superficial-temporal-veins.course: Descend in front of the ear, joined by tributaries from the scalp, and enter the parotid gland.

superior-cerebellar-artery.name: Superior Cerebellar Artery
superior-cerebellar-artery.summary: A branch of the basilar artery near its end. It supplies the top of the cerebellum and parts of the midbrain and pons.
superior-cerebellar-artery.clinical: It often loops near the trigeminal nerve, and compression there can cause trigeminal neuralgia.
superior-cerebellar-artery.course: Passes below the oculomotor nerve and around the midbrain to the top of the cerebellum.
branches: Branches to the pons and midbrain

superior-labial-artery.name: Superior Labial Artery
superior-labial-artery.summary: A branch of the facial artery near the mouth. It supplies the upper lip and part of the nose.
superior-labial-artery.clinical: Both lip arteries join in a ring, so a cut lip bleeds from both ends. Pinching the lip controls bleeding.
superior-labial-artery.from: Facial artery (at the angle of the mouth)
superior-labial-artery.course: Runs in the upper lip between the orbicularis oris muscle and the mucosa.

superior-labial-vein.name: Superior Labial Vein
superior-labial-vein.summary: A vein that drains the upper lip. It empties into the facial vein.
superior-labial-vein.clinical: It lies in the danger triangle of the face, where infection can reach the cavernous sinus.
superior-labial-vein.course: Runs in the upper lip and joins the facial vein near the mouth.

superior-ophtalmic-vein.name: Superior Ophthalmic Vein
superior-ophtalmic-vein.summary: The main vein of the orbit. It links the veins of the face to the cavernous sinus.
superior-ophtalmic-vein.clinical: It has no valves, so face infection can spread to the cavernous sinus through it.
drains: Forehead and root of the nose
superior-ophtalmic-vein.course: Starts near the root of the nose, runs through the orbit, and passes the superior orbital fissure.

superior-ophthalmic-vein.name: Superior Ophthalmic Vein
superior-ophthalmic-vein.summary: The main vein of the orbit. It links the veins of the face to the cavernous sinus.
superior-ophthalmic-vein.clinical: It has no valves, so face infection can spread to the cavernous sinus through it.
drains: Forehead and root of the nose
superior-ophthalmic-vein.course: Starts near the root of the nose, runs through the orbit, and passes the superior orbital fissure.

superior-petrosal-sinus.name: Superior Petrosal Sinus
superior-petrosal-sinus.summary: A small dural sinus that runs along the top of the petrous temporal bone. It links the cavernous sinus to the transverse sinus.
superior-petrosal-sinus.clinical: Infection in the cavernous sinus can spread backward through it to the transverse and sigmoid sinuses.
superior-petrosal-sinus.into: Transverse sinus (at the junction with the sigmoid sinus)
superior-petrosal-sinus.course: Runs along the attached edge of the tentorium cerebelli on the petrous ridge.

superior-sagittal-sinus.name: Superior Sagittal Sinus
superior-sagittal-sinus.summary: A large midline dural sinus along the top of the falx cerebri. It collects blood from the cerebral hemispheres.
superior-sagittal-sinus.clinical: Thrombosis can cause raised intracranial pressure and headache. Arachnoid granulations here return cerebrospinal fluid to the blood.
superior-sagittal-sinus.into: Confluence of sinuses (usually the right transverse sinus)
superior-sagittal-sinus.course: Runs from the crista galli to the internal occipital protuberance in the midline.

superior-thyroid-vein.name: Superior Thyroid Vein
superior-thyroid-vein.summary: A vein that drains the upper part of the thyroid gland. It accompanies the superior thyroid artery.
superior-thyroid-vein.clinical: Surgeons tie it early in thyroid removal to control bleeding.
superior-thyroid-vein.into: Internal jugular vein (sometimes the facial vein)
superior-thyroid-vein.course: Leaves the upper pole of the thyroid and runs upward with the superior thyroid artery.

supra-orbital-arter.name: Supra-orbital Artery
supra-orbital-arter.summary: A branch of the ophthalmic artery. It leaves the orbit with the supra-orbital nerve to supply the forehead and scalp.
supra-orbital-arter.clinical: Forehead cuts near the eyebrow can bleed heavily from this artery.
supra-orbital-arter.course: Runs along the roof of the orbit and exits through the supra-orbital notch or foramen.

supra-orbital-artery.name: Supra-orbital Artery
supra-orbital-artery.summary: A branch of the ophthalmic artery. It leaves the orbit with the supra-orbital nerve to supply the forehead and scalp.
supra-orbital-artery.clinical: Forehead cuts near the eyebrow can bleed heavily from this artery.
supra-orbital-artery.course: Runs along the roof of the orbit and exits through the supra-orbital notch or foramen.

supratrochlear-artery.name: Supratrochlear Artery
supratrochlear-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the ophthalmic artery. It leaves the orbit at its inner upper corner to supply the forehead.
supratrochlear-artery.clinical: Injected filler can enter it and cause skin loss or, rarely, vision loss in the glabella area.
supratrochlear-artery.course: Leaves the orbit above the trochlea with the supratrochlear nerve and ascends over the forehead.

temporo-occipital-branch.name: Temporo-occipital Branch
temporo-occipital-branch.summary: A cortical branch of the middle cerebral artery. It supplies the area where the temporal and occipital lobes meet.
temporo-occipital-branch.clinical: Stroke here can cause visual field loss and trouble with reading or naming.
temporo-occipital-branch.course: Runs backward from the lateral sulcus over the posterior temporal lobe toward the occipital lobe.

transverse-facial-artery.name: Transverse Facial Artery
transverse-facial-artery.summary: A branch of the superficial temporal artery. It crosses the cheek below the zygomatic arch.
transverse-facial-artery.clinical: It is a landmark during facial surgery and lies close to the parotid duct and facial nerve branches.
transverse-facial-artery.from: Superficial temporal artery (within the parotid gland)
transverse-facial-artery.course: Passes forward across the masseter, above the parotid duct, below the zygomatic arch.

transverse-sinus.name: Transverse Sinus
transverse-sinus.summary: A paired dural sinus along the back edge of the tentorium cerebelli. It runs from the confluence of sinuses to the sigmoid sinus.
transverse-sinus.clinical: The right transverse sinus is often larger. Thrombosis raises intracranial pressure and may cause swelling of the optic disc.
transverse-sinus.course: Runs in a groove along the occipital bone, in the attached edge of the tentorium.

vertebral-artery.name: Vertebral Artery
vertebral-artery.summary: The first branch of the subclavian artery. It ascends through the neck to supply the brainstem, cerebellum, and spinal cord.
vertebral-artery.clinical: Neck injury or manipulation can tear it. Reduced flow causes dizziness, double vision, and fainting.
vertebral-artery.course: Ascends through the transverse foramina of C6 to C1, loops over the atlas, and enters the skull through the foramen magnum.
branches: Basilar artery (union with the other side)

vertebral-vein.name: Vertebral Vein
vertebral-vein.summary: A vein that forms around the first cervical vertebra and descends beside the vertebral artery. It drains deep neck structures.
vertebral-vein.clinical: It is a small channel, but it joins the vertebral venous system that links the neck to the spine.
vertebral-vein.course: Descends through the transverse foramina of C1 to C6 as a plexus around the vertebral artery. It then joins the brachiocephalic vein.

anterior-tibial-artery.name: Anterior Tibial Artery
anterior-tibial-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the popliteal artery. It supplies the anterior compartment of the leg and continues as the dorsalis pedis artery.
anterior-tibial-artery.clinical: Swelling in the tight anterior compartment can compress it and cause compartment syndrome.
anterior-tibial-artery.from: Popliteal artery (at the lower border of popliteus)
anterior-tibial-artery.course: Passes through a gap above the interosseous membrane, then descends on the membrane with the deep fibular nerve.
supplies: Anterior compartment muscles of the leg

anterior-tibial-veins.name: Anterior Tibial Veins
anterior-tibial-veins.summary: Paired deep veins that accompany the anterior tibial artery. They drain the front of the leg and the top of the foot.
anterior-tibial-veins.clinical: Deep vein thrombosis can start in the deep leg veins and may travel to the lungs.
drains: Dorsum of the foot (via the dorsal veins of the foot)
anterior-tibial-veins.into: Popliteal vein (with the posterior tibial veins)
anterior-tibial-veins.course: Ascend on the interosseous membrane beside the artery, then pass through its upper gap.

arcuate-artery.name: Arcuate Artery
arcuate-artery.summary: A branch of the dorsalis pedis artery that arches across the bases of the metatarsal bones on the top of the foot.
arcuate-artery.clinical: It links the dorsal arteries of the foot and helps keep blood flow if one route is blocked.
arcuate-artery.course: Runs laterally across the bases of the metatarsals, deep to the extensor tendons.
branches: Second, third, and fourth dorsal metatarsal arteries

calcaneal-branches-of-fibular-artery.name: Calcaneal Branches of Fibular Artery
calcaneal-branches-of-fibular-artery.summary: Small terminal branches of the fibular artery. They supply the lateral and back parts of the heel.
calcaneal-branches-of-fibular-artery.clinical: They join the heel network, which can keep the heel supplied if one source is damaged.
calcaneal-branches-of-fibular-artery.course: Pass behind the lateral malleolus to the heel.
supplies: Skin and fat of the lateral heel

calcaneal-branches-of-posterior-tibial-a.name: Calcaneal Branches of Posterior Tibial Artery
calcaneal-branches-of-posterior-tibial-a.summary: Small branches of the posterior tibial artery. They supply the inner side and heel fat pad.
calcaneal-branches-of-posterior-tibial-a.clinical: Heel pain and heel ulcers depend on this supply. Poor blood flow slows healing.
calcaneal-branches-of-posterior-tibial-a.course: Pass behind the medial malleolus and down to the heel.
supplies: Medial heel skin and fat pad

deep-external-pudendal-artery.name: Deep External Pudendal Artery
deep-external-pudendal-artery.summary: A small branch of the femoral artery. It supplies the skin of the external genitalia.
deep-external-pudendal-artery.clinical: It is at risk of injury during groin surgery or when the femoral vessels are exposed.
deep-external-pudendal-artery.course: Passes medially across the pectineus and adductor longus, then pierces the deep fascia to reach the perineum.
supplies: Skin of the scrotum or labium majus

deep-femoral-artery.name: Deep Femoral Artery
deep-femoral-artery.summary: The largest branch of the femoral artery. It supplies the thigh muscles and the femur.
deep-femoral-artery.clinical: It is the main route of blood flow to the thigh if the femoral artery is blocked below its origin.
deep-femoral-artery.from: Femoral artery (in the femoral triangle, about 3 to 5 cm below the inguinal ligament)
deep-femoral-artery.course: Passes behind the adductor longus and descends between it and the adductor magnus.
supplies: Muscles of all three thigh compartments

deep-femoral-vein.name: Deep Femoral Vein
deep-femoral-vein.summary: A large deep vein that drains the thigh muscles. It joins the femoral vein in the femoral triangle.
deep-femoral-vein.clinical: It can be a site for deep vein thrombosis after long immobility or hip surgery.
deep-femoral-vein.course: Runs with the deep femoral artery in front of the adductor muscles and joins the femoral vein below the inguinal ligament.

deep-plantar-artery.name: Deep Plantar Artery
deep-plantar-artery.summary: A terminal branch of the dorsalis pedis artery. It passes into the sole and completes the plantar arch.
deep-plantar-artery.clinical: It links the blood supply of the top and the sole of the foot.
deep-plantar-artery.course: Passes between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle into the sole.

descending-branch-of-lateral-circumflex-.name: Descending Branch of Lateral Circumflex Femoral Artery
descending-branch-of-lateral-circumflex-.latin: Ramus descendens arteriae circumflexae femoris lateralis
descending-branch-of-lateral-circumflex-.summary: A branch of the lateral circumflex femoral artery. It runs down the front of the thigh on the vastus lateralis.
descending-branch-of-lateral-circumflex-.clinical: Surgeons use it as the blood supply for the anterolateral thigh free flap.
descending-branch-of-lateral-circumflex-.course: Descends on the vastus lateralis beside the nerve to that muscle, toward the knee.

dorsal-digital-veins-of-foot.name: Dorsal Digital Veins of Foot
dorsal-digital-veins-of-foot.summary: Small veins on the top of the toes. They drain into the dorsal metatarsal veins.
dorsal-digital-veins-of-foot.clinical: They are small superficial veins that can be used for IV access in the foot.
dorsal-digital-veins-of-foot.course: Run along the sides of each toe and join near the web spaces.

dorsal-metatarsal-arteries.name: Dorsal Metatarsal Arteries
dorsal-metatarsal-arteries.summary: Four small arteries that run along the metatarsal spaces on the top of the foot. They give branches to the toes.
dorsal-metatarsal-arteries.clinical: They carry blood to the toes and join plantar vessels through perforating branches.
dorsal-metatarsal-arteries.from: Arcuate artery (second to fourth); dorsalis pedis (first)
dorsal-metatarsal-arteries.course: Run forward on the dorsal interosseous muscles and divide into dorsal digital arteries.
branches: Perforating branches to the plantar arteries

dorsal-metatarsal-veins.name: Dorsal Metatarsal Veins
dorsal-metatarsal-veins.summary: Veins that run along the metatarsal spaces on the top of the foot. They drain into the dorsal venous arch.
dorsal-metatarsal-veins.clinical: These small veins are part of the dorsal venous network, which is used to start leg bypass or IV access.
dorsal-metatarsal-veins.into: Dorsal venous arch of the foot
dorsal-metatarsal-veins.course: Run backward along the metatarsal spaces to the arch.

dorsal-venous-arch-of-foot.name: Dorsal Venous Arch of Foot
dorsal-venous-arch-of-foot.summary: A network of veins across the top of the foot. It feeds both saphenous veins.
dorsal-venous-arch-of-foot.clinical: It is visible on the top of the foot and a common site for IV placement.
dorsal-venous-arch-of-foot.into: Great saphenous vein (medially) and small saphenous vein (laterally)
dorsal-venous-arch-of-foot.course: Runs across the foot over the metatarsal bases. Its medial end continues as the great saphenous vein.

dorsalis-pedis-artery.name: Dorsalis Pedis Artery
dorsalis-pedis-artery.summary: The continuation of the anterior tibial artery on the top of the foot. It supplies the dorsum of the foot.
dorsalis-pedis-artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon. It is absent in a small percentage of normal people.
dorsalis-pedis-artery.from: Anterior tibial artery (at the ankle, midway between the malleoli)
dorsalis-pedis-artery.course: Runs forward lateral to the extensor hallucis longus tendon to the first metatarsal space.

external-pudendal-vein.name: External Pudendal Vein
external-pudendal-vein.summary: Veins that drain the skin of the external genitalia. They empty into the great saphenous vein.
external-pudendal-vein.clinical: They are tributaries of the great saphenous vein near the saphenous opening, a landmark in varicose vein surgery.
drains: Skin of the scrotum or labia
external-pudendal-vein.into: Great saphenous vein (near the saphenous opening)
external-pudendal-vein.course: Run laterally across the groin to join the great saphenous vein.

femoral-artery.name: Femoral Artery
femoral-artery.summary: The main artery of the thigh. It continues the external iliac artery below the inguinal ligament.
femoral-artery.clinical: Its pulse is felt at the mid-inguinal point. It is a common site for catheter access to the heart.
femoral-artery.from: External iliac artery (at the inguinal ligament)
femoral-artery.course: Runs down through the femoral triangle and the adductor canal. It becomes the popliteal artery at the adductor hiatus.
supplies: Rest of the lower limb (via its continuation)

femoral-vein.name: Femoral Vein
femoral-vein.summary: The main deep vein of the thigh. It carries blood from the lower limb to the external iliac vein.
femoral-vein.clinical: It is a common site of deep vein thrombosis. It lies medial to the femoral artery, so keep the order in mind during punctures.
femoral-vein.into: External iliac vein (at the inguinal ligament)
femoral-vein.course: Starts at the adductor hiatus and ascends through the adductor canal and femoral triangle, medial to the artery.

fibular-artery.name: Fibular Artery
fibular-artery.summary: A large branch of the posterior tibial artery. It supplies the lateral compartment and the back of the leg.
fibular-artery.clinical: Surgeons use the fibula with this artery as a free flap to rebuild the jaw.
fibular-artery.from: Posterior tibial artery (about 2 to 3 cm below popliteus)
fibular-artery.course: Descends deep in the posterior compartment, close to the fibula and behind the flexor hallucis longus.

fibular-veins.name: Fibular Veins
fibular-veins.summary: Paired deep veins that accompany the fibular artery. They drain the lateral and deep back muscles of the leg.
fibular-veins.clinical: Calf deep vein thrombosis often involves these veins.
fibular-veins.course: Run beside the fibular artery and join the posterior tibial veins.

genicular-veins.name: Genicular Veins
genicular-veins.summary: Small veins that accompany the genicular arteries. They drain the knee joint and its capsule.
genicular-veins.clinical: They are small and can bleed after knee replacement or knee arthroscopy.
genicular-veins.course: Accompany the genicular arteries around the knee and join the popliteal vein.

great-saphenous-vein.name: Great Saphenous Vein
great-saphenous-vein.group: Superficial veins of the lower limb
great-saphenous-vein.summary: The longest vein in the body. It runs up the inner leg and thigh to join the femoral vein.
great-saphenous-vein.clinical: Varicose veins often arise here. Surgeons use it as a bypass graft, and it is used for IV cutdown at the ankle.
drains: Lower abdominal wall and external genitalia
great-saphenous-vein.course: Starts in front of the medial malleolus, ascends behind the medial knee and along the medial thigh.

inferior-lateral-genicular-artery.name: Inferior Lateral Genicular Artery
inferior-lateral-genicular-artery.summary: A branch of the popliteal artery that supplies the outer side of the knee joint.
inferior-lateral-genicular-artery.clinical: It lies close to the lateral meniscus and can be injured in knee surgery.
inferior-lateral-genicular-artery.course: Passes laterally below the lateral head of gastrocnemius and deep to the lateral collateral ligament.

inferior-medial-genicular-artery.name: Inferior Medial Genicular Artery
inferior-medial-genicular-artery.summary: A branch of the popliteal artery that supplies the inner side of the knee joint.
inferior-medial-genicular-artery.clinical: It lies near the medial tibial condyle and can bleed during knee surgery.
inferior-medial-genicular-artery.course: Passes medially below the medial tibial condyle, deep to the medial collateral ligament.

lateral-circumflex-femoral-artery.name: Lateral Circumflex Femoral Artery
lateral-circumflex-femoral-artery.summary: A branch of the deep femoral artery. It wraps around the upper thigh to supply the lateral thigh muscles and hip.
lateral-circumflex-femoral-artery.clinical: It supplies a major flap used in reconstruction, and can bleed in hip fractures.
lateral-circumflex-femoral-artery.from: Deep femoral artery (sometimes the femoral artery)
lateral-circumflex-femoral-artery.course: Passes laterally behind sartorius and rectus femoris, between the branches of the femoral nerve.

lateral-circumflex-femoral-veins.name: Lateral Circumflex Femoral Veins
lateral-circumflex-femoral-veins.summary: Veins that accompany the lateral circumflex femoral artery. They drain the lateral thigh muscles.
lateral-circumflex-femoral-veins.clinical: They are part of the deep venous system and can be involved in thigh vein thrombosis.
lateral-circumflex-femoral-veins.course: Run beside the artery and join the femoral vein in the femoral triangle.

lateral-plantar-artery.name: Lateral Plantar Artery
lateral-plantar-artery.summary: The larger terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery. It supplies the outer sole and forms the plantar arch.
lateral-plantar-artery.clinical: Poor flow here contributes to foot ulcers in diabetes.
lateral-plantar-artery.from: Posterior tibial artery (behind the medial malleolus)
lateral-plantar-artery.course: Runs laterally and forward between flexor digitorum brevis and quadratus plantae, then arches medially.

lateral-plantar-veins.name: Lateral Plantar Veins
lateral-plantar-veins.summary: Deep veins in the outer sole. They accompany the lateral plantar artery and drain the sole.
lateral-plantar-veins.clinical: They are involved in the foot pump that helps push blood up the leg.
lateral-plantar-veins.course: Run with the lateral plantar artery and join the medial plantar veins behind the medial malleolus.

lateral-tarsal-artery.name: Lateral Tarsal Artery
lateral-tarsal-artery.summary: A branch of the dorsalis pedis artery. It supplies the outer part of the tarsal region.
lateral-tarsal-artery.clinical: It adds to the collateral network around the ankle and foot.
lateral-tarsal-artery.course: Runs laterally under the extensor digitorum brevis.

medial-circumflex-femoral-artery.name: Medial Circumflex Femoral Artery
medial-circumflex-femoral-artery.summary: A branch of the deep femoral artery. It wraps around the femoral neck and is the main supply of the femoral head.
medial-circumflex-femoral-artery.clinical: A femoral neck fracture can tear it, leading to death of the femoral head (avascular necrosis).
medial-circumflex-femoral-artery.from: Deep femoral artery (sometimes the femoral artery)
medial-circumflex-femoral-artery.course: Passes backward between pectineus and psoas, then between obturator externus and adductor brevis.
branches: Retinacular arteries to the femoral neck

medial-plantar-artery.name: Medial Plantar Artery
medial-plantar-artery.summary: The smaller terminal branch of the posterior tibial artery. It supplies the inner sole and the great toe.
medial-plantar-artery.clinical: A pulse here is hard to feel. Poor flow can add to foot ischemia.
medial-plantar-artery.from: Posterior tibial artery (behind the medial malleolus)
medial-plantar-artery.course: Runs forward under the abductor hallucis, then splits into superficial and deep branches.

medial-plantar-veins.name: Medial Plantar Veins
medial-plantar-veins.summary: Deep veins in the inner sole. They accompany the medial plantar artery and drain the sole.
medial-plantar-veins.clinical: They are part of the deep calf and foot pump system.
medial-plantar-veins.course: Run with the medial plantar artery and join the lateral plantar veins behind the medial malleolus.

middle-genicular-artery.name: Middle Genicular Artery
middle-genicular-artery.summary: A branch of the popliteal artery. It pierces the back of the knee capsule to supply the inside of the joint.
middle-genicular-artery.clinical: It supplies the cruciate ligaments, which have limited blood supply and heal poorly.
middle-genicular-artery.course: Pierces the oblique popliteal ligament and enters the knee joint.

patellar-anastomosis.name: Patellar Anastomosis
patellar-anastomosis.summary: A network of arteries around the kneecap. Many genicular and other branches join to form it.
patellar-anastomosis.clinical: It gives a backup route of blood flow if the popliteal artery is blocked or injured.
patellar-anastomosis.from: Genicular arteries, descending genicular artery, anterior tibial recurrent artery, and lateral circumflex femoral artery
patellar-anastomosis.course: Lies on the front of the knee over the patella and the patellar ligament.

perforating-femoral-arteries.name: Perforating Femoral Arteries
perforating-femoral-arteries.summary: Three or four branches of the deep femoral artery that pierce the adductor magnus. They supply the back of the thigh.
perforating-femoral-arteries.clinical: A thigh fracture or surgery near the linea aspera can injure them and cause bleeding.
perforating-femoral-arteries.course: Pierce the adductor magnus close to the femur to reach the posterior thigh.

perforating-veins.name: Perforating Veins
perforating-veins.summary: Veins that pass through the deep fascia. They connect the superficial veins to the deep veins.
perforating-veins.clinical: Valves in them direct blood inward. When valves fail, pressure causes varicose veins and venous ulcers.
perforating-veins.into: Deep veins (femoral or deep femoral vein)
perforating-veins.course: Pierce the deep fascia and drain blood from the superficial system into the deep system.

plantar-arch.name: Plantar Arch
plantar-arch.summary: An arterial arch in the sole of the foot. It is formed mainly by the lateral plantar artery and completed by the deep plantar artery.
plantar-arch.clinical: It gives a collateral link between the dorsal and plantar blood supply of the foot.
plantar-arch.from: Lateral plantar artery (joined by the deep plantar artery)
plantar-arch.course: Arches medially across the bases of the metatarsals deep to the oblique head of the adductor hallucis.

plantar-metatarsal-arteries.name: Plantar Metatarsal Arteries
plantar-metatarsal-arteries.summary: Four arteries arising from the plantar arch. They run forward along the metatarsal spaces in the sole.
plantar-metatarsal-arteries.clinical: They supply the toes and can be affected by small vessel disease in diabetes.
plantar-metatarsal-arteries.course: Run forward on the interosseous muscles and divide into plantar digital arteries.
branches: Perforating branches to the dorsal metatarsal arteries

plantar-metatarsal-veins.name: Plantar Metatarsal Veins
