lateral-vein-of-right-lung.name: Lateral Vein of Right Lung
lateral-vein-of-right-lung.latin: Vena lateralis lobi medii pulmonis dextri
lateral-vein-of-right-lung.summary: A tributary of the middle lobe vein. It drains the lateral segment of the right middle lobe.
drains: Lateral segment of the right middle lobe
lateral-vein-of-right-lung.into: Middle lobe vein, then the right superior pulmonary vein
lateral-vein-of-right-lung.course: Runs in the septa between lung segments toward the hilum and joins the medial vein.
lateral-vein-of-right-lung.clinical: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. Middle lobe resection divides the middle lobe vein.

left-atrium.name: Left Atrium
left-atrium.summary: The heart chamber that receives oxygenated blood from the lungs. It forms most of the base (back) of the heart.
left-atrium.location: Posterior part of the heart, directly in front of the esophagus and behind the aortic root.
function: Receives oxygenated blood from four pulmonary veins
Pumps blood through the mitral valve into the left ventricle
blood: Atrial branches of the circumflex artery
Atrial branches of the right coronary artery
left-atrium.nerve: Cardiac plexus (sympathetic fibers from T1 to T4 and vagal fibers)
parts: Smooth posterior wall with four pulmonary vein openings
Interatrial septum with valve of the foramen ovale
left-atrium.clinical: Atrial fibrillation can form clots in the left atrial appendage, causing stroke. A large atrium can press on the esophagus.

left-brachiocephalic-vein.name: Left Brachiocephalic Vein
left-brachiocephalic-vein.summary: The longer of the two brachiocephalic veins. It crosses the upper chest to join the right one and form the superior vena cava.
drains: Left superior intercostal, inferior thyroid, internal thoracic, thymic, and pericardial veins
left-brachiocephalic-vein.into: Superior vena cava, behind the right first costal cartilage
left-brachiocephalic-vein.course: Forms behind the left sternoclavicular joint, passes obliquely right behind the manubrium and in front of the three arch branches and the trachea.
left-brachiocephalic-vein.clinical: An aortic arch aneurysm can compress it. The thoracic duct enters the venous system at its origin, the left venous angle.

left-common-carotid-artery.name: Left Common Carotid Artery
left-common-carotid-artery.summary: The second branch of the aortic arch. It supplies the left side of the head and neck.
left-common-carotid-artery.course: Ascends through the superior mediastinum to the left sternoclavicular joint, then runs in the carotid sheath beside the trachea to the upper thyroid cartilage.
supplies: Left side of the head and neck, brain, and face through its terminal branches
left-common-carotid-artery.clinical: The carotid pulse can be felt at the level of C6. Atherosclerosis at its bifurcation is a major cause of stroke.

left-coronary-artery.name: Left Coronary Artery
left-coronary-artery.summary: The artery that arises from the left aortic sinus. It divides into the anterior interventricular and circumflex arteries.
left-coronary-artery.from: Left aortic sinus of the ascending aorta
left-coronary-artery.course: Passes as a short main stem (1 to 2.5 cm) between the pulmonary trunk and left auricle, then divides.
supplies: Anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum
left-coronary-artery.clinical: Left main stem blockage is life-threatening because it cuts off most of the left ventricle.

left-coronary-leaflet.name: Left Coronary Leaflet
left-coronary-leaflet.summary: One of the three leaflets of the aortic valve. The left coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it.
left-coronary-leaflet.from: Attached to the aortic annulus at the root of the aorta
left-coronary-leaflet.course: A thin pocket that opens upward into the left aortic sinus. Its free edge has a small thickened nodule.
branches: The left coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind this leaflet
supplies: It is not a vessel; the leaflet is largely avascular and fed by diffusion from the blood
left-coronary-leaflet.location: Root of the aorta, on the left posterior side of the valve
function: Opens in systole to let blood leave the left ventricle
Closes in diastole to prevent backflow and fill the coronary arteries
left-coronary-leaflet.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
left-coronary-leaflet.clinical: Fusion of the left and right leaflets is the commonest form of bicuspid aortic valve. During valve replacement, a displaced leaflet can block the left coronary opening.

left-inferior-pulmonary-vein.name: Left Inferior Pulmonary Vein
left-inferior-pulmonary-vein.summary: One of the four pulmonary veins. It carries oxygenated blood from the left lower lobe to the left atrium.
drains: Left lower lobe through the superior vein and the common basal vein
left-inferior-pulmonary-vein.course: Leaves the lower hilum of the left lung, below the left pulmonary artery, and pierces the pericardium to enter the left atrium.
left-inferior-pulmonary-vein.clinical: Its opening is a target for pulmonary vein isolation in atrial fibrillation. Ablation can cause pulmonary vein stenosis.

left-pulmonary-artery.name: Left Pulmonary Artery
left-pulmonary-artery.summary: The shorter of the two pulmonary arteries. It carries deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the left lung.
left-pulmonary-artery.course: Arches over the left main bronchus to reach the back of the bronchus in the hilum. The ligamentum arteriosum attaches to it.
branches: Superior lobar (segmental) arteries to the left upper lobe and lingula
Interlobar artery, giving the inferior lobar arteries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the left lung
left-pulmonary-artery.clinical: Pulmonary embolism may block it. The left recurrent laryngeal nerve passes under the ligamentum arteriosum close to it.

left-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-valv.name: Left Semilunar Leaflet of Pulmonary Valve
left-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-valv.latin: Valvula semilunaris sinistra valvae trunci pulmonalis
left-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-valv.summary: One of the three cup-shaped leaflets of the pulmonary valve. It lies on the left side of the valve opening.
left-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-valv.location: At the base of the pulmonary trunk, at the top of the right ventricular outflow tract.
function: Opens in ventricular systole so blood leaves the right ventricle
Closes with the other leaflets to prevent backflow
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
left-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-valv.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
left-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-valv.clinical: Pulmonary stenosis narrows the valve. Its closure forms the pulmonic part of the second heart sound.

left-subclavian-artery.name: Left Subclavian Artery
left-subclavian-artery.summary: The third branch of the aortic arch. It supplies the left upper limb and parts of the neck, brain, and chest wall.
left-subclavian-artery.from: Aortic arch, behind the left common carotid artery
left-subclavian-artery.course: Ascends to the root of the neck, arches over the cupula of the pleura, and passes over the first rib. It continues as the axillary artery.
supplies: Posterior part of the brain through the vertebral artery
left-subclavian-artery.clinical: Narrowing near its origin can cause subclavian steal syndrome, with reversed flow in the left vertebral artery.

left-subclavian-vein.name: Left Subclavian Vein
left-subclavian-vein.group: Veins of the neck and upper limb
left-subclavian-vein.summary: The continuation of the axillary vein. It drains the left upper limb and joins the left internal jugular vein.
left-subclavian-vein.into: Left brachiocephalic vein, behind the sternoclavicular joint
left-subclavian-vein.course: Begins at the outer border of the first rib, passes in front of scalenus anterior and behind the clavicle. The artery lies behind the muscle.
left-subclavian-vein.clinical: It is a common site for central lines. The thoracic duct enters at the left venous angle, so injury can cause chylothorax.

left-superior-intercostal-veins.name: Left Superior Intercostal Vein
left-superior-intercostal-veins.summary: A vein that drains the upper left intercostal spaces. It crosses the aortic arch to reach the left brachiocephalic vein.
left-superior-intercostal-veins.course: Runs forward over the aortic arch, superficial to the vagus nerve and deep to the phrenic nerve.
left-superior-intercostal-veins.clinical: It forms the aortic nipple on a chest radiograph, a small bump on the aortic knob. It may link with the accessory hemi-azygos vein.

left-superior-pulmonary-vein.name: Left Superior Pulmonary Vein
left-superior-pulmonary-vein.summary: One of the four pulmonary veins. It carries oxygenated blood from the left upper lobe and lingula to the left atrium.
drains: Left upper lobe and lingula through the apicoposterior, anterior, and lingular veins
left-superior-pulmonary-vein.course: Leaves the upper hilum, in front of the left main bronchus and the left pulmonary artery, and pierces the pericardium.
left-superior-pulmonary-vein.clinical: Its opening is a target for pulmonary vein isolation in atrial fibrillation. Ligation is part of left upper lobectomy.

left-ventricle.name: Left Ventricle
left-ventricle.summary: The thick-walled heart chamber that pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta. It forms the apex and most of the left side of the heart.
left-ventricle.location: Left and posterior part of the heart, forming the apex at the left fifth intercostal space.
function: Pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for the systemic circulation
Fills from the left atrium through the mitral valve
left-ventricle.nerve: Cardiac plexus (sympathetic fibers from T1 to T4 and vagal fibers)
left-ventricle.clinical: Most heart attacks damage this chamber. Chronic high blood pressure thickens its wall (hypertrophy).

medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.name: Medial Basal Segmental Artery of Left Lung
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.latin: Arteria segmentalis basalis medialis pulmonis sinistri
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.parent: Inferior lobar artery of left lung
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.summary: A segmental branch of the left pulmonary artery to segment S7. It carries deoxygenated blood to the medial basal segment of the left lower lobe.
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.from: Basal trunk of the inferior lobar artery of the left lung
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the medial basal segment of the left lower lobe
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-left-lu.clinical: On the left this segment is often fused with the anterior basal segment (anteromedial basal segment). Pulmonary embolism can block it.

medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.name: Medial Basal Segmental Artery of Right Lung
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.latin: Arteria segmentalis basalis medialis pulmonis dextri
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.parent: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.summary: A segmental branch of the right pulmonary artery to segment S7. It carries deoxygenated blood to the medial (cardiac) basal segment of the right lower lobe.
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.from: Basal trunk of the inferior lobar artery of the right lung
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the medial (cardiac) basal segment of the right lower lobe
medial-basal-segmental-artery-of-right-l.clinical: This segment lies against the heart and inferior vena cava. Pulmonary embolism can block it.

medial-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.name: Medial Segmental Artery of Right Lung
medial-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.parent: Middle lobar artery of right lung
medial-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.summary: A segmental branch of the right pulmonary artery to segment S5. It carries deoxygenated blood to the medial segment of the right middle lobe.
medial-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.from: Middle lobar artery of the right pulmonary artery
medial-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the medial segment of the right middle lobe
medial-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.clinical: A narrow middle lobe bronchus can be compressed by lymph nodes, causing collapse of the lateral and medial segments (middle lobe syndrome).

medial-vein-of-right-lung.name: Medial Vein of Right Lung
medial-vein-of-right-lung.latin: Vena medialis lobi medii pulmonis dextri
medial-vein-of-right-lung.summary: A tributary of the middle lobe vein. It drains the medial segment of the right middle lobe.
drains: Medial segment of the right middle lobe
medial-vein-of-right-lung.into: Middle lobe vein, then the right superior pulmonary vein
medial-vein-of-right-lung.course: Runs in the septa between segments toward the hilum and joins the lateral vein.
medial-vein-of-right-lung.clinical: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. Middle lobectomy divides the middle lobe vein.

middle-cardiac-vein.name: Middle Cardiac Vein
middle-cardiac-vein.summary: A cardiac vein on the back of the heart. It runs beside the posterior interventricular artery and ends in the coronary sinus.
drains: Posterior part of the interventricular septum
middle-cardiac-vein.into: Coronary sinus, near its right end
middle-cardiac-vein.course: Begins near the apex and ascends in the posterior interventricular groove with the posterior interventricular artery.
middle-cardiac-vein.clinical: It is a possible route for pacing leads, and it may be used for retrograde delivery of cardioplegia.

middle-lobar-artery-of-right-lung.name: Middle Lobar Artery of Right Lung
middle-lobar-artery-of-right-lung.summary: The artery of the right middle lobe. It branches from the front of the right interlobar artery.
middle-lobar-artery-of-right-lung.from: Interlobar part of the right pulmonary artery
middle-lobar-artery-of-right-lung.course: Passes forward and downward beside the middle lobe bronchus and divides into two segmental branches.
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the right middle lobe
middle-lobar-artery-of-right-lung.clinical: Pulmonary embolism can block it. Middle lobe syndrome is collapse of this lobe from bronchial narrowing.

musculophrenic-veins.name: Musculophrenic Veins
musculophrenic-veins.summary: Veins that accompany the musculophrenic arteries along the lower costal margin. They drain the front of the lower chest and diaphragm.
musculophrenic-veins.course: Run along the costal margin behind the costal cartilages from the 7th to 9th spaces and join the internal thoracic veins.
musculophrenic-veins.clinical: They are a small collateral pathway between the abdominal wall and the superior vena cava.

non-coronary-leaflet.name: Non-coronary Leaflet
non-coronary-leaflet.summary: One of the three leaflets of the aortic valve. No coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it.
non-coronary-leaflet.from: Attached to the aortic annulus at the root of the aorta
non-coronary-leaflet.course: A thin pocket that opens upward into the non-coronary (posterior) aortic sinus. It lies against the anterior mitral leaflet.
branches: None; no coronary artery arises from the sinus behind it
supplies: It is not a vessel; the leaflet is largely avascular and fed by diffusion from the blood
non-coronary-leaflet.location: Root of the aorta, on the posterior side of the valve
function: Opens in systole to let blood leave the left ventricle
Closes in diastole to prevent backflow into the left ventricle
non-coronary-leaflet.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
non-coronary-leaflet.clinical: A sinus of Valsalva aneurysm here can rupture into the right atrium. The conduction system lies near the junction with the right leaflet.

posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.name: Posterior Basal Segmental Artery of Left Lung
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.latin: Arteria segmentalis basalis posterior pulmonis sinistri
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.parent: Inferior lobar artery of left lung
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.summary: A segmental branch of the left pulmonary artery to segment S10. It carries deoxygenated blood to the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe.
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.from: Basal trunk of the inferior lobar artery of the left lung
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-left.clinical: In an upright person, aspirated material tends to enter the basal segments of the lower lobes.

posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.name: Posterior Basal Segmental Artery of Right Lung
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.latin: Arteria segmentalis basalis posterior pulmonis dextri
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.parent: Inferior lobar artery of right lung
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.summary: A segmental branch of the right pulmonary artery to segment S10. It carries deoxygenated blood to the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe.
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.from: Basal trunk of the inferior lobar artery of the right lung
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe
posterior-basal-segmental-artery-of-righ.clinical: In an upright person, aspirated material tends to enter the basal segments, and the right side is more often affected.

posterior-intercostal-arteries.name: Posterior Intercostal Arteries
posterior-intercostal-arteries.summary: Nine pairs of arteries that run in the intercostal spaces. They supply the chest wall from behind.
posterior-intercostal-arteries.from: Thoracic aorta (3rd to 11th spaces); the first two spaces come from the supreme intercostal artery
posterior-intercostal-arteries.course: Pass around the chest wall in the costal groove between the internal and innermost intercostal muscles. The vein lies above and the nerve below the artery.
branches: Dorsal branch to the back muscles and spinal canal
supplies: Ribs and skin of the chest wall
Spinal cord and vertebrae through the spinal branch
posterior-intercostal-arteries.clinical: Needles and chest tubes go above the rib to avoid them. In coarctation of the aorta, enlarged intercostal arteries notch the lower rib borders.

posterior-leaflet-of-left-atrioventricul.name: Posterior Leaflet of Left Atrioventricular Valve
posterior-leaflet-of-left-atrioventricul.summary: One of the two leaflets of the mitral valve. It is attached to about two thirds of the valve ring and has three scallops.
posterior-leaflet-of-left-atrioventricul.location: Attached to the posterior part of the mitral annulus, between the left atrium and left ventricle.
function: Closes with the anterior leaflet in systole to seal the mitral orifice
Prevents backflow from the left ventricle into the left atrium
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
posterior-leaflet-of-left-atrioventricul.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
posterior-leaflet-of-left-atrioventricul.clinical: Prolapse or rupture of the middle scallop (P2) is the commonest cause of degenerative mitral regurgitation.

posterior-segmental-artery-of-left-lung.name: Posterior Segmental Artery of Left Lung
posterior-segmental-artery-of-left-lung.parent: Superior lobar artery of left lung
posterior-segmental-artery-of-left-lung.summary: A segmental branch of the left pulmonary artery to segment S2. It carries deoxygenated blood to the posterior segment of the left upper lobe.
posterior-segmental-artery-of-left-lung.from: Superior lobar branches of the left pulmonary artery
posterior-segmental-artery-of-left-lung.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the posterior segment of the left upper lobe
posterior-segmental-artery-of-left-lung.clinical: On the left the posterior segment is commonly fused with the apical segment. Upper lobe segments are common sites for post-primary tuberculosis.

posterior-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.name: Posterior Segmental Artery of Right Lung
posterior-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.parent: Superior lobar artery of right lung
posterior-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.summary: A segmental branch of the right pulmonary artery to segment S2. It carries deoxygenated blood to the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
posterior-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.from: Ascending branch of the right interlobar artery (sometimes the superior trunk)
posterior-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.course: Runs beside the segmental bronchus, usually on its lateral or posterior side, into the bronchopulmonary segment.
branches: Subsegmental branches that end in the pulmonary capillaries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the posterior segment of the right upper lobe
posterior-segmental-artery-of-right-lung.clinical: Upper lobe segments are common sites for post-primary tuberculosis. Its origin varies, so surgeons check it before resection.

posterior-vein-of-right-lung.name: Posterior Vein of Right Lung
posterior-vein-of-right-lung.latin: Vena posterior lobi superioris pulmonis dextri
posterior-vein-of-right-lung.summary: A tributary of the right superior pulmonary vein. It drains the posterior segment of the right upper lobe.
drains: Posterior segment of the right upper lobe
posterior-vein-of-right-lung.course: Runs in the septa between segments toward the hilum and joins the apical and anterior veins.
posterior-vein-of-right-lung.clinical: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. They are divided with the upper lobe in right upper lobectomy.

pulmonary-trunk.name: Pulmonary Trunk
pulmonary-trunk.summary: The large artery that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle toward the lungs. It divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries.
pulmonary-trunk.from: Right ventricle, through the pulmonary valve
pulmonary-trunk.course: About 5 cm long. It runs up, back, and to the left in front of the aorta, inside the pericardium, and ends beneath the aortic arch.
pulmonary-trunk.clinical: A large pulmonary embolus can lodge at its division and cause sudden collapse. High lung pressure enlarges it.

right-atrium.name: Right Atrium
right-atrium.summary: The heart chamber that receives deoxygenated blood from the body. It forms the right border of the heart.
right-atrium.location: Right side of the heart, receiving the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus.
function: Receives deoxygenated blood from the body and heart wall
Pumps blood through the tricuspid valve into the right ventricle
blood: Right coronary artery and its atrial branches
right-atrium.nerve: Cardiac plexus (sympathetic fibers from T1 to T4 and vagal fibers)
parts: Rough pectinate muscles and right auricle
Openings of the venae cavae and coronary sinus
right-atrium.clinical: Central venous catheter tips are placed at the junction with the superior vena cava. Atrial flutter ablation targets the tissue between the IVC and tricuspid valve.

right-brachiocephalic-vein.name: Right Brachiocephalic Vein
right-brachiocephalic-vein.summary: A short, nearly vertical vein behind the right first costal cartilage. It joins the left one to form the superior vena cava.
drains: Right vertebral, internal thoracic, and inferior thyroid veins
right-brachiocephalic-vein.into: Superior vena cava, behind the right first costal cartilage
right-brachiocephalic-vein.course: Forms behind the right sternoclavicular joint and descends about 2.5 cm to meet the left vein.
right-brachiocephalic-vein.clinical: The right lymphatic duct enters near its origin. Central lines on the right take a straighter path to the right atrium.

right-common-carotid-artery.name: Right Common Carotid Artery
right-common-carotid-artery.summary: The artery that supplies the right side of the head and neck. It begins behind the right sternoclavicular joint.
right-common-carotid-artery.from: Brachiocephalic trunk, behind the right sternoclavicular joint
right-common-carotid-artery.course: Ascends in the carotid sheath beside the trachea and esophagus and ends at the upper border of the thyroid cartilage (C3 to C4).
supplies: Right side of the head and neck, brain, and face through its terminal branches
right-common-carotid-artery.clinical: The carotid pulse can be felt at C6. Atherosclerosis at the bifurcation is a major cause of stroke.

right-coronary-artery.name: Right Coronary Artery
right-coronary-artery.summary: The artery that arises from the right aortic sinus. It supplies the right heart and the back of the heart.
right-coronary-artery.from: Right aortic sinus of the ascending aorta
right-coronary-artery.course: Runs in the coronary sulcus between the right atrium and right ventricle, around the right border to the crux of the heart.
supplies: Posterior part of the left ventricle
Posterior third of the interventricular septum
right-coronary-artery.clinical: Blockage causes inferior infarction, often with slow heart rate or heart block because it supplies the nodes.

right-coronary-leaflet.name: Right Coronary Leaflet
right-coronary-leaflet.summary: One of the three leaflets of the aortic valve. The right coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind it.
right-coronary-leaflet.from: Attached to the aortic annulus at the root of the aorta
right-coronary-leaflet.course: A thin pocket that opens upward into the right (anterior) aortic sinus. Its free edge has a small thickened nodule.
branches: The right coronary artery arises from the aortic sinus behind this leaflet
supplies: It is not a vessel; the leaflet is largely avascular and fed by diffusion from the blood
right-coronary-leaflet.location: Root of the aorta, on the anterior side of the valve
function: Opens in systole to let blood leave the left ventricle
Closes in diastole to prevent backflow and fill the coronary arteries
right-coronary-leaflet.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
right-coronary-leaflet.clinical: Fusion with the left leaflet is the commonest form of bicuspid aortic valve. The conduction bundle runs close to the junction with the non-coronary leaflet.

right-inferior-pulmonary-vein.name: Right Inferior Pulmonary Vein
right-inferior-pulmonary-vein.summary: One of the four pulmonary veins. It carries oxygenated blood from the right lower lobe to the left atrium.
drains: Right lower lobe through the superior vein and the common basal vein
right-inferior-pulmonary-vein.course: Leaves the lower hilum of the right lung, below and in front of the bronchus, and passes behind the right atrium to the left atrium.
right-inferior-pulmonary-vein.clinical: Its opening is a target for pulmonary vein isolation in atrial fibrillation. It is the lowest hilar structure and is divided in lower lobectomy.

right-pulmonary-artery.name: Right Pulmonary Artery
right-pulmonary-artery.summary: The longer of the two pulmonary arteries. It carries deoxygenated blood from the pulmonary trunk to the right lung.
right-pulmonary-artery.course: Runs horizontally to the right behind the ascending aorta and superior vena cava and in front of the right main bronchus.
branches: Superior (anterior) trunk to the right upper lobe
Interlobar artery, giving the middle and inferior lobar arteries
supplies: Deoxygenated blood to the right lung
right-pulmonary-artery.clinical: Pulmonary embolism often lodges here or in its branches. It lies in front of the right bronchus, so tumors of the hilum can encase it.

right-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-val.name: Right Semilunar Leaflet of Pulmonary Valve
right-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-val.latin: Valvula semilunaris dextra valvae trunci pulmonalis
right-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-val.summary: One of the three cup-shaped leaflets of the pulmonary valve. It lies on the right side of the valve opening.
right-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-val.location: At the base of the pulmonary trunk, at the top of the right ventricular outflow tract.
function: Opens in ventricular systole so blood leaves the right ventricle
Closes with the other leaflets to prevent backflow
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
right-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-val.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
right-semilunar-leaflet-of-pulmonary-val.clinical: Pulmonary stenosis narrows the valve. The leaflet is a landmark during valve replacement.

right-subclavian-artery.name: Right Subclavian Artery
right-subclavian-artery.summary: The artery that supplies the right upper limb and parts of the neck, brain, and chest wall. It begins behind the right sternoclavicular joint.
right-subclavian-artery.from: Brachiocephalic trunk, behind the right sternoclavicular joint
right-subclavian-artery.course: Arches over the cupula of the pleura, passes behind scalenus anterior, and crosses the first rib. It continues as the axillary artery.
supplies: Posterior part of the brain through the vertebral artery
right-subclavian-artery.clinical: An aberrant right subclavian artery arises from the descending aorta and passes behind the esophagus, sometimes causing difficulty swallowing.

right-subclavian-vein.name: Right Subclavian Vein
right-subclavian-vein.group: Veins of the neck and upper limb
right-subclavian-vein.summary: The continuation of the axillary vein. It drains the right upper limb and joins the right internal jugular vein.
right-subclavian-vein.into: Right brachiocephalic vein, behind the sternoclavicular joint
right-subclavian-vein.course: Begins at the outer border of the first rib, passes in front of scalenus anterior and behind the clavicle.
right-subclavian-vein.clinical: It is a common site for central lines, with a risk of pneumothorax. Effort thrombosis can occur in athletes.

right-superior-intercostal-veins.name: Right Superior Intercostal Vein
right-superior-intercostal-veins.summary: A vein that drains the upper right intercostal spaces. It empties into the arch of the azygos vein.
right-superior-intercostal-veins.course: Descends along the right side of the upper thoracic vertebrae and curves into the azygos arch.
right-superior-intercostal-veins.clinical: It is part of the azygos collateral system that bypasses a blocked superior vena cava.

right-superior-phrenic-vein.name: Right Superior Phrenic Vein
right-superior-phrenic-vein.summary: A small vein that drains the upper surface of the right side of the diaphragm. The model shows it joining the azygos system.
drains: Upper (thoracic) surface of the right diaphragm
right-superior-phrenic-vein.into: Azygos vein (as modeled; other sources give the internal thoracic or other veins)
right-superior-phrenic-vein.course: Runs on the thoracic surface of the diaphragm toward the vertebral column.
right-superior-phrenic-vein.clinical: Its small size makes it clinically minor, but the diaphragm drains to both the caval and azygos systems.

right-superior-pulmonary-vein.name: Right Superior Pulmonary Vein
right-superior-pulmonary-vein.summary: One of the four pulmonary veins. It carries oxygenated blood from the right upper and middle lobes to the left atrium.
drains: Right upper lobe through the apical, anterior, and posterior veins
Right middle lobe through the middle lobe vein
right-superior-pulmonary-vein.course: Leaves the upper hilum, in front of the right pulmonary artery, and passes behind the right atrium and superior vena cava.
right-superior-pulmonary-vein.clinical: Its opening is a target for pulmonary vein isolation in atrial fibrillation. Ablation can narrow it, and it is divided in right upper lobectomy.

right-ventricle.name: Right Ventricle
right-ventricle.summary: The heart chamber that pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs. It forms most of the front surface of the heart.
right-ventricle.location: Right and anterior part of the heart, lying directly behind the sternum.
function: Pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary trunk
Fills from the right atrium through the tricuspid valve
right-ventricle.nerve: Cardiac plexus (sympathetic fibers from T1 to T4 and vagal fibers)
right-ventricle.clinical: Chest trauma often injures it because it lies behind the sternum. It can be damaged in inferior infarction.

second-posterior-intercostal-artery.name: Second Posterior Intercostal Artery
second-posterior-intercostal-artery.summary: The artery of the second intercostal space. It arises from the supreme intercostal artery, not from the aorta.
second-posterior-intercostal-artery.from: Supreme intercostal artery, from the costocervical trunk
second-posterior-intercostal-artery.course: Descends in front of the neck of the second rib and runs forward in the second intercostal space.
branches: Dorsal branch to the back and spinal canal
Anterior connection to the internal thoracic artery
supplies: Muscles and skin of the second intercostal space
second-posterior-intercostal-artery.clinical: It joins the anterior intercostal artery from the internal thoracic artery, forming a loop around the chest wall.

septal-branches-of-anterior-interventric.name: Septal Branches of Anterior Interventricular Artery
septal-branches-of-anterior-interventric.summary: A group of branches that enter the muscular septum from the front. They supply the anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum.
septal-branches-of-anterior-interventric.from: Anterior interventricular artery, along its course in the anterior groove
septal-branches-of-anterior-interventric.course: Pass back at right angles into the interventricular septum and run toward the posterior branches.
branches: Branches within the septum that join septal branches of the posterior interventricular artery
supplies: Anterior two thirds of the interventricular septum
Bundle branches of the conduction system
septal-branches-of-anterior-interventric.clinical: The first septal perforator can be closed by alcohol septal ablation to thin the septum in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

septal-leaflet-of-right-atrioventricular.name: Septal Leaflet of Right Atrioventricular Valve
septal-leaflet-of-right-atrioventricular.summary: One of the three leaflets of the tricuspid valve. It attaches to the interventricular septum.
septal-leaflet-of-right-atrioventricular.location: Attached to the tricuspid annulus along the interventricular septum, near the membranous septum.
function: Closes the valve in ventricular systole with the other two leaflets
Prevents backflow into the right atrium
blood: Mostly avascular; nourished by diffusion from blood in the heart chambers
septal-leaflet-of-right-atrioventricular.nerve: Cardiac plexus; the leaflets have few nerve endings
septal-leaflet-of-right-atrioventricular.clinical: Its attachment lies near the atrioventricular node and bundle. In Ebstein anomaly it is displaced into the right ventricle.

septal-papillary-muscle-of-right-ventric.name: Septal Papillary Muscle of Right Ventricle
septal-papillary-muscle-of-right-ventric.summary: The smallest of the three papillary muscles of the right ventricle. It arises from the interventricular septum.
septal-papillary-muscle-of-right-ventric.location: Rises from the right side of the interventricular septum.
function: Anchors the anterior and septal tricuspid leaflets through chordae tendineae
Helps keep the valve closed in systole
blood: Septal branches of the anterior interventricular artery
septal-papillary-muscle-of-right-ventric.nerve: Cardiac plexus (sympathetic fibers from T1 to T4 and vagal fibers)
septal-papillary-muscle-of-right-ventric.clinical: It lies close to the conduction system, so surgeons take care when repairing septal defects.

superior-basal-vein-of-left-lung.name: Superior Basal Vein of Left Lung
superior-basal-vein-of-left-lung.summary: A basal vein of the left lower lobe. It joins the inferior basal vein to form the common basal vein.
drains: Upper part of the basal segments of the left lower lobe
superior-basal-vein-of-left-lung.into: Common basal vein, then the left inferior pulmonary vein
superior-basal-vein-of-left-lung.course: Runs in the septa between basal segments toward the hilum.
superior-basal-vein-of-left-lung.clinical: Pulmonary veins carry oxygenated blood. They are divided at the hilum in left lower lobectomy.

glossary.def: Moving a limb away from the midline of the body. For the fingers, away from the middle finger.
Moving a limb toward the midline of the body. For the fingers, toward the middle finger.
A connection between two vessels, which gives blood a second route to an area.
Toward the front of the body.
A broad, flat sheet of tendon that attaches a muscle to bone or to another muscle.
A joint, or the place where two bones meet.
A smaller nerve or vessel that leaves a larger one.
A circular movement that combines flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in turn.
A group of muscles, with their nerve and blood supply, held together by fascia.
A rounded knob at the end of a bone that forms part of a joint.
In the brachial plexus, one of three bundles (lateral, posterior, medial) named for their position around the axillary artery.
Farther from the surface of the body.
Lowering a body part downward, such as pulling the shoulders down.
An area of skin supplied by the sensory fibers of a single spinal nerve.
Farther from the trunk or from the point where a limb attaches.
Relating to the back of the hand, or the back surface of a structure.
Lifting a body part upward, such as shrugging the shoulders.
A bump on the side of a bone above a joint surface, where muscles and ligaments attach.
The end of a long bone, which grows from its own center of ossification.
A movement that increases the angle at a joint, such as straightening the elbow.
A sheet of connective tissue that wraps muscles and other structures.
A movement that decreases the angle at a joint, such as bending the elbow.
A hole in a bone through which nerves or vessels pass.
A shallow hollow or depression on a bone.
The nerve supply to a muscle, organ or area of skin.
The attachment of a muscle that usually moves when the muscle contracts, usually farther from the trunk.
Farther from the midline of the body. In the anatomical position, the thumb side of the forearm is lateral.
Turning the front of a limb away from the midline, around its long axis.
A tough band of connective tissue that joins one bone to another.
Closer to the midline of the body. In the anatomical position, the little-finger side of the forearm is medial.
Turning the front of a limb toward the midline, around its long axis.
Bringing the tip of the thumb across the palm to touch another fingertip.
The attachment of a muscle that stays fixed, usually closer to the trunk, when the muscle contracts.
The process of forming bone, usually from cartilage or membrane.
Relating to the palm side of the hand, the same as anterior in the hand.
A network of nerves or vessels that join and then split again.
Toward the back of the body.
A bony projection that sticks out from a bone.
Turning the forearm so the palm faces backward or down.
Moving the scapula forward around the rib cage, away from the spine.
Closer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.
A thick band of fascia that holds tendons close to a joint, such as at the wrist.
Moving the scapula backward toward the spine, as when squeezing the shoulder blades together.
In the brachial plexus, one of the five ventral rami (C5 to T1) that form the plexus. These are not the same as the dorsal and ventral roots attached to the spinal cord.
A small bone that develops inside a tendon, such as the pisiform or kneecap.
A groove on a bone, often where a tendon or nerve runs.
Closer to the surface of the body.
Turning the forearm so the palm faces forward or up.
A tough cord of connective tissue that joins a muscle to a bone.
In the brachial plexus, one of three large nerve bundles (upper, middle, lower) formed from the roots.
A small, rounded bump on a bone, often where a tendon attaches.
A large, rough bump on a bone where a muscle or ligament attaches.
Turning the scapula so the socket faces up, which is needed to raise the arm overhead.
